section: 11.45 Selection for logarithmic models on products
text: Theorem 11.45.9 . 72A7418012F7 Let $a_ j,d_ j>0$ converge to $a,d>0$, let smooth positive functions $b_ j$ converge uniformly to $b$, and let continuous positive functions $H_ j$ converge uniformly to $H$. For any $\sigma _ j>0$ tending to zero, put \[  \begin{aligned}  \theta _ j& =(a_ j+d_ j)\omega _1+b_ j\kappa ,& \psi _ j& =d_ j\log \ell ,& \phi _ j& =\phi _{a_ j,d_ j},\\  f_ j& =N b_ j^ kH_ j,& m_ j& =\int _{\mathbb P^1}H_ j\omega _1,& c_{0,j}& =a_ j/m_ j. \end{aligned}  \] Let $s_ j$ be the greatest solution of ( 11.45.5 ) for these data, and set $v_ j=s_ j-\sup _ Xs_ j$, $c_ j=\mathrm{e}^{\sigma _ j\sup _ Xs_ j}$. Then \[  v_ j\longrightarrow v_0=\psi +w_0-S_0,\qquad s_ j-\sigma _ j^{-1}\log c_{0,j}\longrightarrow s_0=\psi +w_0-J  \] in $L^1(X)$, in capacity, and locally uniformly on $X\setminus D$. Moreover, 97B5C8E6D45D 11.45.10 \begin{equation}  c_ j\longrightarrow c_0,\qquad \sigma _ j^{-1}\log (c_ j/c_{0,j})\longrightarrow S_0-J, \end{equation} and $\mathrm{MA}_{\theta _ j}(v_ j)\to c_0 f\, \mathrm{d}W$ in total variation. The limit has ordinary type $\phi _{a,d}$ and belongs to $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\phi _{a,d})$, with \[  \mathrm{MA}_\theta (v_0)=c_0 f\, \mathrm{d}W.  \] There is no restriction on the relative rates of parameter and exponent convergence. Proof. We construct uniformly bounded residuals on the curve, then use their equation to determine both the normalized limit and the scalar error. Uniform construction. The kernel has uniformly integrable logarithmic tails and $C_ G=\sup _ x\int |G(x,z)|\omega _1(z)<\infty $. These facts follow by rotation invariance and the radial integral of $|\log \ell +1|$ on $0<\ell <1$; the Poincaré–Lelong formula and $\int _0^1\log \ell \, \mathrm{d}\ell =-1$ give its curvature and mean. Truncating the kernel shows that convolution of bounded densities is continuous. Temporarily omit subscripts. On continuous mean-zero functions on the curve define \[  T_\sigma (w)=G*(A(w)-a),\qquad A(w)=\frac{aH\mathrm{e}^{\sigma (\psi +w)}}{Z(w)},\qquad Z(w)=\int _{\mathbb P^1}H\mathrm{e}^{\sigma (\psi +w)}\omega _1.  \] For all late parameters choose fixed bounds $a\leq a_{\max }$, $d\leq d_{\max }$ and $0<h_{\min }\leq H\leq h_{\max }$. Put $B=4a_{\max }h_{\max }/h_{\min }$ and choose $R_0>C_ G(B+a_{\max })$. On the ball $\| w\| _\infty \leq R_0$, for sufficiently small $\sigma $, \[  Z(w)\geq \frac{h_{\min }\mathrm{e}^{-\sigma R_0}}{1+\sigma d_{\max }} \geq h_{\min }/2,\qquad 0\leq A(w)\leq B.  \] Here $\int \ell ^{\sigma d}\omega _1=(1+\sigma d)^{-1}$. Thus $T_\sigma $ maps the mean-zero ball into itself. Since $\int A(w)\omega _1=a$, its density derivative in direction $h$ is \[  \sigma A(w)\left(h-a^{-1}\int hA(w)\omega _1\right).  \] It follows that $\| T_\sigma (w)-T_\sigma (v)\| _\infty \leq 2\sigma B C_ G\| w-v\| _\infty $. The map is a contraction for all sufficiently small exponents, uniformly over the late parameters. Its fixed point $w_ j$ has mean zero and $\| w_ j\| _\infty \leq R_0$. Write $Z_ j=Z(w_ j)$ and $A_ j=A(w_ j)$. The fixed-point equation gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j=(A_ j-a_ j)\omega _1$, and the potential 9E6339686644 11.45.11 \begin{equation}  \psi _ j+w_ j+\sigma _ j^{-1}\log (a_ j/Z_ j) \end{equation} has residual form $A_ j\omega _1+b_ j\kappa $, continuous and semipositive. On coordinate balls, mollification of $w_ j$ converges together with its continuous complex Hessian. The local bounded product, expanded after a common strict smooth correction, therefore equals $N b_ j^ kA_ j\, \mathrm{d}W$. Removing $D$ identifies the singular product with the same measure. The identity \[  N b_ j^ kA_ j=\mathrm{e}^{\sigma _ j(\psi _ j+w_ j)}(a_ j/Z_ j)f_ j  \] shows that ( 11.45.11 ) solves the exponential equation in the ordinary type. By lemma 11.45.4 , it is $s_ j$. Residual and normalized limits. Uniform boundedness and dominated convergence give $Z_ j\to m$ and $A_ j\to A_0$ in $L^1(\omega _1)$, with a common bound on $A_ j$. For uniformly bounded densities $F_ j\to 0$ in $L^1$, one has \[  \| G*F_ j\| _\infty \leq \| F_ j\| _\infty \sup _ x\int _{\{ |G(x,z)|>M\} }|G(x,z)|\omega _1(z) +M\| F_ j\| _1.  \] First letting $j\to \infty $ and then $M\to \infty $ proves $w_ j\to w_0$ uniformly. Although $A_ j=0$ on $D$ and $A_0>0$ there, the $L^1$ convergence suffices for this argument. Put $S_ j=\sup _ X(\psi _ j+w_ j)$. A point with $\ell =1$ supplies a uniformly bounded competing value. Since $d_ j\geq d_{\min }>0$, the upper bound $d_{\min }\log \ell +R_0$ tends uniformly to $-\infty $ near $D$, so all maximizing points stay in a fixed compact subset of $X\setminus D$. Uniform convergence there gives $S_ j\to S_0$. Hence $v_ j=\psi _ j+w_ j-S_ j$ has the asserted $L^1$ and local uniform limits. For capacity convergence, the complements of $\{ \psi <-T\} $ are compact subsets of $X\setminus D$. Choose a fixed Hermitian form for which $\psi $ is plurisubharmonic and apply ( 5.29.4 ); their omitted sublevels have capacity at most $C/T$. Local uniform convergence, followed by $T\to \infty $, proves convergence in capacity, with the common poles omitted. The measure formula and uniform convergence of $b_ j$ give total-variation convergence to $N b^ kA_0\, \mathrm{d}W=c_0 f\, \mathrm{d}W$. The same bounded product calculation gives this equation for $v_0$. The residual extensions in proposition 11.45.3 show directly that $v_0\sim \phi _{a,d}$. Choose $C$ with $v_0\geq \phi _{a,d}-C$. For every $t\geq 1$, the potential $q_ t=\phi _{a,d}-tC$ satisfies \[  t^{-1}q_ t+(1-t^{-1})\phi _{a,d}\leq v_0,  \] which proves membership in the relative envelope class by definition 16.28.61 . Scalar centering. The exact formula is $c_ j=a_ j\mathrm{e}^{\sigma _ j S_ j}/Z_ j$. In the difference quotient \[  \frac{Z_ j-m_ j}{\sigma _ j} =\int H_ j\frac{\mathrm{e}^{\sigma _ j(\psi _ j+w_ j)}-1}{\sigma _ j}\omega _1,  \] the negative part is bounded by $h_{\max }(d_{\max }|\log \ell |+R_0)$ and the positive part by a constant. Dominated convergence gives a limit $\int H(\psi +w_0)\omega _1=mJ$. Since $m_ j\to m>0$, \[  \sigma _ j^{-1}\log (Z_ j/m_ j)\longrightarrow J.  \] The identity $c_ j/c_{0,j}=m_ j\mathrm{e}^{\sigma _ j S_ j}/Z_ j$ proves ( 11.45.10 ). Subtracting $\sigma _ j^{-1}\log c_{0,j}$ in ( 11.45.11 ) leaves $\psi _ j+w_ j-\sigma _ j^{-1}\log (Z_ j/m_ j)$, proving the centered limit in all three topologies. $\square$

text: Corollary 11.45.13 . 86F268014BE0 For the fixed data, $c_0$ is the largest coefficient $c>0$ for which $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $u\preceq \phi _{a,d}$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)\geq c f\, \mathrm{d}W$. Among separated potentials $u=\psi +r(x)\preceq \phi _{a,d}$, the critical subsolutions are exactly the translates of $\psi +w_0$. Thus $v_0$ is their unique supremum-zero member, and $s_0$ is their greatest member with $\int _ Xu\, \mathrm{d}\nu _0\leq 0$. Proof. For a separated critical subsolution, ( 11.45.6 ) and the product expansion give $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{a\omega _1}(r)\geq A_0\omega _1$. Closed curve truncations have mass $a$, so the non-pluripolar measure has mass at most $a$. Since $\int A_0\omega _1=a$, it must equal $A_0\omega _1$. The positive closed current $a\omega _1+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r$ also has mass $a$, so it has no remaining measure on the pole set. Consequently $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r=(A_0-a)\omega _1$ as distributions, and $r=w_0+C$ because harmonic distributions on $\mathbb P^1$ are constant. Supremum zero gives $C=-S_0$, while the mean condition gives $C\leq -J$. For a general $u\preceq \phi _{a,d}$ with coefficient $c>0$, write $u=\psi +r$ by ( 11.45.6 ) and put $B_ r=\sup _ Xr$. Since $\psi \leq 0$, the potential $u+\sigma ^{-1}\log c-B_ r$ is an exponential subsolution for every $\sigma >0$. Greatestness gives \[  u+\sigma ^{-1}\log c-B_ r\leq s_\sigma .  \] At a point off $D$ where $r$ is finite, subtract $\sigma ^{-1}\log c_0$, multiply by $\sigma $ and use the fixed-data case of theorem 11.45.9 . This yields $\log c\leq \log c_0$. The potential $v_0$ attains $c_0$. $\square$ The scalar in the centering follows the varying data. Replacing $c_{0,j}$ by $c_0$ adds $\sigma _ j^{-1}\log (c_{0,j}/c_0)$ to the centered potential, and this term need not vanish. For example, take $a=1$, $d=1/4$, $H=1$ and $b=2+t$, where $t$ is the sphere height. Then $w_0=0$, $S_0=0$, $J=-1/4$ and $c_0=1$, so $s_0=\psi +1/4$ and the scalar-error limit is $1/4$. If $a_ j=1+\sqrt{\sigma _ j}$ and the other data are fixed, the appropriate centering uses $c_{0,j}=a_ j$. Centering by $1$ instead adds \[  \frac{\log (1+\sqrt{\sigma _ j})}{\sigma _ j}\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] These examples can be taken on a non-Kähler manifold by choosing $Y$ to be the scalar Hopf surface with its Hermitian form rescaled to unit volume. The product cannot be Kähler, since a Kähler form would restrict to one on the Hopf fiber. The pole divisor remains present in the selected ordinary type.

text: Lemma 11.45.15 . 85744C3971DC Let $V>0$ be continuous on $\mathbb P^1$, and let $T$ be a finite signed measure such that \[  \int _{\mathbb P^1}(\Delta f-Vf)\, \mathrm{d}T=0 \qquad (f\in C^\infty (\mathbb P^1)).  \] Then $T=0$. Proof. Let $H_ t$ be the sphere heat operator. On spherical harmonics of degree $\ell $, it acts by $\mathrm{e}^{-t\ell (\ell +1)}$. The harmonic series defines a smooth heat solution for $t>0$; for smooth initial functions, the maximum principle gives positivity and contraction in the uniform norm. Density of smooth functions extends $H_ t$ to a positive, strongly continuous contraction on $C(\mathbb P^1)$. Choose $M\geq \max V$ and define \[  R_ Mg=\int _0^\infty \mathrm{e}^{-Mt}H_ tg\, \mathrm{d}t.  \] Then $\| R_ M\| \leq M^{-1}$ and $(M-\Delta )R_ Mg=g$ in distributions. For any $g\in C(\mathbb P^1)$, the map \[  f\longmapsto R_ M((M-V)f-g)  \] contracts by at most $1-\min V/M<1$. Its continuous fixed point satisfies $\Delta f=Vf+g$ in distributions, with a continuous right-hand side. The functions $f_\varepsilon =H_\varepsilon f$ are smooth and satisfy \[  f_\varepsilon \longrightarrow f,\qquad \Delta f_\varepsilon =H_\varepsilon (Vf+g)\longrightarrow Vf+g  \] uniformly. Thus $(\Delta -V)f_\varepsilon \to g$ uniformly. Testing against the finite measure $T$ gives $\int g\, \mathrm{d}T=0$ for every continuous $g$, hence $T=0$. $\square$

Example 11.45.19 . 3C22B09DCF87 Take $a=1$, $d=1/4$, $q=1$, and let $t$ be the sphere height \[  t= rac{|Z_0|^2-|Z_1|^2}{|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2},\qquad b=2+t,\qquad H=A=	frac 12+|t|.  \] Here $c_0=1$ and $F=\log (2bA)$ is Lipschitz but not $C^1$. The residual has continuous positive coefficients with the same loss of differentiability. Its supporting probability differs from normalized Monge–Ampère volume: \[  \int _ X\Omega ^2=4,\qquad \int _ Xt\, \mathrm{d}
u =0,\qquad \int _ Xt\,  rac{\Omega ^2}{4}= rac5{24}.  \] Even for smooth constant $H$, approximation of the pole by globally smooth potentials need not recover the weak adjoint. For $H=a$, so that $w_0=0$ and $
u =\mathrm{d}W$, put \[  \psi _\delta =d\log (\ell +\delta (1-\ell )),\qquad P_\delta =\omega _1+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\psi _\delta /d),\qquad 0<\delta \leq 1.  \] The smooth potentials $\psi _\delta $ decrease pointwise to $\psi $, converge in $L^1$ and smoothly off $D$, but the classical adjoint probabilities of $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _\delta $ converge to \[   rac{a\omega _1+d\delta _ p}{a+d}\wedge \omega _2, \qquad p=\{ Z_0=0\} .  \] This limit assigns mass $d/(a+d)>0$ to $D$, and the weighted currents also retain a nonzero divisor component. Proof. The height $t$ is uniform on $[-1,1]$, so $\int A\omega _1=1$ and $\int tA\omega _1=0$. Since $\Omega ^2=2bA\, \mathrm{d}W$, its mass is four and its normalized height moment is \[   rac12\int _{-1}^1 t^2(	frac 12+|t|)\,  rac{\mathrm{d}t}{2} = rac5{24}.  \] The weight is $1/(2b)$ and $
u =A\, \mathrm{d}W$. Moreover, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}	heta =-2t\, \mathrm{d}W$, so the background has no smooth positive Gauduchon potential perturbation. For the smoothing family, direct differentiation gives \[   rac{P_\delta }{\omega _1} = rac{4\delta }{((1+\delta )+(1-\delta )t)^2}.  \] It is positive of mass one and converges weakly to $\delta _ p$. Thus the positive smooth forms are $\widehat\Omega _\delta =a\omega _1+dP_\delta +b\omega _2$. Their classical weights and probabilities are \[  \widehatho _\delta = rac1{2(a+d)b},\qquad \widehat
u _\delta = rac{a\omega _1+dP_\delta }{a+d}\wedge \omega _2.  \] The weighted forms are closed, so these are the normalized classical adjoints. Their limits follow from the curve measure convergence. In particular, the weighted-current limit contains $d[D]/(2(a+d)b(p))$. These smoothings fill the pole and do not satisfy the fixed-divisor and uniform-residual hypotheses of proposition 11.45.18 . $\square$

section: 11.46 Residual regularity in radial singularity types
text: Subtracting a prescribed singularity separates regularity of the residual from the pole of the solution. On projective space, central radial mass gives an exact inverse for the equation. A relative density error then controls the residual through two derivatives, even when the density is merely integrable at the pole. The inverse also permits smooth crossing of density zeros away from it. The pole is the one used in lemma 15.30.1 ; here its ordinary type is fixed while the density varies.

title: 11.46.1 The prescribed ordinary type
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality

text: Let $k\geq 2$, let $\kappa $ be the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^ k$ with $\int \kappa ^ k=1$, and put $o=[1:0:\cdots :0]$. On the chart $Z_0\ne 0$ write $z_ i=Z_ i/Z_0$ and set \[  r=\sum _{j=1}^ k|z_ j|^2,\qquad P=\frac r{1+r},\qquad T=1-\log P, \qquad u_\alpha =1-T^\alpha \quad (0<\alpha <1).  \] The ratio $P=\sum _{i=1}^ k|Z_ i|^2/\sum _{i=0}^ k|Z_ i|^2$ is global. Give $u_\alpha $ its canonical value $-\infty $ at $o$ and value zero on the hyperplane $Z_0=0$. Primes denote differentiation in $r$, and $b_\alpha =k(1-\alpha )>0$ throughout this section. Lemma 11.46.2 . 3CE4F16CE935 The canonical $u_\alpha $ is $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic and smooth off $o$. Its non-pluripolar measure has a positive density $q_\alpha $ of mass one, in $L^1$ and in no $L^ p$, $p>1$. Distinct $\alpha $ give distinct ordinary types, although all their multiplier ideals are trivial. Proof. Plurisubharmonicity, smoothness off the pole, unit mass and the $L^ p$ assertions are those of lemma 15.30.1 . To fix the profile used in the inverse below, put 81B05A10FA0A 11.46.3 \begin{equation}  \Phi _\alpha =\log (1+r)+u_\alpha ,\qquad Q_\alpha =r\Phi _\alpha '=P+\alpha (1-P)T^{\alpha -1}. \end{equation} The tangential and radial eigenvalues are $Q_\alpha /r$ and $Q_\alpha '$, both positive. Radial determinant integration, with the constant fixed by $\Phi =\log (1+r)$, gives DE57A4B5C703 11.46.4 \begin{equation}  \int _{a<|z|^2<b}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi )^ k=Q(b)^ k-Q(a)^ k, \qquad Q=r\Phi '. \end{equation} Since $Q_\alpha (0)=0$ and $Q_\alpha (\infty )=1$, the density is AF6A825EA4B9 11.46.5 \begin{equation}  q_\alpha =\frac{(Q_\alpha ^ k)'}{(P^ k)'}>0. \end{equation} Smoothness on the hyperplane and the exclusion of the canonical pole in the product leave no further measure. Near $r=0$, with $L=1-\log r$, direct differentiation gives 44CC5DC8E895 11.46.6 \begin{align}  Q_\alpha & \sim \alpha L^{\alpha -1},&  Q_\alpha '& \sim \frac{\alpha (1-\alpha )}rL^{\alpha -2},\\  (Q_\alpha ^ k)'& \sim \frac{k\alpha ^ k(1-\alpha )}rL^{-1-k(1-\alpha )}.\nonumber \end{align} In particular $q_\alpha \sim \alpha ^ k(1-\alpha )r^{-k}L^{-1-b_\alpha }$; the radial volume has order $r^{k-1}\, \mathrm{d}r$, recovering these integrability assertions. The types for different $\alpha $ are ordinarily distinct, since their difference is unbounded at $o$. Yet every $\mathcal I(tu_\alpha )$ is trivial for finite $t>0$: integrability of the constant function reduces near $o$ to $\int ^\infty \mathrm{e}^{-kL+tL^\alpha }\, \mathrm{d}L<\infty $. Ordinary type information here is strictly finer than this ideal information. $\square$

Here “radial” means depending only on $r$ in the displayed chart. The smoothness assumption along the hyperplane includes a smooth profile in $t=1/r$ near $t=0$. Theorem 11.46.8 . title: 11.46.14 Smooth residuals from flat errors
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
section: 11.46 Residual regularity in radial singularity types
text: Proposition 11.46.15 . 33B8FF26FB4B Under the hypotheses of Theorem 11.46.8 , suppose $g=q/q_\alpha -1$ satisfies \[  (r\partial _ r)^ jg=O(r^ N) \quad \text{for every }N,j\ge 0.  \] Then $R-R_0$ extends smoothly across $o$, with every derivative zero there. Proof. Put $x=-\log r$, $a(x)=Q_\alpha (\mathrm{e}^{-x})^ k$ and $E(x)=M(\mathrm{e}^{-x})-a(x)$. The exact central integral is \[  E(x)=\int _ x^\infty g(\mathrm{e}^{-y})[-a'(y)]\, \mathrm{d}y, \qquad E'(x)=g(\mathrm{e}^{-x})a'(x).  \] Every derivative of $a$ has at most polynomial growth in $1+x$, and $a\asymp (1+x)^{-b_\alpha }$. The integral bounds $E$ by an exponential of arbitrarily large rate. Repeated differentiation of $E'$ expresses each derivative as a finite Leibniz sum of flat derivatives of $g$ and polynomially bounded derivatives of $a$; all derivatives of $E$ are therefore exponentially flat. Every derivative of $1/a$ has at most polynomial growth, by ( 11.46.3 ). Thus $E/a$ has the same flatness. Applying smooth composition near one to \[  Q-Q_\alpha =Q_\alpha \bigl [(1+E/a)^{1/k}-1\bigr ]  \] proves flatness of every $x$ derivative of $Q-Q_\alpha $. Since $\mathrm{d}R/\mathrm{d}x=-(Q-Q_\alpha )$, integration from $x$ to infinity proves the same for $R-R_0$, including its zeroth derivative. An ordinary $j$th derivative in $r$ is $r^{-j}$ times a polynomial in $\partial _ x$; arbitrarily strong exponential decay absorbs that factor. All ordinary derivatives extend continuously as zero at $r=0$, and repeated one-dimensional integration verifies smoothness there. Composition with $r=|z|^2$ gives the conclusion. $\square$

text: Proposition 11.46.17 . F4F876167D51 The $C^1$ threshold $\delta =1/2$ and $C^2$ threshold $\delta =1$ are sharp. When $2\delta <1$, the stated Hölder exponent is also sharp. Nontrivial probability-density perturbations with smoothly flat residuals exist. Proof. Choose smooth nonnegative radial cutoffs $\chi _0,\chi _1$ with disjoint supports: $\chi _0=1$ near $r=0$ and vanishes outside a finite small ball; $\chi _1$ is nonzero in a finite annulus. Put 405FC6263C95 11.46.18 \begin{equation}  B=\frac{\int r^\delta \chi _0q_\alpha \kappa ^ k}{\int \chi _1q_\alpha \kappa ^ k},\qquad q_ c=q_\alpha \bigl [1+c(r^\delta \chi _0-B\chi _1)\bigr ]. \end{equation} For sufficiently small $c>0$, $q_ c$ is positive, smooth off $o$ and along the hyperplane, and has total mass exactly one. It is comparable to $q_\alpha $ near $o$, hence is in no $L^ p$, $p>1$. Theorem 11.46.8 gives a compact solution in the prescribed ordinary type. Near $o$ its central flux difference is exactly $c\int _0^ r s^\delta (Q_\alpha ^ k)'\, \mathrm{d}s$. The substitution $s=r\mathrm{e}^{-y}$ and dominated convergence give \[  \int _0^ r s^{\delta -1}(1-\log s)^{-1-b_\alpha }\, \mathrm{d}s \sim \delta ^{-1}r^\delta L^{-1-b_\alpha }.  \] Using ( 11.46.6 ) and the $k$th-root expansion yields \begin{align*}  R_ c'(r)& \sim \frac{c\alpha (1-\alpha )}\delta r^{\delta -1}L^{\alpha -2},\\  R_ c(r)-R_ c(0)& \sim \frac{c\alpha (1-\alpha )}{\delta ^2} r^\delta L^{\alpha -2}. \end{align*} For $\delta <\frac12$, the radial gradient $2\sqrt r\, R_ c'$ diverges, ruling out $C^1$ extension. For $\delta <1$, a tangential real Hessian eigenvalue $2R_ c'$ diverges, ruling out $C^2$ extension. The annular compensation changes no central flux. For $2\delta <1$ the displayed asymptotic also rules out any larger Hölder exponent. The critical derivative thresholds in Theorem 11.46.8 are therefore sharp for this family. Replacing $r^\delta \chi _0$ in ( 11.46.18 ) by $\mathrm{e}^{-1/r}\chi _0$ and adjusting $B$ by the same integral formula gives a nonzero mass-preserving perturbation satisfying every flat-error hypothesis. Proposition 11.46.15 then supplies a smoothly flat residual across the pole. $\square$

text: Proposition 11.46.20 . 7D9147EC36A1 For every $k\ge 2$ and $0<\alpha <1$, there is a nonnegative radial probability density $q_0$, smooth off $o$ and along the hyperplane, which equals $q_\alpha $ near $o$ and vanishes on a nonempty open annulus. Its solution has ordinary type $u_\alpha $ and a globally smooth residual, constant near $o$. Proof. Choose a smooth radial $h$ with $0\le h\le 1$, equal to zero on a nonempty finite annulus and equal to one near $o$ and outside a larger finite annulus. Choose a nonzero nonnegative smooth radial cutoff $\chi $ supported in a disjoint finite annulus where $h=1$. Set \[  C=\frac{\int (1-h)q_\alpha \kappa ^ k}{\int \chi q_\alpha \kappa ^ k}>0, \qquad q_0=q_\alpha (h+C\chi ).  \] This is nonnegative and has integral one. It is smooth at every point off $o$, including the hyperplane, and equals $q_\alpha $ near $o$. It vanishes on the chosen open annulus and is still in no $L^ p$, $p>1$. Theorem 11.46.8 applies, with zero relative density error on a neighborhood of $o$. There the exact central fluxes agree, so $Q=Q_\alpha $ and $R'=0$. Hence $R$ is constant near $o$ and extends smoothly across it. It is smooth everywhere else by the positive-root inverse, including the entire zero annulus. The solution retains its genuine pole; this smoothness assertion concerns the residual. $\square$

text: Let $(X_0,h_0)$ be any connected compact Hermitian $m$-fold with $v_-(h_0)=0$, and write $V_0=\int _{X_0}h_0^ m>0$. On $X=X_0\times \mathbb P^ k$ put $N=m+k$ and $H=\operatorname {pr}_0^*h_0+\operatorname {pr}_ Y^*\kappa $, where $\operatorname {pr}_0$ and $\operatorname {pr}_ Y$ are the two projections. In the product formulas below, $U$ and $R$ denote their pullbacks. Corollary 11.46.22 . 7C248BB2EDD2 The pullback of $U$ has the pulled-back ordinary type and relative envelope-class membership. Its residual retains the proved regularity across $X_0\times \{ o\} $, and its finite Monge–Ampère mass is $\binom Nm V_0$. The background $H$ is nonclosed and $v_-(H)=0$. Proof. The pullback of $U$ obeys \[  \mathrm{MA}_ H(U)=\binom Nm\operatorname {pr}_0^*(h_0^ m) \wedge \operatorname {pr}_ Y^*(q\kappa ^ k), \qquad \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_ H(U)=\binom Nm V_0.  \] Indeed the bounded truncation $\max \{ U,-j\} $ is a pullback. The bounded corrected-product expansion of proposition 5.28.2 , lemma 5.28.4 leaves only the displayed binomial term by dimensions; multiplication by $1_{\{ U>-j\} }$ and increasing $j$ give the exact formula and finite mass. The residual is the pullback of $R$, so its proved regularity extends across $X_0\times \{ o\} $. It is ordinarily equivalent to the pullback of $u_\alpha $ and belongs to the corresponding relative stretching class by the same explicit $v_ t$. Also $v_-(H)=0$: bounded $h_0$-psh potentials with masses tending to zero have pullbacks of mass $\binom Nm$ times those masses. The background is genuinely nonclosed, since a closed positive $h_0$ would have all bounded masses equal to $V_0>0$ by Stokes. title: 11.47 Envelopes for singular radial obstacles
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: The radial inverse of section 11.46 starts with a density. One can instead perturb the singular reference as an obstacle and let the envelope select its measure. The resulting total profile is a convex minorant. Its affine intervals give open regions of zero density, while its contact with the reference at both ends controls the residual across the pole and the hyperplane at infinity. Keep $k\geq 2$, $0<\alpha <1$, the normalized Fubini–Study form $\kappa $ on $\mathbb P^ k$ and the potential $u_\alpha $ of lemma 11.46.2 . Write $r=|z|^2$ on the chart $Z_0\ne 0$, put $x=\log r$, and define \[  A(x)=\log (1+\mathrm e^ x)+u_\alpha (x).  \] Here $u_\alpha (x)$ denotes its radial profile. Throughout this section primes denote derivatives in $x$. For $F\in C_ c^2(\mathbb R;\mathbb R)$, extend $F(\log r)$ by zero near the pole $o$ and the hyperplane at infinity, and set AF49CAB59368 11.47.1 \begin{equation}  E_ F=\left(\sup \{ v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^ k,\kappa ): v\leq u_\alpha +F\  \text{everywhere},\  v\preceq u_\alpha \} \right)^*. \end{equation} The obstacle takes the value $-\infty $ at $o$. Since $F$ is bounded, its pointwise constraint already implies ordinary domination for each competitor. Lemma 11.47.2 . 3CD979065654 The profile $A$ is smooth and strictly convex, with $0<A'<1$, bounded $A''$ and asymptotic slopes $0,1$. Its tangents tend uniformly to $-\infty $ on each compact interval as their point of tangency tends to $-\infty $, and uniformly to the line $y\mapsto y$ as that point tends to $+\infty $. Moreover, $A(x)-x\searrow 0$ at the right end. Proof. Put $p=\mathrm e^ x/(1+\mathrm e^ x)$, $T=1-\log p$ and $a=\alpha T^{\alpha -1}$. Differentiating ( 11.46.3 ) gives \[  A'=p+(1-p)a,\qquad A''=p(1-p)(1-a)+\alpha (1-\alpha )(1-p)^2T^{\alpha -2}.  \] Since $T\geq 1$ and $0<a\leq \alpha <1$, these formulas give the asserted positivity and bounds. On the left, $A(x)=1-(1-x)^\alpha +o(1)$ and $A-xA'$ has leading term $-(1-\alpha )(-x)^\alpha $. On the right, $A=x+(1-\alpha )\mathrm e^{-x}+O(\mathrm e^{-2x})$ and $A'=1-(1-\alpha )\mathrm e^{-x}+O(\mathrm e^{-2x})$. The tangent at $x$ is $y\mapsto A'(x)y+A(x)-xA'(x)$, so both uniform limits follow. Finally $A'-1<0$ gives the decreasing right-end limit. $\square$

title: 11.47.3 The convex minorant and its residual
search_title: The convex minorant and its residual
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Put $g=A+F$, $K_ F=\| F\| _\infty $, and let $C_ F$ be the supremum of all affine functions below $g$ on $\mathbb R$. Since $A-K_ F$ is convex and is the supremum of its supporting lines, 61A86D21F0FE 11.47.4 \begin{equation}  A-K_ F\leq C_ F\leq A+F\leq A+K_ F. \end{equation} In particular $C_ F$ is a finite convex function. Theorem 11.47.5 . 7444FA94A222 The envelope ( 11.47.1 ) is \[  E_ F=C_ F(\log r)-\log (1+r)  \] on the punctured affine chart, with its canonical extensions at both ends. It has ordinary type $u_\alpha $. The residual $R_ F=E_ F-u_\alpha $ off $o$ extends to $C^{1,1}(\mathbb P^ k)$, is zero near $o$ and is smooth near infinity. The function $C_ F$ is affine on each component of $\{ C_ F<g\} $, and, with $L_2=\sup _{\mathbb R}\max (g'',0)$, 7B822F7684AE 11.47.6 \begin{equation}  0\leq C_ F'(b)-C_ F'(a)\leq L_2(b-a)\qquad (a<b). \end{equation} Proof. We first identify the full envelope, then examine contact and the two ends. Every supporting slope of $C_ F$ lies in $[0,1]$, by the left growth $g\to -\infty $ and the right growth $g=x+o(1)$. The sandwich forces its asymptotic slopes to be $0,1$. The competitor family is invariant under the unitary group $U(k)$ acting on the affine coordinates. Its regularized supremum is therefore radial. Adding smooth local potentials of $\kappa $ gives a locally upper-bounded family of plurisubharmonic functions, so the envelope is $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic. The competitor $u_\alpha -K_ F$ prevents collapse, and upper semicontinuity of the obstacle preserves the everywhere bound after regularization, including at $o$. A radial plurisubharmonic total potential $B(\log r)$ has convex profile $B$: restriction to a complex line gives this from radial subharmonicity. Positivity in a direction orthogonal to $z$ gives $B'\geq 0$. Conversely a convex nondecreasing profile has nonnegative tangential and radial Hessian eigenvalues $B'/r$ and $B''/r$, first for smooth profiles and then by convex smoothing on annuli. The envelope's total profile is consequently a convex minorant of $g$, and is at most $C_ F$. The same criterion makes $C_ F(\log r)$ plurisubharmonic on the punctured chart. Its upper bound near $o$ and ( 11.47.4 ) give a removable extension with value $-\infty $. Since $C_ F'\leq 1$, the function $C_ F-x$ is nonincreasing and, by the sandwich, has a finite right-end limit. The proposed $E_ F$ is thus locally bounded above near infinity. Add a local smooth potential of $\kappa $ and apply lemma 5.24.7 across the hyperplane. This gives a global competitor, hence the formula. The sandwich proves ordinary equivalence without subtracting the infinite values at $o$. On a compact interval in the free set the gap $g-C_ F$ is positive. Replacing $C_ F$ on a sufficiently short subinterval by its chord preserves convexity at both endpoints and stays below $g$. Unless $C_ F$ is locally affine this would give a larger minorant. It follows that it is affine on each free component. At a contact point $y$, domination by $g$ gives $C'_{F,-}(y)\geq g'(y)\geq C'_{F,+}(y)$, and convexity reverses the outer inequality. Thus $C_ F$ is differentiable at contacts, with derivative $g'$, and it is differentiable on free intervals as well. Its derivative is continuous. For $a<b$ outside one common free interval, move $a$ to its right contact endpoint and $b$ to its left contact endpoint whenever necessary. These points $a',b'\in [a,b]$ have the same respective derivatives. An unbounded free interval lacking the needed endpoint contains both original points, in which case the difference is zero. Otherwise \[  0\leq C_ F'(b)-C_ F'(a)=g'(b')-g'(a') \leq L_2(b'-a')\leq L_2(b-a),  \] which proves ( 11.47.6 ). For all sufficiently negative $x$, the tangent to $A$ at $x$ lies below $g$ on $\operatorname {supp}F$, by lemma 11.47.2 , and below $A=g$ elsewhere. Hence $C_ F=A$ on a left tail. The residual is zero near $o$. For the other end, put $L_ F=\inf _{\mathbb R}(g(x)-x)\leq 0$. If this infimum is attained at $y$, the affine minorant $x+L_ F$ touches $g$ there. The bound $C_ F'\leq 1$ forces $C_ F=x+L_ F$ for $x\geq y$. A negative infimum is always attained, since $g-x$ tends to $+\infty $ on the left and to zero on the right. With $R=1/r$, the envelope on this tail is E93EE9714FF1 11.47.7 \begin{equation}  E_ F=L_ F-\log (1+R). \end{equation} If $L_ F=0$ is not attained and $F\ne 0$, the continuous function $g(y)-y$ has a positive minimum on $\operatorname {supp}F$. The right tangents of $A$ approach the line $y$ uniformly there, so every sufficiently late tangent lies below $g$ and gives $C_ F=A$ at its contact point. Thus $C_ F=A$ on a right tail; for $F=0$ this holds everywhere. Both alternatives give a smooth residual near infinity, because $R$ and $u_\alpha $ are smooth there. On the intervening finite annulus, \[  |C_ F-A|\leq K_ F,\qquad |C_ F'-A'|\leq 1, \qquad |(C_ F-A)''|\leq L_2+\| A''\| _\infty \quad \text{a.e.}  \] Composing with the smooth coordinate function $x=\log r$ gives $C^{1,1}$ regularity. The exact end formulas extend it over the whole projective space. $\square$ Corollary 11.47.8 . EA98BEE991F7 The non-pluripolar measure of $E_ F$ has mass one and satisfies \[  \operatorname{MA}_\kappa (E_ F)(\{ a<\log r<b\} )=C_ F'(b)^ k-C_ F'(a)^ k \qquad (-\infty <a<b<\infty ).  \] It vanishes on every free interval. For any $F,G\in C_ c^2(\mathbb R;\mathbb R)$, 2FE2F9FAF60D 11.47.9 \begin{equation}  \| R_ F-R_ G\| _{C^0(\mathbb P^ k)}\leq \| F-G\| _\infty . \end{equation} Proof. On an annulus, the radial flux formula ( 11.46.4 ), followed by convex smoothing and bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity, gives the displayed measure. Continuity of $C_ F'$ excludes boundary atoms. The non-pluripolar truncations discard $o$, and smoothness at infinity excludes hyperplane mass. The asymptotic slopes $0,1$ therefore give mass one. An affine profile has zero radial eigenvalue and hence zero top-degree measure. Finally, if $\delta =\| F-G\| _\infty $, subtracting $\delta $ from a competitor for $F$ gives a competitor for $G$, and conversely. The resulting value bound for the envelopes gives ( 11.47.9 ) off $o$, and continuity of the residuals extends it across both ends. $\square$ For example, take a nonnegative smooth compactly supported bump $\chi $ with $\chi (x_0)=1$ and $F=-M\chi $, where $M>A(x_0)-x_0$. Then $L_ F<0$, and ( 11.47.7 ) gives an open free region of zero density. The envelope still has its sublogarithmic pole, while its residual is globally $C^{1,1}$.

For a fixed interval $[a,b]$ and $M>0$, let $\mathcal F_{a,b,M}$ consist of real $C^2$ functions supported in $[a,b]$ with $\| F\| _\infty +\| F''\| _\infty \leq M$. Take all norms in one fixed finite smooth projective atlas. Theorem 11.47.11 . 278AD9E56CEA There is $K=K(k,\alpha ,a,b,M)$ such that \[  \| R_ F\| _{C^{1,1}}\leq K\qquad (F\in \mathcal F_{a,b,M}).  \] For every $0<\gamma <1$ and $F,G\in \mathcal F_{a,b,M}$ with $\delta =\| F-G\| _\infty \leq 1$, \[  \| R_ F-R_ G\| _{C^{1,\gamma }} \leq K_\gamma \delta ^{(1-\gamma )/2},  \] where $K_\gamma $ has the same fixed-parameter dependence. These bounds hold across changes of the infinity alternative in theorem 11.47.5 . Proof. The left tangents of $A$ lie below $A-M$ on $[a,b]$ once their contact point is less than a common $a_0<a$. title: 11.47.13 The full envelope on a Hermitian product
search_title: The full envelope on a Hermitian product
topic: Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality
text: Let $(Y,h_0)$ be a connected compact Hermitian manifold of dimension $m\geq 1$, and on $X=\mathbb P^ k\times Y$ put $H=\operatorname {pr}_1^*\kappa +\operatorname {pr}_2^*h_0$, $N=k+m$ and $V_0=\int _ Yh_0^ m$. Pull $u_\alpha $ and $F$ back to $X$, and define $E_ F^ H$ by ( 11.47.1 ) using the full family $\mathrm{PSH}(X,H)$. Proposition 11.47.14 . E4713F2FEF7D One has $E_ F^ H=\operatorname {pr}_1^*E_ F$ and \[  \operatorname{MA}_ H(E_ F^ H)=\binom Nk\, \operatorname{MA}_\kappa (E_ F)\otimes h_0^ m, \qquad \operatorname{MA}_ H(E_ F^ H)(X)=\binom Nk V_0.  \] The pulled-back residual is globally $C^{1,1}$, and $E_ F^ H$ belongs to $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,H,u_\alpha )$. On each fixed product the uniform bounds and derivative stability of theorem 11.47.11 hold for these residuals. Proof. Every competitor restricts to a projective slice as a $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic function or as $-\infty $ identically. To check the exact lower bound when $H$ is nonclosed, choose a smooth quadratic correction $q$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq H$ on a coordinate polydisk and let $v_\epsilon =(v+q)*\eta _\epsilon -q$ on a smaller polydisk, where $\eta _\epsilon $ is the rescaling of a fixed smooth nonnegative radial probability kernel. Radial plurisubharmonic convolutions decrease to the canonical $v+q$, and \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\epsilon \geq (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q-H)*\eta _\epsilon -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q \geq -H-o(1)\omega _{\mathrm{Eucl}}.  \] Restrict this smooth inequality to a fixed slice. The corrected restrictions decrease either to $-\infty $ or to a plurisubharmonic function in local $L^1$; in the latter case the background error tends to zero distributionally. Subtracting $q$ gives the exact $\kappa $ bound, and these canonical restrictions patch on the connected slice. The everywhere obstacle constraint now gives $v\leq \operatorname {pr}_1^*E_ F$ on every slice. Upper regularization preserves this bound. Conversely every base competitor lifts, since $h_0>0$, proving equality of the full envelopes. The bounded truncations $\max (E_ F^ H,-j)$ are pullbacks. By proposition 5.28.2 , lemma 5.28.4 , dimensional multilinearity leaves only the term with $k$ projective factors and $m$ factor entries. Restrict to strict superlevel sets and let $j\to \infty $ to obtain the stated non-pluripolar measure and its finite mass. The residual regularity and uniform estimates pull back in a fixed smooth product atlas. Finally $E_ F^ H\geq u_\alpha -K_ F$. At $t=1$ take the stretching witness $v_1=E_ F^ H$; for $t>1$ take $v_ t=u_\alpha -tK_ F$, so that \[  t^{-1}v_ t+(1-t^{-1})u_\alpha =u_\alpha -K_ F\leq E_ F^ H.  \] Together with ordinary domination this is definition 16.28.61 , including the canonical values at the common pole. $\square$ Example 11.47.15 . 1E30DC99E57B There is a nonclosed positive background on a non-Kähler fourfold for which the preceding full envelope formula and uniform residual estimates hold. Proof. Take $Y=(\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle \zeta \mapsto \mathrm e\zeta \rangle $. With $s=\log |\zeta |^2$, the form $h_0=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s+\mathrm ds\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s$ is invariant under the quotient. Its two summands are positive on the tangential and radial complex directions, respectively, so it is Hermitian. Moreover $\mathrm dh_0=-\mathrm ds\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s\ne 0$. The Hopf surface is diffeomorphic to $S^3\times S^1$ and has odd first Betti number. Thus $X=\mathbb P^2\times Y$ is a non-Kähler fourfold with $\mathrm dH\ne 0$, and proposition 11.47.14 applies. $\square$

title: 18.2 Multiplier-ideal envelopes and $\mathcal I$-goodness
text: Throughout this chapter, $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n$ and $\theta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, which need not be closed. We fix a smooth positive probability volume form $\mathrm{d}V$ on $X$ and take $L^1$ norms with respect to it. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u)$ denotes the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (u)$ of theorem 13.14.3 ; its total mass may be infinite. We write $u\preceq v$ and $u\sim v$ for the ordinary singularity order and equivalence of definition 16.7.1 , and $u\preceq _{\mathcal I}v$ and $u\sim _{\mathcal I}v$ for inclusion and equality of the multiplier ideals $\mathcal I(ku)$ and $\mathcal I(kv)$ at every weight $k>0$, as in section 5.33 . Finally, $P_\theta [u]$ and $P_{\theta ,F}[u]$ denote the ordinary singularity envelopes of definition 5.40.4 , below zero and below a smooth obstacle $F$, and $V_\theta =P_\theta (0)$ is the potential with minimal singularities of section 5.40 . Multiplier ideals record weighted holomorphic integrability. Two potentials can have the same multiplier ideals at every weight although their ordinary envelopes differ, so passing from the ordinary singularity type of a potential to its multiplier-ideal class loses information. Analytic approximation makes this loss visible: along dyadic Demailly approximations, the envelopes converge to the greatest nonpositive representative of the multiplier-ideal class, which may exceed the ordinary envelope of the original potential. In the Kähler theory, equality of these two envelopes is also characterized by a mass condition. In a nonclosed background the equality remains meaningful even when the potential has infinite mass, and we therefore study both envelopes along analytic approximations. Examples on curves show that this still does not give continuity of mass or completeness, because diffuse polar curvature can disappear in the limit. The same examples explain why the obstacle has to be taken into account when the background changes.

title: 18.3 The Kähler characterization
text: First suppose that $X$ is Kähler, that $\theta $ is a smooth closed big real $(1,1)$-form, and that $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ has positive non-pluripolar mass. Let $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ be the multiplier-ideal envelope of definition 18.4.1 below, and let $d_ S$ be the singularity pseudometric of 16.9 The $d_ S$-pseudometric . The characterization of $\mathcal I$-good singularities in Theorem 18.1.2 states that the following three conditions are equivalent: \[  \begin{gathered} u\text{ lies in the }d_ S\text{-closure of analytic singularities},\\ \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (u) =\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}),\\ P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}. \end{gathered}  \] The last condition involves only envelopes. It therefore offers a starting point for the Hermitian problem even where the metric and the mass characterizations are unavailable. The integral on the right of the middle condition is the multiplier-ideal volume of [ SGPT ] . The upper and lower volumes of definition 16.28.58 , by contrast, vary the potential within its ordinary singularity type. The distinction matters in a nonclosed background, where even a bounded change of the potential can alter its total mass.

title: 18.4 Ideal projection
text: We return to the general setting fixed at the beginning of the chapter. The multiplier-ideal envelope is the greatest nonpositive potential in a multiplier-ideal class. Taking a supremum over the class could a priori enlarge the multiplier ideals; the increasing-limit form of strong openness rules this out, and the envelope is then a projection onto the class. Definition 18.4.1 . F1F202AEE8FD For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ define \[  P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I} :=\left(\sup \{ v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):v\leq 0, \  v\sim _{\mathcal I}u\} \right)^*.  \] As for ordinary envelopes, the members of the defining family are called competitors . The family is nonempty because it contains $u-\sup _ Xu$; bounded perturbations do not change multiplier ideals. Since it is bounded above by zero, its regularized supremum is a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function. The envelope depends only on the multiplier-ideal class of $u$. Theorem 18.4.2 . 7F20FD198864 For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, \[  P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}\sim _{\mathcal I}u,\qquad P_\theta [P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}]_{\mathcal I}=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}.  \] The regularization in definition 18.4.1 does not change the pointwise supremum. Moreover, \[  \sup _ X P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}=0.  \] Proof. Write $q=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. By Choquet's lemma, some sequence from the defining family has regularized supremum $q$. Replacing its terms by successive finite maxima, we obtain by lemma 5.37.4 an increasing sequence $v_ j$ that remains in the family and converges to $q$ almost everywhere. Fix $x\in X$ and $\lambda >0$. On a coordinate ball about $x$, choose one smooth function $r$ such that every $v_ j+r$ and $q+r$ is plurisubharmonic; this is possible because all these functions have complex Hessian bounded below by the same smooth form $-\theta $. The increasing-limit assertion of theorem 5.37.3 gives \[  \mathcal I(\lambda (q+r))_ x =\mathcal I(\lambda (v_ j+r))_ x =\mathcal I(\lambda u)_ x  \] for all large $j$; the second equality holds because smooth additions do not change multiplier ideals. Hence $q\sim _{\mathcal I}u$. Since $q\leq 0$, it belongs to its own defining family. The pointwise supremum is therefore at least $q$, and it is at most its regularization $q$; this proves the assertion about regularization. The defining families for $P_\theta [q]_{\mathcal I}$ and $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ coincide, which proves idempotence. Finally, if $\sup _ Xq<0$, then $q-\sup _ Xq$ would be a larger competitor, which is impossible. $\square$ Ideal projection commutes with pullback by a modification because both the potential class and the all-weight ideal class descend. Proposition 18.4.3 . 9AE7825754C3 Let $\mu :Y\to X$ be a modification of connected compact complex manifolds. For every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$ and every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, \[  P_{\mu ^*\theta }[u\circ \mu ]_{\mathcal I} =P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}\circ \mu .  \] Proof. By proposition 5.43.18 , pullback identifies the potentials in the two backgrounds. Surjectivity of $\mu $ identifies their nonpositivity constraints, and lemma 5.43.24 identifies their all-weight multiplier-ideal classes. Hence pullback gives a bijection of the complete competitor families. The ideal envelope is itself a competitor and is their greatest member by theorem 18.4.2 . Its pullback is therefore the greatest competitor upstairs, which proves the identity. $\square$ Proposition 18.4.4 . 2506B7AD6F19 For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, \[  u-\sup _ Xu\leq P_\theta [u]\leq P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}\leq V_\theta .  \] Moreover, \[  \begin{gathered} P_\theta [u]\sim _{\mathcal I}u,\qquad P_\theta [P_\theta [u]]_{\mathcal I}=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I},\\ P_\theta [P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}. \end{gathered}  \] Proof. Let $h\leq 0$ be a competitor for the ordinary envelope, so that $h\preceq u$. The function $\max (h,u-\sup _ Xu)$ is nonpositive, ordinarily equivalent to $u$, and dominates $h$. Since ordinarily equivalent potentials have the same multiplier ideals, it is a competitor for the ideal envelope. Taking regularized suprema gives $P_\theta [u]\leq P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$; the two outer inequalities follow directly from the defining families. Projection and monotonicity of local integrability now give, for every $\lambda >0$, \[  \mathcal I(\lambda u) \subseteq \mathcal I(\lambda P_\theta [u]) \subseteq \mathcal I(\lambda P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}) =\mathcal I(\lambda u).  \] Thus the ordinary envelope preserves all multiplier ideals, and it has the same ideal envelope as $u$. For $q=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$, the inequalities already proved and idempotence give $q\leq P_\theta [q]\leq P_\theta [q]_{\mathcal I}=q$. $\square$ We call $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ normalized if $\sup _ Xu=0$. Recall from definition 5.40.4 that $u$ is an ordinary model, or envelope fixed point, if $P_\theta [u]=u$; we call $u$ an ideal model if $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}=u$. Models of either kind are normalized, and by the last identity in proposition 18.4.4 every ideal model is an ordinary model. The map $u\mapsto P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ is called ideal projection . Corollary 18.4.5 . B853F2E6C70B If $\theta $ is semipositive and big, then $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ has finite extended Monge–Ampère mass for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Proof. By the last identity in corollary 18.4.4 , $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ is an ordinary model, that is, an envelope fixed point. The mass estimate for envelope fixed points in proposition 16.28.7 applies. $\square$ Proposition 18.4.6 . EAFF378DAF48 For $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, \[  u\preceq _{\mathcal I}v\quad \Longrightarrow \quad P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}\leq P_\theta [v]_{\mathcal I}.  \] For $a>0$ one has $P_{a\theta }[a u]_{\mathcal I}=aP_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. For smooth real $(1,1)$-forms $\theta _ i$ and potentials $u_ i\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta _ i)$, $i=1,2$, \[  P_{\theta _1}[u_1]_{\mathcal I}+P_{\theta _2}[u_2]_{\mathcal I} \leq P_{\theta _1+\theta _2}[u_1+u_2]_{\mathcal I}.  \] Proof. Let $h$ be a competitor for $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. Since $h\sim _{\mathcal I}u\preceq _{\mathcal I}v$, the Lelong-number criterion in theorem 5.37.3 shows that $\max (h,v-\sup _ Xv)$ is multiplier-ideal equivalent to $v$. This function is nonpositive and dominates $h$, so it is a competitor for $P_\theta [v]_{\mathcal I}$; taking the supremum over $h$ proves that the envelope preserves the order. Multiplication by $a$ is a bijection between the defining families in the scaling identity. For the sum, $P_{\theta _1}[u_1]_{\mathcal I}+P_{\theta _2}[u_2]_{\mathcal I}$ is nonpositive and $(\theta _1+\theta _2)$-plurisubharmonic, and it is multiplier-ideal equivalent to $u_1+u_2$ by projection and lemma 5.37.4 . It is therefore a competitor for the envelope on the right. $\square$

title: 18.4.7 Analytic and divisorial singularities
text: For a potential $a$ with analytic singularities, the multiplier-ideal order controls the ordinary order: by lemma 5.38.11 , every quasi-plurisubharmonic $v$ with $v\preceq _{\mathcal I}a$ satisfies $v\preceq a$. The ideal envelope of $a$ is then a competitor for its ordinary envelope, and the two envelopes coincide. Proposition 18.4.8 . EB95710FF4D7 Let $a\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have analytic singularities. Then \[  a\sim P_\theta [a]=P_\theta [a]_{\mathcal I}.  \] In particular the common envelope has analytic singularities with the same coefficient and ideal as $a$, up to a bounded remainder. Proof. Set $q=P_\theta [a]_{\mathcal I}$. Projection gives $q\sim _{\mathcal I}a$, so lemma 5.38.11 gives $q\preceq a$. Since $q\leq 0$, it is a competitor for $P_\theta [a]$. section: 18.5 Changes of background and envelope mass
text: A smooth change of representative $(\theta ,u)\mapsto (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f,u-f)$ preserves the current $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ but moves the zero obstacle. The resulting envelopes remain ordinarily equivalent after transport. In a nonclosed background, however, their masses can differ. Proposition 18.5.1 . 07B0D783C3F0 Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$. Set $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$, $u'=u-f$, $m=\min _ Xf$ and $M=\max _ Xf$. Then \[  P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}+m \leq P_{\theta '}[u']_{\mathcal I}+f \leq P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}+M.  \] The same inequalities hold for the ordinary envelopes. Proof. If $v$ is a competitor for $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$, then $v-f+m$ is $\theta '$-plurisubharmonic, nonpositive and multiplier-ideal equivalent to $u'$. Therefore $v\leq P_{\theta '}[u']_{\mathcal I}+f-m$, and taking the envelope gives the first inequality. Conversely, a competitor $v'$ in the new background gives the competitor $v'+f-M$ in the old one, which proves the second inequality. For the ordinary envelopes, the same calculation applies with the ordinary singularity order in place of multiplier-ideal equivalence. $\square$ For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, put \[  W_\theta (u)=\int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\theta (P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I})\in [0,+\infty ].  \] This quantity depends on the decomposition of the current, even for smooth potentials. Proposition 18.5.2 . 6E8985733CBC There are two smooth decompositions of the same positive current for which the corresponding values of $W$ are different. Proof. Use the Hermitian form $\omega $ and the smooth function $g=u_ t$ of example 11.1.12 , with $t\ne 0$ sufficiently small. Both $\omega $ and $\omega '=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ are Hermitian, and \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}0=\omega '+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(-g).  \] For a smooth potential in a Hermitian background, all multiplier ideals are trivial and zero is a competitor for its multiplier-ideal envelope, so that envelope is zero. Consequently \[  W_\omega (0)=\int _ X\omega ^2,\qquad W_{\omega '}(-g)=\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g)^2.  \] By the explicit formula ( 11.1.13 ), the two integrals differ. $\square$ The underlying torus is Kähler; the dependence comes from the chosen nonclosed background. In the closed theory, the invariance of mass under bounded changes of the potential gives the missing step after proposition 18.5.1 . Singularity volumes, on the other hand, range over the entire ordinary type, so the bijection of competitors in the gauge change preserves them. Under bounded mass, proposition 13.25.1 accordingly transports ordinary models of positive volume and preserves their upper-volume comparison.

title: 18.6 $L^1$ geometry of ideal classes
text: Ideal projection selects a canonical representative of each multiplier-ideal class, so the $L^1$ distance between these representatives defines a metric on the classes. Since the representatives have supremum zero, normalized compactness makes this metric totally bounded and its completion compact. The points added in the completion, however, need not be ideal models. On a curve this happens as badly as possible: approximating curvature measures by finite atomic measures shows that the completion contains every normalized potential. Let \[  \mathfrak S_{\mathcal I}(X,\theta ) =\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )/{\sim _{\mathcal I}},\qquad \mathfrak M_{\mathcal I}(X,\theta ) =\{ q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ):P_\theta [q]_{\mathcal I}=q\}   \] be the set of multiplier-ideal classes and the set of ideal models, and write $[u]_{\mathcal I}$ for the multiplier-ideal class of $u$. By theorem 18.4.2 , the map $[u]_{\mathcal I}\mapsto P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ identifies these two sets, and every ideal envelope has supremum zero. Proposition 18.6.1 . 47A414940A74 The formula CE9BB18A9158 18.6.2 \begin{equation}  d_{\mathcal I,\theta ,\mathrm{d}V}([u]_{\mathcal I},[v]_{\mathcal I}) =\int _ X|P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}-P_\theta [v]_{\mathcal I}|\, \mathrm{d}V \end{equation} defines a finite metric on $\mathfrak S_{\mathcal I}(X,\theta )$. This metric space is totally bounded. Its metric completion is canonically the $L^1$ closure of $\mathfrak M_{\mathcal I}(X,\theta )$ inside the compact space $\mathcal K_\theta $ of normalized $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions in theorem 5.25.2 . Changing $\mathrm{d}V$ to another smooth positive probability volume form gives a bi-Lipschitz equivalent metric. Proof. The ideal envelopes are integrable and depend only on the ideal classes, so the formula is well defined and finite; symmetry and the triangle inequality are those of the $L^1$ norm. If the distance is zero, the two envelopes agree almost everywhere, hence everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 , and projection shows that the two ideal classes coincide. Conversely, equal ideal classes have the same envelope. By the normalized compactness theorem, $\mathfrak M_{\mathcal I}$ lies in the compact space $\mathcal K_\theta $. Every subset of a compact metric space is totally bounded, and its completion is its closure in that space. Finally, the ratio of two smooth positive volume forms on the compact manifold $X$ is bounded above and below by positive constants, and multiplying the integral by these bounds proves the last assertion. $\square$

title: 18.6.5 Mass and capacity convergence
text:
The approximation in theorem 18.6.4 loses all non-pluripolar mass. For the nonconstant smooth $u$ at the end of its proof, the approximants $q_ j$ have zero non-pluripolar measure, whereas $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (u)=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. After normalization to mean zero, the same sequence converges in the Gauduchon trace metric of corollary 11.31.6 . Nevertheless, the sequence $q_ j$ does not converge to $u$ in capacity. Otherwise, since $q_ j,u\leq 0$, theorem 13.15.9 would give \[  0=\mathrm{e}^{q_ j}\mathrm{MA}_	heta (q_ j) ightharpoonup \mathrm{e}^{u}(	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u),  \] contradicting the strict positivity of the limiting measure. Thus weak convergence of traces and $L^1$ convergence do not imply convergence in capacity, even on a curve. The same sequence shows that ideal projection is not continuous for the $L^1$ topology: $P_	heta [q_ j]_{\mathcal I}=q_ j	o u$, whereas $P_	heta [u]_{\mathcal I}=0$. The completion therefore distinguishes smooth normalized potentials that the quotient by multiplier-ideal equivalence identifies. The loss of mass also occurs along sequences of fixed positive mass. Proposition 18.6.6 . 8B21A468DD06 In the curve setting above, for every rational $0<	au <1$ there are ideal models $r_ j$ with analytic singularities such that \[   egin{gathered} d_{\mathcal I,	heta ,\mathrm{d}V}([r_ j]_{\mathcal I},[0]_{\mathcal I})\longrightarrow 0,\ \mathrm{MA}_	heta (r_ j)(Y)=	au , \qquad \mathrm{MA}_	heta (r_ j)ightharpoonup 	au 	heta . \end{gathered}  \] In particular, non-pluripolar mass is not continuous for this metric, even on a family whose masses have a fixed positive lower bound. Proof. Choose finitely supported probability measures $
u _ j$ with rational weights converging weakly to $	heta $, and let $q_ j$ be their normalized Green potentials; the preceding proof gives $q_ j	o 0$ in $L^1$. u _ j\geq 0.  \] Since $aq_ j$ is a competitor, $aq_ j\leq r_ j\leq 0$, and hence $r_ j	o 0$ in $L^1$. By projection, $r_ j$ is an ideal model. title: Proposition 18.6.6
text:
Proposition 18.6.6 . 8B21A468DD06 In the curve setting above, for every rational $0<	au <1$ there are ideal models $r_ j$ with analytic singularities such that \[   egin{gathered} d_{\mathcal I,	heta ,\mathrm{d}V}([r_ j]_{\mathcal I},[0]_{\mathcal I})\longrightarrow 0,\ \mathrm{MA}_	heta (r_ j)(Y)=	au , \qquad \mathrm{MA}_	heta (r_ j)ightharpoonup 	au 	heta . \end{gathered}  \] In particular, non-pluripolar mass is not continuous for this metric, even on a family whose masses have a fixed positive lower bound. Proof. Choose finitely supported probability measures $
u _ j$ with rational weights converging weakly to $	heta $, and let $q_ j$ be their normalized Green potentials; the preceding proof gives $q_ j	o 0$ in $L^1$. Put $a=1-	au $ and $r_ j=P_	heta [a q_ j]_{\mathcal I}$. The scaled potential lies in the same background, since \[  	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(aq_ j)=(1-a)	heta +a
u _ j\geq 0.  \] Since $aq_ j$ is a competitor, $aq_ j\leq r_ j\leq 0$, and hence $r_ j	o 0$ in $L^1$. By projection, $r_ j$ is an ideal model. By proposition 18.4.8 , it has exactly the logarithmic coefficients of $aq_ j$, which are rational, with bounded local remainders, and it is locally bounded away from the finite pole set. On the curve, removing the polar part of the curvature therefore gives \[  \mathrm{MA}_	heta (r_ j)=	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r_ j-a
u _ j.  \] By distributional Stokes, this measure has total mass $1-a=	au $. The positive curvature measures $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}r_ j$ have mass one and converge as distributions, hence weakly, to $	heta $. Since $
u _ jightharpoonup 	heta $, the last identity gives $\mathrm{MA}_	heta (r_ j)ightharpoonup 	au 	heta $. Finally, $P_	heta [0]_{\mathcal I}=0$, so the distance in the statement is $\int _ Y|r_ j|\, \mathrm{d}V$, which tends to zero. The limiting potential $0$ has non-pluripolar measure $	heta $, of mass one. $\square$

title: 18.6.7 Comparison with scalar normalization
text: We return to $X$ of arbitrary dimension, with the fixed volume form $\mathrm{d}V$. The scalar pseudometric $\Delta $ of ( 11.39.3 ) compares the normalization scalars $B_\varphi $ of section 11.33 uniformly over all continuous logarithmic densities. When an analytic singularity is shrunk to zero, the estimate in a smaller background makes this scalar distance tend to zero. At a fixed mass, however, the normalization scalar in a closed background does not see the location of the poles. Example 18.6.8 . 0F685C3DE85F Let $\theta $ be semipositive and big, and let $a\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have analytic singularities with $a\leq 0$. Use the normalization scalars $B_\varphi $ and the sets $\mathcal A_\varphi (G)$ of supporting probabilities from section 11.33 , section 11.34 , defined with the fixed volume form $\mathrm{d}V$. Set \[  \varphi _ t=P_\theta [ta],\qquad t\in \mathbb Q\cap (0,1).  \] By proposition 18.4.8 , $\varphi _ t\sim ta$; since the ordinary envelope depends only on the ordinary type, $P_\theta [\varphi _ t]=\varphi _ t$. Moreover $ta\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,t\theta )$ and $ta\leq \varphi _ t$, so the envelope $P_{t\theta }(\varphi _ t)$ in the smaller background is not identically $-\infty $. By proposition 11.39.1 , \[  \sup _{G\in C(X)}|B_{\varphi _ t}(G)-B_0(G)| \leq -n\log (1-t)\longrightarrow 0 \qquad (t\downarrow 0).  \] When $\theta $ is Hermitian and $G$ is fixed and smooth, every choice in $\mathcal A_{\varphi _ t}(G)$ converges weakly in $L^1$ to the smooth Gauduchon adjoint probability, by corollary 11.39.6 , theorem 11.34.9 . By contrast, the projective references in example 11.42.3 have equal mass and identical normalization functionals, although their poles and multiplier ideals differ.

title: 18.7 Limits of analytic envelopes
text:
By the curve construction of theorem 18.6.4 , convergence of potentials alone does not determine the limit of their ideal envelopes. Two further conditions do: a common lower bound in the multiplier-ideal order, and convergence of all divisorial Lelong numbers. Together they force every cluster value of the envelopes to have the multiplier ideals of the limiting potential, and maximality of the envelope then identifies the cluster value. The dyadic analytic approximants satisfy both conditions. In this section, $	heta $ is again an arbitrary smooth real $(1,1)$-form. We fix $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$ and a Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, which will absorb the curvature errors of the approximants. Recall from section 5.38 that a local divisor $E$ over $X$ is a prime divisor on a smooth modification $\pi $ of a coordinate neighborhood in $X$, and that $
u _ E(u)=
u (u\circ \pi ,E)$ is the generic Lelong number of the pullback of $u$ along $E$. Proposition 18.7.1 . B727D2CB45A6 Let $\epsilon _ j\geq 0$ tend to zero, and let $a_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta +\epsilon _ jh)$ satisfy \[  u\preceq _{\mathcal I}a_ j,\qquad 
u _ E(a_ j)\longrightarrow 
u _ E(u) \quad 	ext{for every local divisor }E	ext{ over }X.  \] Then \[  P_{	heta +\epsilon _ jh}[a_ j]_{\mathcal I} \longrightarrow P_	heta [u]_{\mathcal I} \quad 	ext{in }L^1.  \] If the $a_ j$ have analytic singularities, their ordinary envelopes converge to $P_	heta [u]$ in $L^1$ if and only if $P_	heta [u]=P_	heta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. Proof. Set $p=P_	heta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ and $q_ j=P_{	heta +\epsilon _ jh}[a_ j]_{\mathcal I}$. Projection and the ideal order give \[  p\leq P_{	heta +\epsilon _ jh}[p]_{\mathcal I}\leq q_ j\leq 0.  \] The first inequality holds because $p$ is a competitor in the larger background, and the second follows from proposition 18.4.6 , since $p\sim _{\mathcal I}u\preceq _{\mathcal I}a_ j$. All $q_ j$ have supremum zero and belong to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta +Ch)$ for a fixed $C\geq \sup _ j\epsilon _ j$. By normalized compactness, every subsequence therefore has a further subsequence converging in $L^1$. Let $q$ be such a limit. Passing to the limit in the current inequalities gives $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,	heta )$, and lemma 5.24.3 gives $p\leq q\leq 0$. Fix a local modification $\pi :Z	o U$ and a prime divisor $E\subset Z$. By lemma 5.43.19 , the chosen subsequence still converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ after pullback. Since $q_ j\sim _{\mathcal I}a_ j$, the two functions have the same divisorial Lelong numbers, and the pointwise semicontinuity in lemma 5.38.7 yields \[  
u _ E(q)\geq \limsup _ j
u _ E(q_ j) =\lim _ j
u _ E(a_ j)=
u _ E(u).  \] Indeed, at every point of $E$ the pullback of each $q_ j$ has Lelong number at least $
u _ E(q_ j)$; it remains to apply the pointwise inequality at a point of $E$ where the pullback of $q$ has Lelong number $
u _ E(q)$. On the other hand, $p\leq q$ gives $
u _ E(q)\leq 
u _ E(p)=
u _ E(u)$. Thus $q$ and $u$ have the same Lelong numbers along all local divisors. Blowing up a point of any local modification recovers the pointwise Lelong number there as a generic divisorial number; on a curve the point is already a divisor. By theorem 5.37.3 , $q\sim _{\mathcal I}u$. Consequently $q$ is a competitor for $p$, so $q\leq p$. Every cluster value is therefore $p$, which proves convergence of the whole sequence. For analytic $a_ j$, proposition 18.4.8 identifies the ordinary and ideal envelopes, and the last assertion follows from uniqueness of $L^1$ limits and lemma 5.24.3 . $\square$ The divisorial convergence follows from inclusions of multiplier ideals at fixed weights. The local Bergman estimate bounds the error in terms of the log discrepancy, and this error tends to zero after division by the weight. u _ E(u)-A  \] for all large $j$. Taking the lower limit in $j$ first, and then letting $m	o \infty $ and $\delta \downarrow 0$, we obtain $\liminf _ j
u _ E(a_ j)\geq 
u _ E(u)$. The opposite inequality $
u _ E(a_ j)\leq

Example 18.7.3 . 504A5958272F On a compact connected curve $Y$ with a positive form $	heta $ of total mass one, there are normalized $a_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,	heta )$ with analytic singularities and a smooth $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,	heta )$ such that \[  a_ j\longrightarrow u	ext{ in }L^1,\qquad 
u _ E(a_ j)\longrightarrow 
u _ E(u)	ext{ for every local divisor }E,  \] but $P_	heta [a_ j]=P_	heta [a_ j]_{\mathcal I}	o u
e P_	heta [u]=P_	heta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ in $L^1$. Proof. Choose $u$ smooth, nonconstant and normalized, with $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$, and apply the construction in theorem 18.6.4 to the smooth probability measure $
u =	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. Since $
u $ has no atoms, the largest mass of a cell tends to zero along partitions of vanishing diameter. Choose the rational approximations of the weights so that their total absolute error tends to zero. The resulting atomic probability measures $
u _ j$ converge weakly to $
u $, and their largest atoms tend to zero. By the same theorem, their normalized Green potentials $a_ j$ have analytic singularities, satisfy $P_	heta [a_ j]=P_	heta [a_ j]_{\mathcal I}=a_ j$, and converge to $u$ in $L^1$. At every point $y\in Y$, \[  0\leq 
u (a_ j,y)=
u _ j(\{ y\} ) \leq \max _{z\in Y}
u _ j(\{ z\} )\longrightarrow 0=
u (u,y).  \] Since local modifications of a smooth curve are isomorphisms, this gives all the required divisorial limits. As $u$ is bounded and $	heta >0$, both of its envelopes are zero, and since $u$ is not constant, the envelopes do not converge to them. Each $a_ j$ has a logarithmic pole, so $u\preceq _{\mathcal I}a_ j$ fails. $\square$

title: 18.7.4 Dyadic regularization
text: Demailly regularization provides the common ideal bound, since its approximants lie above $u$, and the Bergman estimate gives convergence of each divisorial Lelong number. Along dyadic indices, subadditivity of multiplier ideals also orders the ordinary singularity types of the approximants, which makes their envelopes decrease pointwise. This is the mechanism used in Theorem 18.1.2 . Apply theorem 5.36.1 to $u$, with $\gamma =-\theta $, along the indices $m_ j=2^ j$, starting at a sufficiently large index. Denote the resulting potentials by $a_ j$, and choose numbers $\epsilon _ j>0$ decreasing to zero such that E93CF05C13A8 18.7.5 \begin{equation}  a_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta +\epsilon _ jh),\qquad a_ j\geq u,\qquad a_ j\text{ has type }(1/m_ j,\mathcal I(m_ ju)). \end{equation} These approximants satisfy $a_ j\to u$ in $L^1$. Their values need not decrease, but their ordinary singularity types do: the subadditivity property in ( 5.37.6 ) gives \[  \mathcal I(2m_ ju)\subseteq \mathcal I(m_ ju)^2, \qquad a_{j+1}\preceq a_ j,  \] where the ordinary comparison follows by taking logarithms of local generators, with a constant that may depend on $j$. Theorem 18.7.6 . EA60F3EAF248 For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and every choice in ( 18.7.5 ), put \[  q_ j=P_{\theta +\epsilon _ jh}[a_ j].  \] Then $q_ j$ has analytic singularities, and \[  q_ j=P_{\theta +\epsilon _ jh}[a_ j]_{\mathcal I} \searrow P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}  \] pointwise and in $L^1$. The limit is independent of the choice of the approximants $a_ j$, of the error bounds $\epsilon _ j$ and of the metric $h$. Proof. By proposition 18.4.8 , $q_ j=P_{\theta +\epsilon _ jh}[a_ j]_{\mathcal I}\sim a_ j$. Since the backgrounds decrease and $a_{j+1}\preceq a_ j$, the function $q_{j+1}$ is a competitor for $P_{\theta +\epsilon _ jh}[a_ j]$. Hence $q_{j+1}\leq q_ j$. The inequality $a_ j\geq u$ gives $u\preceq _{\mathcal I}a_ j$. For every local divisor $E$, lemma 5.38.9 gives \[  \nu _ E(a_ j)=\frac1{m_ j}\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathcal I(m_ ju) \longrightarrow \nu _ E(u).  \] By proposition 18.7.1 , $q_ j\to p:=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ in $L^1$, and $p\leq q_ j\leq 0$. The decreasing limit of the $q_ j$ is therefore bounded below by $p$; it is a $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function that agrees with $p$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere. This identifies the limit in terms of $\theta $ and the multiplier-ideal class of $u$ alone, which proves the asserted independence. $\square$ Corollary 18.7.7 . E941DFE18F1D For the sequence above, the following are equivalent: \[  P_\theta [u]=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I},\qquad q_ j\longrightarrow P_\theta [u]\text{ in }L^1, \qquad q_ j\searrow P_\theta [u]\text{ pointwise}.  \] They hold for one choice in ( 18.7.5 ) if and only if they hold for every such choice. For the fixed volume form $\mathrm{d}V$, \[  \lim _ j\int _ X(q_ j-P_\theta [u])\, \mathrm{d}V =\int _ X(P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}-P_\theta [u])\, \mathrm{d}V\geq 0,  \] and the vanishing of this limit is a further equivalent condition. Proof. The theorem identifies both limits of the $q_ j$ as $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ for every such choice, and its $L^1$ convergence gives the integral formula. By proposition 18.4.4 , the limiting difference is nonnegative. Its integral therefore vanishes exactly when the two envelopes agree almost everywhere, hence everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 . This proves all the equivalences. $\square$

title: 18.7.8 Absorbing the curvature error
text: When $\theta =\omega $ is Hermitian, we can take $h=\omega $, and dividing the approximants by $1+\epsilon _ j$ absorbs the curvature error. If the error bounds are rational, the analytic coefficients remain rational, so the whole approximation takes place in the fixed class $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. Corollary 18.7.9 . A08D826CFAD4 Let $\omega $ be Hermitian and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. There are $b_ j\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with analytic singularities and decreasing ordinary singularity types, such that $b_ j\to u$ in $L^1$ and \[  P_\omega [b_ j]=P_\omega [b_ j]_{\mathcal I}\searrow P_\omega [u]_{\mathcal I}.  \] Consequently the classes of potentials with analytic singularities are dense in the whole metric space of ideal classes of proposition 18.6.1 . The equality $P_\omega [u]=P_\omega [u]_{\mathcal I}$ is equivalent to convergence of these ordinary envelopes to $P_\omega [u]$ in $L^1$. Proof. Use $h=\omega $ in ( 18.7.5 ). Enlarge the error bounds to positive rational numbers $\epsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, and set \[  c_ j=\frac1{1+\epsilon _ j},\qquad b_ j=c_ ja_ j.  \] Then $c_ j\uparrow 1$ is rational and \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ j =c_ j\bigl ((1+\epsilon _ j)\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j\bigr )\geq 0.  \] The analytic coefficient of $b_ j$ is $c_ j/m_ j$. Moreover $b_ j\to u$ in $L^1$, since $a_ j\to u$ there and the sequence has bounded $L^1$ norm. Because $a_{j+1}\preceq a_ j$, $c_{j+1}\geq c_ j$, and each $a_ j$ is bounded above, one has $b_{j+1}\preceq b_ j$. Put $q_ j=P_{(1+\epsilon _ j)\omega }[a_ j]=P_{(1+\epsilon _ j)\omega }[a_ j]_{\mathcal I}$. The preceding theorem gives $q_ j\searrow P_\omega [u]_{\mathcal I}$ pointwise and in $L^1$. Since $b_ j$ has analytic singularities, proposition 18.4.8 and the homogeneity in proposition 18.4.6 give \[  r_ j:=P_\omega [b_ j]=P_\omega [b_ j]_{\mathcal I}=c_ jq_ j.  \] Here $q_ j\leq 0$ decreases and $c_ j\uparrow 1$, so $r_ j$ also decreases, with pointwise limit $P_\omega [u]_{\mathcal I}$. section: 18.8 A topology on ordinary singularity types
text:
The ordinary and the ideal envelope of a potential record different parts of its singularity. If a topology on ordinary singularity types requires both envelopes to converge, their equality becomes a closed condition, which every limit of analytic singularity types satisfies. For the converse, the dyadic approximants of a potential with equal envelopes must converge to it. We therefore add coordinates that these approximants control in a fixed Hermitian background: controlled inclusions of multiplier ideals, and the weighted total variation of divisorial Lelong numbers on each fixed modification. The closure of the analytic types is then exactly the set of types with equal envelopes, on the whole space of ordinary types. This topology depends on the zero obstacle hidden in the envelopes, and a smooth change of background moves that obstacle. Testing all smooth obstacles removes this dependence, and raises the question whether equality of the envelopes below zero implies equality below every obstacle. Examples of zero volume built from divisors in fibrations and products over curves answer this question on explicit classes of potentials. On these classes, polar curvature on the curve factors also gives complete metrics, which we compare with the complete topologies known in positive volume at the end of the section. From 18.11 on, several constructions use the volume comparison of ordinary models and the curve models of section 13.16 ; those results do not depend on the present section, and the reader may consult them as they are cited. Fix a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$ and write \[  \mathfrak S(X,\omega )=\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )/{\sim }.  \] In this section $[u]$ denotes the ordinary class of $u$, that is, its class modulo bounded differences. For each smooth compact modification $\pi :Y	o X$, fix a Hermitian form $\gamma _\pi $ on $Y$. For a prime divisor $E\subset Y$, set $w_ E=\int _ E\gamma _\pi ^{n-1}$, and let $
u _ E(u)=
u (u\circ \pi ,E)$ be the generic Lelong number of section 5.38 . Lemma 18.8.1 . 8FA80F8B6F5A For $u,v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, the sum D93497D2DEF1 18.8.2  egin{equation}  d_\pi ([u],[v])=\sum _{E\subset Y	ext{ prime}}w_ E|
u _ E(u)-
u _ E(v)| \end{equation} is finite and defines a pseudometric on $\mathfrak S(X,\omega )$. Changing $\gamma _\pi $ gives an equivalent pseudometric for the fixed modification $\pi $. Proof. The current $T=\pi ^*\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi )$ is positive. Divisorial removal in lemma 5.38.1 gives, for every finite family of prime divisors, \[  \sum _ Ew_ E
u _ E(u)\leq \int _ YT\wedge \gamma _\pi ^{n-1}<\infty .  \] Taking the supremum over finite families shows that the sum converges and that only countably many coefficients are positive. The same bound holds for $v$. Bounded changes of $u$ or $v$ do not affect the coefficients, and the triangle inequality holds term by term. Finally, two Hermitian forms on the compact manifold $Y$ bound one another by fixed positive multiples, and so do the corresponding divisor weights. $\square$ For $t>0$ and $a>1$, let 91C58D64DE57 18.8.3  egin{equation}  \mathcal U(t,a)=\{ ([u],[v]):\mathcal I(atu)\subseteq \mathcal I(tv),\quad \mathcal I(atv)\subseteq \mathcal I(tu)\} . \end{equation} These are relations between ordinary classes, since a bounded change leaves every multiplier ideal unchanged. Let $d_ I$ be the pullback of the metric ( 18.6.2 ), in background $\omega $, under $[u]\mapsto [u]_{\mathcal I}$, and put \[  d_ O([u],[v])=\| P_\omega [u]-P_\omega [v]\| _{L^1(\mathrm dV)}.  \] Both are pseudometrics on ordinary classes: $d_ I$ compares the ideal envelopes, whereas $d_ O$ also detects differences of ordinary envelopes within a single multiplier-ideal class. Proposition 18.8.4 . B919F0D14EE2 Finite intersections of the relations $d_ O<r$, $d_ I<r$, $d_\pi <r$ and $\mathcal U(t,a)$, with $r,t>0$ and $a>1$, form a base of entourages for a uniformity on $\mathfrak S(X,\omega )$. Denote its topology by $	au _{\omega ,0}$, where the subscript $0$ records the zero obstacle in the envelopes. A net $[u_ j]$ converges to $[u]$ if and only if both envelopes converge in $L^1$, $d_\pi ([u_ j],[u])	o 0$ for every fixed $\pi $, and $([u_ j],[u])\in \mathcal U(t,a)$ eventually for every fixed $t,a$. Smooth positive choices of $\mathrm dV$ and of the $\gamma _\pi $ do not change the uniformity. Proof. All generators are symmetric and contain the diagonal. Multiplier ideals decrease as the weight increases, as one sees from local integrability after subtracting a local upper bound from the potential. For $b=\sqrt a$, put $\mathcal V=\mathcal U(t,b)\cap \mathcal U(bt,b)$. If $([x],[y]),([y],[z])\in \mathcal V$, then \[  \mathcal I(atx)\subseteq \mathcal I(bty)\subseteq \mathcal I(tz),  \] and the same argument with $x$ and $z$ exchanged shows that $\mathcal V\circ \mathcal V\subseteq \mathcal U(t,a)$. For the pseudometric relations, halving the radius gives the corresponding refinement under composition. Taking finite intersections of these refinements proves the axioms of a uniformity, and convergence in it means eventual membership in each generating entourage. Bounded ratios of smooth positive volume forms and lemma 18.8.1 show that the auxiliary choices do not matter. $\square$ Each entourage involves only finitely many fixed modifications. The definition therefore requires neither a countable cofinal family of modifications nor convergence that is uniform over all modifications.

title: 18.9 Analytic closure
text:
We now show that the dyadic approximants of corollary 18.7.9 converge in $	au _{\omega ,0}$ exactly when the two envelopes agree. Let $\mathcal A_\omega $ be the set of ordinary classes with analytic singularities, with rational coefficients as in section 5.34 ; the rational curvature correction in corollary 18.7.9 keeps the approximants in this set. In the controlled ideal relations, the scale factor of that correction has to be taken into account. Theorem 18.9.1 . 867EFC7DCD8D The closure and the sequential closure of $\mathcal A_\omega $ in $	au _{\omega ,0}$ are both equal to 27F9EF4DC38B 18.9.2  egin{equation}  \mathcal G_\omega =\{ [u]:P_\omega [u]=P_\omega [u]_{\mathcal I}\} . \end{equation} For every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, the dyadic sequence $b_ j$ of corollary 18.7.9 satisfies \[  [b_ j]\longrightarrow [u]	ext{ in }	au _{\omega ,0} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad [u]\in \mathcal G_\omega .  \] The approximants may be chosen with one positive rational analytic coefficient on all charts.
