title: 18.10 Separation and mass
text: The topology $\tau _{\omega ,0}$ sees an ordinary class only through its envelopes, its multiplier ideals and its divisorial Lelong numbers. Distinct ordinary types can have the same ordinary envelope, and such types cannot be separated. Proposition 18.10.1 . 3B87EFC632CF Two classes have the same $\tau _{\omega ,0}$ neighborhoods if and only if their ordinary envelopes coincide. This topology is not $T_0$ and cannot be induced by a metric on $\mathfrak S(X,\omega )$. Proof. The coordinate $d_ O$ distinguishes different ordinary envelopes. Conversely, potentials with equal ordinary envelopes have equal multiplier ideals at every weight by corollary 18.4.4 . Their ideal envelopes and all their divisorial coefficients therefore agree, so every generating entourage has identical sections at the two classes. To produce distinct classes of this kind, choose a cutoff logarithmic pole $w\leq 0$ supported in a coordinate ball, plurisubharmonic near its pole and smooth on the annulus where the cutoff varies. After multiplication by a small positive constant, $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. Put $\chi (s)=1-\sqrt{1-s}$ for $s\leq 0$ and $u=\chi (w)$. The inequalities $0<\chi '\leq 1/2$ and $\chi ''\geq 0$, applied first to bounded truncations, give $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. In local coordinates $z$ centered at the pole, $u$ has size comparable to $\sqrt{-\log |z|^2}$, so it is unbounded and $\mathrm e^{-tu}$ is integrable for every $t>0$. Hence all its multiplier ideals are trivial and $P_\omega [u]_{\mathcal I}=0$. For every $0<\delta \leq 1$, the function $\delta s-\chi (s)$ is bounded above on $(-\infty ,0]$. Hence $\delta w\preceq u$, and $\delta w$ is a competitor for the ordinary envelope of $u$. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ off the pole gives $P_\omega [u]=0$. Thus $[u]$ and $[0]$ are distinct classes with the same neighborhoods. $\square$ By theorem 13.14.3 , the two envelopes have the extended masses \[  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\omega (P_\omega [u]),\qquad \int _ X\mathrm{MA}_\omega (P_\omega [u]_{\mathcal I}).  \] In the present positive background, both are at most $\int _ X\omega ^ n$. For the ideal envelope this follows from corollary 18.4.4 , proposition 16.28.7 . For the ordinary envelope, normalize $u\leq 0$ and put $p_ j=P_\omega (u+j,0)$ and $p=P_\omega [u]$, with the obstacle envelopes of section 5.40 . Then $p_ j\to p$ in capacity by lemma 5.29.19 . For $k>0$, set $\eta _ k=\min \{ 1,(u+k)_+\} $. If $j>k$, the contact set of $p_ j$ with $u+j$ lies outside $\{ \eta _ k>0\} $, so proposition 16.28.6 gives $\eta _ k\mathrm{MA}_\omega (p_ j)\leq \eta _ k\omega ^ n$. Testing against a nonnegative continuous function and applying lemma 13.14.8 , we obtain the same inequality for $p$. Letting $k\to \infty $ proves $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (p)\leq \omega ^ n$, since the remaining set $\{ u=-\infty \} $ is pluripolar. The potential itself can nevertheless have infinite mass: proposition 18.5.5 gives such a $u$ whose two envelopes are both zero. Its ordinary class belongs to $\mathcal G_\omega $. Thus the topology and its analytic-closure criterion need no mass condition on the representative, whereas the two canonical envelopes never have infinite mass in a Hermitian background.

title: 18.11 Transport with an obstacle
text: A smooth change of background $\omega '=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $ identifies $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega ')$ by $u\mapsto u-\chi $, but it moves the zero obstacle to $-\chi $. To compare the topologies in different backgrounds, we therefore need envelopes below an arbitrary smooth obstacle. For a smooth real obstacle $F$, we use the ordinary envelope $P_{\omega ,F}[u]$ of definition 5.40.4 , and we write $P_{\omega ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I}$ for the ideal envelope defined with $v\leq F$ in place of $v\leq 0$. The competitor family of the latter contains a translate of $u$. Replacing a competitor by its maximum with this translate shows that the ideal envelope may equivalently be defined with the condition $v\preceq _{\mathcal I}u$. The same notation applies to any smooth real background that admits $u$. Define $\tau _{\omega ,F}$ by replacing the two envelope coordinates in proposition 18.8.4 by these obstacle envelopes. Proposition 18.11.1 . 760C8726BAE2 Let $\chi \in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$ and $\omega '=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi >0$. The map $[u]\mapsto [u-\chi ]$ is a uniform isomorphism \[  (\mathfrak S(X,\omega ),\tau _{\omega ,F}) \longrightarrow (\mathfrak S(X,\omega '),\tau _{\omega ',F-\chi }).  \] For $s>0$, $[u]\mapsto [su]$ is a uniform isomorphism from $\tau _{\omega ,F}$ to $\tau _{s\omega ,sF}$. Both maps transport the ordinary and the ideal envelopes exactly. Proof. For either envelope operator $P$, the correspondence of competitors gives \[  P_{\omega ',F-\chi }[u-\chi ]=P_{\omega ,F}[u]-\chi , \qquad P_{s\omega ,sF}[su]=sP_{\omega ,F}[u].  \] Smooth additions leave all multiplier ideals and divisorial Lelong numbers unchanged. Scaling multiplies the divisorial and envelope distances by $s$ and changes the ideal weights by $t\mapsto st$. Each map and its inverse therefore transport the generating entourages to generating entourages. $\square$ For two smooth obstacles, translation of competitors gives \[  P_{\omega ,F}[u]+\min _ X(G-F) \leq P_{\omega ,G}[u] \leq P_{\omega ,F}[u]+\max _ X(G-F),  \] and the same inequalities hold for the ideal envelopes. By the local construction in theorem 13.14.3 , the extended measures satisfy $\mathrm{MA}_{\omega '}(u-\chi )=\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)$ and $\mathrm{MA}_{s\omega }(su)=s^ n\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)$, also when the total mass is infinite. If instead the zero obstacle is kept in both backgrounds, the transport gives $P_{\omega ',0}[u-\chi ]=P_{\omega ,\chi }[u]-\chi $, so the change of background compares the obstacles $0$ and $\chi $. The bounded comparison of obstacles does not make this change continuous, even on a curve. Proposition 18.11.2 . 8B44DB3F02D3 Let $Y$ be a compact connected Riemann surface and $\theta >0$ a smooth form of mass one. If $F$ is a nonconstant smooth function with $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F>0$, then the bijection \[  \Gamma _ F:(\mathfrak S(Y,\theta ),\tau _{\theta ,0}) \longrightarrow (\mathfrak S(Y,\theta '),\tau _{\theta ',0}), \qquad [u]\longmapsto [u-F],  \] and its inverse are both discontinuous. Equivalently, $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ and $\tau _{\theta ,F}$ are incomparable topologies on the same space of ordinary types. Proof. The smooth function $\theta '/\theta $ has integral one against the probability measure $\theta $, and it is not constant: otherwise $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F=0$, and the harmonic function $F$ would be constant on $Y$. Choose $c$ with $\min _ Y(\theta '/\theta )<c<1$, so that $\theta '\not\geq c\theta $. Next choose probability measures $\mu _ j$ without atoms, each carried by a polar set, that converge weakly to $\theta $. To construct them, start with finite atomic probability measures converging weakly to $\theta $, as in theorem 18.6.4 , and replace each atom by a nonatomic probability measure carried by a polar Cantor set in a small coordinate disk about that atom, keeping its weight; the construction in example 13.28.14 provides such measures in every disk. If the diameters of the disks tend to zero uniformly, uniform continuity of continuous test functions preserves weak convergence, and the finite union of the polar carriers is polar. Let $q_ j$ be the normalized Green potentials with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_ j=\mu _ j$ and $\sup _ Yq_ j=0$. By normalized compactness, the sequence has $L^1$ cluster values, and each of them has curvature $\theta $ and supremum zero, hence vanishes. Thus $q_ j\to 0$ in $L^1$. Put $u_ j=cq_ j$. Then \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j=(1-c)\theta +c\mu _ j,\qquad u_ j\leq P_\theta [u_ j]\leq 0.  \] Since $\mu _ j$ has no atoms, all point Lelong numbers of $u_ j$ vanish. Because modifications of a smooth curve are isomorphisms, theorem 5.37.3 gives trivial multiplier ideals at every weight. Thus $P_\theta [u_ j]_{\mathcal I}=0$, all controlled ideal relations with $[0]$ hold, and every divisorial distance to $[0]$ vanishes. The bounds above give convergence of the ordinary envelopes to zero in $L^1$. Consequently $[u_ j]\to [0]$ in $\tau _{\theta ,0}$. Set $v_ j=P_{\theta ,F}[u_ j]$. Every competitor $h\preceq u_ j$ satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\geq c\mu _ j$, by corollary 5.27.15 . The family of competitors below $F$ contains a translate of $u_ j$ and is stable under finite maxima, so Choquet selection and distributional convergence of increasing maxima show that $v_ j$ satisfies the same inequality. If $[u_ j]\to [0]$ in $\tau _{\theta ,F}$, the ordinary-envelope coordinate would give $v_ j\to P_{\theta ,F}[0]=F$ in $L^1$, because $F$ is a bounded $\theta $-plurisubharmonic competitor. Passing to the limit in the current inequality would then give $\theta '\geq c\theta $, a contradiction. By proposition 18.11.1 , $[u]\mapsto [u-F]$ is a uniform isomorphism from $\tau _{\theta ,F}$ onto $\tau _{\theta ',0}$, so the sequence above shows that $\Gamma _ F$ is discontinuous. The same argument applied to $\theta '$ and $-F$ shows that the inverse is discontinuous. Under this transport, continuity of $\Gamma _ F$ and of its inverse are precisely the two comparisons between $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ and $\tau _{\theta ,F}$, which proves incomparability. $\square$ The sequence $u_ j$ has trivial multiplier ideals, and its polar curvature in the sense of subsection 5.27.13 , that is, the restriction $\mathbf1_{\{ u_ j=-\infty \} }(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)$ of its curvature to its pole set, is $c\mu _ j$. By the classification of curve models through their polar curvature in lemma 13.28.1 and the bounded obstacle comparison, its ordinary envelopes in both backgrounds have non-pluripolar mass $1-c$. The discontinuity therefore persists among models whose masses are bounded below by a fixed positive constant. On the same curve, the total variation of polar curvature is a complete metric on ordinary models, by theorem 13.28.4 , and after ordinary projection it is invariant under smooth changes of background; it keeps the diffuse curvature that the sequence above loses.

title: Proposition 18.11.1
text: Proposition 18.11.1 . 760C8726BAE2 Let $\chi \in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$ and $\omega '=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi >0$. The map $[u]\mapsto [u-\chi ]$ is a uniform isomorphism \[  (\mathfrak S(X,\omega ),\tau _{\omega ,F}) \longrightarrow (\mathfrak S(X,\omega '),\tau _{\omega ',F-\chi }).  \] For $s>0$, $[u]\mapsto [su]$ is a uniform isomorphism from $\tau _{\omega ,F}$ to $\tau _{s\omega ,sF}$. Both maps transport the ordinary and the ideal envelopes exactly. Proof. For either envelope operator $P$, the correspondence of competitors gives \[  P_{\omega ',F-\chi }[u-\chi ]=P_{\omega ,F}[u]-\chi , \qquad P_{s\omega ,sF}[su]=sP_{\omega ,F}[u].  \] Smooth additions leave all multiplier ideals and divisorial Lelong numbers unchanged. Scaling multiplies the divisorial and envelope distances by $s$ and changes the ideal weights by $t\mapsto st$. Each map and its inverse therefore transport the generating entourages to generating entourages. $\square$

title: Proposition 18.11.2
text: Proposition 18.11.2 . 8B44DB3F02D3 Let $Y$ be a compact connected Riemann surface and $\theta >0$ a smooth form of mass one. If $F$ is a nonconstant smooth function with $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F>0$, then the bijection \[  \Gamma _ F:(\mathfrak S(Y,\theta ),\tau _{\theta ,0}) \longrightarrow (\mathfrak S(Y,\theta '),\tau _{\theta ',0}), \qquad [u]\longmapsto [u-F],  \] and its inverse are both discontinuous. Equivalently, $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ and $\tau _{\theta ,F}$ are incomparable topologies on the same space of ordinary types. Proof. The smooth function $\theta '/\theta $ has integral one against the probability measure $\theta $, and it is not constant: otherwise $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F=0$, and the harmonic function $F$ would be constant on $Y$. Choose $c$ with $\min _ Y(\theta '/\theta )<c<1$, so that $\theta '\not\geq c\theta $. Next choose probability measures $\mu _ j$ without atoms, each carried by a polar set, that converge weakly to $\theta $. To construct them, start with finite atomic probability measures converging weakly to $\theta $, as in theorem 18.6.4 , and replace each atom by a nonatomic probability measure carried by a polar Cantor set in a small coordinate disk about that atom, keeping its weight; the construction in example 13.28.14 provides such measures in every disk. If the diameters of the disks tend to zero uniformly, uniform continuity of continuous test functions preserves weak convergence, and the finite union of the polar carriers is polar. Let $q_ j$ be the normalized Green potentials with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_ j=\mu _ j$ and $\sup _ Yq_ j=0$. By normalized compactness, the sequence has $L^1$ cluster values, and each of them has curvature $\theta $ and supremum zero, hence vanishes. Thus $q_ j\to 0$ in $L^1$. Put $u_ j=cq_ j$. Then \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j=(1-c)\theta +c\mu _ j,\qquad u_ j\leq P_\theta [u_ j]\leq 0.  \] Since $\mu _ j$ has no atoms, all point Lelong numbers of $u_ j$ vanish. Because modifications of a smooth curve are isomorphisms, theorem 5.37.3 gives trivial multiplier ideals at every weight. Thus $P_\theta [u_ j]_{\mathcal I}=0$, all controlled ideal relations with $[0]$ hold, and every divisorial distance to $[0]$ vanishes. The bounds above give convergence of the ordinary envelopes to zero in $L^1$. Consequently $[u_ j]\to [0]$ in $\tau _{\theta ,0}$. Set $v_ j=P_{\theta ,F}[u_ j]$. Every competitor $h\preceq u_ j$ satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h\geq c\mu _ j$, by corollary 5.27.15 . The family of competitors below $F$ contains a translate of $u_ j$ and is stable under finite maxima, so Choquet selection and distributional convergence of increasing maxima show that $v_ j$ satisfies the same inequality. If $[u_ j]\to [0]$ in $\tau _{\theta ,F}$, the ordinary-envelope coordinate would give $v_ j\to P_{\theta ,F}[0]=F$ in $L^1$, because $F$ is a bounded $\theta $-plurisubharmonic competitor. Passing to the limit in the current inequality would then give $\theta '\geq c\theta $, a contradiction. By proposition 18.11.1 , $[u]\mapsto [u-F]$ is a uniform isomorphism from $\tau _{\theta ,F}$ onto $\tau _{\theta ',0}$, so the sequence above shows that $\Gamma _ F$ is discontinuous. The same argument applied to $\theta '$ and $-F$ shows that the inverse is discontinuous. Under this transport, continuity of $\Gamma _ F$ and of its inverse are precisely the two comparisons between $\tau _{\theta ,0}$ and $\tau _{\theta ,F}$, which proves incomparability. $\square$

title: 18.12 All smooth obstacles
text: We return to the Hermitian background $\omega $ on $X$. By proposition 18.11.2 , a smooth change of background need not preserve convergence when the obstacle is kept at zero. Requiring convergence below every smooth obstacle gives a topology that is stable under such changes. The dyadic approximation still determines its analytic closure, which is now described by equality of the two envelopes below every obstacle. Let $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_\omega $ be the topology of the uniformity generated by all the uniformities $\tau _{\omega ,F}$ with $F\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$. Thus an entourage involves finitely many distances between obstacle envelopes, together with finitely many of the controlled ideal relations and divisorial distances defined above. Proposition 18.12.1 . DAA4A0418197 A countable family $\{ F_ k\} _{k\geq 1}\subset C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$ that is dense for the uniform norm suffices for the obstacle coordinates of $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_\omega $. For smooth $\chi $ with $\omega '=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi >0$, the map $[u]\mapsto [u-\chi ]$ is a uniform isomorphism between $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_\omega $ and $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_{\omega '}$. For $s>0$, positive scaling gives the corresponding uniform isomorphism onto $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_{s\omega }$. This topology is not $T_0$ on ordinary classes. Proof. For either envelope operator, the obstacle comparison gives \[  \| P_{\omega ,F}[u]-P_{\omega ,G}[u]\| _{L^1(\mathrm dV)} \leq \| F-G\| _\infty .  \] Hence the two envelope distances for a pair $[u],[v]$ differ by at most $2\| F-G\| _\infty $, uniformly in the pair. The space $C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$ contains a countable subset that is dense for the uniform norm: approximate each member of a countable dense subset of $C(X)$ by smooth functions with errors $1/m$, $m\geq 1$. Given an entourage, we approximate each of its finitely many obstacles by a member of the family and shrink the radii accordingly; this proves that the family generates the same uniformity. The divisorial coordinates still range over all fixed compact modifications. The transport in proposition 18.11.1 relabels the entire family of smooth obstacles by $F\mapsto F-\chi $, or by $F\mapsto sF$. These are bijections of the family, which proves both isomorphisms. For nonseparation, use the unbounded function $u=1-\sqrt{1-w}$ of proposition 18.10.1 . It has trivial multiplier ideals and zero divisorial Lelong numbers, and $\delta w\preceq u$ for $0<\delta \leq 1$. Fix $F$ and put $q=P_\omega (F)$, the envelope of the obstacle $F$ in the sense of section 5.40 . Since $\omega >0$, the constant $\min _ XF$ is a competitor, so $q$ is bounded and $q\leq F$. The function \[  h_\delta =(1-\delta )q+\delta w-\delta \| F\| _\infty  \] is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic, lies below $F$, and satisfies $h_\delta \preceq u$. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ off the pole of $w$ gives $P_{\omega ,F}[u]=q=P_{\omega ,F}[0]$. Since $u$ and $0$ have the same multiplier ideals, their ideal envelopes below $F$ also agree. Every generating entourage therefore has identical sections at $[u]$ and $[0]$, although these ordinary classes differ. $\square$ Below a smooth obstacle, the ideal envelope is the ordinary envelope of the ideal model obtained with the zero obstacle. Equality of the two envelopes below every obstacle therefore reduces to a question about ordinary envelopes alone. Proposition 18.12.2 . 84E9AB1A05B4 Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and put $q=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. For every smooth real $F$, \[  P_{\theta ,F}[q]=P_{\theta ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I}\sim q.  \] If $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,q)$, then also \[  P_{\theta ,F}[u]=P_{\theta ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} \quad \text{for every smooth real }F.  \] Proof. Set $q_ F=P_{\theta ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I}$. Translation of competitors gives \[  q+\min _ XF\leq q_ F\leq q+\max _ XF,  \] so $q_ F\sim q$. The identity $q_ F-F=P_{\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F}[u-F]_{\mathcal I}$ and theorem 18.4.2 give $q_ F\sim _{\mathcal I}u$. Since $q_ F\leq F$ and $q_ F\sim q$, it is a competitor for $P_{\theta ,F}[q]$. Conversely, the maximum of a competitor for $P_{\theta ,F}[q]$ with a sufficiently low translate of $q$ is a competitor for $P_{\theta ,F}[q]_{\mathcal I}$, and this ideal envelope equals $q_ F$ because $q\sim _{\mathcal I}u$. These bounds give \[  q_ F\leq P_{\theta ,F}[q]\leq P_{\theta ,F}[q]_{\mathcal I}=q_ F.  \] The last assertion follows from proposition 16.28.65 , which gives $P_{\theta ,F}[u]=P_{\theta ,F}[q]$. $\square$ Theorem 18.12.3 . 26068B87D99A The closure and the sequential closure of $\mathcal A_\omega $ in $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_\omega $ are both equal to \[  \mathcal G^{\mathrm{all}}_\omega =\{ [u]:P_{\omega ,F}[u]=P_{\omega ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} \text{ for every smooth }F\} .  \] It suffices to test equality on the countable dense family above. The dyadic sequence $b_ j$ of corollary 18.7.9 converges to $[u]$ in this topology if and only if $[u]\in \mathcal G^{\mathrm{all}}_\omega $. Proof. Fix a smooth obstacle $F$. As in the preceding proof, transport of the obstacle and theorem 18.4.2 give $P_{\omega ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I}\sim _{\mathcal I}u$. For $a$ with analytic singularities, lemma 5.38.11 therefore makes this ideal envelope a competitor for the ordinary envelope, so $P_{\omega ,F}[a]=P_{\omega ,F}[a]_{\mathcal I}$. Write $p=P_{\omega ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I}$ and $q_ j=P_{\omega ,F}[b_ j]_{\mathcal I}$. The dyadic construction gives $u\preceq _{\mathcal I}b_ j$, decreasing ordinary types, and convergence of every local divisorial Lelong number of $b_ j$ to that of $u$. The ideal envelope preserves the ideal order, as one sees by taking maxima with a translate of $b_ j$ below $F$, so $p\leq q_ j\leq F$. Since $q_ j=P_{\omega ,F}[b_ j]$ and the ordinary types decrease, the sequence $q_ j$ decreases. Its limit $q$ is bounded below by $p$, so it is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic, and $p\leq q\leq F$; the same bounds give convergence in $L^1$. Convergence after pullback and semicontinuity of Lelong numbers, as in proposition 18.7.1 , give $\nu _ E(q)\geq \nu _ E(u)$ for every local divisor $E$, and $p\leq q$ gives the reverse inequality. The Lelong-number criterion of theorem 5.37.3 yields $q\sim _{\mathcal I}u$. Since $q\leq F$, it is a competitor for $p$, which proves \[  P_{\omega ,F}[b_ j]=P_{\omega ,F}[b_ j]_{\mathcal I} \searrow P_{\omega ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I}.  \] The controlled ideal relations and all divisorial distances on fixed modifications converge by the proof of theorem 18.9.1 ; they do not depend on $F$. Consequently this one dyadic sequence converges in $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_\omega $ exactly when the stated envelope equalities hold. For each $F$, equality of the two $L^1$ envelope coordinates is a closed condition. Analytic classes satisfy all these equalities, so the closure of the analytic classes under nets lies in $\mathcal G^{\mathrm{all}}_\omega $, and the dyadic sequence proves the converse. Finally, the uniform obstacle bound in the proof of proposition 18.12.1 extends equality from a dense family to every smooth obstacle. $\square$ Before turning to examples, we record how the envelopes and the relative envelope classes behave under finite unramified coverings; this will be used for fibrations with disconnected fibers. Recall from definition 16.28.61 that $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi )$ means that $u\preceq \varphi $ and that, for every $a\in (0,1)$, there is a stretching competitor $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $a\varphi +(1-a)h\leq u$; here $a=1-b^{-1}$ in the notation of that definition. Pullback of competitors and the maximum over the fibers of the covering identify the envelopes upstairs and downstairs, and the same fiber maximum transfers stretching competitors from the covering space to the base. Proposition 18.12.4 . 625C5E3FF1B3 Let $r:Y\to X$ be a finite unramified holomorphic covering between connected compact complex manifolds. Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, let $u,\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, and put $\theta '=r^*\theta $ and $u'=u\circ r$. For every $F\in C(X,\mathbb R)$, \[  \begin{split}  P_{\theta ',F\circ r}[u']& =P_{\theta ,F}[u]\circ r,\\  P_{\theta ',F\circ r}[u']_{\mathcal I} & =P_{\theta ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I}\circ r. \end{split}  \] Moreover, \[  u'\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\theta ',\varphi \circ r) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,\varphi ).  \] Proof. For $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta ')$, define \[  v_{\max }(x)=\max _{y\in r^{-1}(x)}v(y).  \] Over a sufficiently small ball in $X$, this is the finite maximum of the functions obtained by composing $v$ with the local inverse branches of $r$. Each of them is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, so $v_{\max }\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ by lemma 5.24.1 . If $v\preceq u'$, then $v_{\max }\preceq u$. If $v\sim _{\mathcal I}u'$, a local biholomorphic change of variables makes each branch multiplier-ideal equivalent to $u$, and the maximum rule in lemma 5.37.4 gives $v_{\max }\sim _{\mathcal I}u$. The obstacle bound $v\leq F\circ r$ gives $v_{\max }\leq F$. Thus every competitor upstairs is dominated by the pullback of a corresponding competitor downstairs. Conversely, pullback of a competitor downstairs preserves the background inequality, the ordinary order or multiplier-ideal equivalence, and the obstacle bound. These two correspondences between the competitor families give the envelope identities; upper regularization commutes with $r$, since $r$ is locally biholomorphic. Since $r$ is surjective, it reflects the ordinary order: $u'\preceq \varphi \circ r$ if and only if $u\preceq \varphi $. Fix $a\in (0,1)$. Pullback takes any stretching competitor $h$ with $a\varphi +(1-a)h\leq u$ to a stretching competitor upstairs. Conversely, if $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta ')$ satisfies \[  a\varphi \circ r+(1-a)v\leq u',  \] then taking the maximum over the fibers gives $a\varphi +(1-a)v_{\max }\leq u$; this also holds at poles, because the convex sums are defined there. Applying the definition of the relative class for every $a$ proves the last assertion. $\square$ Taking $F=0$ gives $\mathcal G^{\mathrm{all}}_\omega \subseteq \mathcal G_\omega $. For the reverse inclusion, let $q=P_\omega [u]_{\mathcal I}$. By proposition 18.12.2 , it suffices to show that $P_{\omega ,F}[u]=P_{\omega ,F}[q]$ for every $F$, and membership $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\omega ,q)$ is sufficient for this. Under bounded mass and positive lower volume of $q$, this membership is equivalent to equality of the envelopes below zero, by proposition 13.24.2 . On curves the two closures coincide even at zero mass, by proposition 13.28.22 . We do not know whether the reverse inclusion holds in general. The following subsections prove equality for explicit classes of potentials in higher dimension, including types of zero volume. The reduction along a divisor in a fibration gives such classes over curves, and one example of this kind has a base potential in the required relative envelope class and an ambient background with unbounded mass (example 18.14.8 ). Although $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_\omega $ removes the dependence on a fixed obstacle, it still has incomplete curve families and is strictly weaker than polar total variation on ordinary curve models, by proposition 13.28.24 . On the product and fibration model loci constructed below, complete metrics come instead from polar curvature.

title: Proposition 18.12.2
text: Proposition 18.12.2 . 84E9AB1A05B4 Let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and put $q=P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$. For every smooth real $F$, \[  P_{\theta ,F}[q]=P_{\theta ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I}\sim q.  \] If $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta ,q)$, then also \[  P_{\theta ,F}[u]=P_{\theta ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} \quad \text{for every smooth real }F.  \] Proof. title: Theorem 18.12.3
text: Theorem 18.12.3 . 26068B87D99A The closure and the sequential closure of $\mathcal A_\omega $ in $\tau ^{\mathrm{all}}_\omega $ are both equal to \[  \mathcal G^{\mathrm{all}}_\omega =\{ [u]:P_{\omega ,F}[u]=P_{\omega ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} \text{ for every smooth }F\} .  \] It suffices to test equality on the countable dense family above. text: Proposition 18.12.4 . 625C5E3FF1B3 Let $r:Y\to X$ be a finite unramified holomorphic covering between connected compact complex manifolds. title: 18.13 Countable poles and all obstacles
text: A fixed potential that is more singular than every finite stretch of a given potential supplies ordinary competitors below all continuous obstacles. We construct such a pair with poles on any prescribed countable set. The potentials have trivial multiplier ideals even when their poles are dense, so both envelopes lose this ordinary singularity information. Let $h$ be a Hermitian form on the connected compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n\geq 1$, and fix a smooth positive probability volume form $\mathrm dV$. Below a continuous obstacle we use the same competitor definitions as in definition 5.40.4 , definition 18.4.1 , with the bound $v\leq F$. Theorem 18.13.1 . 6529F0A74D79 For every nonempty finite or countably infinite subset $\{ x_ j\} \subset X$, there are nonpositive $u,w\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ such that \[  h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u,\  h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq \tfrac 34h, \qquad u(x_ j)=w(x_ j)=-\infty .  \] The same $w$ satisfies $tw\preceq u$ for every $0<t\leq 1$, and \[  u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,h,0),\qquad \mathrm e^{-su},\  \mathrm e^{-sw}\in L^1(X,\mathrm dV) \quad (s>0).  \] Thus $\mathcal I(su)=\mathcal I(sw)=\mathcal O_ X$ for every $s>0$. If the prescribed set is dense, both potentials are unbounded on every nonempty open set. Proof. Fix $0<\beta <\beta '<1$. Choose a finite atlas of relatively compact charts with larger coordinate neighborhoods, on which the coefficients of $\mathrm dV$ are uniformly bounded. For each $x_ j$, choose a coordinate ball of radius $r_ j\leq 1$ centered at $z_ j$, contained in one of the larger charts. Let $\chi $ be a smooth cutoff supported inside the unit ball, with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ and $\chi =1$ near zero. On this ball set \[  \chi _ j(z)=\chi ((z-z_ j)/r_ j),\qquad L_ j=1-\log (|z-z_ j|^2/r_ j^2).  \] The functions $-\chi _ jL_ j^\sigma $, for $\sigma =\beta ,\beta '$, extend by zero outside the ball. Near the center they are plurisubharmonic: for $s=\log (|z-z_ j|^2/r_ j^2)$ the profile $q_\sigma (s)=-(1-s)^\sigma $ has \[  q_\sigma '=\sigma (1-s)^{\sigma -1}>0, \qquad q_\sigma ''=\sigma (1-\sigma )(1-s)^{\sigma -2}>0.  \] To justify the extension across the center, take a smooth nondecreasing $\zeta $ equal to zero on $(-\infty ,-2]$ and one on $[-1,+\infty )$. For large $A$ put \[  q_{\sigma ,A}'(s)=q_\sigma '(s)\zeta (s/A),\qquad q_{\sigma ,A}(s)=q_\sigma (0)-\int _ s^0q_{\sigma ,A}'(v)\, \mathrm dv.  \] These profiles are convex and increasing, constant near the center, and agree with $q_\sigma $ on $s\geq -A$. As $A$ increases they decrease to $q_\sigma $, including its value $-\infty $ at the center. Radial integrability gives convergence in $L^1$. The cutoff annulus is unchanged for large $A$, and its Hessian has a finite lower bound. After a fixed local quadratic correction, the decreasing-limit theorem gives the canonical quasi-plurisubharmonic extension; its current bound passes to the limit. Put $e_ j=2^{-j-2}$. Scale both profiles by the same $0<\delta _ j\leq 2^{-j}$ so that the nonpositive functions F52CC5DA3364 18.13.2 \begin{equation}  a_ j=-\delta _ j\chi _ jL_ j^\beta , \qquad c_ j=-\delta _ j\chi _ jL_ j^{\beta '}, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_ j,\  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}c_ j\geq -e_ jh \end{equation} have these lower bounds globally. This is possible because only the smooth cutoff annulus can contribute a negative Hessian. Coordinate rescaling and the finite atlas give \[  \| a_ j\| _{L^1}+\| c_ j\| _{L^1}\leq C\delta _ j.  \] Consequently the nonpositive partial sums decrease with uniformly bounded $L^1$ norms. By corollary 5.25.3 , they define potentials \[  u=\sum _ j a_ j,\qquad w=\sum _ j c_ j  \] with the stated canonical values and with currents at least $(1-\sum _ j e_ j)h\geq 3h/4$. Each prescribed point is a pole of its own summand. This also proves the assertion when the prescribed set is dense. For $b\geq 1$ let \[  S=\sum _ j\delta _ j>0,\qquad M_ b=\max \{ 0,\sup _{L\geq 1}(bL^\beta -L^{\beta '})\} <\infty .  \] Multiplying the defining inequality by $\delta _ j\chi _ j$ and summing gives 1696AB66FF1D 18.13.3 \begin{equation}  w\leq bu+M_ bS. \end{equation} The inequality first holds for finite sums and then for their decreasing limits, including common poles. Taking $b=1/t$ gives $tw\preceq u$. Since $h>0$, convexity with zero makes $tw$ $h$-plurisubharmonic. Also $w-M_ bS\leq bu$ is an $h$-plurisubharmonic stretching competitor for every $b\geq 1$, so definition 16.28.61 gives $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,h,0)$. It remains to prove integrability at every positive exponential scale. Fix $s>0$ and use Jensen's inequality with weights $\delta _ j/S$, assigning the unused weight in each finite sum to zero: \[  \mathrm e^{-s\sum _{j\leq N}a_ j} \leq 1-\sum _{j\leq N}\frac{\delta _ j}{S} +\sum _{j\leq N}\frac{\delta _ j}{S} \mathrm e^{sS\chi _ jL_ j^\beta }.  \] The integrals on the right are bounded uniformly in $j$, since coordinate rescaling reduces the contribution inside the ball to a constant times \[  \int _0^1\exp \bigl (sS(1-\log R^2)^\beta \bigr )R^{2n-1}\, \mathrm dR.  \] With $x=-\log R^2$, its exponent is $-nx+sS(1+x)^\beta $, which is at most $-nx/2$ for large $x$. Integrating the Jensen inequality and using monotone convergence proves $\mathrm e^{-su}\in L^1$. The same calculation with $\beta '$ proves the assertion for $w$. Every holomorphic germ is bounded on a smaller coordinate neighborhood, so definition 6.8.5 gives the stated trivial ideals. $\square$ Proposition 18.13.4 . AB19DE43A7F6 For the potentials of theorem 18.13.1 and every $F\in C(X,\mathbb R)$, \[  P_{h,F}[u]=P_{h,F}[u]_{\mathcal I}=P_ h(F).  \] In particular, $P_ h[u]=P_ h[u]_{\mathcal I}=0$. Proof. Put $Q=P_ h(F)$. The constant $\min _ XF$ is a competitor. The envelope construction of section 5.40 , which preserves the exact lower current bound for the nonclosed form $h$, gives $Q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$ and \[  \min _ XF\leq Q\leq F\leq \max _ XF.  \] Since $Q$ is bounded, all its multiplier ideals are trivial. Thus $Q\sim _{\mathcal I}u$, making $Q$ itself a competitor for the ideal envelope below $F$. Every ideal competitor is an unrestricted competitor for $P_ h(F)$, so $P_{h,F}[u]_{\mathcal I}=Q$. For $0<t<1$ set \[  A_ t=(1-t)Q+tw-t\| F\| _\infty .  \] Convexity gives $A_ t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,h)$, and $w\leq 0$ implies $A_ t\leq (1-t)F-t\| F\| _\infty \leq F$. Boundedness of $Q$ and ( 18.13.3 ) with $b=1/t$ give $A_ t\preceq u$. Hence the ordinary envelope $O=P_{h,F}[u]$ has a competitor and satisfies $A_ t\leq O\leq Q$. Its regularized supremum is $h$-plurisubharmonic by the same envelope construction. Where $w$ is finite, $A_ t\to Q$ as $t\downarrow 0$. Thus $O=Q$ almost everywhere, and lemma 5.24.3 gives equality everywhere. For $F=0$, zero is an unrestricted competitor, so $P_ h(0)=0$. $\square$ For a dense prescribed set, the ordinary type of $u$ differs from the bounded type, although their envelopes agree below every continuous obstacle. The construction applies to every positive Hermitian background, including one with unbounded upper mass or zero lower mass. It does not decide whether equality below zero alone implies all-obstacle equality for an arbitrary potential and an admissible smooth background.

title: 18.14 Relative divisors and fiber obstacles
text:
To test equality of the envelopes below all obstacles beyond curves, we need potentials whose envelopes can be computed. Consider a holomorphic submersion with compact connected fibers, and a potential that is the sum of a logarithmic potential $\Psi $ with fixed weights along some divisors and the pullback of a potential $w$ on the base. Every competitor has at least the poles of $\Psi $, and removing them leaves a current pulled back from the base. Since the fibers are compact and connected, the remaining potential descends to the base, and minimizing the obstacle over the fibers reduces both envelopes to envelopes on the base. Over a fiber contained in the divisor the induced obstacle is infinite, but normalized compactness still bounds the competitors. Because the remaining current comes from a base of smaller dimension, all these potentials have zero top-degree mass. The reduction gives criteria on the base for membership in relative envelope classes and for equality of the envelopes below all obstacles. The divisors may be singular or ramified over the base; only the explicit product formula for the multiplier ideals requires relative normal crossings. Let $p:M	o Y$ be a surjective holomorphic submersion between connected compact complex manifolds, with connected fibers, and put $d=\dim Y$ and $n=\dim M$, where $1\leq d<n$. Let $H_1,\ldots ,H_ s$ be a nonempty finite family of distinct prime divisors on $M$ and put $H= igcup _ jH_ j$. For positive real weights $\lambda _ j$, choose smooth Hermitian metrics $h_ j$ on $\mathcal O_ M(H_ j)$, with canonical sections $s_ j$ and Chern curvatures $\kappa _ j$. Set \[  A=\sum _{j=1}^ s\lambda _ jH_ j,\qquad \Psi =\sum _{j=1}^ s\lambda _ j\log |s_ j|_{h_ j}^2,\qquad \kappa _ A=\sum _{j=1}^ s\lambda _ j\kappa _ j.  \] Thus $\kappa _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi =[A]=\sum _ j\lambda _ j[H_ j]$. For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $ eta $ on $Y$ and $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y, eta )$, put \[  \Theta =p^* eta +\kappa _ A,\qquad u=\Psi +w\circ p.  \] The form $ eta $ need not be closed or positive. Envelopes below continuous real obstacles are defined by the same competitor families as for smooth obstacles. Let \[  Z=\{ y\in Y:p^{-1}(y)\subset H\}   \] be the set of points over which the whole fiber lies in $H$. Proposition 18.14.1 . 1195E1B9B18D For every $F\in C(M,\mathbb R)$, the function \[  \widehat F(y)=\inf _{x\in p^{-1}(y)\setminus H}\{ F(x)-\Psi (x)\} , \qquad \inf \varnothing =+\infty ,  \] is continuous in the extended real sense, finite on $Y\setminus Z$ and equal to $+\infty $ on $Z$. Defining the base envelopes below this extended-real obstacle by the usual competitor families, one has EDA13205415C 18.14.2  egin{equation}   egin{split}  P_{\Theta ,F}[u]& =\Psi +P_{ eta ,\widehat F}[w]\circ p,\  P_{\Theta ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} & =\Psi +P_{ eta ,\widehat F}[w]_{\mathcal I}\circ p. \end{split} \end{equation} Every representative of the ordinary type of $u$ or of $P_\Theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ has zero extended mass. Consequently both singularity volumes of these types are zero. If the ordinary and ideal envelopes of $w$ agree below every smooth obstacle on $Y$, then those of $u$ agree below every smooth obstacle on $M$. Proof. We first study the induced obstacle and bound the base competitors, then describe all competitors upstairs by divisorial removal and descent, and finally prove the mass assertion. Step 1: the induced obstacle. Since $p$ is open, $Y\setminus Z=p(M\setminus H)$ is open and nonempty. The function $F-\Psi $ is bounded below by $\min _ MF-\sup _ M\Psi $ and tends to $+\infty $ near $H$, because $\Psi 	o -\infty $ there. On every fiber that meets $M\setminus H$, its infimum is therefore attained outside $H$. A local holomorphic section through a minimizer gives upper semicontinuity of $\widehat F$. Conversely, let $y_ j	o y$ with bounded fiber minima. By compactness, a subsequence of the minimizers converges, and its limit lies outside $H$ because $F-\Psi $ remains bounded along it; this gives lower semicontinuity. If $y\in Z$, the same limit would lie in $H$, a contradiction. Thus $\widehat F	o +\infty $ at $Z$, and $\widehat F$ is continuous in the extended sense. Step 2: a uniform bound for the base competitors. Choose a relatively compact nonempty ball $U$ in the base and a holomorphic section $s$ of $p$ on a neighborhood of $\overline U$ with image outside $H$. There is a finite $C_ U$ with $\widehat F\leq F\circ s-\Psi \circ s\leq C_ U$ on $U$. Fix a smooth probability volume form $\mathrm dV$ on $Y$. For every $b\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y, eta )$ below $\widehat F$, normalized compactness in theorem 5.25.2 gives \[  -C_ eta \leq \int _ U(b-\sup _ Yb)\, \mathrm dV \leq (C_ U-\sup _ Yb)\int _ U\mathrm dV.  \] Hence every such $b$ satisfies $\sup _ Yb\leq K_ F=C_ U+C_ eta /\int _ U\mathrm dV$. A sufficiently low translate of $w$ belongs to both base competitor families. Their regularized suprema are therefore $ eta $-plurisubharmonic functions, not identically $-\infty $, and by the extended continuity of $\widehat F$ they still lie below $\widehat F$. Step 3: the competitors upstairs. The pullback of $w$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic, so its generic Lelong numbers are nonnegative, and $
u (u,H_ j)=\lambda _ j+
u (w\circ p,H_ j)\geq \lambda _ j$. Let $v$ be an ordinary competitor for $u$, or an ideal competitor with $v\sim _{\mathcal I}u$. By the ordinary order or by theorem 5.37.3 , its generic Lelong number along $H_ j$ is at least $\lambda _ j$. Divisorial removal in lemma 5.38.1 gives \[  \Theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v-[A]\geq 0.  \] Hence $v-\Psi $ has a quasi-plurisubharmonic representative $a$ satisfying $p^* eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\geq 0$. Descent along the compact connected fibers, proposition 5.43.5 , gives $a=b\circ p$ for a unique $b\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y, eta )$, and $v=\Psi +b\circ p$ for the canonical representatives. Conversely, every potential of this form is $\Theta $-plurisubharmonic. For such $v$, one has $v\preceq u$ if and only if $b\preceq w$. Indeed, canceling $\Psi $ outside $H$ gives the base inequality almost everywhere, by Fubini's theorem in product charts, hence everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 ; the reverse implication follows by pullback and addition. Similarly, $v\sim _{\mathcal I}u$ if and only if $b\sim _{\mathcal I}w$: lemma 5.37.4 permits both addition and cancellation of $\Psi $, the pullback formula in lemma 5.37.7 then gives one direction, and restriction of the extended ideals along any local section gives the other. This comparison of ideals does not need a section outside $H$. If the divisors have relative simple normal crossings, the ideals have an explicit form. Here this means that near every point there are product coordinates $(y,z)$ with $p(y,z)=y$ in which the components through the point are distinct coordinate hyperplanes in the fiber variables. Then 336B6FB1D279 18.14.3  egin{equation}  \mathcal I igl (t(\Psi +b\circ p) igr ) =\mathcal O_ M\! \left(-\sum _ j\lfloor t\lambda _ jfloor H_ jight)  igl (\mathcal I(tb)\mathcal O_ M igr ) \qquad (t>0). \end{equation} To see this, work in such coordinates. Up to a smooth correction, $\Psi $ is the sum of the weights $\lambda _ j\log |z_ j|^2$ over the components through the point. Since $b$ is locally bounded above, integrability forces vanishing to order at least $\lfloor t\lambda _ jfloor $ along each hyperplane. After this product of coordinate powers is factored out, the remaining fiber weight is \[  \prod _ j|z_ j|^{-2(t\lambda _ j-\lfloor t\lambda _ jfloor )}.  \] It is integrable and bounded below by a positive constant on a small polydisk. Integrability of the quotient against this weight therefore implies integrability against the pullback of $\mathrm e^{-tb}$ alone, and lemma 5.37.7 puts the quotient in the extension of $\mathcal I(tb)$. Conversely, local generators of that ideal are weighted-integrable against the integrable product weight, by Fubini's theorem. Outside $H$ the formula is the same pullback lemma. For one smooth divisor of weight one transverse to the fibers, the first factor is the ideal sheaf of the divisor raised to the power $\lfloor tfloor $. Step 4: the envelope identities. The bound $v\leq F$ is equivalent to $b\leq \widehat F$, with no constraint over $Z$. The competitor families upstairs and on the base therefore correspond to each other, which gives ( 18.14.2 ) outside $H$, since regularization commutes with pullback in product coordinates there. On $H$ both sides equal $-\infty $: every competitor is at most $\Psi +K_ F$, by the bound $b\leq K_ F$, and this upper semicontinuous function equals $-\infty $ on $H$, so regularization does not change the values there. Step 5: equality below all obstacles. Suppose that the two base envelopes agree below every smooth obstacle. Uniform obstacle comparison extends this equality to continuous real obstacles. The functions $G_ j=\min (\widehat F,j)$ are continuous and real-valued. Every base competitor below $\widehat F$ has finite supremum and hence lies below $G_ j$ for every sufficiently large integer $j$. Each full competitor family is thus the union of its subfamilies below the $G_ j$, and equality for all $G_ j$ gives equality below $\widehat F$ after taking regularized suprema. By the reduction, the envelopes upstairs agree below every smooth obstacle. Step 6: zero mass. Take any $b\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y, eta )$ and write $a=\Psi +b\circ p$. On a relatively compact chart outside $H$, the functions $b_ j=\max (b,-j)$ are locally bounded and quasi-plurisubharmonic, and there \[  \Theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Psi +b_ j\circ p)=p^*( eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ j).  \] Since $n>d$, the $n$th bounded product of this current is zero by lemma 5.28.4 . This identity does not require $b_ j$ to be $ eta $-plurisubharmonic: proposition 5.28.2 defines the products for locally bounded quasi-plurisubharmonic potentials. By plurifine locality, this zero product agrees with $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\Theta (a)$ on $\{ b\circ p>-j\} $ in the chart. These sets cover the locus where $b\circ p$ is finite, while the remaining pole set and $H$ receive no extended mass. Thus $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\Theta (a)=0$. By divisorial removal and descent, every representative ordinarily equivalent to $u$ has this form. By the identity already proved, the ideal model is also of this form, with base potential $P_{ eta ,\widehat0}[w]_{\mathcal I}$, where $\widehat0$ is the induced obstacle for $F=0$. The same removal and descent apply to every representative of its ordinary type. All these masses are zero, which proves both volume assertions. $\square$ Proposition 18.14.4 . A399EFC10B9E For $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y, eta )$ put $v=\Psi +\varphi \circ p$. Then \[  u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(M,\Theta ,v) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad w\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y, eta ,\varphi ).  \] In particular, for $q_ M=P_\Theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ and $q_ Y=P_ eta [w]_{\mathcal I}$, \[  u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(M,\Theta ,q_ M) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad w\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y, eta ,q_ Y).  \] Every ordinary representative of $u$ or $q_ M$ has zero extended mass, so both singularity volumes of these types vanish. Proof. The ordinary order $u\preceq v$ is equivalent to $w\preceq \varphi $. One implication follows by addition and pullback. Conversely, cancel $\Psi $ outside $H$, which has smooth volume zero; Fubini's theorem in product charts gives the base inequality almost everywhere, and lemma 5.24.3 makes it hold everywhere. Membership in the relative envelope class requires, for every $a\in (0,1)$, a stretching competitor $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(M,\Theta )$ with \[  av+(1-a)h\leq u.  \] A base competitor $c\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y, eta )$ with $a\varphi +(1-a)c\leq w$ gives such an $h$, namely $h=\Psi +c\circ p$. Conversely, put $ho _ j=
u (w\circ p,H_ j)$ and $\sigma _ j=
u (\varphi \circ p,H_ j)$. The ordinary order $w\preceq \varphi $ gives $ho _ j\geq \sigma _ j\geq 0$. Comparing generic Lelong numbers along $H_ j$ in the inequality above gives \[  a(\lambda _ j+\sigma _ j)+(1-a)
u (h,H_ j) \geq \lambda _ j+ho _ j.  \] Consequently $
u (h,H_ j)\geq \lambda _ j+(ho _ j-a\sigma _ j)/(1-a)\geq \lambda _ j$. Divisorial removal and descent along the fibers give $h=\Psi +c\circ p$ with $c\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y, eta )$. Canceling $\Psi $ outside $H$ and the pole sets, and applying Fubini's theorem, we obtain $a\varphi +(1-a)c\leq w$ almost everywhere on the base, and hence on all of $Y$ by lemma 5.24.3 . This proves the first equivalence. For the ideal reference, theorem 18.4.2 gives $q_ M\sim _{\mathcal I}u$. The generic divisorial coefficients of $q_ M$ are therefore at least $\lambda _ j$, and removal and descent give \[  q_ M=\Psi +b\circ p,\qquad b\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y, eta ).  \] Cancellation in lemma 5.37.4 gives $b\circ p\sim _{\mathcal I}w\circ p$. By lemma 5.37.7 , these ideals are extensions of the base ideals, so restriction along any local section gives $b\sim _{\mathcal I}w$, even over a fiber contained in $H$. Put $C=\max \{ 0,\sup _ M\Psi \} $ and $K=\max \{ 0,\sup _ Yb\} $. The potential $\Psi +q_ Y\circ p-C$ is nonpositive and multiplier-ideal equivalent to $u$, so it is a competitor for $q_ M$. Likewise, $b-K$ is a competitor for $q_ Y$. Canceling $\Psi $ in the first inequality almost everywhere and extending as above gives \[  q_ Y-C\leq b\leq q_ Y+K.  \] Thus $b\sim q_ Y$. The first equivalence with reference $b$, together with the invariance of the class under ordinarily equivalent references in proposition 16.28.62 , proves the second equivalence. This argument works with the ideal model itself and does not require the induced fiber obstacle to be finite. If $w$ belongs to the base relative class, proposition 18.12.2 gives equality of the two envelopes upstairs below every smooth obstacle. For any ordinary representative of $u$ or $q_ M$, removal and descent give the form $\Psi +c\circ p$ with $c\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y, eta )$. Outside $H$, replace $c$ locally by $\max (c,-k)$ and keep $\Psi $. The resulting bounded quasi-plurisubharmonic potentials have currents pulled back from the $d$-dimensional base, so their $n$th products vanish by lemma 5.28.4 , since $n>d$. By plurifine locality, this product agrees with the original extended measure on $\{ c\circ p>-k\} $. These sets cover the locus where $c\circ p$ is finite, and the pole sets and $H$ receive no mass. This proves the mass and volume assertions. $\square$ Corollary 18.14.5 . 0B566FB6A5E6 The ordinary and ideal envelopes of $u$ agree below every smooth obstacle on $M$ if and only if those of $w$ agree below every smooth obstacle on $Y$. Put $q=P_ eta [w]_{\mathcal I}$. If $w\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y, eta ,q)$, then \[  P_{\Theta ,F}[u]=P_{\Theta ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} \quad 	ext{for every smooth real }F.  \] If $Y$ is a curve, write \[  T_ w= eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w,\qquad \mu _ w=\mathbf1_{\{ w=-\infty \} }T_ w,\qquad D_ w=\sum _{y\in Y}
u (w,y)\delta _ y  \] for the curvature measure of $w$, its polar part and its atomic part. Then equality of the two envelopes of $u$ below zero, the equality $\mu _ w=D_ w$, and equality of the two envelopes of $u$ below every smooth obstacle are equivalent. They are also equivalent to \[  u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(M,\Theta ,P_\Theta [u]_{\mathcal I}).  \] These equivalences also hold when $\int _ Y eta =0$. Proof. The forward implication is part of proposition 18.14.1 . For the converse, we approximate a smooth obstacle on the base by the induced obstacles of continuous obstacles upstairs. Suppose that the envelopes upstairs agree below every smooth obstacle. Uniform obstacle comparison extends this equality to continuous real obstacles. Fix a smooth real function $B$ on $Y$ and put $G=\widehat0$. The continuous obstacles \[  F_ j=B\circ p+\max (\Psi ,-j)\qquad (j\geq 1)  \] have induced base obstacles \[  G_ j=B+\max (G-j,0),  \] with value $+\infty $ on $Z$. By the reduction and the assumed equality, \[  q_ j=P_{ eta ,G_ j}[w]_{\mathcal I}=P_{ eta ,G_ j}[w].  \] Write $q_ B=P_{ eta ,B}[w]_{\mathcal I}$. Then $q_ B\leq q_ j\leq q_1$, and the $q_ j$ decrease to a $ eta $-plurisubharmonic potential $r$, not identically $-\infty $, with convergence in $L^1$; indeed, their negative parts are bounded by that of $q_ B$, and corollary 5.25.3 applies. The set $Z$ has smooth volume zero: in each product chart of the submersion, the preimage of $Z$ lies in $H$, which has smooth volume zero, and Fubini's theorem gives the assertion on the base. Off $Z$, the bounds $q_ j\leq G_ j\downarrow B$ give $r\leq B$, and almost-everywhere order in lemma 5.24.3 extends the inequality to all of $Y$. Each $q_ j$ is multiplier-ideal equivalent to $w$. To see this without assuming $G_ j$ finite, put $Q_0=P_\Theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ and $Q_ j=P_{\Theta ,F_ j}[u]_{\mathcal I}$. Translation of the competitor families gives \[  Q_0+\min _ MF_ j\leq Q_ j\leq Q_0+\max _ MF_ j.  \] Thus $Q_ j\sim Q_0\sim _{\mathcal I}u$ by theorem 18.4.2 . Since $Q_ j=\Psi +q_ j\circ p$, cancellation and reflection of multiplier ideals under submersions, lemma 5.37.4 , lemma 5.37.7 , give $q_ j\sim _{\mathcal I}w$. The same bounded comparison with $P_ eta [w]_{\mathcal I}$ gives $q_ B\sim _{\mathcal I}w$. Let $\pi $ be any smooth local modification of a coordinate neighborhood in the base. The bounds $q_ B\circ \pi \leq q_ j\circ \pi \leq q_1\circ \pi $ give decreasing local $L^1$ convergence to $r\circ \pi $. At every point $x$ of this modification, lemma 5.38.7 and the ordinary order give \[  
u (w\circ \pi ,x) \leq 
u (r\circ \pi ,x) \leq 
u (q_ B\circ \pi ,x)=
u (w\circ \pi ,x).  \] All these Lelong numbers are therefore equal, and theorem 5.37.3 gives $r\sim _{\mathcal I}w$. Together with $r\leq B$, this makes $r$ a competitor for $q_ B$. Hence $r=q_ B$. Put $\epsilon _ j=\max \{ 0,\sup _ Y(q_ j-B)\} $. The moving-point estimate in lemma 5.25.1 gives $\epsilon _ j	o 0$: otherwise a subsequence of maximizers of $q_ j-B$ converges to some $y$, where that estimate contradicts $q_ B(y)\leq B(y)$. Every ordinary competitor $b$ below $G_ j$ satisfies $b\leq q_ j$, so $b-\epsilon _ j\leq B$ and $b-\epsilon _ j\preceq w$. Taking regularized suprema yields \[  q_ j-\epsilon _ j\leq P_{ eta ,B}[w].  \] Since $q_ B\leq q_ j$, letting $j	o \infty $ proves $q_ B\leq P_{ eta ,B}[w]$. The reverse inequality always holds, so the two envelopes agree below $B$. Since $B$ was arbitrary, this proves the converse. Under the relative-class hypothesis, proposition 18.12.2 gives equality of the two base envelopes below every smooth obstacle, and the equivalence just proved gives the stated equality upstairs. In the curve case, put $G=\widehat0$ and $L=-\sup _ M\Psi $. The uniform bound in Step 2 of the proof of proposition 18.14.1 gives a finite $K$ with $\sup _ Yb\leq K$ for every $b\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y, eta )$ below $G$. Since $G\geq L$, translation of the two competitor families gives \[   egin{split}  P_ eta [w]+L& \leq P_{ eta ,G}[w] \leq P_ eta [w]+K,\  q+L& \leq P_{ eta ,G}[w]_{\mathcal I} \leq q+K. \end{split}  \] By proposition 13.29.1 , corollary 5.27.15 , the polar curvatures of these two base envelopes are $\mu _ w$ and $D_ w$, respectively. Thus equality of the envelopes upstairs below zero forces $\mu _ w=D_ w$. Conversely, under this equality of measures, corollary 13.29.2 gives equality below every smooth obstacle on the base. As in Step 5 of the proof of proposition 18.14.1 , this extends to every induced obstacle $\widehat F$, and the reduction gives equality upstairs below every smooth obstacle. Taking $F=0$ proves the remaining implication. The same curve criterion identifies the equality of measures with membership of $w$ in the base relative envelope class of $q$, and the equivalence for ideal references in proposition 18.14.4 gives the last assertion upstairs. $\square$ The normal-crossing hypothesis is needed only for the explicit formula ( 18.14.3 ). The reduction of the envelopes holds without it. Example 18.14.6 . 8119F7E76588 On $M=\mathbb P^1	imes \mathbb P^1$, let $p,r$ be the projections and let $\sigma $ be the probability Fubini–Study form. With homogeneous coordinates $[y_0:y_1]$ and $[z_0:z_1]$, the divisor \[  H=\{ y_0z_0^2+y_1z_1^2=0\}   \] is smooth, meets every fiber properly and ramifies over the first factor. Give $\mathcal O_ M(H)=\mathcal O_ M(1,2)$ its product metric, with logarithmic divisor potential $\Psi $ and curvature $\kappa _ H=p^*\sigma +2r^*\sigma $. Put $\Theta =2p^*\sigma +2r^*\sigma $ and choose $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^1,\sigma )$ with $\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=\delta _{[0:1]}$. Both obstacle envelopes of $u=\Psi +w\circ p$ reduce to the base, but the product formula for its multiplier ideals fails at a ramification point. Proof. For each $[z_0:z_1]$ there is a unique point $[y_0:y_1]=[-z_1^2:z_0^2]$ on $H$, so $H$ is a smooth graph over the second factor, and its projection to the base has degree two. In particular no fiber of $p$ lies in $H$. Since $\Theta =p^*\sigma +\kappa _ H$, proposition 18.14.1 gives both envelope identities. Near $([0:1],[1:0])$, use $y=y_0/y_1$ and $z=z_1/z_0$. Up to smooth additions, \[  \Psi =\log |y+z^2|^2,\qquad w=\log |y|^2, \qquad u=\log |y(y+z^2)|^2.  \] At $t=3/4$, each of the two weights separately has trivial multiplier ideal, so the right side of ( 18.14.3 ) would be $\mathcal O_ M$. However, $1
otin \mathcal I(3u/4)$ at this point. Indeed, consider the region where $y=cz^2$ with $|c-1|<1/4$ and $0<|z|<\epsilon $; for fixed $z$, it has area comparable to $|z|^4$ in the $y$ variable. The weighted integral of $1$ is therefore bounded below by a positive constant times \[  \int _{0<|z|<\epsilon }|z|^{-6}|z|^4\, \mathrm d\lambda _ z =2\pi \int _0^\epsilon  rac{\mathrm dr}{r}=+\infty ,  \] where $\mathrm d\lambda _ z$ is planar area. Thus the multiplier ideal is proper. The envelope identities follow instead from the behavior of multiplier-ideal equivalence under addition, and do not require the product formula. $\square$ If the divisor contains an entire fiber, the induced obstacle is infinite over that fiber. The next example still admits an explicit model for the zero obstacle. Example 18.14.7 . A467F501617F Let $M=\mathbb P^2	imes \mathbb P^1$, with projections $p,r$, and let $\sigma _ j$ be the standard Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^ j$. In the positive closed background \[  \Theta =2p^*\sigma _2+r^*\sigma _1,  \] there is a logarithmic potential $\Psi $ of a smooth prime divisor containing the fiber over $E=[0:0:1]$. Its fiber infimum for the zero obstacle is finite and continuous off $E$ and tends to $+\infty $ at $E$. Nevertheless, \[  P_\Theta [\Psi ]=P_\Theta [\Psi ]_{\mathcal I}=\Psi +q\circ p,  \] where $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^2,\sigma _2)$ is bounded, $0\leq q\leq \log 4$ and $q(E)=\log 4$. Every ordinary representative of this model has zero extended mass, so both singularity volumes vanish. The two envelopes also agree below every smooth obstacle. Proof. Use homogeneous coordinates $[y_0:y_1:y_2]$ and $[z_0:z_1]$, and take \[  H=\{ y_0z_0+y_1z_1=0\} ,\qquad \Psi =\log  rac{|y_0z_0+y_1z_1|^2}{(|y_0|^2+|y_1|^2+|y_2|^2)(|z_0|^2+|z_1|^2)}.  \] Outside $E$, the divisor is the graph $[z_0:z_1]=[-y_1:y_0]$. Its closure contains the whole fiber over $E$, so $H$ is prime. It is smooth outside that fiber by the graph description, and smooth along it because the derivatives in the $y_0$ and $y_1$ directions are $z_0$ and $z_1$, which cannot both vanish. Its product metric has curvature $p^*\sigma _2+r^*\sigma _1$, hence \[  \Theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi =p^*\sigma _2+[H].  \] Writing $S=|y_0|^2+|y_1|^2$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives the fiber obstacle \[  G(y)=-\max _{z\in \mathbb P^1}\Psi (y,z) =\log  rac{S+|y_2|^2}{S},\qquad G(E)=+\infty .  \] It has no finite continuous extension at $E$. We claim that the largest $\sigma _2$-plurisubharmonic potential below $G$ is \[  q(y)= egin{cases}  \displaystyle \log  rac{4|y_2|^2}{S+|y_2|^2},&  S\leq |y_2|^2,\[6pt] \displaystyle \log  rac{S+|y_2|^2}{S},&  S\geq |y_2|^2. \end{cases}  \] To see that $q$ is $\sigma _2$-plurisubharmonic, work on $y_2
e 0$ with $x=(y_0/y_2,y_1/y_2)$ and $t=\log |x|^2$. Adding the Fubini–Study potential $L(x)=\log (1+|x|^2)$ gives \[  q+L= egin{cases}  \log 4,& t\leq 0,\  2\log (1+\mathrm e^ t)-t,& t\geq 0. \end{cases}  \] This function and its first derivative are continuous at $t=0$. For $t>0$, its first two derivatives are $(\mathrm e^ t-1)/(\mathrm e^ t+1)\geq 0$ and $2\mathrm e^ t/(1+\mathrm e^ t)^2>0$. It is therefore a convex nondecreasing function of $t$, hence plurisubharmonic in $x$, across the unit sphere as well. The expression is constant near $x=0$, and $q=G$ is smooth near $y_2=0$, so $q$ is globally $\sigma _2$-plurisubharmonic and bounded. If $b\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^2,\sigma _2)$ lies below $G$, then $b+L\leq \log 4$ on $|x|=1$, and the maximum principle on the unit ball gives $b\leq q$ inside it. Outside the ball, the obstacle already gives $b\leq G=q$. For $0<R=|x|^2\leq 1$, the inequality $q\leq G$ reads $4R\leq (1+R)^2$, and at $E$ it is automatic. The formula for $q$ also gives the asserted bounds, which proves the claim. For every ordinary or ideal competitor $v$ for $\Psi $, the ordinary order or theorem 5.37.3 gives $
u (v,H)\geq 1$. Divisorial removal and descent along the fibers, lemma 5.38.1 , proposition 5.43.5 , give $v=\Psi +b\circ p$ with $b\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^2,\sigma _2)$. The bound $v\leq 0$ gives $b\leq G$ off $E$, hence everywhere with the extended value at $E$. Thus $v\leq \Psi +q\circ p$. Conversely, this upper bound is a competitor for both envelopes, since it is nonpositive and differs boundedly from $\Psi $. This proves the envelope identities directly. On $M\setminus H$, bounded local truncations of $b$ have products pulled back from a two-dimensional base, so their third products vanish by lemma 5.28.4 , and plurifine locality gives zero extended mass. Divisorial removal puts every ordinary representative of the model in this form, which proves both volume assertions. Finally, since the model is ordinarily equivalent to $\Psi $, proposition 16.28.62 gives $\Psi \in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(M,\Theta ,P_\Theta [\Psi ]_{\mathcal I})$, and proposition 18.12.2 gives equality below every smooth obstacle. $\square$ Example 18.14.8 . 68E397A3AF5C There is a Hermitian background $\Theta $ on a compact fourfold that fails the bounded mass property and admits a potential $u$ without an analytic ordinary type such that \[  P_\Theta [u]=P_\Theta [u]_{\mathcal I}=\Psi , \qquad u
ot\sim \Psi .  \] Both envelopes agree below every smooth obstacle, and their common model for the zero obstacle has both singularity volumes zero. Proof. Let $(Y,\omega )$ be the Hopf threefold of theorem 23.1.1 . On $\mathbb P^1$, let $\sigma $ be the probability Fubini–Study form, choose a point $D$ and a logarithmic potential $\psi $ with $\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =[D]$ and $\sup \psi =0$. On $M=Y	imes \mathbb P^1$, with projections $p,r$, put \[  \Theta =p^*\omega +r^*\sigma ,\qquad H=Y	imes D,\qquad \Psi =\psi \circ r.  \] Take the potential $U\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y,\omega ,0)$ of infinite mass from proposition 16.28.72 , which satisfies $P_\omega [U]=0$. Its multiplier ideals are trivial, so also $P_\omega [U]_{\mathcal I}=0$. Set $u=\Psi +U\circ p$. Here $\widehat0=0$, so proposition 18.14.1 , corollary 18.14.5 give the envelope identities, the equality below all obstacles and the vanishing of the singularity volumes. Moreover $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(M,\Theta ,\Psi )$ by proposition 18.14.4 . Since $U$ has infinite extended mass, it is unbounded; restriction to a section outside $H$ therefore proves $u
ot\sim \Psi $. If a potential $a$ with analytic singularities were ordinarily equivalent to $u$, proposition 18.4.8 would give $u\sim a\sim P_\Theta [a]=P_\Theta [u]=\Psi $, a contradiction. Finally, let $V_ j$ be the smooth potentials of theorem 23.1.1 . Their pullbacks are bounded and $\Theta $-plurisubharmonic, and proposition 20.3.59 gives \[  \int _ M\mathrm{MA}_\Theta (V_ j\circ p) =4\int _ Y\mathrm{MA}_\omega (V_ j)\longrightarrow +\infty .  \] Thus $\Theta $ itself fails the bounded mass property. $\square$ The descent of potentials uses that the fibers are connected. Otherwise the residual potential can take independent values on different components of a fiber, as a finite isogeny shows. Example 18.14.9 . 75FBCB1F7EC3 There is a surjective holomorphic submersion $p:M	o Y$ from a connected compact Kähler surface to an elliptic curve, with four components in every fiber, for which both identities in ( 18.14.2 ) fail. The pole divisor is smooth and maps onto $Y$, and the obstacle upstairs is smooth. Proof. Let $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z)$, let $ eta $ be its flat probability form, and let $q:E	o E$ be multiplication by two. On $M=E	imes \mathbb P^1$, denote the projections by $a,r$ and put $p=q\circ a$. Then $q$ is an unramified covering of degree four and $q^* eta =4 eta $. The manifold $M$ is connected, whereas every fiber of $p$ is the disjoint union of four projective lines. On $\mathbb P^1$ take the probability Fubini–Study form $\sigma $, a point $D$ and a logarithmic potential $\psi $ with $\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =[D]$ and $\sup \psi =0$. Put \[  H=E	imes D,\qquad \Psi =\psi \circ r,\qquad \Theta =p^* eta +r^*\sigma =4a^* eta +r^*\sigma .  \] Thus $\Theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Psi =p^* eta +[H]$, which corresponds to the base potential $w=0$. Choose $\epsilon >0$ so small that \[  f(\zeta )=\epsilon \cos (2\pi \operatorname {Re}\zeta ) \in \mathrm{PSH}(E,4 eta ),  \] and set $F=f\circ a$. The function $f$ is well defined and smooth on $E$. Since it changes sign under translation by $1/2$, it is not constant on the fibers of $q$. Apply proposition 18.14.1 to the projection $a$, which has connected fibers, with base background $4 eta $ and base potential zero. Its induced obstacle is $f$, since $\sup \psi =0$. The bounded potential $f$ is a competitor for both base envelopes and equals their obstacle, so \[  P_{\Theta ,F}[\Psi ]=P_{\Theta ,F}[\Psi ]_{\mathcal I} =\Psi +f\circ a.  \] For the map $p$, the fiber obstacle of proposition 18.14.1 would instead be \[  \widehat F(y)=\min _{q(\zeta )=y}f(\zeta ).  \] Every expression $\Psi +b\circ p$ is invariant under translation of the first factor by points of the kernel of $q$. The computed envelope is not invariant under translation by $1/2$, because $\Psi $ is unchanged and $f$ changes sign. It therefore cannot equal either right side of ( 18.14.2 ) for $p$. $\square$ The correct formula takes the fiber minimum over each connected component of a fiber separately. These components are the points of the finite covering of the base in lemma 5.43.4 . Corollary 18.14.10 . 20390B807B79 Let $p:M	o Y$ be a surjective holomorphic submersion between connected compact complex manifolds, with $1\leq \dim Y<\dim M$; its fibers may be disconnected. Use the weighted divisor data $A,H,\Psi ,\kappa _ A$ above, let $ eta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $Y$, and let $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y, eta )$. Put \[  \Theta =p^* eta +\kappa _ A,\qquad u=\Psi +w\circ p.  \] For the factorization $p=r\circ \pi $ of lemma 5.43.4 , set $ eta '=r^* eta $ and $w'=w\circ r$. For $F\in C(M,\mathbb R)$ define \[  \widehat F_{\mathrm{comp}}(y') =\inf _{x\in \pi ^{-1}(y')\setminus H}\{ F(x)-\Psi (x)\} , \qquad \inf \varnothing =+\infty .  \] This obstacle is continuous in the extended real sense on $Y'$, and \[   egin{split}  P_{\Theta ,F}[u] & =\Psi +P_{ eta ',\widehat F_{\mathrm{comp}}}[w']\circ \pi ,\  P_{\Theta ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} & =\Psi +P_{ eta ',\widehat F_{\mathrm{comp}}}[w']_{\mathcal I}\circ \pi . \end{split}  \] Every representative of the ordinary type of $u$ or of $P_\Theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ has zero extended mass, and both singularity volumes of these types are zero. The ordinary and ideal envelopes of $u$ agree below every smooth obstacle on $M$ if and only if those of $w'$ agree below every smooth obstacle on $Y'$. For $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y, eta )$, put $v=\Psi +\varphi \circ p$. Then \[  u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(M,\Theta ,v) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad w\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y, eta ,\varphi ).  \] For $q_ M=P_\Theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ and $q_ Y=P_ eta [w]_{\mathcal I}$, one also has \[  u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(M,\Theta ,q_ M) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad w\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y, eta ,q_ Y).  \] If $Y$ is a curve, let $\mu _ w,D_ w$ be the polar and atomic measures of corollary 18.14.5 . Then equality of the envelopes of $u$ below zero, the equality $\mu _ w=D_ w$, and equality of the envelopes of $u$ below every smooth obstacle are equivalent. They are also equivalent to $u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(M,\Theta ,q_ M)$. Proof. The covering map $r$ preserves the curvature inequality, so $w'\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y', eta ')$. Moreover $\dim Y'=\dim Y<\dim M$, and \[  \Theta =\pi ^* eta '+\kappa _ A,\qquad u=\Psi +w'\circ \pi .  \] Applying proposition 18.14.1 to the submersion $\pi $, which has connected fibers, gives the obstacle identities and the mass assertions, and corollary 18.14.5 for the same submersion gives the equivalence for all obstacles. In example 18.14.9 , this factorization has $Y'=E$, $r=q$ and $\pi =a$, so it recovers the computed envelope. For the assertions on relative classes, apply proposition 18.14.4 to $\pi $, with reference $\varphi \circ r$ on $Y'$, and then transfer membership through $r$ by proposition 18.12.4 . That proposition, applied with the zero obstacle, also gives \[  P_{ eta '}[w']_{\mathcal I}=q_ Y\circ r.  \] Applying the same two equivalences with these ideal references proves the assertion for $q_ M$ and $q_ Y$. In the curve case, $Y'$ is a curve. The covering is locally biholomorphic, so curvature measures and point Lelong numbers pull back without multiplicities. The pole set of $w'$ is $r^{-1}\{ w=-\infty \} $, and therefore \[  \mu _{w'}=r^*\mu _ w,\qquad D_{w'}=r^*D_ w,  \] where the pullback of a measure is defined on each sheet through the local inverse of $r$. Such pullbacks reflect equality: over every sufficiently small ball in $Y$, the restriction of a measure is recovered from any sheet over that ball. Hence $\mu _{w'}=D_{w'}$ if and only if $\mu _ w=D_ w$. The curve case of corollary 18.14.5 , applied to $\pi $, identifies the former equality with the equality of the envelopes upstairs below zero, with their equality below every smooth obstacle and with membership in the relative envelope class upstairs. This proves the last assertion. $\square$

title: Proposition 18.14.1
text: Proposition 18.14.1 . 1195E1B9B18D For every $F\in C(M,\mathbb R)$, the function \[  \widehat F(y)=\inf _{x\in p^{-1}(y)\setminus H}\{ F(x)-\Psi (x)\} , \qquad \inf \varnothing =+\infty ,  \] is continuous in the extended real sense, finite on $Y\setminus Z$ and equal to $+\infty $ on $Z$. Defining the base envelopes below this extended-real obstacle by the usual competitor families, one has EDA13205415C 18.14.2 \begin{equation}  \begin{split}  P_{\Theta ,F}[u]& =\Psi +P_{\beta ,\widehat F}[w]\circ p,\\  P_{\Theta ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} & =\Psi +P_{\beta ,\widehat F}[w]_{\mathcal I}\circ p. \end{split} \end{equation} Every representative of the ordinary type of $u$ or of $P_\Theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ has zero extended mass. Consequently both singularity volumes of these types are zero. If the ordinary and ideal envelopes of $w$ agree below every smooth obstacle on $Y$, then those of $u$ agree below every smooth obstacle on $M$. Proof. We first study the induced obstacle and bound the base competitors, then describe all competitors upstairs by divisorial removal and descent, and finally prove the mass assertion. Step 1: the induced obstacle. Since $p$ is open, $Y\setminus Z=p(M\setminus H)$ is open and nonempty. The function $F-\Psi $ is bounded below by $\min _ MF-\sup _ M\Psi $ and tends to $+\infty $ near $H$, because $\Psi \to -\infty $ there. On every fiber that meets $M\setminus H$, its infimum is therefore attained outside $H$. A local holomorphic section through a minimizer gives upper semicontinuity of $\widehat F$. Conversely, let $y_ j\to y$ with bounded fiber minima. By compactness, a subsequence of the minimizers converges, and its limit lies outside $H$ because $F-\Psi $ remains bounded along it; this gives lower semicontinuity. If $y\in Z$, the same limit would lie in $H$, a contradiction. Thus $\widehat F\to +\infty $ at $Z$, and $\widehat F$ is continuous in the extended sense. Step 2: a uniform bound for the base competitors. Choose a relatively compact nonempty ball $U$ in the base and a holomorphic section $s$ of $p$ on a neighborhood of $\overline U$ with image outside $H$. There is a finite $C_ U$ with $\widehat F\leq F\circ s-\Psi \circ s\leq C_ U$ on $U$. Fix a smooth probability volume form $\mathrm dV$ on $Y$. For every $b\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\beta )$ below $\widehat F$, normalized compactness in theorem 5.25.2 gives \[  -C_\beta \leq \int _ U(b-\sup _ Yb)\, \mathrm dV \leq (C_ U-\sup _ Yb)\int _ U\mathrm dV.  \] Hence every such $b$ satisfies $\sup _ Yb\leq K_ F=C_ U+C_\beta /\int _ U\mathrm dV$. A sufficiently low translate of $w$ belongs to both base competitor families. Their regularized suprema are therefore $\beta $-plurisubharmonic functions, not identically $-\infty $, and by the extended continuity of $\widehat F$ they still lie below $\widehat F$. Step 3: the competitors upstairs. The pullback of $w$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic, so its generic Lelong numbers are nonnegative, and $\nu (u,H_ j)=\lambda _ j+\nu (w\circ p,H_ j)\geq \lambda _ j$. Let $v$ be an ordinary competitor for $u$, or an ideal competitor with $v\sim _{\mathcal I}u$. By the ordinary order or by theorem 5.37.3 , its generic Lelong number along $H_ j$ is at least $\lambda _ j$. Divisorial removal in lemma 5.38.1 gives \[  \Theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v-[A]\geq 0.  \] Hence $v-\Psi $ has a quasi-plurisubharmonic representative $a$ satisfying $p^*\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\geq 0$. Descent along the compact connected fibers, proposition 5.43.5 , gives $a=b\circ p$ for a unique $b\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\beta )$, and $v=\Psi +b\circ p$ for the canonical representatives. Conversely, every potential of this form is $\Theta $-plurisubharmonic. For such $v$, one has $v\preceq u$ if and only if $b\preceq w$. Indeed, canceling $\Psi $ outside $H$ gives the base inequality almost everywhere, by Fubini's theorem in product charts, hence everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 ; the reverse implication follows by pullback and addition. Similarly, $v\sim _{\mathcal I}u$ if and only if $b\sim _{\mathcal I}w$: lemma 5.37.4 permits both addition and cancellation of $\Psi $, the pullback formula in lemma 5.37.7 then gives one direction, and restriction of the extended ideals along any local section gives the other. This comparison of ideals does not need a section outside $H$. If the divisors have relative simple normal crossings, the ideals have an explicit form. Here this means that near every point there are product coordinates $(y,z)$ with $p(y,z)=y$ in which the components through the point are distinct coordinate hyperplanes in the fiber variables. Then 336B6FB1D279 18.14.3 \begin{equation}  \mathcal I\bigl (t(\Psi +b\circ p)\bigr ) =\mathcal O_ M\! \left(-\sum _ j\lfloor t\lambda _ j\rfloor H_ j\right) \bigl (\mathcal I(tb)\mathcal O_ M\bigr ) \qquad (t>0). \end{equation} To see this, work in such coordinates. Up to a smooth correction, $\Psi $ is the sum of the weights $\lambda _ j\log |z_ j|^2$ over the components through the point. Since $b$ is locally bounded above, integrability forces vanishing to order at least $\lfloor t\lambda _ j\rfloor $ along each hyperplane. After this product of coordinate powers is factored out, the remaining fiber weight is \[  \prod _ j|z_ j|^{-2(t\lambda _ j-\lfloor t\lambda _ j\rfloor )}.  \] It is integrable and bounded below by a positive constant on a small polydisk. Integrability of the quotient against this weight therefore implies integrability against the pullback of $\mathrm e^{-tb}$ alone, and lemma 5.37.7 puts the quotient in the extension of $\mathcal I(tb)$. Conversely, local generators of that ideal are weighted-integrable against the integrable product weight, by Fubini's theorem. Outside $H$ the formula is the same pullback lemma. For one smooth divisor of weight one transverse to the fibers, the first factor is the ideal sheaf of the divisor raised to the power $\lfloor t\rfloor $. Step 4: the envelope identities. The bound $v\leq F$ is equivalent to $b\leq \widehat F$, with no constraint over $Z$. The competitor families upstairs and on the base therefore correspond to each other, which gives ( 18.14.2 ) outside $H$, since regularization commutes with pullback in product coordinates there. On $H$ both sides equal $-\infty $: every competitor is at most $\Psi +K_ F$, by the bound $b\leq K_ F$, and this upper semicontinuous function equals $-\infty $ on $H$, so regularization does not change the values there. Step 5: equality below all obstacles. Suppose that the two base envelopes agree below every smooth obstacle. Uniform obstacle comparison extends this equality to continuous real obstacles. The functions $G_ j=\min (\widehat F,j)$ are continuous and real-valued. Every base competitor below $\widehat F$ has finite supremum and hence lies below $G_ j$ for every sufficiently large integer $j$. Each full competitor family is thus the union of its subfamilies below the $G_ j$, and equality for all $G_ j$ gives equality below $\widehat F$ after taking regularized suprema. By the reduction, the envelopes upstairs agree below every smooth obstacle. Step 6: zero mass. Take any $b\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\beta )$ and write $a=\Psi +b\circ p$. On a relatively compact chart outside $H$, the functions $b_ j=\max (b,-j)$ are locally bounded and quasi-plurisubharmonic, and there \[  \Theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Psi +b_ j\circ p)=p^*(\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_ j).  \] Since $n>d$, the $n$th bounded product of this current is zero by lemma 5.28.4 . This identity does not require $b_ j$ to be $\beta $-plurisubharmonic: proposition 5.28.2 defines the products for locally bounded quasi-plurisubharmonic potentials. By plurifine locality, this zero product agrees with $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\Theta (a)$ on $\{ b\circ p>-j\} $ in the chart. These sets cover the locus where $b\circ p$ is finite, while the remaining pole set and $H$ receive no extended mass. Thus $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\Theta (a)=0$. By divisorial removal and descent, every representative ordinarily equivalent to $u$ has this form. By the identity already proved, the ideal model is also of this form, with base potential $P_{\beta ,\widehat0}[w]_{\mathcal I}$, where $\widehat0$ is the induced obstacle for $F=0$. The same removal and descent apply to every representative of its ordinary type. All these masses are zero, which proves both volume assertions. $\square$

title: Equation 18.14.2
text: EDA13205415C 18.14.2 \begin{equation}  \begin{split}  P_{\Theta ,F}[u]& =\Psi +P_{\beta ,\widehat F}[w]\circ p,\\  P_{\Theta ,F}[u]_{\mathcal I} & =\Psi +P_{\beta ,\widehat F}[w]_{\mathcal I}\circ p. \end{split} \end{equation}

title: Equation 18.14.3
text: 336B6FB1D279 18.14.3 \begin{equation}  \mathcal I\bigl (t(\Psi +b\circ p)\bigr ) =\mathcal O_ M\! \left(-\sum _ j\lfloor t\lambda _ j\rfloor H_ j\right) \bigl (\mathcal I(tb)\mathcal O_ M\bigr ) \qquad (t>0). \end{equation}

title: Proposition 18.14.4
text:
Proposition 18.14.4 . A399EFC10B9E For $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(Y, eta )$ put $v=\Psi +\varphi \circ p$. Then \[  u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(M,\Theta ,v) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad w\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y, eta ,\varphi ).  \] In particular, for $q_ M=P_\Theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ and $q_ Y=P_ eta [w]_{\mathcal I}$, \[  u\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(M,\Theta ,q_ M) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad w\in \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(Y, eta ,q_ Y).  \] Every ordinary representative of $u$ or $q_ M$ has zero extended mass, so both singularity volumes of these types vanish. Proof. The ordinary order $u\preceq v$ is equivalent to $w\preceq \varphi $. One implication follows by addition and pullback. Conversely, cancel $\Psi $ outside $H$, which has smooth volume zero; Fubini's theorem in product charts gives the base inequality almost everywhere, and lemma 5.24.3 makes it hold everywhere. Membership in the relative envelope class requires, for every $a\in (0,1)$, a stretching competitor $h\in \mathrm{PSH}(M,\Theta )$ with \[  av+(1-a)h\leq u.  \] A base competitor $c\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y, eta )$ with $a\varphi +(1-a)c\leq w$ gives such an $h$, namely $h=\Psi +c\circ p$. Conversely, put $ho _ j=
u (w\circ p,H_ j)$ and $\sigma _ j=
