title: 17.16 Perron interpolation and the geodesic equation
search_title: Perron interpolation and the geodesic equation
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 17.16 Perron interpolation and the geodesic equation
text: Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form. Fix a smooth positive volume form $\mathrm{d}V$ for the $L^1(X)$ topology. This part studies two operations on singular potentials: interpolation between two potentials along an auxiliary real parameter, and restriction to a complex submanifold. A one-parameter family of $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions can be regarded as a single function on the product of $X$ with a strip in $\mathbb C$, and positivity of its curvature current on the product is a convexity condition in the parameter. The largest such family with prescribed endpoints, the Perron envelope, interpolates between two potentials; in Kähler geometry it gives the weak geodesics of the space of potentials. A Legendre transform in the parameter relates rays made of Perron segments to concave decreasing families of envelope fixed points, the test curves of section 17.17 . Restriction behaves differently: the restriction of a potential to a submanifold can acquire poles that are invisible to its multiplier ideals, and section 20.3 works instead with the information carried by the restricted multiplier ideals. All these constructions use only positivity of currents, so they apply to nonclosed backgrounds. In Kähler geometry, the smooth geodesic equation for the Mabuchi $L^2$ metric on potentials is a homogeneous Monge–Ampère equation on such a product. Positivity on the product still defines Perron interpolation for a nonclosed background, but the two constructions can now differ: integration by parts in the $L^2$ action produces torsion terms. Even a smooth Perron segment given by translation by constants can fail to be stationary for that action. The Perron construction itself rests on convexity and barriers. Convexity in the parameter bounds every admissible path by the chord between its endpoints, while a lower barrier ensures that the envelope attains the endpoints. For two potentials of the same ordinary singularity type, two affine barriers suffice and give a Lipschitz bound in the parameter. Maximality on each finite subinterval is the property that links Perron segments with Legendre duality in section 17.17 .

title: 17.16.1 Subgeodesics and endpoint bounds
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 17.16 Perron interpolation and the geodesic equation
text: As in lemma 5.41.1 , for a nonempty open interval $I\subset \mathbb R$ write \[  S_ I=\{ z\in \mathbb C:\operatorname{Re}z\in I\} ,\qquad \pi :X\times S_ I\longrightarrow X,  \] where $\pi $ is the projection. A family $u_ t\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, $t\in I$, is a subgeodesic if its complexification $U(x,z)=u_{\operatorname{Re}z}(x)$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic and satisfies $\pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U\geq 0$ on $X\times S_ I$. For finite $a<b$ and $u_ a,u_ b\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, a subgeodesic on $(a,b)$ runs from $u_ a$ to $u_ b$ if $u_ t\to u_ a$ in $L^1(X)$ as $t\downarrow a$ and $u_ t\to u_ b$ as $t\uparrow b$. The elementary operations below produce lower barriers. Convexity in $t$, given by lemma 5.41.1 , and the minimum principle of section 5.41 then give the continuity and upper bounds needed for the Perron envelope. Proposition 17.16.2 . 1A5A4BBF82E3 Subgeodesics are preserved by adding an affine function of $t$, by a positive affine reparametrization of time, by finite maxima, and by convex combinations. For $h\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$, replacing $\theta $ by $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h$ and $u_ t$ by $u_ t-h$ also preserves them. Proof. Affine functions of $\operatorname{Re}z$ have zero complex Hessian, and a positive affine change of time is induced by a holomorphic affine change of the strip coordinate. Convex combinations preserve the inequality between currents, and the change $(\theta ,u_ t)\mapsto (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h,u_ t-h)$ preserves the current itself. Maxima are covered by lemma 5.24.1 . $\square$ Proposition 17.16.3 . 15E98759958F A subgeodesic is continuous in $L^1(X)$ on the interior of its parameter interval. If the interval is $(a,b)$ with $a<b$ finite, and the subgeodesic runs from $u_ a$ to $u_ b$, where $u_ a,u_ b\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, then 3E2013A813CD 17.16.4 \begin{equation}  u_ t\leq \frac{b-t}{b-a}u_ a+\frac{t-a}{b-a}u_ b, \qquad a<t<b. \end{equation} Moreover, the following upper limits, taken jointly in space and time, hold at the endpoints: \[  \limsup _{\substack {y\to x\\ t\downarrow a}}u_ t(y)\leq u_ a(x), \qquad \limsup _{\substack {y\to x\\ t\uparrow b}}u_ t(y)\leq u_ b(x).  \] Proof. For a compact interval $J\Subset I$, choose $a'<\inf J\leq \sup J<b'$ in $I$. By lemma 5.41.1 , the path lies below the chord through $u_{a'}$ and $u_{b'}$, hence below a constant on $J$, and by proposition 5.41.3 the function $\inf _{a'<t<b'}u_ t$ is an integrable lower bound. For almost every $x$, the function $t\mapsto u_ t(x)$ is finite and convex, hence continuous, and dominated convergence proves continuity in $L^1$ on $J$. For the chord bound, choose sequences of times tending to $a$ and $b$ along which the assumed $L^1$ convergence holds almost everywhere. Applying convexity between these times and passing to the limit proves ( 17.16.4 ) almost everywhere in $x$, for each $t$, and hence everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 . For the joint upper limit at $a$, note that in ( 17.16.4 ) the coefficient of $u_ a$ tends to one, while the term involving $u_ b$ has a vanishing coefficient and a uniform upper bound. Upper semicontinuity of $u_ a$ gives the assertion when $u_ a(x)$ is finite. At a pole of $u_ a$, bound $u_ a$ near $x$ above by an arbitrary real number, take the joint upper limit, and let that number tend to $-\infty $. The argument at $b$ is the same. $\square$

title: 17.16.5 Perron segments
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 17.16 Perron interpolation and the geodesic equation
text: The chord bound survives taking a regularized supremum, and a single competitor attaining the endpoints bounds that supremum from below and forces the same endpoint limits. Fix $u_0,u_1\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and call a subgeodesic on $(0,1)$ admissible if its joint upper limits at $t=0$ and $t=1$, in the sense of proposition 17.16.3 , are at most $u_0$ and $u_1$, respectively. Define the Perron envelope \[  U=\left(\sup \{ V:V\text{ is an admissible complexification}\} \right)^*,  \] where the upper semicontinuous regularization is taken on $X\times S_{(0,1)}$, and denote the slices of $U$ by $u_ t^{\mathrm P}$. When these slices form a subgeodesic running from $u_0$ to $u_1$, they define the Perron segment from $u_0$ to $u_1$, and we set $u_0^{\mathrm P}=u_0$ and $u_1^{\mathrm P}=u_1$. An affine change of parameter gives the same construction on any finite interval. Proposition 17.16.6 . 5D2A9C4885B8 If an admissible subgeodesic exists, the Perron envelope is the largest admissible subgeodesic. If some admissible subgeodesic runs from $u_0$ to $u_1$, so does the envelope, which is then the Perron segment. In that case, for every $[a,b]\subset [0,1]$ with $a<b$, its restriction to $[a,b]$ is the Perron segment between $u_ a^{\mathrm P}$ and $u_ b^{\mathrm P}$. Proof. Convexity in $t$ and the upper limits at the endpoints bound every competitor by $(1-t)u_0+t u_1$. This bound is jointly upper semicontinuous on the interior and locally bounded above, so it persists after regularization. The local envelope theorem of section 5.40 shows that $U$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic with $\pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U\geq 0$, and $U$ is still independent of $\Im z$. Since it dominates an admissible competitor, each slice belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. The chord bound gives the joint upper limits at the endpoints, by the argument at the end of the proof of proposition 17.16.3 . The envelope therefore belongs to its defining family and is its largest member. If a competitor $w_ t$ runs from $u_0$ to $u_1$, then \[  w_ t\leq u_ t^{\mathrm P}\leq (1-t)u_0+t u_1.  \] In particular, almost everywhere, \[  |u_ t^{\mathrm P}-u_0|\leq |w_ t-u_0|+t|u_1-u_0|,  \] which proves $u_ t^{\mathrm P}\to u_0$ in $L^1$ as $t\downarrow 0$. The argument at $t=1$ is the same. For $0\leq a<b\leq 1$, let $v_ t$ be the Perron envelope on $(a,b)$ between $u_ a^{\mathrm P}$ and $u_ b^{\mathrm P}$. The original path restricted to $(a,b)$ runs between these endpoints and is admissible by proposition 17.16.3 . Thus $v_ t$ also runs between them and dominates $u_ t^{\mathrm P}$. The joint upper limits of $v_ t$ at $a$ and $b$ allow us to glue its complexification to $U$ outside the smaller strip, by lemma 5.24.2 ; if $a=0$ or $b=1$, the same upper limits show that the glued family is still admissible for $u_0,u_1$. The resulting competitor cannot exceed $U$, which proves $v_ t=u_ t^{\mathrm P}$ on $(a,b)$. $\square$ When the endpoints differ by a bounded function, an explicit lower barrier is available. Theorem 17.16.7 . 66E38862017F Suppose that $u_0\sim u_1$, and choose $C\geq 0$ with $u_0-C\leq u_1\leq u_0+C$. Then the Perron segment from $u_0$ to $u_1$ exists, every slice has the ordinary singularity type of $u_0$ and $u_1$, and \[  u_0-Ct\leq u_ t^{\mathrm P}\leq u_0+Ct, \qquad u_1-C(1-t)\leq u_ t^{\mathrm P}\leq u_1+C(1-t).  \] Moreover, away from the common pole set, \[  |u_ t^{\mathrm P}-u_ s^{\mathrm P}|\leq C|t-s|, \qquad 0\leq s,t\leq 1.  \] Proof. Consider the barrier \[  w_ t=\max \{ u_0-Ct,\  u_1-C(1-t)\} .  \] It is a subgeodesic by proposition 17.16.2 , and the bounded difference gives $w_0=u_0$ and $w_1=u_1$. Upper semicontinuity gives the joint upper limits at the endpoints. Off the common poles, $|w_ t-u_0|\leq Ct$ and $|w_ t-u_1|\leq C(1-t)$, so $w_ t$ runs from $u_0$ to $u_1$, and proposition 17.16.6 applies. The lower bounds follow from $w_ t\leq u_ t^{\mathrm P}$, and the upper bounds from the chord estimate; together they give the asserted singularity type. Off the common poles, put $f(t)=u_ t^{\mathrm P}(x)$. For $0<s<t<1$, monotonicity of the slopes of secants of the convex function $f$ gives \[  -C\leq \frac{f(s)-f(0)}s \leq \frac{f(t)-f(s)}{t-s} \leq \frac{f(1)-f(t)}{1-t}\leq C.  \] The two-sided estimates at the endpoints cover the cases $s=0$ and $t=1$, which proves the Lipschitz bound on $[0,1]$. $\square$ For endpoints of different types, a common lower potential still gives an admissible constant path, so the envelope exists. Attaining the endpoints requires a barrier approaching the prescribed values; proposition 17.16.6 separates this requirement from the existence of the envelope.

title: 17.16.8 The smooth product equation
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
section: 17.16 Perron interpolation and the geodesic equation
text:
For a smooth path, positivity on the product compares the acceleration with the spatial gradient of the velocity. Let $u_ t$ be smooth in $(x,t)\in X\times I$, suppose that $\eta _ t=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t>0$, and write, in local holomorphic coordinates $(x_1,\ldots ,x_ n)$, \[  \theta =\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\sum _{i,j=1}^ n g_{i\bar j}\, \mathrm dx_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar x_ j, \qquad H=(g_{i\bar j}+\partial _ i\partial _{\bar j}u), \qquad \xi =(\partial _ i\dot u)_{i=1}^ n.  \] Here dots denote derivatives in $t$, $\xi $ is a column vector, and $\xi ^*$ is its conjugate transpose. Since $t=\operatorname{Re}z$, the form $\pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$ on the product has, in the coordinates $(x_1,\ldots ,x_ n,z)$, the coefficient matrix \[  \begin{pmatrix}  H

& \tfrac 12\xi 

\\  \tfrac 12\xi ^*

& \tfrac 14\ddot u 

\end{pmatrix}.  \] Proposition 17.16.9 . 5885FD8F9550 The form $\pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U$ is semipositive exactly when \[  \ddot u\geq \xi ^*H^{-1}\xi .  \] Its $(n+1)$st power vanishes exactly when equality holds. Equivalently, the homogeneous Monge–Ampère equation on the product is F12E6A9111B5 17.16.10 \begin{equation}  \ddot u\, \eta _ t^ n =n\, \mathrm{d}\dot u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\dot u\wedge \eta _ t^{n-1}. \end{equation} Proof. The Schur complement of $H$ in the block matrix is $(\ddot u-\xi ^*H^{-1}\xi )/4$. Since $H>0$, the block matrix is semipositive exactly when this complement is nonnegative, and its determinant, which is $\det H$ times the complement, vanishes exactly when the complement vanishes. To rewrite the equation in terms of forms, note that \[  \mathrm{d}\dot u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\dot u=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial \dot u\wedge \bar\partial \dot u, \qquad n\frac{\mathrm{d}\dot u\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\dot u\wedge \eta _ t^{n-1}}{\eta _ t^ n} =\operatorname {tr}(H^{-1}\xi \xi ^*)=\xi ^*H^{-1}\xi .  \] Multiplying the second identity by $\eta _ t^ n>0$ gives ( 17.16.10 ). $\square$ This calculation identifies the homogeneous equation for smooth paths. Whether nonsmooth Perron segments solve a weak form of this equation is a separate question, which we do not address.

text: The homogeneous equation on the product involves the spatial form $\eta _ t$ only pointwise. In the $L^2$ action, integration by parts also differentiates the powers of $\eta _ t$, which produces terms absent from that equation. Fix a Hermitian form $\omega $, write $\omega _ u=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, and recall from section 11.1 the space $\mathcal H_\omega $ of smooth real functions $u$ with $\omega _ u>0$. On $\mathcal H_\omega $ consider the Riemannian metric \[  G_ u(v,w)=\int _ Xvw\, \omega _ u^ n, \qquad v,w\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R).  \] For a smooth path $u_ t\in \mathcal H_\omega $, $0\leq t\leq 1$, its action is \[  \mathscr S(u)=\frac12\int _0^1\int _ X\dot u_ t^{\, 2}\, \omega _{u_ t}^ n\, \mathrm{d}t.  \] Stationarity under smooth variations fixing both endpoints is the formal geodesic equation of this metric. Theorem 17.16.12 . 7A7AE56CA513 Let $u_ t\in \mathcal H_\omega $, $0\leq t\leq 1$, be a smooth path, and put $\eta _ t=\omega _{u_ t}$ and $T_ t=\eta _ t^{n-1}$. The path is stationary for $\mathscr S$ if and only if DCC8DA6D179E 17.16.13 \begin{equation}  \begin{split}  \ddot u_ t\, \eta _ t^ n={}& n\, \mathrm{d}\dot u_ t\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\dot u_ t\wedge T_ t\\ & +n\dot u_ t\bigl (\mathrm{d}\dot u_ t\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}T_ t -\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\dot u_ t\wedge \mathrm{d}T_ t\bigr ) +\frac n2\dot u_ t^{\, 2}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_ t. \end{split} \end{equation} All differentials on the right act only in the $X$ variable. Proof. Vary the path as $u_ t+s v_ t$, where $v_ t$ is smooth in $(x,t)$ and $v_0=v_1=0$, and put $f=\dot u_ t$. Differentiating the action at $s=0$, using $\partial _ s(\omega _{u_ t+sv_ t}^ n)|_{s=0}=n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ t\wedge T_ t$, gives \[  \delta \mathscr S =\int _0^1\left(\int _ X f\dot v_ t\, \eta _ t^ n +\frac n2\int _ X f^2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ t\wedge T_ t\right)\mathrm{d}t.  \] We integrate by parts in $t$ in the first term, using $\partial _ t(\eta _ t^ n)=n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge T_ t$, and on $X$ in the second, using lemma 11.1.2 with the whole form $f^2T_ t$. Thus \[  \delta \mathscr S =\int _0^1\int _ Xv_ t\left(-\ddot u_ t\eta _ t^ n -nf\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge T_ t+\frac n2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(f^2T_ t)\right)\mathrm{d}t.  \] The product rule gives \[  \begin{split}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(f^2T_ t)={}& 2f\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge T_ t +2\mathrm{d}f\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge T_ t\\ & +2f\bigl (\mathrm{d}f\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}T_ t-\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \mathrm{d}T_ t\bigr ) +f^2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_ t. \end{split}  \] After the term $nf\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge T_ t$ cancels, the integrand is $v_ t$ times the difference between the right-hand and left-hand sides of ( 17.16.13 ). Since $\eta _ t>0$ on the compact set $X\times [0,1]$, every smooth $v_ t$ gives an admissible variation for small $|s|$, and the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations gives both implications. $\square$ For a Kähler background, $\mathrm{d}T_ t=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}T_ t=0$, and the equation reduces to ( 17.16.10 ). The Gauduchon condition $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T_ t=0$ on $\eta _ t$ removes only the last term. Translations by constants isolate that term and give an exact test for stationarity. Corollary 17.16.14 . BE24BBA15991 Fix $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $ and a nonzero constant $a$. The path $u_ t=u+at$, $0\leq t\leq 1$, is a Perron segment and solves the homogeneous equation ( 17.16.10 ). It is stationary for the $L^2$ action if and only if \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega _ u^{n-1})=0.  \] For $n\geq 2$, this means that $\omega _ u$ is a Gauduchon metric. Proof. The path is admissible and equals the chord between its endpoints, so by the chord bound no admissible competitor can be larger; it is therefore the Perron segment. Its acceleration and the spatial derivatives of its velocity vanish, which proves ( 17.16.10 ). In ( 17.16.13 ), the only remaining term is $\frac n2a^2\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega _ u^{n-1})$, which vanishes exactly under the stated condition. $\square$ The three-dimensional torus in example 11.23.5 carries a Gauduchon form $\omega $ and a smooth potential $u\in \mathcal H_\omega $ for which $\omega _ u$ is not Gauduchon. Thus $u_ t=u+t$ is a smooth Perron segment that is not stationary for the $L^2$ action. On a surface, the Gauduchon condition persists under perturbation of the potential by proposition 11.23.4 , but it does not cancel the terms in ( 17.16.13 ) involving first derivatives of $T_ t$. On the Hopf background, basic potentials give a complete metric whose geodesics are the full Perron segments. Its relation to the raw action reveals a further distinction between stationarity and minimization.

title: 17.16.15 Basic finite energy potentials on a Hopf manifold
search_title: Basic finite energy potentials on a Hopf manifold

text: The Hopf geometry of subsection 23.1.32 gives a nonclosed background for which a distinguished family of potentials has a complete geodesic metric. Its Perron envelope uses all subgeodesics, although the metric measures lengths within the distinguished family. The distinction matters: allowing additional smooth paths can decrease the length. Fix $n\geq 3$ and put $d=n-1$. Write \[  X=H_ n,\qquad Y=\mathbb P^ d,\qquad \pi =p_ n, \qquad \omega =\omega _ n=\alpha _ n+\beta _ n.  \] Let $\kappa $ be the mass-one Fubini–Study form on $Y$, so $\alpha _ n=\pi ^*\kappa $. On the cover, $r=\log |z|^2$ is defined modulo two and $\beta _ n=\mathrm dr\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}r$. The compact elliptic group \[  E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+2\pi \mathrm i\mathbb Z)  \] acts by scalar multiplication, preserves $\omega $, and acts transitively on each fiber. A potential is basic if it is invariant under this action; such a potential is exactly $\pi ^*v$. These manifolds are not products of positive-dimensional compact complex manifolds. Indeed, $H_ n$ is diffeomorphic to $S^{2n-1}\times S^1$, whose intermediate positive even-degree real cohomology vanishes. A product with a compact complex factor of dimension $k$, $0<k<n$, would have a nonzero degree-$2k$ class: pullback of that factor's top class is injective because projection has a smooth section. Thus the fiber reduction below takes place on a nonproduct manifold. Proposition 17.16.16 . 0290ABD0E348 Let $S$ be a strip and $V$ a genuine quasi-plurisubharmonic function on $Y\times S$. Then \[  \operatorname {pr}_ X^*\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\pi \times \mathrm{id})^*V\geq 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \operatorname {pr}_ Y^*\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V\geq 0.  \] For every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\kappa )$, the extended non-pluripolar measure satisfies 4A3521DF9F72 17.16.17 \begin{equation}  \operatorname{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (\pi ^*v) =n\beta _ n\wedge \pi ^*\operatorname{MA}_\kappa (v). \end{equation} In particular, for every nonnegative Borel function $F$, 6D09A14331E6 17.16.18 \begin{equation}  \int _ X\pi ^*F\, \operatorname{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (\pi ^*v) =2n\int _ YF\, \operatorname{MA}_\kappa (v). \end{equation} If the base Perron family between $v_0,v_1$ is nonempty, the full Hermitian Perron envelope between $\pi ^*v_0,\pi ^*v_1$ is the pullback of the base envelope. Proof. Write $\alpha =\alpha _ n$ and $\beta =\beta _ n$. Locally $\beta =(\mathrm i/(2\pi ))\partial r\wedge \bar\partial r$, and $\partial r$ has a nonzero vertical component. Every vector on $Y\times S$ therefore has a lift annihilated by $\partial r$. Testing the current on these lifts removes $\beta $; integrating the resulting distributional inequality against a nonnegative compact fiber density gives positivity on the base. Conversely, pullback of a positive base current plus $\beta $ is positive. An invariant genuine potential descends canonically by restricting to local holomorphic sections, so the argument also applies to singular potentials. For bounded $v$, the local product with smooth corrections from section 13.14 gives \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\pi ^*v)^ n =(\beta +\pi ^*(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v))^ n =n\beta \wedge \pi ^*(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ d.  \] All other terms vanish by $\beta ^2=0$ and the dimension of $Y$. Apply this identity to $\max (v,-j)$ and restrict to $\{ v>-j\} $. Increasing finite-level limits give ( 17.16.17 ), without assigning mass to the pole set. The identity $\int _{\pi ^{-1}(y)}\beta =2$ from subsection 23.1.32 gives ( 17.16.18 ). The full Perron competitor family is preserved by $E$. Its supremum and upper semicontinuous regularization are invariant. The chord bound and a pulled-back base competitor make this envelope a genuine subgeodesic by proposition 17.16.6 . Positivity descent makes its descended envelope a base competitor with the prescribed joint boundary upper bounds. Conversely, every base competitor pulls back to a full competitor. The two envelopes consequently agree; in submersion charts, upper semicontinuous regularization commutes with pullback. $\square$ Let $\mathcal E^2(Y,\kappa )$ denote the canonical $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic potentials of non-pluripolar mass one and finite squared energy. Define \[  \mathcal B_\infty =\{ \pi ^*v:v\in C^\infty (Y),\  \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0\} , \qquad \mathcal B_2=\pi ^*\mathcal E^2(Y,\kappa ).  \] Thus $\mathcal B_2$ consists precisely of the basic potentials of extended mass $2n$ with $\int _ X|u|^2\operatorname{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)<\infty $. On $\mathcal B_\infty $, let $d_ B$ be the infimum of the lengths of smooth basic paths for the metric $G$ above. A geodesic metric space $(Z,\delta )$ is CAT$(0)$ if every constant-speed geodesic $\gamma :[0,1]\to Z$ satisfies \[  \begin{aligned}  \delta (z,\gamma _ t)^2\leq {}&  (1-t)\delta (z,\gamma _0)^2+t\delta (z,\gamma _1)^2\\ & -t(1-t)\delta (\gamma _0,\gamma _1)^2 \end{aligned}  \] for $z\in Z$ and $0\leq t\leq 1$. In particular, its geodesics are unique. We use the classical Kähler completion theorem: the $L^2$ length metric for $\int _ Y\xi \eta (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ d$ has completion $\mathcal E^2(Y,\kappa )$, is a CAT$(0)$ metric, and its geodesic between two points is their Perron segment. That segment has capacity endpoint limits and all its slices lie in $\mathcal E^2$. We also use the full-mass characterization $P_\kappa [v]=0$ for $v\in \mathcal E^2$. These are closed-background inputs on $Y$; their exact source and operator normalization are specified in 25.14 . Theorem 17.16.19 . B0CA576B1836 The completion of $(\mathcal B_\infty ,d_ B)$ is $\mathcal B_2$. It is a CAT$(0)$ space, and its unique constant-speed geodesic between two points is their full Hermitian Perron segment. This segment attains both endpoints in $L^1(X,\mathrm dV)$ for every smooth positive volume form $\mathrm dV$. For every $u\in \mathcal B_2$ and $c\in \mathbb R$, \[  d_ B(u,u+c)=\sqrt{2n}|c|.  \] Proof. Fiber integration gives the exact restricted metric D40B24211305 17.16.20 \begin{equation}  G_{\pi ^*v}(\pi ^*\xi ,\pi ^*\eta ) =2n\int _ Y\xi \eta (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ d. \end{equation} The Kähler completion theorem therefore gives the stated completion and CAT$(0)$ property after multiplying base distances by $\sqrt{2n}$. If $\widetilde d_ D$ denotes the completed metric written with operator $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial $ and background $\kappa $, the normalization is explicitly 58F89D956FBF 17.16.21 \begin{equation}  d_ B(\pi ^*v,\pi ^*w) =2\pi \sqrt{2n}\, \widetilde d_ D(v/(2\pi ),w/(2\pi )), \end{equation} because $\kappa +\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial (v/(2\pi ))=\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. The preceding proposition identifies its unique geodesic with the full Hermitian Perron envelope. The base capacity endpoint limits give $L^1(Y)$ convergence. Since \[  \int _ X|\pi ^*(v-w)|\frac{\omega ^ n}{2n} =\int _ Y|v-w|\kappa ^ d,  \] the same holds on $X$; every smooth positive $\mathrm dV$ has bounded density ratio with $\omega ^ n$ on compact $X$. For smooth $v$, the constant translation is a base geodesic with speed $|c|$. Smooth metric approximation and translation by the same constant extend the distance formula to every $v\in \mathcal E^2$. $\square$ For an absolutely continuous curve $\gamma :[0,1]\to \mathcal B_2$, define its metric action by \[  \mathcal A_ B(\gamma )=\frac12\int _0^1|\dot\gamma |_{d_ B}^{\, 2}\, \mathrm dt.  \] Here the metric derivative is the almost everywhere defined limit \[  |\dot\gamma _ t|_{d_ B} =\lim _{h\to 0}\frac{d_ B(\gamma _{t+h},\gamma _ t)}{|h|}.  \] The action is defined even when the potentials are unbounded; it does not require a Riemannian tensor at a singular potential. Proposition 17.16.22 . 2B828BD01DBB The unique action minimizer between two points of $\mathcal B_2$ is their constant-speed Perron segment, and its action is half their squared distance. On every smooth path in $\mathcal B_\infty $, $\mathcal A_ B$ equals the raw action $\mathscr S$. Every smooth basic Perron segment with strictly positive spatial forms is stationary for $\mathscr S$ under all smooth fixed-endpoint variations on $X$. Proof. The length inequality and Cauchy–Schwarz give \[  d_ B(\gamma _0,\gamma _1)^2 \leq \left(\int _0^1|\dot\gamma |_{d_ B}\, \mathrm dt\right)^2 \leq 2\mathcal A_ B(\gamma ).  \] Equality holds for the constant-speed geodesic. Equality for a connecting curve forces constant speed and equality between length and endpoint distance, hence forces a geodesic; uniqueness follows from the CAT$(0)$ property. For a smooth basic path $\pi ^*v_ s$, put $h=v_{s+\delta }-v_ s$. On its short base Perron segment, parametrized by $0\leq \tau \leq 1$, the chord bounds above, and \[  v_ s+\tau h-C\delta ^2\tau (1-\tau )  \] bounds below. Indeed, the spatial forms along the chord have a uniform positive lower bound, $\mathrm dh=O(\delta )$, and proposition 17.16.9 makes the displayed path a subgeodesic for a fixed sufficiently large $C$. The right initial velocity of the Perron segment is therefore $h+O(\delta ^2)$ uniformly. The classical smooth-endpoint Kähler distance formula gives \[  \lim _{\delta \to 0}\frac{d_ B(\pi ^*v_ s,\pi ^*v_{s+\delta })^2}{\delta ^2} =2n\int _ Y\dot v_ s^{\, 2}(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ s)^ d.  \] Integration proves $\mathcal A_ B=\mathscr S$ along this path. For stationarity, let $L(w)$ be the first variation at a smooth basic Perron path. Uniform spatial positivity allows every smooth endpoint-zero variation. Group invariance of the action and of the path gives $L(g^*w)=L(w)$ for $g\in E$. Average over Haar probability measure to obtain \[  L(w)=L\left(\int _ Eg^*w\, \mathrm dg\right)=L(\pi ^*q)  \] for a smooth endpoint-zero base variation $q$. Fiber integration reduces this to $2n$ times the closed-base first variation. With $\eta _ t=\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ t$, integration by parts gives that variation as \[  \int _0^1\int _ Yq_ t\left[-\ddot v_ t\eta _ t^ d +d\, \mathrm d\dot v_ t\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\dot v_ t\wedge \eta _ t^{d-1}\right]\mathrm dt.  \] The bracket vanishes by the smooth base homogeneous equation. Thus $L(w)=0$ for every variation on $X$. $\square$ The metric action minimizes over curves in $\mathcal B_2$. The stationarity assertion allows all smooth variations. It does not imply minimization over all smooth Hermitian paths. Likewise, the initial-velocity formula used above has smooth endpoints; it is not a definition of the metric on all of $\mathcal B_2$.

text: Theorem 17.16.19 . B0CA576B1836 The completion of $(\mathcal B_\infty ,d_ B)$ is $\mathcal B_2$. It is a CAT$(0)$ space, and its unique constant-speed geodesic between two points is their full Hermitian Perron segment. This segment attains both endpoints in $L^1(X,\mathrm dV)$ for every smooth positive volume form $\mathrm dV$. For every $u\in \mathcal B_2$ and $c\in \mathbb R$, \[  d_ B(u,u+c)=\sqrt{2n}|c|.  \] Proof. Fiber integration gives the exact restricted metric D40B24211305 17.16.20 \begin{equation}  G_{\pi ^*v}(\pi ^*\xi ,\pi ^*\eta ) =2n\int _ Y\xi \eta (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ d. \end{equation} The Kähler completion theorem therefore gives the stated completion and CAT$(0)$ property after multiplying base distances by $\sqrt{2n}$. If $\widetilde d_ D$ denotes the completed metric written with operator $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial $ and background $\kappa $, the normalization is explicitly 58F89D956FBF 17.16.21 \begin{equation}  d_ B(\pi ^*v,\pi ^*w) =2\pi \sqrt{2n}\, \widetilde d_ D(v/(2\pi ),w/(2\pi )), \end{equation} because $\kappa +\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial (v/(2\pi ))=\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$. The preceding proposition identifies its unique geodesic with the full Hermitian Perron envelope. The base capacity endpoint limits give $L^1(Y)$ convergence. Since \[  \int _ X|\pi ^*(v-w)|\frac{\omega ^ n}{2n} =\int _ Y|v-w|\kappa ^ d,  \] the same holds on $X$; every smooth positive $\mathrm dV$ has bounded density ratio with $\omega ^ n$ on compact $X$. For smooth $v$, the constant translation is a base geodesic with speed $|c|$. Smooth metric approximation and translation by the same constant extend the distance formula to every $v\in \mathcal E^2$. $\square$

text: Proposition 17.16.22 . 2B828BD01DBB The unique action minimizer between two points of $\mathcal B_2$ is their constant-speed Perron segment, and its action is half their squared distance. On every smooth path in $\mathcal B_\infty $, $\mathcal A_ B$ equals the raw action $\mathscr S$. Every smooth basic Perron segment with strictly positive spatial forms is stationary for $\mathscr S$ under all smooth fixed-endpoint variations on $X$. Proof. The length inequality and Cauchy–Schwarz give \[  d_ B(\gamma _0,\gamma _1)^2 \leq \left(\int _0^1|\dot\gamma |_{d_ B}\, \mathrm dt\right)^2 \leq 2\mathcal A_ B(\gamma ).  \] Equality holds for the constant-speed geodesic. Equality for a connecting curve forces constant speed and equality between length and endpoint distance, hence forces a geodesic; uniqueness follows from the CAT$(0)$ property. For a smooth basic path $\pi ^*v_ s$, put $h=v_{s+\delta }-v_ s$. On its short base Perron segment, parametrized by $0\leq \tau \leq 1$, the chord bounds above, and \[  v_ s+\tau h-C\delta ^2\tau (1-\tau )  \] bounds below. Indeed, the spatial forms along the chord have a uniform positive lower bound, $\mathrm dh=O(\delta )$, and proposition 17.16.9 makes the displayed path a subgeodesic for a fixed sufficiently large $C$. The right initial velocity of the Perron segment is therefore $h+O(\delta ^2)$ uniformly. The classical smooth-endpoint Kähler distance formula gives \[  \lim _{\delta \to 0}\frac{d_ B(\pi ^*v_ s,\pi ^*v_{s+\delta })^2}{\delta ^2} =2n\int _ Y\dot v_ s^{\, 2}(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ s)^ d.  \] Integration proves $\mathcal A_ B=\mathscr S$ along this path. For stationarity, let $L(w)$ be the first variation at a smooth basic Perron path. Uniform spatial positivity allows every smooth endpoint-zero variation. Group invariance of the action and of the path gives $L(g^*w)=L(w)$ for $g\in E$. Average over Haar probability measure to obtain \[  L(w)=L\left(\int _ Eg^*w\, \mathrm dg\right)=L(\pi ^*q)  \] for a smooth endpoint-zero base variation $q$. Fiber integration reduces this to $2n$ times the closed-base first variation. With $\eta _ t=\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ t$, integration by parts gives that variation as \[  \int _0^1\int _ Yq_ t\left[-\ddot v_ t\eta _ t^ d +d\, \mathrm d\dot v_ t\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\dot v_ t\wedge \eta _ t^{d-1}\right]\mathrm dt.  \] The bracket vanishes by the smooth base homogeneous equation. Thus $L(w)=0$ for every variation on $X$. $\square$

text: On this Hopf background, constant Perron translations are stationary. Radial variations detect the failure of minimization. Every smooth two-periodic function of $r$ defines a smooth function on $X$, and for a radial path $u(t,r)$, \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=(1+u_ r)\alpha _ n+(1+u_{rr})\beta _ n.  \] For $\langle F\rangle =\frac12\int _0^2F(r)\, \mathrm dr$, fiber integration therefore gives 905CCA72845B 17.16.24 \begin{equation}  \mathscr S(u)=n\int _0^1 \left\langle u_ t^2(1+u_ r)^ d(1+u_{rr})\right\rangle \mathrm dt. \end{equation} Changing the local base section shifts the start of the full period and leaves the average unchanged. Theorem 17.16.25 . 944944D6FF68 For every nonzero constant $c$, the full Perron segment $u_ t=ct$ is stationary for the raw action, whose Hessian has an infinite-dimensional negative subspace. The infimum of raw lengths over all smooth strictly positive paths from $0$ to $c$ is strictly smaller than $d_ B(0,c)=\sqrt{2n}|c|$. Proof. The constant path is basic, equals the chord, and is the full Perron segment by corollary 17.16.14 . Its stationarity also follows from proposition 17.16.22 . Let $w(t,r)$ be smooth, two-periodic in $r$, and zero at $t=0,1$. The paths $ct+\varepsilon w$ have positive spatial forms for sufficiently small $|\varepsilon |$. Expanding ( 17.16.24 ) to second order gives \[  2n\int _0^1\left\langle w_ t^2+2cw_ t(dw_ r+w_{rr}) +c^2\left(\frac{d(d-1)}2w_ r^2+dw_ rw_{rr}\right) \right\rangle \mathrm dt.  \] The integral of $w_ rw_{rr}$ over a period vanishes, while $\int _0^1\langle w_ tw_{rr}\rangle \mathrm dt =-\frac12[\langle w_ r^2\rangle ]_0^1=0$. Completing the square gives the Hessian F20F3B72C244 17.16.26 \begin{equation}  2n\int _0^1\left\langle (w_ t+dcw_ r)^2-\frac{d(d+1)}2c^2w_ r^2 \right\rangle \mathrm dt. \end{equation} For a positive integer $k$, take \[  w_ k(t,r)=\sin (\pi t)\cos \bigl (\pi k(r-dct)\bigr ).  \] Then $w_{k,t}+dcw_{k,r}=\pi \cos (\pi t)\cos (\pi k(r-dct))$, and ( 17.16.26 ) is \[  \frac{n\pi ^2}2\left(1-\frac{d(d+1)}2c^2k^2\right).  \] It is negative for all sufficiently large $k$. Distinct modes and their derivatives are orthogonal under the $r$ average, so the quadratic form is negative on every nonzero finite combination of these modes. Each combination gives a positive path for sufficiently small variation parameter and has action strictly below $nc^2$. Its raw length satisfies $L^2\leq 2\mathscr S$ on the unit interval, so it is strictly below $\sqrt{2n}|c|$. $\square$ These competing paths need not be subgeodesics. The strict length inequality does not establish definiteness or completeness of the unrestricted length infimum. For $n=3$ and $c=1$, a concrete path is \[  u_\varepsilon (t,r)=t+\varepsilon \sin (\pi t)\cos \bigl (\pi (r-2t)\bigr ).  \] Its spatial coefficients are at least $1-\pi |\varepsilon |$ and $1-\pi ^2|\varepsilon |$. Its exact action is 00E6402ACAB5 17.16.27 \begin{equation}  \mathscr S(u_\varepsilon ) =3-\frac{3\pi ^2}2\varepsilon ^2+\frac{111\pi ^4}{64}\varepsilon ^4. \end{equation} Indeed, put $f=\sin (\pi t)$, $p=f'$, and $\vartheta =\pi (r-2t)$. Substitute $u_ t=1+\varepsilon (p\cos \vartheta +2\pi f\sin \vartheta )$, $u_ r=-\varepsilon \pi f\sin \vartheta $, and $u_{rr}=-\varepsilon \pi ^2f\cos \vartheta $ into ( 17.16.24 ). Odd powers have zero periodic average. The averaged quadratic coefficient is $(p^2-3\pi ^2f^2-2\pi ^2fp)/2$, and the quartic coefficient is $\pi ^2f^2(p^2+6\pi ^2fp+12\pi ^2f^2)/8$. The identities \[  \begin{gathered} \int _0^1fp\, \mathrm dt=\int _0^1f^3p\, \mathrm dt=0, \\ \int _0^1f^2\, \mathrm dt=\frac12, \quad \int _0^1p^2\, \mathrm dt=\frac{\pi ^2}2,\\ \int _0^1f^4\, \mathrm dt=\frac38, \quad \int _0^1f^2p^2\, \mathrm dt=\frac{\pi ^2}8 \end{gathered}  \] give ( 17.16.27 ). Taking $\varepsilon =1/100$ gives a positive path with action $2.9985212487\ldots <3$.

text: Diagonal projective automorphisms give smooth nonconstant geodesics. For real $a_0,\ldots ,a_{n-1}$, set \[  v_ t([z])=\log \frac{\sum _{j=0}^{n-1}\mathrm e^{ta_ j}|z_ j|^2}{\sum _{j=0}^{n-1}|z_ j|^2}.  \] The family is spatially nonconstant when the $a_ j$ are not all equal. Proposition 17.16.29 . A3E893F6A601 The pullback $\pi ^*v_ t$ is the full Hermitian Perron segment and is stationary under all smooth fixed-endpoint variations. Its distance and action are \[  \begin{aligned}  d_ B(0,\pi ^*v_1)^2& =\frac{2[(\sum _ ja_ j)^2+\sum _ ja_ j^2]}{n+1},\\  \mathscr S(\pi ^*v)& =\mathcal A_ B(\pi ^*v) =\frac{(\sum _ ja_ j)^2+\sum _ ja_ j^2}{n+1}. \end{aligned}  \] Proof. On the strip, the holomorphic map $F([z],s)=[\mathrm e^{a_0s/2}z_0:\cdots :\mathrm e^{a_{n-1}s/2}z_{n-1}]$ satisfies $\operatorname {pr}_ Y^*\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}V=F^*\kappa $. The imaginary-time phases are unitary, so $V$ depends only on $\operatorname{Re}s$. This form has rank $d$, strictly positive spatial slices, and zero $(d+1)$st power. The classical bounded Kähler Dirichlet uniqueness identifies it with the base Perron segment; proposition 17.16.16 , proposition 17.16.22 give the full segment and its stationarity. For $x_ j=|z_ j|^2/\sum |z_ j|^2$, the initial velocity is $\sum _ ja_ jx_ j$. A standard complex Gaussian vector has independent exponential squared coordinates, and its projective direction has distribution $\kappa ^ d$. Dividing those coordinates by their sum gives the uniform simplex distribution, with moments \[  \int _ Yx_ i^2\kappa ^ d=\frac2{n(n+1)}, \qquad \int _ Yx_ ix_ j\kappa ^ d=\frac1{n(n+1)}\quad (i\ne j).  \] The smooth distance formula and ( 17.16.20 ) give the claimed squared distance; the action is half of it. $\square$ For instance, $n=3$ and $(a_0,a_1,a_2)=(1,-1,0)$ give squared distance one and action $1/2$. The completed space also contains potentials with different ordinary singularity types. Put $o=[1:0:\cdots :0]\in Y$ and \[  \psi =\log \frac{\sum _{j=1}^ d|z_ j|^2}{\sum _{j=0}^ d|z_ j|^2}, \qquad v_ a=1-(1-\psi )^ a,\qquad 0<a<1,  \] with the canonical value $v_ a(o)=-\infty $. Proposition 17.16.30 . 9355B610E2C3 Every $v_ a$ has non-pluripolar mass one, and \[  v_ a\in \mathcal E^2(Y,\kappa ) \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad a<\frac d{d+2}.  \] At equality its squared energy diverges logarithmically. The pullback has mass $2n$ and pole set $\pi ^{-1}(o)$. If $0<a<b<d/(d+2)$, the two pullbacks have different ordinary singularity types and finite positive $d_ B$ distance. Proof. In the chart $z_0=1$, write $s=\log |z'|^2$, $L=\log (1+\mathrm e^ s)$, $P=\mathrm e^ s/(1+\mathrm e^ s)$, and $T=1+L-s\geq 1$. The local potential $\Phi =L+1-T^ a$ has derivative \[  A=P+a(1-P)T^{a-1},\qquad A'=P'(1-aT^{a-1})+a(1-a)(1-P)^2T^{a-2}>0.  \] Both $A$ and $A'$ are positive, so the radial complex Hessian is positive. Its bounded-above local potential extends plurisubharmonically across $o$ by lemma 5.24.7 . The function extends smoothly across the hyperplane at infinity. Its bounded plurisubharmonic truncations decrease to a nontrivial canonical potential: near $o$, $|v_ a|=O((1-s)^ a)$ is integrable against radial smooth volume $O(\mathrm e^{ds})\, \mathrm ds$. The radial mass flux is $Q(s)=A(s)^ d$. Its sphere coefficient is one, since $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\log |z'|^2$ integrates to one on the Hopf circle and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z'|^2$ induces mass-one Fubini–Study on $\mathbb P^{d-1}$. Stokes on an annulus gives mass $Q(s_2)-Q(s_1)$. Since $Q(-\infty )=0$ and $Q(+\infty )=1$, finite-level locality and annular exhaustion give non-pluripolar mass one. The pole has no atom, and smoothness gives no mass on the hyperplane at infinity. As $s\to -\infty $, \[  |v_ a|^2\sim T^{2a},\qquad Q'(s)\sim d a^ d(1-a)T^{-d(1-a)-1},\qquad T\sim 1-s.  \] The squared energy therefore converges exactly when $2a-d(1-a)<0$. At equality the integrand has order $T^{-1}$, giving logarithmic divergence. All other compact regions have smooth potentials and measures. Fiber integration gives the pullback assertions. Finally, $v_ a-v_ b=T^ b-T^ a\to +\infty $ at $o$, so mutual bounded comparison fails. Both points lie in the completed metric space and are distinct, giving finite positive distance. $\square$

text: The distance just constructed retains information about the potentials that their ordinary model projection forgets. This distinction connects the example with the singularity spaces studied earlier and with the Legendre construction in the next chapter. Proposition 17.16.32 . DE987FD1A354 For every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\kappa )$, \[  P_\omega [\pi ^*v]=\pi ^*P_\kappa [v].  \] Consequently every point of $\mathcal B_2$ has ordinary model projection zero. Pullback commutes with the forward and backward Legendre transforms of base ordinary model test curves. If a base Perron ray has every finite slice, including its initial potential, in $\mathcal E^2(Y,\kappa )$, each finite segment of its pullback is a $d_ B$ geodesic and minimizes the metric action with its prescribed endpoints. Proof. For finite $C$, the obstacle $\pi ^*\min (v+C,0)$ and the full competitor family are invariant under $E$. The same argument as in proposition 17.16.16 gives \[  P_\omega (\pi ^*\min (v+C,0)) =\pi ^*P_\kappa (\min (v+C,0)).  \] Increasing limits and their upper semicontinuous regularizations commute with pullback in submersion charts, proving the model identity. The classical full-mass characterization on $Y$ gives $P_\kappa [v]=0$ for every $v\in \mathcal E^2$, hence the assertion for $\mathcal B_2$. Pullback preserves parameterwise concavity, order, ordinary-model normalization and cutoff values of a base model test curve. It commutes with pointwise infima, and the submersion property makes it commute with upper semicontinuous regularization of suprema. Thus it commutes with both Legendre transforms. Finally, the Perron descent identifies every finite ray segment with the full Hermitian segment; its finite-energy endpoints and theorem 17.16.19 , proposition 17.16.22 give the geodesic and minimizing assertions. $\square$ For ordinary-equivalent endpoints, theorem 17.16.7 already gives their common type throughout the segment. The basic mass formula computes the mass of a chosen basic potential; it does not compute the lower or upper volume of its entire ordinary type, which also includes nonbasic potentials. A separating complete metric on all ordinary models, with compatibility under modifications and changes of background, remains open.

title: 17.17 Test curves and Legendre duality
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form. Fix $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ with $P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi $, where $P_\theta [\cdot ]$ is the ordinary singularity envelope of definition 5.40.4 ; thus $\varphi \leq 0$ and $\sup _ X\varphi =0$. A fixed smooth positive volume form defines the $L^1(X)$ topology. Legendre duality in the parameter exchanges two maximality conditions: each member of a test curve is a fixed point of the singularity envelope, while every finite segment of the corresponding ray is a Perron segment in the sense of section 17.16 . Replacing a finite segment of the ray by the Perron segment with the same endpoints changes each inverse transform only by a bounded amount, so the envelope condition forces Perron maximality. Conversely, comparison with affine paths built from obstacle envelopes shows that the inverse transforms of a ray of Perron segments are envelope fixed points. The argument uses only convexity, the minimum principle and the Perron construction, and therefore applies to nonclosed backgrounds as well as to Kähler forms. The transforms are the pointwise Legendre transforms of subsection 5.41.4 , and the proofs follow the envelope arguments for the Ross–Witt Nyström correspondence in 17.13 Ross–Witt Nyström correspondence .

title: 17.17.1 Envelope test curves and rays
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: The members of a test curve become more singular as the parameter increases. The cutoff of the curve becomes the slope of the transformed ray, while its limit as the parameter tends to $-\infty $ gives the initial potential. Definition 17.17.2 . 7D4FF1072CEF An envelope test curve with initial potential $\varphi $ consists of a real number $c$ and potentials $\Gamma _\tau \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ for $\tau <c$ such that $\tau \mapsto \Gamma _\tau $ is pointwise concave and decreasing; $P_\theta [\Gamma _\tau ]=\Gamma _\tau $ for every $\tau <c$; $(\sup _{\tau <c}\Gamma _\tau )^*=\varphi $. Its cutoff is $c$. We extend it by \[  \Gamma _ c=\lim _{\tau \uparrow c}\Gamma _\tau , \qquad \Gamma _\tau \equiv -\infty \quad (\tau >c).  \] Each $\Gamma _\tau $ is an envelope fixed point and hence has supremum zero, so theorem 5.25.2 , corollary 5.25.3 give $\Gamma _ c\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Definition 17.17.3 . ECDB430D0021 An envelope ray with initial potential $\varphi $ and slope $c$ is a subgeodesic $u_ t$, $t>0$, such that $u_ t\to \varphi $ in $L^1(X)$ as $t\downarrow 0$, and, with $u_0=\varphi $, the restriction of the ray to every interval $(a,b)$ with $0\leq a<b<\infty $ is the Perron segment from $u_ a$ to $u_ b$; $P_\theta [u_ t]=\varphi $ for every $t>0$; $\sup _ Xu_ t=ct$ for every $t>0$. For an envelope test curve, write $U_ t$ for its forward transform ( 5.41.6 ), the pointwise supremum of $\Gamma _\tau +t\tau $ over $\tau <c$. For a family $(u_ t)_{t>0}$, write $\widehat u_\tau $ for its inverse transform ( 5.41.7 ), the pointwise infimum of $u_ t-t\tau $ over $t>0$. title: 17.17.4 Perron maximality
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: The slope and the singularity envelope of the transformed ray follow directly from the normalization of the test curve. To prove Perron maximality, we replace the transform on a finite interval by the Perron segment with the same endpoints. The estimate ( 17.17.6 ) keeps each inverse transform in its original ordinary singularity type, where the envelope condition forces equality. Theorem 17.17.5 . 548B64628B04 The forward transform of an envelope test curve with cutoff $c$ is an envelope ray with the same initial potential and slope $c$. Moreover, $U_ t-ct$ decreases as $t$ increases. Proof. By theorem 5.41.9 , $U_ t$ is a subgeodesic. The inequalities \[  \Gamma _\tau +t\tau \leq U_ t\leq \varphi +ct  \] give $\sup _ XU_ t\geq t\tau $ for each $\tau <c$, since $\sup _ X\Gamma _\tau =0$, and $\sup _ XU_ t\leq ct$. Letting $\tau \uparrow c$ proves $\sup _ XU_ t=ct$. The formula \[  U_ t-ct=\sup _{\tau <c}\bigl (\Gamma _\tau -t(c-\tau )\bigr )  \] shows that $U_ t-ct$ is decreasing in $t$. Since $\Gamma _\tau \preceq U_ t\preceq \varphi $, monotonicity of the singularity envelope gives \[  \Gamma _\tau =P_\theta [\Gamma _\tau ]\leq P_\theta [U_ t] \leq P_\theta [\varphi ]=\varphi .  \] Taking the regularized supremum in $\tau $ proves $P_\theta [U_ t]=\varphi $. The local envelope theorem in section 5.40 gives $\sup _{\tau <c}\Gamma _\tau =\varphi $ almost everywhere, and at those points the bounds $\Gamma _\tau +t\tau \leq U_ t\leq \varphi +ct$ imply $U_ t\to \varphi $ as $t\downarrow 0$. For any fixed $\tau _0<c$ and $0<t\leq 1$, they also give \[  \Gamma _{\tau _0}-|\tau _0|\leq U_ t\leq \varphi +|c|.  \] Both bounds are integrable, so dominated convergence gives $U_ t\to \varphi $ in $L^1$ as $t\downarrow 0$. It remains to prove Perron maximality. Fix $0\leq a<b$ and replace $U_ t$ on $(a,b)$ by the Perron segment from $U_ a$ to $U_ b$, with $U_0=\varphi $ when $a=0$; it exists by proposition 17.16.6 , because the restriction of $U_ t$ itself runs between these endpoints. The joint upper limits of the Perron segment at $a$ and $b$ allow gluing by lemma 5.24.2 , proposition 17.16.3 . The resulting subgeodesic $v_ t$ dominates $U_ t$ and equals it outside $(a,b)$, where therefore $v_ t\leq ct$. On $(a,b)$, the chord bound ( 17.16.4 ) together with $U_ a\leq ca$ and $U_ b\leq cb$ gives $v_ t\leq ct$ as well. For $\tau <c$, put $\chi _\tau =\inf _{t>0}(v_ t-t\tau )$. Since $v_ t-t\tau \geq U_ t-t\tau \geq \Gamma _\tau $, proposition 5.41.3 gives $\chi _\tau \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. We claim that DD25DD31A00B 17.17.6 \begin{equation}  \Gamma _\tau \leq \chi _\tau \leq \Gamma _\tau +(b-a)(c-\tau ). \end{equation} The first inequality was just noted. For the second, let $s>0$. If $s\in [a,b]$, then $v_ b=U_ b$, and since $U_ t-ct$ is decreasing, \[  \chi _\tau \leq U_ b-b\tau \leq U_ s-s\tau +(b-s)(c-\tau ).  \] If $s\notin [a,b]$, then $\chi _\tau \leq v_ s-s\tau =U_ s-s\tau $. In both cases $\chi _\tau \leq U_ s-s\tau +(b-a)(c-\tau )$. Taking the infimum over $s>0$ and using lemma 5.41.8 proves ( 17.17.6 ). Moreover, $v_ t\leq ct$ gives $\chi _\tau \leq t(c-\tau )$ for every $t>0$, hence $\chi _\tau \leq 0$. By ( 17.17.6 ), $\chi _\tau $ has the ordinary type of $\Gamma _\tau $, so it is a competitor for $P_\theta [\Gamma _\tau ]=\Gamma _\tau $. Thus $\chi _\tau =\Gamma _\tau $. Recovering $v_ t$ from its inverse transforms by lemma 5.41.5 gives $v_ t=U_ t$, which proves Perron maximality on every finite interval. $\square$

title: 17.17.7 Recovering the singularity envelopes
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: The minimum principle shows that the inverse transforms are $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, but their envelope property uses the whole ray. For an inverse transform $g$ and $C>0$, the envelope $P_\theta (g+C,0)$ of the obstacle $\min (g+C,0)$ gives an admissible affine path on every interval $[0,M]$, lying below the ray translated by an affine function of $t$. Letting the length $M$ vary, and then letting the relative time $t/M$ tend to zero, removes the additive constant $C$. Theorem 17.17.8 . 062DEC0E6527 If $u_ t$ is an envelope ray of slope $c$ with initial potential $\varphi $, its inverse transform is an envelope test curve with cutoff $c$ and initial potential $\varphi $. The forward and inverse transforms are mutually inverse bijections between the envelope test curves of definition 17.17.2 and the envelope rays of definition 17.17.3 with initial potential $\varphi $. Proof. By lemma 5.41.1 , for each $x$ the function $t\mapsto u_ t(x)-ct$ is either finite and convex or identically $-\infty $. It is bounded above by zero, so it is decreasing. Since $\sup _ X(u_ t-ct)=0$, theorem 5.25.2 , corollary 5.25.3 give \[  \widehat u_ c=\inf _{t>0}(u_ t-ct)\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta ).  \] For $\tau <c$, we have $\widehat u_ c\leq \widehat u_\tau \leq u_1-\tau $, so proposition 5.41.3 gives $\widehat u_\tau \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Also \[  \widehat u_\tau \leq \inf _{t>0}t(c-\tau )=0 \quad (\tau \leq c),  \] while the bound $\widehat u_\tau \leq t(c-\tau )$ with $t\to \infty $ shows $\widehat u_\tau \equiv -\infty $ for $\tau >c$. Concavity and monotonicity in $\tau $ hold because $\widehat u_\tau $ is an infimum of affine functions of $\tau $ with negative slopes $-t$. Fix $\tau <c$ and write $g=\widehat u_\tau $. The inequality $g\leq u_ M-M\tau $, valid for every $M>0$, gives \[  P_\theta [g]\leq P_\theta [u_ M]=\varphi .  \] For $C>0$ put $q_ C=P_\theta (g+C,0)$. Since $g\leq 0$, the function $g$ is a competitor, so $q_ C\not\equiv -\infty $, and \[  g\leq q_ C\leq P_\theta [g]\leq \varphi , \qquad q_ C-C\leq g\leq u_ M-M\tau .  \] The affine path $q_ C-Ct/M$ is admissible for the endpoints $\varphi $ and $u_ M-M\tau $ on $[0,M]$. Adding $-t\tau $ gives a bijection between the competitor families for the endpoints $\varphi ,u_ M$ and $\varphi ,u_ M-M\tau $, by proposition 17.16.2 , so the Perron segment for the latter endpoints is $u_ t-t\tau $. For $0<s\leq 1$ this yields \[  q_ C-Cs\leq u_{sM}-sM\tau .  \] Taking the infimum over $M>0$ gives $q_ C-Cs\leq g$, and letting $s\downarrow 0$ gives $q_ C\leq g$. Thus $q_ C=g$ for every $C>0$, and letting $C\to \infty $ in the definition of $P_\theta [g]$ proves $P_\theta [g]=g$. Let $\psi =(\sup _{\tau <c}\widehat u_\tau )^*$; since $\widehat u_\tau =P_\theta [\widehat u_\tau ]\leq \varphi $, we have $\psi \leq \varphi $. Because $u_ t-ct$ is decreasing in $t$, the limit of $u_ t(x)$ as $t\downarrow 0$ exists at every $x$, and an almost everywhere convergent sequence given by the $L^1$ convergence $u_ t\to \varphi $ identifies it with $\varphi $ almost everywhere. At these points, the endpoint identity in lemma 5.41.5 gives \[  \sup _{\tau <c}\inf _{t>0}(u_ t(x)-t\tau )=\varphi (x).  \] Therefore $\psi =\varphi $ by lemma 5.24.3 . As $\tau \uparrow c$, the transforms decrease to $\widehat u_ c$, since the infima over $t>0$ and over $\tau <c$ commute; this is the convention for the value at the cutoff. Finally, lemma 5.41.5 recovers $u_ t$ from its inverse transforms, also at points where $t\mapsto u_ t(x)$ is identically $-\infty $, and lemma 5.41.8 recovers each test curve from its forward transform. Hence the correspondence is a bijection. $\square$

title: 17.17.9 A logarithmic pole on the projective line
search_title: A logarithmic pole on the projective line
topic: Energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves
text: Let $X=\mathbb P^1$ and $\varphi =0$. The envelope of a multiple of a logarithmic pole is obtained by replacing part of a convex function by a tangent line. The corresponding ray is smooth, and all its slices are bounded; the pole appears only in the behavior of the ray as $t\to \infty $. In the affine coordinate $z$, take \[  \theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2),\qquad g(z)=\log \frac{|z|^2}{1+|z|^2}.  \] The form $\theta $ extends to the Fubini–Study form of $\mathbb P^1$, which has integral one. The potential $g$ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, has a logarithmic pole at zero, and extends smoothly across infinity, with value zero there. Put $H(\lambda )=-\lambda \log \lambda -(1-\lambda )\log (1-\lambda )$ for $0<\lambda <1$, with $H(0)=H(1)=0$. For $0<\lambda <1$, define 3B7363400CA2 17.17.10 \begin{equation}  \Gamma _\lambda (z)= \begin{cases}  \lambda \log |z|^2-\log (1+|z|^2)+H(\lambda ), &  |z|^2\leq \lambda /(1-\lambda ),\\  0, &  |z|^2\geq \lambda /(1-\lambda ). \end{cases} \end{equation} Set $\Gamma _\lambda =0$ for $\lambda \leq 0$, $\Gamma _1=g$, and $\Gamma _\lambda =-\infty $ for $\lambda >1$. Proposition 17.17.11 . 377F0AD20B28 The family $(\Gamma _\lambda )$ is an envelope test curve with initial potential zero and cutoff one. Its forward transform is 9BA75154C113 17.17.12 \begin{equation}  U_ t(z)=\log \frac{1+\mathrm{e}^ t|z|^2}{1+|z|^2},\qquad t>0. \end{equation} At $z=0$ its value is zero, and at infinity its value is $t$. Proof. Fix $0<\lambda <1$. For $s=\log |z|^2$, let $q_\lambda (s)=\Gamma _\lambda (z)+\log (1+\mathrm{e}^ s)$. In the first region of ( 17.17.10 ) this is the affine function $\lambda s+H(\lambda )$, which is tangent to $\log (1+\mathrm{e}^ s)$ at $s_\lambda =\log (\lambda /(1-\lambda ))$, and in the second region it is $\log (1+\mathrm{e}^ s)$. Its derivative is continuous at the junction and nondecreasing, so $q_\lambda $ is convex. By corollary 5.41.2 , $\Gamma _\lambda $ is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic away from zero, and it extends across its logarithmic pole by lemma 5.24.7 . It vanishes near infinity and has the ordinary type of $\lambda g$. To prove $\Gamma _\lambda =P_\theta [\lambda g]$, let $v\leq 0$ be a competitor with $v\preceq \lambda g$. On the punctured disk $0<|z|^2<\lambda /(1-\lambda )$, the function \[  v-\Gamma _\lambda =v+\log (1+|z|^2)-\lambda \log |z|^2-H(\lambda )  \] is subharmonic, since $v+\log (1+|z|^2)$ is subharmonic and $\log |z|^2$ is harmonic there. Since $v\preceq \lambda g$, this difference is bounded above near zero, so it extends subharmonically across zero by lemma 5.24.7 . Its upper limits at the boundary circle are at most zero, since $v\leq 0$ and $\Gamma _\lambda =0$ there. The maximum principle gives $v\leq \Gamma _\lambda $ on the disk (at zero both have the value $-\infty $), and outside the disk the same inequality follows from $\Gamma _\lambda =0$. Thus every competitor lies below $\Gamma _\lambda $, which is itself a competitor, so $\Gamma _\lambda =P_\theta [\lambda g]$. Since the envelope depends only on the ordinary type, also $P_\theta [\Gamma _\lambda ]=\Gamma _\lambda $. The zero potential is an envelope fixed point as well. For a fixed $0<|z|<\infty $, put $p=|z|^2/(1+|z|^2)$. The function $\lambda \mapsto \Gamma _\lambda (z)$ is zero for $\lambda \leq p$. For $p<\lambda <1$ its derivative is \[  \log |z|^2+\log \frac{1-\lambda }{\lambda }.  \] It vanishes at $\lambda =p$ and decreases in $\lambda $, which proves that $\lambda \mapsto \Gamma _\lambda (z)$ is concave and decreasing. At $z=0$, the function is zero for $\lambda \leq 0$ and $-\infty $ for $\lambda >0$; at $z=\infty $, it is zero for $\lambda \leq 1$. These functions are concave and decreasing as well. Finally, $\sup _{\lambda <1}\Gamma _\lambda =0$, and the limit as $\lambda \uparrow 1$ is $g$, so the family is an envelope test curve with cutoff one. For finite nonzero $z$ and $t>0$, the supremum defining $U_ t(z)$ is attained at a parameter $\lambda >p$, namely at \[  \lambda =\frac{\mathrm{e}^ t|z|^2}{1+\mathrm{e}^ t|z|^2},  \] and substituting this value into the first line of ( 17.17.10 ) gives ( 17.17.12 ). At $z=0$, only the parameters $\lambda \leq 0$ give finite values, and the supremum is zero; at $z=\infty $, the supremum of $t\lambda $ over $\lambda <1$ is $t$. In the coordinate $w=1/z$, the formula reads $\log ((|w|^2+\mathrm e^ t)/(|w|^2+1))$, so the ray is smooth in both charts. $\square$ Each slice of this ray is bounded and has envelope zero, whereas its inverse transforms for $0<\lambda \leq 1$ have logarithmic poles. At $z=0$, the parameters $\lambda \leq 0$ determine the transform: omitting them would give the wrong value $U_ t(0)=-\infty $. Since $v\preceq \lambda g$, this difference is bounded above near zero, so it extends subharmonically across zero by lemma 5.24.7 . Its upper limits at the boundary circle are at most zero, since $v\leq 0$ and $\Gamma _\lambda =0$ there. The maximum principle gives $v\leq \Gamma _\lambda $ on the disk (at zero both have the value $-\infty $), and outside the disk the same inequality follows from $\Gamma _\lambda =0$. Thus every competitor lies below $\Gamma _\lambda $, which is itself a competitor, so $\Gamma _\lambda =P_\theta [\lambda g]$. Since the envelope depends only on the ordinary type, also $P_\theta [\Gamma _\lambda ]=\Gamma _\lambda $. The zero potential is an envelope fixed point as well. For a fixed $0<|z|<\infty $, put $p=|z|^2/(1+|z|^2)$. The function $\lambda \mapsto \Gamma _\lambda (z)$ is zero for $\lambda \leq p$. For $p<\lambda <1$ its derivative is \[  \log |z|^2+\log \frac{1-\lambda }{\lambda }.  \] It vanishes at $\lambda =p$ and decreases in $\lambda $, which proves that $\lambda \mapsto \Gamma _\lambda (z)$ is concave and decreasing. At $z=0$, the function is zero for $\lambda \leq 0$ and $-\infty $ for $\lambda >0$; at $z=\infty $, it is zero for $\lambda \leq 1$. These functions are concave and decreasing as well. Finally, $\sup _{\lambda <1}\Gamma _\lambda =0$, and the limit as $\lambda \uparrow 1$ is $g$, so the family is an envelope test curve with cutoff one. For finite nonzero $z$ and $t>0$, the supremum defining $U_ t(z)$ is attained at a parameter $\lambda >p$, namely at \[  \lambda =\frac{\mathrm{e}^ t|z|^2}{1+\mathrm{e}^ t|z|^2},  \] and substituting this value into the first line of ( 17.17.10 ) gives ( 17.17.12 ). At $z=0$, only the parameters $\lambda \leq 0$ give finite values, and the supremum is zero; at $z=\infty $, the supremum of $t\lambda $ over $\lambda <1$ is $t$. In the coordinate $w=1/z$, the formula reads $\log ((|w|^2+\mathrm e^ t)/(|w|^2+1))$, so the ray is smooth in both charts. $\square$

title: 20.3 Restriction and intrinsic trace data
text: Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold, let $Y\subset X$ be a connected compact complex submanifold of positive dimension, and fix a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $u\in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ whose generic Lelong number along $Y$ vanishes: $\nu (u,Y)=\inf _{y\in Y}\nu (u,y)=0$. Even when all multiplier ideals of $u$ are trivial, its restriction to $Y$ can have logarithmic poles. To keep only information determined by the multiplier ideals of $u$ on $X$, we restrict the ideals themselves and take their asymptotic vanishing orders on modifications of $Y$. These orders form the divisorial trace data. Subadditivity of multiplier ideals and analytic approximation make the trace data additive under sums of potentials. The next question is whether a potential on $Y$ realizes these numbers. On a curve, they form an atomic measure, whose Green potential has exactly the prescribed Lelong numbers. In higher dimension, restricted analytic envelopes converge to the largest potential satisfying the trace inequalities, but Lelong semicontinuity gives only a lower bound for its divisorial Lelong numbers. When $Y$ is Kähler, convergence in a sufficiently large closed background gives the reverse bound. Pullback from a curve gives another exact realization on non-Kähler targets. On a scalar Hopf manifold, elliptic symmetry and extraction of divisors on its projective base extend this construction to projective pullback data of arbitrary dimension. The product examples show that exact trace data still does not determine the Monge–Ampère mass. The final ruled family computes both mass extremes within one unbounded ordinary type, and a blowup separates positivity of its lower volume from existence of a strict current in that type. Choose a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ with $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$. We use the analytic approximants $u_ m$ of corollary 5.36.2 : they have analytic type $(1/m,\mathcal I(mu))$ in the sense of section 5.34 and satisfy $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ m\geq -\epsilon _ m\omega $ with $\epsilon _ m\downarrow 0$. By corollary 5.43.26 , their restrictions to $Y$ are quasi-plurisubharmonic, in particular not identically $-\infty $. As in section 13.14 , $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ denotes the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure, also written $\mathrm{MA}$ when its total mass is finite.

title: 20.3.1 Restricted ideals and trace data
text:
The restriction of a multiplier ideal to $Y$ records the vanishing of its local generators along $Y$. Its vanishing order along a divisor on a modification of $Y$ can grow with the weight, even when the ideal is generically trivial on $Y$. For $t>0$ put \[  \mathfrak a_ t(u;Y)=\mathcal I(tu)\mathcal O_ Y.  \] Here $\mathcal I(tu)\mathcal O_ Y$ denotes the image of $\mathcal I(tu)$ under the restriction map $\mathcal O_ X	o \mathcal O_ Y$. This is a coherent ideal sheaf on $Y$, and it is nonzero: since $
u (u,Y)=0$, there is $y\in Y$ with $
u (u,y)<1/t$, and Skoda's integrability theorem gives $\mathcal I(tu)_ y=\mathcal O_{X,y}$. In this chapter, a divisor over $Y$ is a prime divisor $E$ on a connected smooth compact modification $\pi :Z	o Y$. For a nonzero coherent ideal $\mathfrak a$ on $Y$, let $\operatorname {ord}_ E(\mathfrak a)$ be the generic vanishing order along $E$ of the ideal generated by its pullback to $Z$; it is a nonnegative integer. Theorem 20.3.2 . 7CD874C73EC9 For every divisor $E$ over $Y$, the limit 66AFB7F7397B 20.3.3  egin{equation}  	au _{Y,u}(E) :=\lim _{t	o \infty } rac{\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathfrak a_ t(u;Y)}{t} =\sup _{t>0} rac{\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathfrak a_ t(u;Y)}{t} \end{equation} exists and is finite, and it equals the limit along positive integers. These numbers depend only on the multiplier-ideal equivalence class of $u$ on $X$. Proof. Fix the modification $\pi :Z	o Y$ carrying $E$, and write $b(t)=\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathfrak a_ t(u;Y)$ for $t>0$. For $s,t>0$, the subadditivity of multiplier ideals (the second inclusion in ( 5.37.6 )), followed by restriction to $Y$, gives \[  \mathfrak a_{s+t}\subseteq \mathfrak a_ s\mathfrak a_ t, \qquad b(s+t)\geq b(s)+b(t).  \] Moreover, $b(t)\geq 0$. For fixed $s>0$ and $t=ks+r$ with $k$ a nonnegative integer and $0\leq r<s$, repeated superadditivity gives $b(t)\geq k b(s)$. Hence \[  \liminf _{t	o \infty } rac{b(t)}t\geq  rac{b(s)}s.  \] Taking the supremum over $s$ proves the existence of the limit and the supremum formula, with the value $+\infty $ allowed at this stage. In particular, the limit along positive integers is the same. For every sufficiently large integer $m$, the restriction $u_ m|_ Y$ has analytic type $(1/m,\mathfrak a_ m(u;Y))$ by section 5.34 , and therefore \[   rac{b(m)}m =
u  igl ((u_ m|_ Y)\circ \pi ,E igr ).  \] These numbers are uniformly bounded by corollary 5.43.26 , so the limit along integers, and hence the supremum, is finite. Finally, the ideals $\mathfrak a_ t(u;Y)$ are unchanged when $u$ is replaced by a potential with the same multiplier ideals, which proves the last assertion. $\square$ We call the function $E\mapsto 	au _{Y,u}(E)$, defined on all divisors over $Y$, the divisorial trace data of $u$ along $Y$. Inclusions of ideals give monotonicity and homogeneity of the trace data directly. For sums, subadditivity of multiplier ideals gives one inequality; for the reverse inequality, an analytic approximant of the sum controls sufficiently fine approximants of both summands. Proposition 20.3.4 . 89D22AB4CBD8 Let $v\in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ also have zero generic Lelong number along $Y$, and recall that $u\preceq _{\mathcal I}v$ means $\mathcal I(ku)\subseteq \mathcal I(kv)$ for every real $k>0$ (section 5.33 ). Then, as functions on divisors over $Y$, $u\preceq _{\mathcal I}v$ implies $	au _{Y,u}\geq 	au _{Y,v}$; $	au _{Y,au}=a	au _{Y,u}$ for every $a>0$; $	au _{Y,u+v}=	au _{Y,u}+	au _{Y,v}$; $	au _{Y,\max (u,v)}\leq \min \{ 	au _{Y,u},	au _{Y,v}\} $. Proof. The inclusions of ideals defining $\preceq _{\mathcal I}$ persist after restriction and reverse the vanishing orders, which proves (1). Replacing $t$ by $at$ in ( 20.3.3 ) proves (2). Moreover, \[  \mathcal I(tu)+\mathcal I(tv)\subseteq \mathcal I(t\max (u,v)).  \] Since the order of a sum of ideals is the minimum of their orders, restriction and passage to the limit prove (4); note that $\max (u,v)$ also has zero generic Lelong number along $Y$. Generic Lelong numbers of sums add, so $u+v$ has zero generic Lelong number along $Y$ as well. For (3), subadditivity of multiplier ideals gives $	au _{Y,u+v}\geq 	au _{Y,u}+	au _{Y,v}$. For the reverse inequality, fix a sufficiently large integer $k$ and the analytic approximant $S_ k$ of $u+v$ given by theorem 5.36.1 , of analytic type $(1/k,\mathcal I(k(u+v)))$; that theorem gives $u+v\leq S_ k$. Let $U_ m,V_ m$ be the corresponding approximants of $u$ and $v$. Lemma 5.38.12 gives \[  U_ m+V_ m\leq (1-\delta _ m)S_ k+O(1),\qquad \delta _ m\downarrow 0.  \] Here both $\delta _ m$ and the bounded error may depend on the fixed $k$. The restrictions of $U_ m$, $V_ m$ and $S_ k$ to $Y$ are not identically $-\infty $ by corollary 5.43.26 . Restricting, pulling back to a fixed modification and taking the generic Lelong number along a divisor $E$ on it, we obtain \[   rac{\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathfrak a_ m(u;Y)}m + rac{\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathfrak a_ m(v;Y)}m \geq (1-\delta _ m)  rac{\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathfrak a_ k(u+v;Y)}k.  \] Letting first $m	o \infty $, with $k$ fixed, and then $k	o \infty $, the finite limits of theorem 20.3.2 give the reverse inequality. $\square$

title: Theorem 20.3.2
text: Theorem 20.3.2 . 7CD874C73EC9 For every divisor $E$ over $Y$, the limit 66AFB7F7397B 20.3.3 \begin{equation}  \tau _{Y,u}(E) :=\lim _{t\to \infty }\frac{\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathfrak a_ t(u;Y)}{t} =\sup _{t>0}\frac{\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathfrak a_ t(u;Y)}{t} \end{equation} exists and is finite, and it equals the limit along positive integers. These numbers depend only on the multiplier-ideal equivalence class of $u$ on $X$. Proof. Fix the modification $\pi :Z\to Y$ carrying $E$, and write $b(t)=\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathfrak a_ t(u;Y)$ for $t>0$. For $s,t>0$, the subadditivity of multiplier ideals (the second inclusion in ( 5.37.6 )), followed by restriction to $Y$, gives \[  \mathfrak a_{s+t}\subseteq \mathfrak a_ s\mathfrak a_ t, \qquad b(s+t)\geq b(s)+b(t).  \] Moreover, $b(t)\geq 0$. For fixed $s>0$ and $t=ks+r$ with $k$ a nonnegative integer and $0\leq r<s$, repeated superadditivity gives $b(t)\geq k b(s)$. Hence \[  \liminf _{t\to \infty }\frac{b(t)}t\geq \frac{b(s)}s.  \] Taking the supremum over $s$ proves the existence of the limit and the supremum formula, with the value $+\infty $ allowed at this stage. In particular, the limit along positive integers is the same. For every sufficiently large integer $m$, the restriction $u_ m|_ Y$ has analytic type $(1/m,\mathfrak a_ m(u;Y))$ by section 5.34 , and therefore \[  \frac{b(m)}m =\nu \bigl ((u_ m|_ Y)\circ \pi ,E\bigr ).  \] These numbers are uniformly bounded by corollary 5.43.26 , so the limit along integers, and hence the supremum, is finite. Finally, the ideals $\mathfrak a_ t(u;Y)$ are unchanged when $u$ is replaced by a potential with the same multiplier ideals, which proves the last assertion. $\square$

text: Proposition 20.3.4 . 89D22AB4CBD8 Let $v\in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ also have zero generic Lelong number along $Y$, and recall that $u\preceq _{\mathcal I}v$ means $\mathcal I(ku)\subseteq \mathcal I(kv)$ for every real $k>0$ (section 5.33 ). Proof. The inclusions of ideals defining $\preceq _{\mathcal I}$ persist after restriction and reverse the vanishing orders, which proves (1). Replacing $t$ by $at$ in ( 20.3.3 ) proves (2). Let $U_ m,V_ m$ be the corresponding approximants of $u$ and $v$. title: 20.3.5 Comparison with ordinary restriction
text:
When the restriction $u|_ Y$ is not identically $-\infty $, the restriction theorem for multiplier ideals bounds the trace data by its divisorial Lelong numbers. For analytic singularities, comparison with the approximants gives the reverse inequality. Proposition 20.3.6 . FE94B20EED19 If $v=u|_ Y$ is not identically $-\infty $, then \[  	au _{Y,u}(E)\leq 
u (v\circ \pi ,E)  \] for every divisor $E$ over $Y$. If $u$ has analytic singularities, equality holds. Proof. The restriction theorem, which is the first inclusion in ( 5.37.6 ), and lemma 5.38.9 , applied on $Y$, give for every $t>0$ \[  \operatorname {ord}_ E\mathfrak a_ t(u;Y) \leq \operatorname {ord}_ E\mathcal I(tv) \leq t
u (v\circ \pi ,E).  \] Divide by $t$ and use theorem 20.3.2 . If $u$ has analytic singularities, apply lemma 5.38.12 to the pair $(u,0)$, with $s=u$, $U_ m=u_ m$ and $V_ m=0$. It gives \[  u_ m\leq (1-\delta _ m)u+O(1),\qquad \delta _ m\downarrow 0.  \] Restricting to $Y$, pulling back by $\pi $ and taking the generic Lelong number along $E$, we obtain, since $u_ m$ has analytic type $(1/m,\mathcal I(mu))$, \[   rac1m\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathfrak a_ m(u;Y) \geq (1-\delta _ m)
u ((u|_ Y)\circ \pi ,E).  \] Letting $m	o \infty $ proves the reverse inequality, hence equality. All the restrictions involved are quasi-plurisubharmonic, because $
u (u,Y)=0$. $\square$ The inequality can be strict, as the following local example shows. On a small bidisk in $\mathbb C^2$ with coordinates $(z,w)$, write \[  u(z,w)=\max \{ -\log (-\log |z|^2),\  \log |w|^2\} , \qquad Y=\{ z=0\} .  \] The bidisk is chosen with $|z|<\mathrm{e}^{-1}$, and the first function is extended by $-\infty $ along $z=0$. It is plurisubharmonic, since $s\mapsto -\log (-s)$ is increasing and convex for $s<0$, and hence so is the maximum. For every $t>0$, \[  \mathrm{e}^{-tu}\leq (-\log |z|^2)^ t,  \] which is locally integrable. Thus all multiplier ideals of $u$ are trivial and the trace data vanishes, whereas $u|_ Y=\log |w|^2$ has Lelong number one at the origin.

title: 20.3.7 Logarithmic divisors with a small-curvature residual
search_title: Logarithmic divisors with a small-curvature residual
text: An ambient residual can be invisible to every multiplier ideal even when its restriction to $Y$ is identically $-\infty $. The restricted ideals then recover the imposed logarithmic divisor directly. Proposition 20.3.8 . C4231F8A37FD Let $q\in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ satisfy ( 18.27.1 ), and let $\Delta $ and $\sigma _\Delta $ be as in theorem 18.27.4 . For every $t>0$, \[  \mathcal I\bigl (t(\sigma _\Delta +q)\bigr ) =\mathcal I(t\sigma _\Delta ).  \] If $\Delta $ has simple normal crossings and $Y$ is contained in none of its positive-coefficient components, then for every divisor $E$ on every smooth connected compact modification $\rho :Z\to Y$, \[  \tau _{Y,\sigma _\Delta +q}(E) =\sum _ ja_ j\operatorname {ord}_ E\rho ^*(D_ j|_ Y).  \] The formula imposes no condition on the naive restriction $q|_ Y$. Proof. The first equality follows from lemma 18.27.2 , lemma 5.37.5 . In normal crossing coordinates, the weight for $t\sigma _\Delta $ is a smooth positive factor times $\prod _ j|z_ j|^{-2ta_ j}$. One-variable polar integration gives the exact formula \[  \mathcal I(t\sigma _\Delta ) =\mathcal O_ X\left(-\sum _ j\lfloor ta_ j\rfloor D_ j\right).  \] Indeed, integrability of a germ of transverse order $k$ requires $k+1>ta_ j$, so $k\geq \lfloor ta_ j\rfloor $; equality at the preceding order is divergent when $ta_ j$ is an integer. Necessity follows on an open set of the other variables where the leading coefficient is nonzero. After division by these powers, the remaining product weight is integrable, proving sufficiency. Since $Y$ is contained in no $D_ j$, each restricted defining equation is a nonzero holomorphic germ on $Y$. Its pullback to $Z$ is nonzero and has a finite nonnegative order $N_{j,E}$ along $E$. Restriction of the displayed principal ideal and then pullback therefore give the exact order $\sum _ j\lfloor ta_ j\rfloor N_{j,E}$. Dividing by $t$ proves the trace formula, including along all real weights. Moreover $\nu (\sigma _\Delta +q,Y)=0$: outside the finitely many divisors both summands have zero point Lelong number. Thus these orders are the intrinsic data of theorem 20.3.2 . When $\Delta =0$, the ideal is $\mathcal O_ X$ and every trace is zero. $\square$
