title: 20.3.63 Ordinary trace volumes on a nonclosed ruled surface
search_title: Ordinary trace volumes on a nonclosed ruled surface
text: The preceding product formula computes the mass of a separated representative. When the background itself varies along the curve, even bounded changes of the representative can change its mass. On a product of projective lines we can optimize over the entire ordinary singularity type, including potentials depending on both factors. The residual pole will be unbounded with zero Lelong number. Its multiplier ideals see the imposed divisor, whereas its ordinary type also retains this residual pole. In this section let $Y=\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$, let $w$ be the probability Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^1$, and denote its pullbacks by $w_1,w_2$. Fix $p\in \mathbb P^1$, and let $G_ p\leq 0$ be the Green potential satisfying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}G_ p=[p]-w$ and $\sup G_ p=0$. Functions on the first factor are also viewed as functions on $Y$. Put \[  D=\{ p\} \times \mathbb P^1,\qquad U=1-(1-G_ p)^\alpha ,\qquad r=bG_ p+U, \qquad 0<\alpha <1,  \] where $b\geq 0$. The term $bG_ p$ is identically zero when $b=0$. Choose $c>0$ and a smooth positive function $a$ on the first curve, and set 691AF485D1C2 20.3.64 \begin{equation}  \theta =cw_1+aw_2. \end{equation} Thus $\theta $ is Hermitian and is nonclosed precisely when $a$ is nonconstant. The function $r$ specifies an ordinary type; whether that type has $\theta $-plurisubharmonic representatives will follow from the next theorem. Lemma 20.3.65 . 72230836D2EE There are $U_ L\sim U$ with $\sup U_ L=0$, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}U_ L\geq -\epsilon _ Lw$ and $\epsilon _ L\downarrow 0$, such that $U_ L\to 0$ in $L^1(\mathbb P^1)$. Each has zero Lelong number at $p$ and is locally bounded off $p$. Proof. For $t\leq 0$ put $\chi (t)=1-(1-t)^\alpha $. Then \[  \chi '(t)=\alpha (1-t)^{\alpha -1}>0,\qquad \chi ''(t)=\alpha (1-\alpha )(1-t)^{\alpha -2}>0.  \] For $L>0$ set $\epsilon _ L=\chi '(-L)$, $C_ L=-\epsilon _ LL-\chi (-L)$, and define \[  \chi _ L(t)= \begin{cases}  \chi (t)+C_ L,& t<-L,\\  \epsilon _ Lt,& -L\leq t\leq 0. \end{cases}  \] The values and first derivatives match, and $\chi _ L$ is convex and increasing with derivative at most $\epsilon _ L$. Off $p$, the chain rule gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi _ L(G_ p)\geq -\epsilon _ Lw$. Canonical extension across $p$ retains this bound by the removable-singularity theorem, so $U_ L=\chi _ L(G_ p)$ has the required curvature. Near $p$ it differs from $U$ by $C_ L$, and elsewhere both are bounded. Its growth is sublogarithmic, hence its Lelong number is zero. Writing $x=1+L$, we have $C_ L=(1-\alpha )x^\alpha +\alpha x^{\alpha -1}-1\geq 0$. Also $\chi (t)\leq \epsilon _ Lt$ for $-L\leq t\leq 0$, by integrating $\chi '\geq \epsilon _ L$ on this interval. It follows that $U\leq U_ L\leq 0$. Since $\epsilon _ L\to 0$, the functions tend to zero off $p$, and dominated convergence gives the $L^1$ limit. $\square$ Theorem 20.3.66 . 9EDE5892D63B The ordinary type of $r$ has $\theta $-plurisubharmonic representatives if and only if $b<c$. In this range it contains a strict current: some $v\sim r$ satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq \delta (w_1+w_2)$ with $\delta >0$. Every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$ with $v\sim r$ has positive finite extended mass, given by EEBF58093B80 20.3.67 \begin{equation}  \int _ Y\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (v) =\int _ Y\theta ^2-2b a(p)+2\int _ Yv\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\theta . \end{equation} The volumes of definition 16.28.58 are 9099C8F4472B 20.3.68 \begin{equation}  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (v)=2(c-b)\min a, \qquad \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (v)=2(c-b)\max a. \end{equation} Both values are limits of masses of representatives of this ordinary type. Proof. We first remove the logarithmic divisor. If $v\sim r$, then $\nu (v,D)=b$, so lemma 5.38.1 gives $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v-b[D]\geq 0$. Taking $q=v-bG_ p$ in $L^1$ and then its quasi-plurisubharmonic representative gives \[  q\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\beta ),\qquad q\sim U,\qquad \beta =kw_1+aw_2,\qquad k=c-b.  \] Indeed the ordinary inequalities hold off $D$ and extend canonically across it. Conversely such a $q$ gives $v=bG_ p+q$ with \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=b[D]+\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q.  \] Their locally bounded products agree off $D$, and both extended measures give $D$ zero mass. Thus their extended measures agree everywhere. If $k>0$, choose $L$ with $\epsilon _ L<k/2$. The potential $bG_ p+U_ L$ belongs to the specified type and satisfies \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(bG_ p+U_ L) \geq b[D]+(k-\epsilon _ L)w_1+aw_2 \geq \min (k/2,\min a)(w_1+w_2).  \] For necessity, average $q$ over the unitary group acting transitively on the second projective line, with its Haar probability measure. The background is invariant. The average has a genuine first-factor representative $q_0\sim U$ and $kw+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_0\geq 0$. One can first average in $L^1$ and then take the canonical representative; the curvature inequality and the ordinary bounds pass to it. The positive curve measure has total mass $k$, excluding $k<0$. When $k=0$, $q_0$ is harmonic on the compact curve and therefore constant, contradicting $q_0\sim U$. It remains to compute the mass for every competitor, before using the average. Choose a closed Kähler form $K=C(w_1+w_2)\geq \beta $ and a fixed $u_0=U_ L$ as above. The closed positive current $S_0=K+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0$ has no coefficient mass on $D$, since its first-factor curvature has no atom at $p$. The product formula gives \[  \langle S_0\rangle =S_0,\qquad \langle S_0^2\rangle =2C(Cw_1+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0)\wedge w_2, \qquad \int _ Y\langle S_0^2\rangle =\int _ YK^2.  \] For $S=K+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q$, both $S$ and $S_0$ are closed positive currents in the same Kähler class, with bounded difference of potentials and small unbounded locus $D$. The classical closed-class comparison of non-pluripolar products, applied in both singularity orders in degrees one and two, gives \[  \{ \langle S\rangle \} =\{ K\} ,\qquad \int _ Y\langle S^2\rangle =\int _ YK^2.  \] Here the degree-one non-pluripolar current is the restriction of $S$ off $D$ and is closed. Hence the positive current $S-\langle S\rangle $ has zero trace against $K$, and vanishes. This proves $\langle S\rangle =S$. Equivalently, absence of polar coefficient mass follows from proposition 5.46.3 . The closed comparison is used only for $K$. Put $R=\beta -K$. Bedford–Taylor expansion off $D$, followed by extension by zero, now yields \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\beta (q) =\langle S^2\rangle +2R\wedge S+R^2.  \] The first term is finite by closed comparison, the second has finite variation because $S$ has finite trace, and the last is smooth. Since none has coefficient mass on $D$, this is also an identity on $Y$. Distributional Stokes therefore gives F060F71204CB 20.3.69 \begin{equation}  \int _ Y\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\beta (q) =\int _ Y\beta ^2+2\int _ Yq\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\beta =2\int _{\mathbb P^1}a(kw+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_0). \end{equation} The pairing uses only $q\in L^1$. Averaging preserves it, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge w_2$. The last measure is positive of total mass $k$, proving the bounds in ( 20.3.68 ) for all original competitors. Substituting $q=v-bG_ p$ and $\int G_ p\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a=a(p)-\int aw$ proves ( 20.3.67 ). To approach either bound, choose a point $x$ where $a$ takes the corresponding extreme value, smooth strictly positive measures $\zeta _ j$ of mass $k$ tending weakly to $k\delta _ x$, and smooth $g_ j$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ j=\zeta _ j-kw$. Choose $L_ j$ so that $\epsilon _{L_ j}$ is less than half the minimum density of $\zeta _ j$ relative to $w$ and $|\int U_{L_ j}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a|<1/j$. Then \[  v_ j=bG_ p+g_ j+U_{L_ j}\sim r,\qquad \beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g_ j+U_{L_ j})\geq \tfrac 12\zeta _ j+aw_2>0.  \] Their masses tend to $2ka(x)$ by ( 20.3.69 ). $\square$ No finite first moment is used here. For the reference $u_0=U_ L$, the closed first moment $\int _ Y(-u_0)\langle (K+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0)^2\rangle $ is finite exactly when $\alpha <1/2$. Near $p$ put $t=-G_ p$. Then $-u_0\asymp t^\alpha $ and $\chi ''(G_ p)\asymp t^{\alpha -2}$, while angular integration of $\mathrm dG_ p\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}G_ p$ is comparable to $\mathrm dt$. The singular contribution is thus comparable to $\int ^\infty t^{2\alpha -2}\, \mathrm dt$. The smooth contributions are integrable, and the mass formula includes the divergent range.

Every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$ with $v\sim r$ has positive finite extended mass, given by EEBF58093B80 20.3.67 \begin{equation}  \int _ Y\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (v) =\int _ Y\theta ^2-2b a(p)+2\int _ Yv\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\theta . \end{equation} The volumes of definition 16.28.58 are 9099C8F4472B 20.3.68 \begin{equation}  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (v)=2(c-b)\min a, \qquad \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (v)=2(c-b)\max a. \end{equation} Both values are limits of masses of representatives of this ordinary type. Taking $q=v-bG_ p$ in $L^1$ and then its quasi-plurisubharmonic representative gives \[  q\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\beta ),\qquad q\sim U,\qquad \beta =kw_1+aw_2,\qquad k=c-b.  \] Indeed the ordinary inequalities hold off $D$ and extend canonically across it. Conversely such a $q$ gives $v=bG_ p+q$ with \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=b[D]+\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q.  \] Their locally bounded products agree off $D$, and both extended measures give $D$ zero mass. Thus their extended measures agree everywhere. If $k>0$, choose $L$ with $\epsilon _ L<k/2$. The potential $bG_ p+U_ L$ belongs to the specified type and satisfies \[  \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(bG_ p+U_ L) \geq b[D]+(k-\epsilon _ L)w_1+aw_2 \geq \min (k/2,\min a)(w_1+w_2).  \] For necessity, average $q$ over the unitary group acting transitively on the second projective line, with its Haar probability measure. The background is invariant. The average has a genuine first-factor representative $q_0\sim U$ and $kw+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_0\geq 0$. One can first average in $L^1$ and then take the canonical representative; the curvature inequality and the ordinary bounds pass to it. The positive curve measure has total mass $k$, excluding $k<0$. When $k=0$, $q_0$ is harmonic on the compact curve and therefore constant, contradicting $q_0\sim U$. It remains to compute the mass for every competitor, before using the average. Choose a closed Kähler form $K=C(w_1+w_2)\geq \beta $ and a fixed $u_0=U_ L$ as above. The closed positive current $S_0=K+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0$ has no coefficient mass on $D$, since its first-factor curvature has no atom at $p$. The product formula gives \[  \langle S_0\rangle =S_0,\qquad \langle S_0^2\rangle =2C(Cw_1+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0)\wedge w_2, \qquad \int _ Y\langle S_0^2\rangle =\int _ YK^2.  \] For $S=K+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q$, both $S$ and $S_0$ are closed positive currents in the same Kähler class, with bounded difference of potentials and small unbounded locus $D$. The classical closed-class comparison of non-pluripolar products, applied in both singularity orders in degrees one and two, gives \[  \{ \langle S\rangle \} =\{ K\} ,\qquad \int _ Y\langle S^2\rangle =\int _ YK^2.  \] Here the degree-one non-pluripolar current is the restriction of $S$ off $D$ and is closed. Hence the positive current $S-\langle S\rangle $ has zero trace against $K$, and vanishes. This proves $\langle S\rangle =S$. Equivalently, absence of polar coefficient mass follows from proposition 5.46.3 . The closed comparison is used only for $K$. Put $R=\beta -K$. Bedford–Taylor expansion off $D$, followed by extension by zero, now yields \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\beta (q) =\langle S^2\rangle +2R\wedge S+R^2.  \] The first term is finite by closed comparison, the second has finite variation because $S$ has finite trace, and the last is smooth. Since none has coefficient mass on $D$, this is also an identity on $Y$. Distributional Stokes therefore gives F060F71204CB 20.3.69 \begin{equation}  \int _ Y\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\beta (q) =\int _ Y\beta ^2+2\int _ Yq\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\beta =2\int _{\mathbb P^1}a(kw+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_0). \end{equation} The pairing uses only $q\in L^1$. Averaging preserves it, since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge w_2$. The last measure is positive of total mass $k$, proving the bounds in ( 20.3.68 ) for all original competitors. Substituting $q=v-bG_ p$ and $\int G_ p\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a=a(p)-\int aw$ proves ( 20.3.67 ). To approach either bound, choose a point $x$ where $a$ takes the corresponding extreme value, smooth strictly positive measures $\zeta _ j$ of mass $k$ tending weakly to $k\delta _ x$, and smooth $g_ j$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g_ j=\zeta _ j-kw$. Choose $L_ j$ so that $\epsilon _{L_ j}$ is less than half the minimum density of $\zeta _ j$ relative to $w$ and $|\int U_{L_ j}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a|<1/j$. Then \[  v_ j=bG_ p+g_ j+U_{L_ j}\sim r,\qquad \beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g_ j+U_{L_ j})\geq \tfrac 12\zeta _ j+aw_2>0.  \] Their masses tend to $2ka(x)$ by ( 20.3.69 ). $\square$

title: 20.3.70 Ambient ideal orders and ordinary type
search_title: Ambient ideal orders and ordinary type
text: To realize these data as intrinsic traces, set $X=Y\times \mathbb P^1$ and identify $Y$ with $Y\times \{ z_0\} $ for a fixed $z_0$. Write $w_3$ for the third-factor form and let $\operatorname {pr}_ Y:X\to Y$ be the projection. With $L$ as in the theorem, put \[  \Theta =\operatorname {pr}_ Y^*\theta +w_3, \qquad u_ X=\operatorname {pr}_ Y^*(bG_ p+U_ L), \qquad D_ X=D\times \mathbb P^1.  \] Then $u_ X\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\Theta )$ and $\nu (u_ X,Y)=0$. Proposition 20.3.71 . C33DAF9C7870 For every real $s>0$, \[  \mathcal I(su_ X)=\mathcal O_ X(-\lfloor sb\rfloor D_ X), \qquad \mathcal I(su_ X)\mathcal O_ Y =\mathcal O_ Y(-\lfloor sb\rfloor D).  \] For every prime divisor $E$ on every smooth compact modification $\pi :Y'\to Y$, the intrinsic trace data are \[  \tau _{Y,u_ X}(E)=b\operatorname {ord}_ E(\pi ^*D).  \] Nevertheless the ordinary type of $bG_ p+U_ L$ has no analytic representative. Proof. Near $D_ X$, choose a transverse coordinate $z_1$. A germ whose exact transverse order is $j$ has a nonzero leading tangential coefficient. With $t=-\log |z_1|^2$, its radial integrability against $\mathrm e^{-su_ X}$ is determined by \[  \exp \bigl (-(j+1-sb)t+s t^\alpha \bigr ).  \] Bounded errors in this exponent do not change convergence. It is integrable exactly when $j+1>sb$, and diverges at equality. Local holomorphic bounds give sufficiency, and a region where the leading tangential coefficient is nonzero gives necessity by Fubini. This proves the ambient ideal formula in the book's convention $|f|^2\mathrm e^{-su_ X}$. Restriction and pullback of this principal ideal give order $\lfloor sb\rfloor \operatorname {ord}_ E(\pi ^*D)$. Divide by $s$ and use theorem 20.3.2 . The residual $U_ L$ has trivial multiplier ideals at every weight, but is unbounded. At a generic point of $D$, an analytic type with divisorial coefficient $b$ is $b\log |z_1|^2+O(1)$. Our residual tends to $-\infty $ like $-t^\alpha $, excluding ordinary equivalence. This also covers $b=0$. $\square$

title: 20.3.72 Pullback and strict representatives
text: The lower volume above is positive, and its type contains a strict current on $Y$. A modification preserves both optimized masses but can destroy this last property when the ordinary type is fixed. Proposition 20.3.73 . 55D866148BAF For every modification $\pi :Y'\to Y$ and $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$ with $v\sim r$, \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\pi ^*\theta }(\pi ^*v) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (v),\qquad \overline{\operatorname {vol}}_{\pi ^*\theta }(\pi ^*v) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\theta (v).  \] These masses and the ideal orders are also unchanged by a smooth gauge $(\theta ,v,r)\mapsto (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f,v-f,r-f)$. Proof. By proposition 5.43.18 , every $\pi ^*\theta $-plurisubharmonic potential descends. Since $\pi $ is surjective, ordinary inequalities are equivalent before and after pullback. Thus the competitors are in bijection. On the locus where $\pi $ is an isomorphism, locality identifies their products. Both extended products give the excluded analytic subsets zero mass, so \[  \pi _*\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{\pi ^*\theta }(\pi ^*v) =\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta (v).  \] Taking the infimum and supremum proves the identities. Smooth gauge preserves the actual currents and measures; it preserves multiplier ideals because $\mathrm e^{sf}$ is locally bounded above and below. $\square$ Proposition 20.3.74 . E91643D06F3E Suppose $b<c$ and let $\pi :Y'\to Y$ be a nonempty finite composition of point blowups. There is a strict current $\pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v'$ with $v'\leq \pi ^*r+C$, but none with $v'\sim \pi ^*r$. Both ordinary-type volumes retain the values in ( 20.3.68 ). Blowup centers may lie on $D$ or on earlier exceptional curves. Proof. Put $\beta =(c-b)w_1+aw_2$. The representatives of lemma 20.3.65 show that $U$ satisfies ( 18.27.1 ); by lemma 18.27.2 so does $\pi ^*U$. The logarithmic divisor is $b\pi ^*D$, whose smooth curvature is $b\pi ^*w_1$, so its residual background is $\pi ^*\beta $. If a strict current existed in the ordinary type of $\pi ^*r$, theorem 18.27.4 would give a smooth $f$ with $\pi ^*\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f>0$. The exceptional curve $E$ of the last blowup is contracted by the composite map. Restriction to this smooth curve would give $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(f|_ E)>0$, contrary to its zero integral by Stokes. Only the smooth function $f$ is restricted, so this argument applies also when the original potential has a pole along $E$. For the one-sided assertion, start with the strict representative $v_0=bG_ p+U_ L$ from theorem 20.3.66 . Suppose $v_ j$ is strict with lower bound $\delta _ jh_ j>0$ on the current surface, and let $\pi _{j+1}$ be the next point blowup. For its exceptional divisor $E_{j+1}$, choose a smooth metric on $\mathcal O(E_{j+1})$ with curvature $\eta _{j+1}$ negative along the vertical tangent, and write $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\ell _{j+1}=[E_{j+1}]-\eta _{j+1}$. For all sufficiently small $t_ j>0$, $\pi _{j+1}^*h_ j-t_ j\eta _{j+1}>0$. To see this, in a blowup chart $(x,z)\mapsto (x,xz)$ the pullback has a uniformly positive horizontal coefficient, mixed coefficient $O(|x|)$ and Schur complement at least $c_1|x|^2$. The perturbation adds a positive vertical term at least $t_ jc_2$, while its error in the Schur complement is bounded by $C(t_ j|x|+t_ j|x|^2+t_ j^2)$. Shrink the exceptional neighborhood and then choose $t_ j$ small; on its compact complement positivity persists under small perturbations. Thus \[  v_{j+1}=\pi _{j+1}^*v_ j+\delta _ jt_ j\ell _{j+1}  \] is strict. These genuine quasi-plurisubharmonic pullbacks are defined even over pole centers. The logarithmic terms are bounded above, so induction gives $v'\leq \pi ^*r+C$. Finally proposition 20.3.73 preserves both volumes in the pulled-back ordinary type. The additional exceptional poles of the one-sided witness are not competitors in that fixed type. $\square$ For example take $c=1$, $b=1/4$, $\alpha =3/4$ and $a=2+\tau $, where $\tau =(|z|^2-1)/(|z|^2+1)$ is the height on the first sphere. The lower and upper volumes are $3/2$ and $9/2$. The choice $L=31$ has $\epsilon _ L=(3/4)32^{-1/4}<3/8$ and gives a strict representative with infinite closed first moment. The intrinsic ideal orders are $\frac14\operatorname {ord}_ E(\pi ^*D)$. Every nonempty finite composition of point blowups, including centers on $D$, preserves both volumes and permits one-sided strictness while excluding a strict representative in the same ordinary type.

title: 19.8 Holomorphic sections and Hermitian mass
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: On a projective manifold, holomorphic sections of line bundles connect singularities with geometry: a singular weight selects the sections whose vanishing compensates for its poles, and the growth of the selected section spaces is governed by Monge–Ampère masses. On a compact Hermitian manifold the curvature of a Hermitian line bundle is still closed, whereas the background form of the Monge–Ampère operator need not be. This part of the book asks what section spaces, and the geometric models attached to sections and singularities, can still detect. Gauduchon degrees often take the place of intersection numbers: they bound the vanishing orders of sections, the valuations along a flag and the divisorial parts of positive currents on modifications. Two kinds of geometric models appear. A complete flag turns vanishing orders into lattice points and section growth into the volume of a convex body, and the elliptic fibration of a Hopf manifold over projective space reduces its sections and its descended potentials to the base. Compact modifications carry the divisorial part of a singularity: on each model, the divisorial Lelong numbers or trace numbers sum to a closed positive current, and subtracting it from the pulled-back background gives residual classes that form b-divisor classes. Finally, positive Hermitian perturbations of a background organize multiplier-ideal envelopes into compatible systems; the limit of such a system in the original background need not recover it. In this chapter, $X$ is a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n$, $L$ is a holomorphic line bundle on $X$ with a smooth Hermitian metric $h$, $u\in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$ is a fixed weight, and $\mathrm{d}V$ is a smooth positive volume form. In a local holomorphic frame $e$ of $L$, write $|e|_ h^2=\mathrm{e}^{-\chi }$. The form $\beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $ does not depend on the frame; it is the smooth closed curvature form of $h$. The weight selects the global sections of $L^ m$ that are square integrable against $h^ m\mathrm{e}^{-mu}$, and the Bergman kernels of these finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces produce closed positive currents in the curvature class of $L$. Pairing the Poincaré–Lelong formula with a Gauduchon metric bounds the vanishing that a nonzero section can carry; on a submanifold, this gives a necessary condition for realizing the trace data of section 20.3 by restricted sections. When $X$ is a curve, $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ and $u$ has finitely many logarithmic poles, Riemann–Roch identifies the leading growth of the section spaces with the extended Monge–Ampère mass of $u$. In higher dimensions this identification depends on the background. Homogeneous sections on a Hopf manifold grow only like the sections on its projective base, and a potential of infinite Hermitian mass with trivial multiplier ideals leaves every section space unchanged. Section counts therefore cannot recover a mass computed in a Hermitian background unrelated to the curvature of $L$.

title: 19.8.1 Weighted sections and Bergman currents
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: The multiplier ideals of $mu$ determine which sections of $L^ m$ have finite weighted $L^2$ norm. Evaluation at points of the resulting Hilbert space defines a Bergman kernel, and its extremal characterization turns comparisons of norms into comparisons of the associated potentials. For every positive integer $m$, set \[  \mathcal H_ m(u)=H^0(X,L^ m\otimes \mathcal I(mu)),\qquad \| s\| _{m,u}^2=\int _ X|s|_{h^ m}^2\mathrm{e}^{-mu}\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The integrand is defined off the pole set $\{ u=-\infty \} $, which has volume zero. A section $s\in H^0(X,L^ m)$ belongs to $\mathcal H_ m(u)$ if and only if $\| s\| _{m,u}<\infty $. Indeed, if the local coefficients of $s$ lie in $\mathcal I(mu)$, the integrand is locally integrable, and a finite covering of the compact manifold $X$ gives a finite integral; conversely, a finite integral gives local integrability on every coordinate ball. Thus $\mathcal H_ m(u)$, a subspace of the finite-dimensional space $H^0(X,L^ m)$, is a Hilbert space for this norm. Write $N_ m=\dim \mathcal H_ m(u)$. Let $v\in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$. If $u\preceq _{\mathcal I}v$, that is, $\mathcal I(ku)\subseteq \mathcal I(kv)$ for every real $k>0$ (section 5.33 ), then $\mathcal H_ m(u)\subseteq \mathcal H_ m(v)$ for every $m$. In particular, weights of the same ordinary singularity type (definition 16.7.1 ) have the same section spaces, by proposition 5.33.2 . When the two weights differ by a bounded function, their Hilbert norms are also comparable. Below, $\| s\| _{m,v,\mathrm{d}V'}$ denotes the norm defined with $v$ and $\mathrm{d}V'$ in place of $u$ and $\mathrm{d}V$. Proposition 19.8.2 . F2503E6C53F2 Let $v\in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$, let $D,E\geq 0$, and let $F\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$. Suppose that $|u-v|\leq D$ outside the union of the pole sets of $u$ and $v$, and that $\mathrm{d}V'=\mathrm{e}^ F \mathrm{d}V$ with $|F|\leq E$. Then $u$ and $v$ have the same section spaces, and for every positive integer $m$ and every $s$ in the common space $\mathcal H_ m(u)=\mathcal H_ m(v)$, \[  \mathrm{e}^{-mD-E}\| s\| _{m,u}^2 \leq \| s\| _{m,v,\mathrm{d}V'}^2 \leq \mathrm{e}^{mD+E}\| s\| _{m,u}^2.  \] Proof. Off the pole sets, the integrand of $\| s\| _{m,v,\mathrm{d}V'}^2$ is that of $\| s\| _{m,u}^2$ multiplied by $\mathrm{e}^{-m(v-u)+F}$, a function with values between $\mathrm{e}^{-mD-E}$ and $\mathrm{e}^{mD+E}$. Hence one norm is finite if and only if the other is, so the section spaces coincide, and integration gives both estimates. $\square$ Fix $m\geq 1$ and choose an orthonormal basis $s_1,\ldots ,s_{N_ m}$ of $\mathcal H_ m(u)$. Define $K_{m,u}$ on $X$ and $B_{m,u}$ off the pole set by \[  K_{m,u}(x)=\sum _{j=1}^{N_ m}|s_ j(x)|_{h^ m}^2, \qquad B_{m,u}(x)=K_{m,u}(x)\mathrm{e}^{-mu(x)},  \] and set $B_{m,u}=0$ on the pole set. When $N_ m=0$, both functions are zero. Since two orthonormal bases differ by a unitary matrix, $K_{m,u}$ does not depend on the choice of basis. We call $\Phi _ m=m^{-1}\log K_{m,u}$ the Bergman potential ; when $N_ m>0$, $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ m$ is its Bergman current . For $N_ m=0$, we have $\Phi _ m\equiv -\infty $. Proposition 19.8.3 . 9E7A6E9D52A6 If $N_ m>0$, then \[  K_{m,u}(x)=\sup _{0\neq s\in \mathcal H_ m(u)} \frac{|s(x)|_{h^ m}^2}{\| s\| _{m,u}^2}, \qquad \int _ X B_{m,u}\, \mathrm{d}V=N_ m.  \] Moreover, the Bergman potential $\Phi _ m=m^{-1}\log K_{m,u}$ is not identically $-\infty $, has analytic singularities, and satisfies \[  \beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ m\geq 0.  \] In particular, the Bergman current $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ m$ is a closed positive current. Proof. Write a section as $s=\sum _ ja_ js_ j$ and trivialize the fiber of $L^ m$ at $x$ by a unit vector. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $|s(x)|_{h^ m}^2\leq \| s\| _{m,u}^2K_{m,u}(x)$, with equality when the coefficient vector $(a_ j)$ is proportional to the complex conjugate of $(s_ j(x))$. If $K_{m,u}(x)=0$, both sides of the extremal formula vanish. This proves the extremal formula. Integrating the finite sum defining $B_{m,u}$ gives $\sum _ j\| s_ j\| _{m,u}^2=N_ m$. Locally $s_ j=f_ j e^{\otimes m}$ with holomorphic functions $f_ j$, so \[  \Phi _ m=\frac1m\log \sum _ j|f_ j|^2-\chi , \qquad \beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ m=\frac1m\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \sum _ j|f_ j|^2\geq 0.  \] Since $X$ is connected, a nonzero section cannot vanish identically on an open set; hence the sum $\sum _ j|f_ j|^2$ does not vanish identically. The local expression therefore shows that $\Phi _ m$ is a quasi-plurisubharmonic function with analytic singularities, not identically $-\infty $. It also shows directly that $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ m$ is closed. $\square$ Write $\Phi _ m(u,\mathrm{d}V)$ when the dependence on the weight and the volume form matters. Under the hypotheses of proposition 19.8.2 , and provided that the common section space is nonzero, the extremal formula gives \[  |\Phi _ m(u,\mathrm{d}V)-\Phi _ m(v,\mathrm{d}V')|\leq D+E/m  \] outside the common base locus. Both potentials equal $-\infty $ on that locus. In particular, the two potentials have the same ordinary singularity type, and for a fixed weight a change of the smooth volume form changes the Bergman potential by $O(m^{-1})$. A simultaneous change of metric and weight leaves the weighted norm unchanged. Let $a\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$, replace the metric by $h'=h\mathrm{e}^{-a}$, so that $|\cdot |_{h'}^2=|\cdot |_ h^2\mathrm{e}^{-a}$, and replace the weight by $u'=u-a$. Then $h'^ m\mathrm{e}^{-mu'}=h^ m\mathrm{e}^{-mu}$, so the Hilbert space, its norm and the density $B_{m,u}\, \mathrm{d}V$ are unchanged, while \[  \beta '=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a,\qquad \Phi '_ m=\Phi _ m-a.  \] Consequently the Bergman current $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ m$ does not change.

title: Proposition 19.8.2
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Proposition 19.8.2 . F2503E6C53F2 Let $v\in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$, let $D,E\geq 0$, and let $F\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$. Suppose that $|u-v|\leq D$ outside the union of the pole sets of $u$ and $v$, and that $\mathrm{d}V'=\mathrm{e}^ F \mathrm{d}V$ with $|F|\leq E$. Then $u$ and $v$ have the same section spaces, and for every positive integer $m$ and every $s$ in the common space $\mathcal H_ m(u)=\mathcal H_ m(v)$, \[  \mathrm{e}^{-mD-E}\| s\| _{m,u}^2 \leq \| s\| _{m,v,\mathrm{d}V'}^2 \leq \mathrm{e}^{mD+E}\| s\| _{m,u}^2.  \] Proof. Off the pole sets, the integrand of $\| s\| _{m,v,\mathrm{d}V'}^2$ is that of $\| s\| _{m,u}^2$ multiplied by $\mathrm{e}^{-m(v-u)+F}$, a function with values between $\mathrm{e}^{-mD-E}$ and $\mathrm{e}^{mD+E}$. Hence one norm is finite if and only if the other is, so the section spaces coincide, and integration gives both estimates. $\square$

title: Proposition 19.8.3
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: Proposition 19.8.3 . 9E7A6E9D52A6 If $N_ m>0$, then \[  K_{m,u}(x)=\sup _{0\neq s\in \mathcal H_ m(u)} \frac{|s(x)|_{h^ m}^2}{\| s\| _{m,u}^2}, \qquad \int _ X B_{m,u}\, \mathrm{d}V=N_ m.  \] Moreover, the Bergman potential $\Phi _ m=m^{-1}\log K_{m,u}$ is not identically $-\infty $, has analytic singularities, and satisfies \[  \beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ m\geq 0.  \] In particular, the Bergman current $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ m$ is a closed positive current. Proof. Write a section as $s=\sum _ ja_ js_ j$ and trivialize the fiber of $L^ m$ at $x$ by a unit vector. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $|s(x)|_{h^ m}^2\leq \| s\| _{m,u}^2K_{m,u}(x)$, with equality when the coefficient vector $(a_ j)$ is proportional to the complex conjugate of $(s_ j(x))$. If $K_{m,u}(x)=0$, both sides of the extremal formula vanish. This proves the extremal formula. Integrating the finite sum defining $B_{m,u}$ gives $\sum _ j\| s_ j\| _{m,u}^2=N_ m$. Locally $s_ j=f_ j e^{\otimes m}$ with holomorphic functions $f_ j$, so \[  \Phi _ m=\frac1m\log \sum _ j|f_ j|^2-\chi , \qquad \beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ m=\frac1m\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \sum _ j|f_ j|^2\geq 0.  \] Since $X$ is connected, a nonzero section cannot vanish identically on an open set; hence the sum $\sum _ j|f_ j|^2$ does not vanish identically. The local expression therefore shows that $\Phi _ m$ is a quasi-plurisubharmonic function with analytic singularities, not identically $-\infty $. It also shows directly that $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ m$ is closed. $\square$

title: 19.8.4 Gauduchon degree and vanishing
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: The zero divisor of a holomorphic section is effective, and the Poincaré–Lelong formula expresses its integration current as the curvature form of the line bundle plus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of a global function. Pairing with a Gauduchon metric removes the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ term, so the size of the divisor is bounded by a degree of the line bundle. Recall that a Hermitian form $\gamma $ is Gauduchon if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0$ (definition 11.4.1 ); every Hermitian form on a curve is Gauduchon. Write $h^0(X,L^ m)=\dim H^0(X,L^ m)$. For a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ on $X$, define the degree \[  \deg _\gamma L=\int _ X\beta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] A change of the smooth metric on $L$ changes $\beta $ by $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$ for a smooth real function $a$, and the integral of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a$ against $\gamma ^{n-1}$ vanishes by Stokes' theorem. Hence the degree does not depend on the smooth metric on $L$. Theorem 19.8.5 . 1DFDCCEF325D If $\deg _\gamma L<0$, then $H^0(X,L^ m)=0$ for every $m\geq 1$. If $\deg _\gamma L=0$ and $H^0(X,L^ m)\neq 0$, then $L^ m$ is holomorphically trivial and $h^0(X,L^ m)=1$. At degree zero, each nonzero weighted subspace $\mathcal H_ m(u)$ is also one-dimensional. Proof. Let $s$ be a nonzero section of $L^ m$ and let $D$ be its zero divisor. The function $\log |s|_{h^ m}^2$ is locally integrable, and the Poincaré–Lelong formula gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |s|_{h^ m}^2=[D]-m\beta .  \] Since $\gamma $ is Gauduchon, integration by parts against $\gamma ^{n-1}$ annihilates the left-hand side, and therefore \[  m\deg _\gamma L=\int _ D\gamma ^{n-1}\geq 0,  \] where the components of $D$ are counted with multiplicities. If $D\neq 0$, the right-hand side is strictly positive, because $\gamma $ is positive on the regular locus of each component. Hence negative degree is impossible. At degree zero we obtain $D=0$, so $s$ has no zeros and trivializes $L^ m$. Every other section of $L^ m$ is then a holomorphic function times $s$, and holomorphic functions on the connected compact manifold $X$ are constant. Thus $h^0(X,L^ m)=1$, and every nonzero subspace $\mathcal H_ m(u)\subseteq H^0(X,L^ m)$ is one-dimensional. $\square$ The degree constrains positive curvature currents in the same way. If $T=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$, the trace identity of proposition 11.5.1 gives \[  \deg _\gamma L=\int _ X T\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\geq 0.  \] If the degree is zero, the positivity of $T$ and the strict positivity of $\gamma $ imply $T=0$.

title: 19.8.6 Restricted sections and trace data
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text:
Let $Y\subset X$ be a connected compact complex submanifold of dimension $r\geq 1$, and suppose that the generic Lelong number $

Recall from subsection 20.3.1 the image ideals $\mathfrak a_ m=\mathfrak a_ m(u;Y)=\mathcal I(mu)\mathcal O_ Y$ and the divisorial trace data $	au _{Y,u}(E)$ of a prime divisor $E$ on a smooth compact modification of $Y$, defined in ( 20.3.3 ) as the limit of $\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathfrak a_ m/m$. Put \[  V_ m=\operatorname {im} igl (\mathcal H_ m(u)\longrightarrow H^0(Y,L^ m|_ Y) igr ).  \] The local coefficients of a restricted section lie in $\mathfrak a_ m$, so $V_ m\subseteq H^0(Y,L^ m|_ Y\otimes \mathfrak a_ m)$; the right-hand space can contain sections that do not extend to $X$. Theorem 19.8.7 . 165328A043C0 Suppose that $V_ m
eq 0$ for arbitrarily large integers $m$. Equip this line bundle with the metric induced by $h$ and the chosen metrics. One $m$th of the logarithm of the squared norm of this section is a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $w_ m$ on $Z$, and the Poincaré–Lelong formula gives \[  \Theta _ m+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ m= rac1m[D_ m]\geq 0.  \] By theorem 20.3.2 , $b_ i(m)/m	o 	au _{Y,u}(E_ i)$ as $m	o \infty $ through all integers, hence also along the chosen degrees, so $\Theta _ m	o \Theta $ smoothly. Consequently a single Hermitian form $\Lambda $ on $Z$ dominates all the forms $\Theta _ m$, and every $w_ m$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(Z,\Lambda )$. Normalize $\sup _ Zw_ m=0$. Finally, pair this current with $\gamma ^{r-1}$, where $\gamma ^{r-1}=1$ if $r=1$. Integration by parts removes $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w$ because $\gamma $ is Gauduchon, and the Poincaré–Lelong formula for the canonical section of $\mathcal O_ Z(E_ i)$ gives $\int _ Z eta _ i\wedge \gamma ^{r-1}=\int _{E_ i}\gamma ^{r-1}$. The nonnegativity of the pairing is exactly the stated degree inequality. $\square$ Equivalently, if one of these inequalities fails for some choice of $Z$, $E_1,\ldots ,E_ q$ and $\gamma $, then $V_ m=0$ for all sufficiently large $m$. The converse of the theorem fails in general. Let $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm{i}\mathbb Z)$ be the square elliptic curve, choose an irrational real number $a$, and let $L$ be the flat line bundle on $E$ with multipliers $\mathrm{e}^{2\pi \mathrm{i} a}$ and $1$ along the two generators: its sections lift to holomorphic functions $f$ on $\mathbb C$ with $f(z+1)=\mathrm{e}^{2\pi \mathrm{i} a}f(z)$ and $f(z+\mathrm{i})=f(z)$. The constant metric on $L$ has curvature zero. Take $u=0$ and $Y=X=E$. Then every trace number is zero, and the class in the theorem is zero, hence pseudoeffective. Nevertheless no positive tensor power of $L$ has a nonzero holomorphic section. Indeed, a nonzero section of $L^ m$ would have a zero divisor of degree zero and would therefore be nowhere zero. The logarithm of its norm would be harmonic on $E$, hence constant, so its lift $f$ would be a holomorphic function of constant modulus on $\mathbb C$, and thus constant. Since $ma

title: 19.8.8 Bounded weighted sections
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: The spaces $\mathcal H_ m(u)$ need not be closed under multiplication: the product of two sections with integrable weighted squared norms need not have an integrable weighted squared norm, as the following logarithmic example shows. Requiring the weighted pointwise norm to be bounded rather than integrable gives spaces that do multiply. They form the graded algebra used in section 19.9 . Example 19.8.9 . D1A2270A67A3 Let $X=\mathbb P^1$ with affine coordinate $z$, and let $\delta _0$ be the Dirac mass at the origin. Take $L=\mathcal O(1)$ with its Fubini–Study metric, whose curvature form is $\beta $, and let \[  u(z)=\frac35\log \frac{|z|^2}{1+|z|^2}.  \] Then $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\frac25\beta +\frac35\delta _0\geq 0$, $\mathcal I(u)=\mathcal O$ and $\mathcal I(2u)=\mathcal O(-[0])$. A section of $L$ that does not vanish at $0$ belongs to $\mathcal H_1(u)$, but its square does not belong to $\mathcal H_2(u)$. Proof. The curvature formula follows from the Poincaré–Lelong formula $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z|^2=\delta _0$ and from $\beta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+|z|^2)$ on $\mathbb C$. The weight is bounded near infinity and equals $\frac35\log |z|^2+O(1)$ near zero, its only singularity. The one-variable calculation of example 5.33.3 therefore gives the two stated ideals: $\mathcal I(u)$ is trivial, while $\mathcal I(2u)$ consists of the functions vanishing at the origin. A section of $L$ with $s(0)\neq 0$ thus lies in $\mathcal H_1(u)$, whereas $s^2$ does not vanish at the origin and so does not lie in $\mathcal H_2(u)$. $\square$ We return to the general data $(X,L,h,u)$. Define $\mathcal W_0=\mathbb C$ and, for $m\geq 1$, \[  \mathcal W_ m(u)=\{ s\in H^0(X,L^ m): |s|_{h^ m}^2\mathrm{e}^{-mu}\text{ is bounded off }\{ u=-\infty \} \} .  \] These are vector spaces, since $|s+t|^2\leq 2|s|^2+2|t|^2$; they are finite-dimensional and do not depend on the smooth metric, because the ratio of two smooth metrics is bounded above and below on $X$. Since $X$ has finite volume, they are contained in $\mathcal H_ m(u)$. For positive integers $m,k$, $s\in \mathcal W_ m(u)$ and $t\in \mathcal W_ k(u)$, the identity \[  |st|_{h^{m+k}}^2\mathrm{e}^{-(m+k)u} =\bigl (|s|_{h^ m}^2\mathrm{e}^{-mu}\bigr ) \bigl (|t|_{h^ k}^2\mathrm{e}^{-ku}\bigr )  \] proves $\mathcal W_ m(u)\mathcal W_ k(u)\subseteq \mathcal W_{m+k}(u)$. Thus $\bigoplus _ m\mathcal W_ m(u)$ is a graded subalgebra of the section ring $\bigoplus _{m\geq 0}H^0(X,L^ m)$ of $L$. On a smooth projective variety, for big line bundles with metrics of positive curvature current and positive multiplier-ideal volume, the almost-semigroup construction of 19.4 Algebraic partial Okounkov bodies works with the integrable section spaces themselves.

title: 19.8.10 Section growth on a curve
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: On a curve, a weight with logarithmic poles imposes vanishing orders at the poles. Integrability rounds the required order down and boundedness rounds it up, so the two resulting divisors differ by a bounded amount, and Riemann–Roch gives the same leading growth for both section spaces. Throughout this section, $X$ is a compact Riemann surface and $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. Let $p_1,\ldots ,p_ r$ be distinct points such that $u$ is locally bounded on $X\setminus \{ p_1,\ldots ,p_ r\} $ and, in coordinates $z_ i$ centered at $p_ i$, \[  u=c_ i\log |z_ i|^2+O(1),\qquad c_ i>0.  \] Set $\ell =\deg L=\int _ X\beta $ and $d=\sum _ i c_ i$. Recall that $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\beta (u)$ denotes the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of theorem 13.14.3 . Theorem 19.8.11 . 1E6D5AA611CC In this situation $0\leq d\leq \ell $, and \[  \begin{split}  \mathcal H_ m(u)& =H^0\left(X,L^ m\Bigl (-\sum _ i\lfloor mc_ i\rfloor p_ i\Bigr )\right),\\  \mathcal W_ m(u)& =H^0\left(X,L^ m\Bigl (-\sum _ i\lceil mc_ i\rceil p_ i\Bigr )\right). \end{split}  \] Moreover, \[  \lim _{m\to \infty }\frac{\dim \mathcal H_ m(u)}m =\lim _{m\to \infty }\frac{\dim \mathcal W_ m(u)}m =\ell -d =\int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\beta (u).  \] Proof. Step 1: the section spaces. A germ of a section of $L^ m$ vanishing to order $k$ at $p_ i$ has weighted squared norm comparable to $|z_ i|^{2(k-mc_ i)}$. As in example 5.33.3 , it is locally integrable if and only if $k-mc_ i>-1$, that is, $k\geq \lfloor mc_ i\rfloor $; it is bounded if and only if $k\geq mc_ i$, that is, $k\geq \lceil mc_ i\rceil $. Away from the points $p_ i$ the weight is locally bounded and imposes no condition. Since $X$ is compact, this gives the displayed global identifications. Step 2: the mass. The positive measure $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ has total mass $\ell $, and it has an atom of mass $c_ i$ at $p_ i$. Subtracting these atoms leaves a positive measure, which proves $d\leq \ell $. This remaining measure does not charge polar sets: after subtraction of the logarithmic singularity, its local potential has a bounded quasi-plurisubharmonic representative, and by proposition 5.28.2 its curvature gives polar sets zero mass. Thus the remaining measure is exactly the extended measure, and its mass is $\ell -d$. Step 3: growth. If $\ell >d$, the degrees of both line bundles in the display equal $m(\ell -d)+O(1)$ and tend to infinity. Let $g$ be the genus of $X$. By Riemann–Roch and Serre duality, $h^0=\deg +1-g$ once the degree exceeds $2g-2$. Dividing by $m$ proves both limits. If $\ell =d$, both degrees remain bounded. A line bundle of negative degree has no nonzero section, and one of nonnegative degree $k$ has at most $k+1$ independent sections: the sections vanishing at $k+1$ given distinct points are sections of a line bundle of negative degree, hence zero. Therefore both dimensions are uniformly bounded, and both limits vanish. These arguments include the case $r=0$. $\square$

text: On a scalar Hopf manifold, a holomorphic section of a line bundle lifts to a function on $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $ with an exact homogeneity property under the contraction. Hartogs extension reduces the section spaces to spaces of homogeneous polynomials, and the invariance of the metric makes the Bergman kernel constant. The resulting growth is of order $m^{n-1}$, reflecting the dimension of the projective base rather than that of the manifold. Let $n\geq 2$, let $z=(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)$ be the coordinates on $\mathbb C^ n$, and set \[  X_ n=(\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle z\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{-1}z\rangle .  \] On the covering space put \[  s=\log |z|^2,\qquad \alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s,\qquad \zeta =\mathrm{d}s\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s,\qquad \omega =\alpha +\zeta .  \] The contraction changes $s$ by the constant $-2$, so these forms descend to $X_ n$. The calculation proving ( 23.1.3 ), written in section 23.1 for $n=3$ and with $\beta $ in place of $\zeta $, applies in every dimension and gives \[  \alpha ^ n=0,\qquad \zeta ^2=0,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\zeta =-\alpha ^2, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\omega ^{n-1})=-(n-1)\alpha ^ n=0.  \] Thus $\omega $ is a Gauduchon form. Projectivization defines a holomorphic map $\pi :X_ n\to \mathbb P^{n-1}$ with elliptic fibers, and $\alpha $ is the pullback of the Fubini–Study form normalized to have total mass one. Since $\zeta $ restricts to twice the normalized area form on each fiber, as in the proof of proposition 23.1.4 , and $\omega ^ n=n\alpha ^{n-1}\wedge \zeta $, we obtain \[  \int _{X_ n}\alpha ^{n-1}\wedge \zeta =2, \qquad \int _{X_ n}\omega ^ n=2n.  \] Set $\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^ n/(2n)$, a probability measure. For an integer $k\geq 0$, let $L_ k$ be the line bundle on $X_ n$ obtained from $(\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} )\times \mathbb C$ through the identification \[  (z,t)\sim (\mathrm{e}^{-1}z,\mathrm{e}^{-k}t).  \] Give it the metric $|t|_{h_ k}^2=|t|^2|z|^{-2k}$. Under the identification the two factors change by $\mathrm{e}^{-2k}$ and $\mathrm{e}^{2k}$, so this metric descends. In the frame $t=1$ the squared norm is $|z|^{-2k}$, and the curvature form is $k\alpha $. We apply the constructions of subsection 19.8.1 with $X=X_ n$, $L=L_ k$, $h=h_ k$ and this probability volume form. Proposition 19.8.13 . 4ABE18AC08D2 For $m\geq 1$ and the weight $u=0$, \[  N_ m:=h^0(X_ n,L_ k^ m)=\binom {km+n-1}{n-1}, \qquad B_{m,0}=N_ m.  \] The Bergman potential is the constant $m^{-1}\log N_ m$, and the Bergman current is $k\alpha $. Moreover, \[  \deg _\omega L_ k=2k(n-1),\qquad \lim _{m\to \infty }m^{-n}N_ m=0, \qquad (k\alpha )^ n=0,  \] whereas $\int _{X_ n}\omega ^ n=2n>0$. Proof. A section of $L_ k^ m$ lifts to a holomorphic function $f$ on $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $ satisfying \[  f(\mathrm{e}^{-1}z)=\mathrm{e}^{-km}f(z).  \] Since $n\geq 2$, Hartogs' theorem extends $f$ holomorphically to $\mathbb C^ n$. In its Taylor series, a monomial of total degree $j$ is multiplied by $\mathrm{e}^{-j}$ under the contraction, so comparing coefficients shows that only monomials of degree $km$ occur. Conversely, every homogeneous polynomial of that degree has the required equivariance. Counting monomials gives the binomial coefficient; when $k=0$, only the constant polynomials remain. The inner product defined by $h_ k^ m$ and $\mathrm{d}V$ is invariant under the unitary group $U(n)$, so the basis-independent function $K_{m,0}$ is $U(n)$-invariant. It is also invariant under positive radial dilations: every section is homogeneous of degree $km$, and the factor $|z|^{-2km}$ in its squared norm cancels the effect of a dilation. Unitary transformations and positive radial dilations act transitively on $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $, so $K_{m,0}$ is constant. By proposition 19.8.3 its integral is $N_ m$, and $\mathrm{d}V$ has mass one. Thus $K_{m,0}=B_{m,0}=N_ m$. The statements about the Bergman potential and current follow immediately. Since $\alpha ^ n=0$ and $\zeta ^2=0$, \[  \int _{X_ n}k\alpha \wedge \omega ^{n-1} =k(n-1)\int _{X_ n}\alpha ^{n-1}\wedge \zeta =2k(n-1).  \] The binomial coefficient grows at most like $m^{n-1}$, which proves the normalized limit, and $\alpha ^ n=0$ proves the vanishing of the curvature mass. $\square$ For $n=3$, $X_3$ is the Gauduchon threefold of theorem 23.1.1 , on which Hermitian Monge–Ampère masses are unbounded; for $k>0$, the line bundles $L_ k$ nevertheless have positive degree and quadratic section growth. In the notation of example 11.21.4 , $L_ k$ is the line bundle $E_ a$ on $X_ q$ with $q=\mathrm e^{-1}$ and $a=\mathrm e^{-k}$. Hence, for every $n\geq 2$ and $k>0$, the complement $\mathbb P(\mathcal O\oplus L_ k)\setminus \mathbb P(\mathcal O)$ of 11.21 has least smooth convexity index two, that is, it is $2$-convex but not $1$-convex in the sense of 11.17 . When $k=0$, the line bundle is trivial and the least smooth convexity index of its complement is $n+1$, by the same example.

title: 19.8.14 Section counts and infinite Hermitian mass
search_title: Section counts and infinite Hermitian mass
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
text: We return to a connected compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n$ and fix a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$. A weight with trivial multiplier ideals leaves every integrable section space unchanged. When $X$ fails the bounded mass property of definition 13.14.14 , theorem 13.14.18 provides such a weight $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with infinite extended mass. For the trivial line bundle with constant metric, $\mathcal H_ m(U)$ consists of constants and every Bergman current vanishes. Thus section growth in a closed curvature class does not determine the mass in an unrelated Hermitian background. Proposition 19.8.15 . 6400AAE4BA1E Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian metric on $X$ with $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $. There is a potential $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ such that, with $L=\mathcal O_ X$ and its constant metric, \[  \dim \mathcal H_ m(U)=1\quad \hbox{for every }m\geq 1, \qquad \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U)=+\infty .  \] All Bergman currents of $U$ are identically zero. Proof. Take $U$ from theorem 13.14.18 ; its extended mass is infinite, and $\mathcal I(tU)=\mathcal O_ X$ for every $t>0$. Global holomorphic functions on $X$ are constant, and the constant function $1$ lies in $\mathcal H_ m(U)$ because $\mathcal I(mU)=\mathcal O_ X$ and $X$ is compact. Hence every weighted section space is one-dimensional, and its orthonormal basis consists of a nonzero constant. Each Bergman potential $\Phi _ m$ is therefore constant. Since the trivial metric has curvature zero, every Bergman current is zero. $\square$

title: 19.9 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
search_title: Flags, convex bodies and section growth
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
section: 19.9 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text: Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n$, and let $L$ be a holomorphic line bundle on $X$. Along a complete flag of compact complex submanifolds, successive vanishing orders turn each section of $L^ m$ into a lattice point, and the Gauduchon degree bounds of section 19.8 keep the normalized points in a compact convex body. For a graded algebra of sections with some nonzero piece of positive degree, counting these points gives the growth exponent and the leading coefficient of its graded pieces: the exponent is the transcendence degree of the field of section ratios, and the coefficient is an intrinsic lattice volume of the body. A smooth metric on $L$ supplies an additional bound: its maximal curvature rank on the semipositive locus bounds the growth dimension, even if its curvature has no global sign. Not every compact complex manifold carries such a flag, but the blowup of a point does, and Hartogs extension identifies the sections on the blowup with those on $X$; the count therefore applies to every compact complex manifold. Growth of the maximal order $m^ n$ forces $X$ to admit a modification from a projective manifold, and hence to have the bounded mass property. On the Hopf threefold, where Hermitian masses are unbounded, positive-degree line bundles still have bodies that are triangles: their area detects quadratic section growth, although their three-dimensional volume vanishes.

title: 19.9.5 The body of a graded section algebra

section: 19.9 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text:
The valuations of the nonzero homogeneous elements of a graded algebra of sections form a semigroup whose part in degree $m$ has exactly as many elements as the dimension of the degree-$m$ piece. The linear bound of theorem 19.9.3 places this semigroup in a cone with compact height-one slice, and a semigroup counting theorem relates the asymptotic count to the volume of this slice. Let $W_ ullet = igoplus _{m\geq 0}W_ m$ be a graded subalgebra of the section ring $ igoplus _{m\geq 0}H^0(X,L^ m)$, with $W_0=\mathbb C$. For a weight $u\in \mathrm{QPSH}(X)$, the bounded weighted section algebra $\mathcal W_ ullet (u)$ of subsection 19.8.8 is an example. Set \[  S=\{ (0,0)\} \cup \{ (
u (s),m):m\geq 1,\  0
eq s\in W_ m\} .  \] This is an additive semigroup, because the product of two nonzero sections on the connected manifold $X$ is nonzero and valuations add. Choose constants $C_ i$ as in theorem 19.9.3 . Then $S$ lies in the closed cone \[  \{ (x,t)\in \mathbb R^ n	imes \mathbb R:t\geq 0,\  0\leq x_ i\leq C_ i t\} ,  \] whose only point at height zero is the origin. Define \[  \Delta (W_ ullet )= \overline{\operatorname {conv}} \{ m^{-1}
u (s):m\geq 1,\  0
eq s\in W_ m\} ,  \] where $\overline{\operatorname {conv}}$ denotes the closed convex hull. If some positive-degree piece of $W_ ullet $ is nonzero, this is a compact convex subset of $\mathbb R^ n$; equivalently, it is the height-one slice of the closed convex cone generated by $S$. If every positive-degree piece is zero, $\Delta (W_ ullet )=\varnothing $. Write $\operatorname {vol}_{\mathbb R^ n}$ for Euclidean volume. Proposition 19.9.6 . E6B4502ECB3B For every such algebra, \[  \limsup _{m	o \infty }m^{-n}\dim W_ m \leq \operatorname {vol}_{\mathbb R^ n}\Delta (W_ ullet ).  \] In particular, if $\Delta (W_ ullet )$ has empty interior, then $\dim W_ m=o(m^ n)$. Proof. The empty case is immediate. Otherwise, let $S_ m=\{ 
u (s):0
eq s\in W_ m\} $. By lemma 19.9.2 , $S_ m$ has $\dim W_ m$ elements, and $m^{-1}S_ m\subseteq \Delta (W_ ullet )$. Attach to each $a\in S_ m$ the half-open cube $m^{-1}(a+[0,1)^ n)$. These cubes are disjoint, their total volume is $m^{-n}\dim W_ m$, and their union is contained in \[  \Delta (W_ ullet )+[0,m^{-1}]^ n.  \] These compact neighborhoods decrease to $\Delta (W_ ullet )$ as $m	o \infty $, so their volumes converge to its volume. This proves the inequality. A compact convex set has positive $n$-dimensional volume exactly when it has nonempty interior, which gives the last statement. $\square$ We use the following semigroup counting theorem, recalled in Theorem 19.7.20 (Kaveh–Khovanskii) . Let $r\geq 0$, and let $\Sigma \subset \mathbb Z^{r+1}$ be an additive semigroup that generates $\mathbb Z^{r+1}$ as a group and lies in a closed convex cone in $\mathbb R^ r	imes \mathbb R_{\geq 0}$ whose height-one slice is compact and whose only point at height zero is the origin. Then the number of points of $\Sigma $ at height $m$, divided by $m^ r$, converges to the Euclidean volume of the height-one slice of the closed convex cone generated by $\Sigma $. Corollary 19.9.7 . 071721B08FC2 If the subgroup generated by $S$ is all of $\mathbb Z^{n+1}$, then \[  \lim _{m	o \infty }m^{-n}\dim W_ m =\operatorname {vol}_{\mathbb R^ n}\Delta (W_ ullet ).  \] Proof. The semigroup $S$ satisfies the cone conditions established above and, by hypothesis, generates $\mathbb Z^{n+1}$. The semigroup counting theorem therefore applies to it. By lemma 19.9.2 , the number of points of $S$ at height $m$ is $\dim W_ m$, and the height-one slice of the closed convex cone generated by $S$ is $\Delta (W_ ullet )$. $\square$

title: 19.9.8 Intrinsic dimension, lattice and growth
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
section: 19.9 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text:
A body of zero volume in $\mathbb R^ n$ can still detect growth of lower order. The group generated by the valuation semigroup determines a degree period and a lattice in which the body is full-dimensional, and counting in this lattice gives the growth exponent and the leading coefficient. Ratios of sections identify the exponent with a transcendence degree, and since the coefficient is a limit of graded dimensions, it does not depend on the flag. Throughout this section, some positive-degree piece of $W_ ullet $ is nonzero. Let $G\subset \mathbb Z^{n+1}$ be the subgroup generated by $S$, and let $\operatorname {pr}_{n+1}$ be the projection to the last coordinate. Define the degree period $e\geq 1$ by \[  \operatorname {pr}_{n+1}(G)=e\mathbb Z.  \] Thus $e$ is the greatest common divisor of the degrees $m$ with $W_ m
eq 0$. Set \[  \Lambda =G\cap (\mathbb R^ n	imes \{ 0\} ), \qquad d=\operatorname {rank}\Lambda .  \] We regard $\Lambda $ as a lattice in its real span, a $d$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb R^ n	imes \{ 0\} $. Its lattice measure assigns volume one to a fundamental parallelepiped. On each translate of this span we use the translated measure, denoted by $\operatorname {vol}_\Lambda $; when $d=0$, a point has volume one. Theorem 19.9.9 . title: 19.9.11 Moishezon manifolds and bounded mass
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
section: 19.9 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text: A compact complex manifold of dimension $n$ is Moishezon if it has $n$ algebraically independent meromorphic functions. By Moishezon's theorem, a compact irreducible complex space of dimension $n$ with $n$ algebraically independent meromorphic functions admits a modification from a smooth projective manifold; the source of this form of the theorem is given in section 25.16 . Such a modification bounds the masses of Hermitian potentials on $X$: the pulled-back Hermitian form is dominated by a fixed Kähler form, whose Monge–Ampère mass does not change when a smooth potential is added. Recall that $X$ has the bounded mass property if the masses $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ of bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $v$ are uniformly bounded for one, equivalently every, Hermitian form $\omega $ (definition 13.14.14 , proposition 13.14.15 ). Lemma 19.9.12 . 976C06708A77 If a compact complex manifold $X$ admits a modification $\pi :Z\to X$ from a compact Kähler manifold, then $X$ has the bounded mass property. Proof. Fix a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$ and a Kähler form $\kappa $ on $Z$, and choose $C>0$ with $\pi ^*\omega \leq C\kappa $. By proposition 13.14.15 , it suffices to bound the masses of smooth functions $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$. Their pullbacks satisfy \[  0\leq \pi ^*\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi ) \leq C\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi ).  \] Taking top powers and integrating gives \[  \begin{split}  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n & =\int _ Z(\pi ^*\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi ))^ n\\ & \leq \int _ Z(C\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi ))^ n =C^ n\int _ Z\kappa ^ n. \end{split}  \] The first equality follows by change of variables on the set where $\pi $ is biholomorphic, since smooth top-degree forms give the exceptional analytic sets zero mass. The inequality follows by expanding in the smooth semipositive difference $C\kappa -\pi ^*\omega $, and the last equality follows from Stokes' theorem because $\kappa $ is closed. The bound does not depend on $u$, which proves the bounded mass property. $\square$ Theorem 19.9.13 . 0F8B7237A1BA If $X$ fails the bounded mass property, then for every complete flag on $X$, every holomorphic line bundle $L$ and every graded subalgebra $W_\bullet $ of its section ring as above, \[  \operatorname {vol}_{\mathbb R^ n}\Delta (W_\bullet )=0, \qquad \dim W_ m=o(m^ n).  \] Proof. If $\Delta (W_\bullet )$ had nonempty interior, $X$ would have $n$ algebraically independent meromorphic functions by proposition 19.9.10 . Moishezon's theorem would then give a modification of $X$ from a smooth projective, hence Kähler, manifold, contradicting lemma 19.9.12 . The body therefore has empty interior, and proposition 19.9.6 gives both conclusions. $\square$

title: 19.9.14 Flags on a point blowup
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
section: 19.9 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text:
We now remove the assumption that $X$ carries a complete flag. A curve always does, since any point completes the flag. In dimension at least two, the exceptional divisor of the blowup of a point is a projective space and carries a complete flag of linear subspaces, while Hartogs extension identifies the sections on the blowup with those on $X$. The growth formula on the blowup therefore counts the original section spaces. Lemma 19.9.15 . 744C8C462232 Every connected compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n\geq 1$ admits a smooth compact modification $\pi :\widetilde X	o X$ such that $\widetilde X$ carries a complete flag and, for every holomorphic line bundle $L$ on $X$ and every $m\geq 0$, pullback is an isomorphism \[  H^0(X,L^ m)\simeq H^0(\widetilde X,\pi ^*L^ m).  \] These isomorphisms are compatible with products. Proof. If $n=1$, take $\pi $ to be the identity and any point as the last member of the flag; the remaining assertions are then immediate. If $n\geq 2$, blow up a point $p\in X$. The local description of the blowup of $\mathbb C^ n$ at the origin shows that $\widetilde X$ is smooth and that its exceptional divisor is $E\simeq \mathbb P^{n-1}$. A nested sequence of linear subspaces of $E$, together with $\widetilde X$, gives a flag \[  \widetilde X\supset E\supset \mathbb P^{n-2} \supset \cdots \supset \mathbb P^0.  \] Each member is smooth, compact and connected, and is a prime divisor in the preceding member. The modification is an isomorphism off $E$. Let $s$ be a section of $\pi ^*L^ m$. Off $E$, it gives a section of $L^ m$ on $X\setminus \{ p\} $. In a trivialization of $L^ m$ on a coordinate ball centered at $p$, its coefficient is holomorphic on the punctured ball, and by Hartogs' extension theorem, valid since $n\geq 2$, it extends holomorphically across $p$. The extension glues with the section away from $p$ to a section of $L^ m$ on $X$. Its pullback agrees with $s$ off $E$, hence everywhere by the identity theorem. This proves surjectivity; injectivity and compatibility with products follow because pullback is an isomorphism on the dense open set $\widetilde X\setminus E$. $\square$ Given a graded subalgebra $W_ ullet $ of the section ring of $L$, choose a complete flag on the modification of lemma 19.9.15 and apply the constructions of subsection 19.9.5 on $\widetilde X$ to the pulled-back algebra $\widetilde W_ m=\pi ^*W_ m\subseteq H^0(\widetilde X,\pi ^*L^ m)$. The shape of the resulting body may depend on the point and on the flag, but its dimension and its normalized count are determined by $W_ ullet $. Theorem 19.9.16 . 1EBEF54DB76D Assume that some positive-degree piece of $W_ ullet $ is nonzero. There are an integer $0\leq d\leq n$, a degree period $e\geq 1$, and a number $V(W_ ullet )>0$ such that \[  \lim _{q	o \infty } rac{\dim W_{eq}}{(eq)^ d}=V(W_ ullet ), \qquad W_ m=0\quad \hbox{if }e
mid m.  \] Here $d$ is the transcendence degree of the section-ratio field $K(W_ ullet )$, $e$ is the greatest common divisor of the degrees $m$ with $W_ m
eq 0$, and $V(W_ ullet )$ is the intrinsic lattice volume of every body constructed on such a modification. In particular, these three quantities do not depend on the choice of the modification or the flag. Proof. Pullback preserves the graded dimensions and the degrees with nonzero sections. Applying theorem 19.9.3 , theorem 19.9.9 on $\widetilde X$ gives the displayed limit and the positivity of the lattice volume. Pullback also identifies the section-ratio fields, since their elements are the corresponding ratios and pullback is injective on the dense set where $\pi $ is an isomorphism. Thus proposition 19.9.10 identifies $d$ with the transcendence degree of the original field. The unchanged degrees with nonzero sections determine $e$, and the limit of the unchanged dimensions determines $V(W_ ullet )$. None of the three depends on the auxiliary choices. $\square$ Corollary 19.9.17 . EECB2B1DF1A4 For every holomorphic line bundle $L$ on a connected compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n$, \[  h^0(X,L^ m)=O(m^ n).  \] If $X$ is not Moishezon, then, for each $L$, either all positive-degree section spaces of $L$ vanish, or there is an integer $d<n$ for which \[  h^0(X,L^ m)=O(m^ d).  \] In particular $m^{-n}h^0(X,L^ m)	o 0$. These conclusions apply when $X$ fails the bounded mass property. Proof. If all positive-degree section spaces vanish, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, apply the theorem to the full section ring. Since $W_ m=0$ for $e
mid m$, the limit gives $h^0(X,L^ m)=O(m^ d)$ for all degrees, with $d\leq n$. If $d=n$, the section-ratio field contains $n$ algebraically independent meromorphic functions on $X$, so $X$ is Moishezon. Thus $d<n$ when $X$ is not Moishezon. Finally, by Moishezon's theorem a Moishezon manifold admits a modification from a projective, hence Kähler, manifold, so it has the bounded mass property by lemma 19.9.12 . The contrapositive gives the last assertion. $\square$ Since the multiplier-ideal section spaces $\mathcal H_ m(u)$ of subsection 19.8.1 are contained in $H^0(X,L^ m)$, the same upper bounds hold for them. Identifying weighted section spaces on a modification, however, requires a correction by the Jacobian; lemma 5.43.22 gives the corresponding formula involving the relative canonical bundle.

title: 19.9.18 Curvature rank and section growth
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
section: 19.9 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text:
The dimension of a section-ratio field can be bounded by a smooth curvature form, even when that form changes rank and has no global sign. The key is to arrange that a maximum of a section norm occurs where the section map has its maximal rank. This gives a pointwise restriction on the growth counted by the preceding sections. Keep the connected compact complex manifold $X$ and line bundle $L$, and choose a smooth Hermitian metric $h$ on $L$. In a local frame write $|e|_ h^2=\mathrm e^{-\chi }$ and put $ eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $, with the normalization of subsection 19.8.1 . Let $r=\max _ X\operatorname {rank} eta $. No positivity of $ eta $, constant-rank condition or Kähler metric is assumed. Set $S_ h=\{ x: eta _ x\geq 0\} $; when $S_ h$ is nonempty, let $r_ h^+=\max _{S_ h}\operatorname {rank} eta $. Proposition 19.9.19 . C8B2CB1B6819 For a nonzero subspace $W\subset H^0(X,L^ p)$, $p\geq 1$, let $B_ W$ be its common zero set and let $\Phi _ W:X\setminus B_ W	o \mathbb P(W^*)$ be its section map. If $d$ is the maximal rank of its differential, there is $x_*
otin B_ W$ such that \[  \operatorname {rank}\mathrm d\Phi _ W|_{x_*}=d, \qquad  eta _{x_*}\geq 0, \qquad \operatorname {rank} eta _{x_*}\geq d.  \] Proof. Choose a basis $s_0,\ldots ,s_ N$ of $W$. title: 19.9.26 The Hopf flag and its lower-dimensional body
search_title: The Hopf flag and its lower-dimensional body
topic: Sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies
section: 19.9 Flags, convex bodies and section growth
text: On a scalar Hopf manifold, the coordinate subspaces give a complete flag ending at a point of an elliptic fiber. Along this flag, a homogeneous section reduces to a nowhere-vanishing section on the elliptic fiber, so the last coordinate of its valuation is zero; the remaining coordinates fill a simplex whose intrinsic volume gives the section growth. Let $X_ n$ and $L_ k$, with $n\geq 2$ and $k\geq 0$, be as in subsection 19.8.12 . In the covering coordinates $z_1,\ldots ,z_ n$, the image of $\{ z_1=\cdots =z_{n-1}=0\} \setminus \{ 0\} $ in $X_ n$ is an elliptic curve; choose a point $p$ on it. Consider the flag $Y_0=X_ n$, \[  Y_ i=\{ z_1=\cdots =z_ i=0\} /\langle \mathrm{e}^{-1}\rangle \quad (1\leq i\leq n-1),\qquad Y_ n=\{ p\} \subset Y_{n-1},  \] where $/\langle \mathrm e^{-1}\rangle $ denotes the quotient of the punctured linear subspace by the contraction $z\mapsto \mathrm e^{-1}z$. Each member is smooth, compact and connected, and is a prime divisor in the preceding member. Take $W_ m=H^0(X_ n,L_ k^ m)$. Proposition 19.9.27 . 987D754E15F6 For this flag, \[  \{ \nu (s):0\neq s\in W_ m\}  =\{ (a_1,\ldots ,a_{n-1},0):a_ i\in \mathbb N, \  \textstyle \sum _ i a_ i\leq km\} .  \] Consequently \[  \Delta (W_\bullet )= \{ (x_1,\ldots ,x_{n-1},0):x_ i\geq 0, \  \textstyle \sum _ i x_ i\leq k\} .  \] Its $n$-dimensional volume is zero. When $k>0$, its volume in the coordinate hyperplane $x_ n=0$, with the Euclidean measure for which the coordinate lattice has covolume one, is \[  \frac{k^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} =\lim _{m\to \infty }\frac{\dim W_ m}{m^{n-1}}.  \] For $k=0$ the body is a point and $\dim W_ m=1$. Proof. By proposition 19.8.13 , sections of $L_ k^ m$ are homogeneous polynomials of degree $km$. Dividing successively by the highest powers of $z_1,\ldots ,z_{n-1}$ that divide the section, and restricting at each step, leaves a nonzero multiple of $z_ n^{km-a_1-\cdots -a_{n-1}}$, where $a_ i$ is the $i$th valuation. This residual section has no zeros on $Y_{n-1}$, so the last valuation is zero, and the preceding ones are nonnegative with sum at most $km$. Conversely, every such tuple is the valuation of the monomial \[  z_1^{a_1}\cdots z_{n-1}^{a_{n-1}} z_ n^{km-a_1-\cdots -a_{n-1}}.  \] The normalized values lie in the displayed simplex and, for $m=1$, include all its vertices, so their closed convex hull is the simplex. For $k>0$, its coordinate-lattice volume is $k^{n-1}/(n-1)!$, the leading coefficient of the binomial count in proposition 19.8.13 . For $k=0$, only the constant polynomials remain. $\square$ 555D3252DD76 19.9.28 For the Hopf threefold and $k>0$, the body is a triangle in a coordinate plane. Its area gives the quadratic section growth, while its ambient volume vanishes.

title: 21.14 Hopf fibrations and toric potentials
text: Let $n\geq 2$ and let $X_ n$ be the scalar Hopf manifold of subsection 19.8.12 , which fibers over $\mathbb P^{n-1}$ with compact elliptic fibers. A potential in a pulled-back closed class is constant on each fiber and therefore descends to the base. For such a weight, the weighted section integrands also descend, and fiber integration identifies the section norms and Bergman kernels on the two spaces. A potential of the standard Gauduchon form may vary along the fibers. For one that descends, the vertical part of this form supplies a single factor in the Hermitian Monge–Ampère measure, and fiber integration reduces the equation to the projective base. For bounded descended potentials, closedness on the base determines the normalizing constant and gives uniqueness up to additive constants. On the Hopf threefold, the descended masses are at most six, so unbounded masses require variation along the fibers. On the base, invariance under separate rotations of the homogeneous coordinates gives a real convex description in logarithmic coordinates. Strict positivity of the curvature makes the gradient a parametrization of the relative interior of a simplex. Write $\pi :X_ n\to \mathbb P^{n-1}$ for the projection. The forms $\alpha ,\zeta ,\omega $ and the probability volume form $\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^ n/(2n)$ are as in subsection 19.8.12 . Write $\sigma $ for the Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^{n-1}$ normalized by $\int _{\mathbb P^{n-1}}\sigma ^{n-1}=1$, and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ for the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of theorem 13.14.3 . The fiber calculations use the following identities, where $y\in \mathbb P^{n-1}$: \[  \alpha =\pi ^*\sigma ,\qquad \omega =\alpha +\zeta ,\qquad \zeta ^2=0,\qquad \mathrm{d}V=\tfrac 12\alpha ^{n-1}\wedge \zeta ,\qquad \int _{\pi ^{-1}(y)}\zeta =2.  \]

title: 21.14.1 Weighted sections on the projective base
search_title: Weighted sections on the projective base
text: For an integer $k\geq 0$, the line bundle $L_ k$ of subsection 19.8.12 , with its metric $h_ k$, is the pullback of $\mathcal O(k)$ with its Fubini–Study metric. By the proof of proposition 19.8.13 , sections of $L_ k^ m$ are represented by homogeneous polynomials $f$ of degree $km$ in the covering coordinates $z\in \mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $, exactly as sections of $\mathcal O(km)$ on $\mathbb P^{n-1}$, and the pointwise squared norm $|f(z)|^2|z|^{-2km}$ is invariant under every nonzero complex scalar. If the weight also descends, the weighted integrand is a function on the base, and fiber integration identifies the norms and Bergman kernels of subsection 19.8.1 on the two spaces. Theorem 21.14.2 . DCED1F266D4F Let $k\geq 0$ be an integer and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X_ n,k\alpha )$. Then $u=\pi ^*v$ for a unique $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^{n-1},k\sigma )$. For every positive integer $m$, pullback identifies the weighted section spaces isometrically: for a section $s$ in the space on the base, \[  \begin{split}  H^0\bigl (\mathbb P^{n-1},\mathcal O(km)\otimes \mathcal I(mv)\bigr ) & \simeq H^0\bigl (X_ n,L_ k^ m\otimes \mathcal I(mu)\bigr ),\\  \| \pi ^*s\| _{X_ n,m,u}^2& =\| s\| _{\mathbb P^{n-1},m,v}^2. \end{split}  \] Here the norm on the base is defined with the Fubini–Study metric and the volume form $\sigma ^{n-1}$. The kernels $K$ and, off their pole sets, $B$ on $X_ n$ are the pullbacks of the corresponding kernels on the base. Pullback also identifies the bounded weighted section algebras $\mathcal W_\bullet (v)$ and $\mathcal W_\bullet (u)$. Proof. The descent of the potential follows from proposition 5.43.5 . By the proof of proposition 19.8.13 , the unweighted section spaces on both manifolds consist of the same homogeneous polynomials of degree $km$, and the pointwise norms of corresponding sections agree because the metrics correspond. For every nonnegative Borel function $F$ on the base, fiber integration gives \[  \int _{X_ n}(F\circ \pi )\, \mathrm{d}V =\frac12\int _{\mathbb P^{n-1}}F\sigma ^{n-1} \int _{\pi ^{-1}(y)}\zeta =\int _{\mathbb P^{n-1}}F\sigma ^{n-1}.  \] Applied to $F=|s|^2\mathrm{e}^{-mv}$, with arbitrary values on the pole set, this formula gives equality of the two possibly infinite integrals. Finally, a nonnegative function on the base is bounded if and only if its pullback is bounded, so pullback also identifies the bounded weighted sections, compatibly with multiplication. $\square$
