title: 21.14.3 Descended measures and equations
text:
The pulled-back curvature of a descended potential has no component in the fiber direction; the form $\zeta $ supplies it. Since $\zeta ^2=0$, the Hermitian top power of a descended potential consists of a single mixed term, and fiber integration of this term determines the mass and reduces the Monge–Ampère equation for descended potentials to the base. For a positive Borel measure $
u $ on $\mathbb P^{n-1}$, we write $\pi ^*
u \wedge \zeta $ for the measure on $X_ n$ defined, on nonnegative Borel functions $F$, by \[  \int _{X_ n}F\, \pi ^*
u \wedge \zeta =\int _{\mathbb P^{n-1}} \left(\int _{\pi ^{-1}(y)}F\zeta ight)\mathrm{d}
u (y).  \] When $
u $ is given by a smooth top-degree form, this agrees with the pullback of the form wedged with $\zeta $. Theorem 21.14.4 . 94243AEE3360 For a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $v$ on $\mathbb P^{n-1}$, the pullback $u=\pi ^*v$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X_ n,\omega )$ if and only if $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^{n-1},\sigma )$. In this case \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u) =n\, \pi ^*\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\sigma (v)\wedge \zeta .  \] Consequently \[  \int _{X_ n}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u) =2n\int _{\mathbb P^{n-1}}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\sigma (v) \leq 2n,  \] with equality for bounded $v$. For an integer $k\geq 0$ and $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^{n-1},k\sigma )$, \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k\alpha }(\pi ^*v)=0  \] as a measure on the $n$-dimensional manifold $X_ n$. Proof. If $v$ is $\sigma $-plurisubharmonic, then \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\pi ^*(\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)+\zeta \geq 0.  \] Conversely, suppose that the left-hand side is positive. Wedge it with the smooth semipositive form $\zeta $ and push the result forward to the base. Since $\zeta ^2=0$ and the fiber integral of $\zeta $ is two, \[  \pi _* igl ((\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge \zeta  igr ) =2(\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)\geq 0;  \] this identity of currents follows by testing against smooth forms on the base and integrating over the fibers. It proves the converse. For the measure formula, first let $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^{n-1},\sigma )$ be bounded. By lemma 5.28.4 , its bounded products commute with $\pi ^*$. Since $\zeta ^2=0$ and the base has dimension $n-1$, expanding the power gives \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n =n\, \pi ^*(\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-1}\wedge \zeta ,  \] and fiber integration identifies the right-hand side with the measure defined above. For general $v$, normalize $v\leq 0$ and set $v_ j=\max (v,-j)$. Since $\sigma $ is positive, these are bounded $\sigma $-plurisubharmonic functions, and their pullbacks are exactly $u_ j=\max (u,-j)$. Multiply the bounded identity by the common indicator function $\mathbf1_{\{ u>-j\} }=\pi ^*\mathbf1_{\{ v>-j\} }$ and pass to the increasing limits defining the extended measures. Fiber integration of nonnegative functions justifies the limit on the right-hand side, including over the poles. The mass formula follows because each fiber has $\zeta $-mass two. The extended mass on the base is at most one: on $\{ v>-j\} $, its truncated measure is bounded above by the full bounded product, whose mass is $\int \sigma ^{n-1}=1$ by Stokes' theorem for the closed form $\sigma $. For bounded $v$ nothing is removed, and equality holds. For the last assertion, take bounded truncations of $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^{n-1},k\sigma )$. By lemma 5.28.4 , the $n$th powers of their pulled-back currents vanish. Restricting to the truncation levels and taking the increasing limit shows that the extended measure is zero; this includes the case $k=0$. $\square$ If an $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potential is constant on the fibers, the local-section argument in proposition 5.43.5 shows that it descends to a quasi-plurisubharmonic function on the base. The theorem therefore bounds its Hermitian mass by $2n$. On the Hopf threefold this bound is six, so the unbounded masses of section 23.1 require potentials that vary along the fibers. For the equation, let $p>1$ and let $f\geq 0$ belong to $L^ p(\mathbb P^{n-1},\sigma ^{n-1})$, with $\int f\sigma ^{n-1}>0$. For potentials $u=\pi ^*v$ with bounded $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(\mathbb P^{n-1},\sigma )$, the equation D50C510DA3A9 21.14.5  egin{equation} \index{Monge--Ampere equation@Monge--Amp\` ere equation!Hopf reduction} (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=c(f\circ \pi )\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad c>0, \end{equation} is equivalent to the base equation \[  (\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-1}= rac{c}{2n}f\sigma ^{n-1}.  \] Indeed, the base equation implies ( 21.14.5 ) by theorem 21.14.4 and the formula for $\mathrm{d}V$. Conversely, pushing ( 21.14.5 ) forward to the base gives $2n(\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-1}=cf\sigma ^{n-1}$. Integrating the base equation determines the constant: \[  c= rac{2n}{\int _{\mathbb P^{n-1}}f\sigma ^{n-1}}.  \] Since $\sigma $ is closed, it satisfies the Guan–Li condition ( 14.25.1 ). Applied to $(\mathbb P^{n-1},\sigma )$, 14.25.2 gives a continuous solution of the base equation with this constant, unique up to additive constants among bounded $\sigma $-plurisubharmonic functions. Consequently ( 21.14.5 ) has a continuous solution, unique up to additive constants among bounded descended potentials. For smooth positive $f$, theorem 14.2.1 on the base gives a smooth solution $v$, and the constant is again determined by Stokes' theorem. For a real parameter $\lambda $, the same calculation shows that the equation with right-hand side $c\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}(f\circ \pi )\mathrm{d}V$ is equivalent to the base equation with right-hand side $(c/(2n))\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v}f\sigma ^{n-1}$.

title: 21.14.6 Logarithmic coordinates and the gradient simplex
search_title: Logarithmic coordinates and the gradient simplex
text:
For potentials invariant under rotations of the individual coordinates, the complex Hessian becomes the real Hessian of a function of the logarithmic coordinates. Invariance under complex scaling gives this Hessian a null direction; transverse to it, positivity becomes convexity, and boundedness of the potential confines the gradient to a simplex. Logarithmic growth makes every interior point of the simplex a gradient value, and strict positivity on the base makes the gradient injective modulo the null direction. In this section, $k>0$ is a real number. Let $v$ be a smooth real function on $\mathbb P^{n-1}$ that is invariant under the torus action \[  [z_1:\cdots :z_ n]\longmapsto [\mathrm e^{\mathrm it_1}z_1:\cdots :\mathrm e^{\mathrm it_ n}z_ n], \qquad t\in \mathbb R^ n,  \] and put $u=\pi ^*v$. On the locus where all covering coordinates $z_ i$ are nonzero, set $x_ i=\log |z_ i|^2$. By this invariance, $u$ is a function of $x=(x_1,\ldots ,x_ n)$, which we denote by $u(x)$, and we set \[  F(x)=k\log \left(\sum _{i=1}^ n \mathrm{e}^{x_ i}ight)+u(x).  \] Write $
abla F=(F_ i)$ and $D^2F=(F_{ij})$ for its Euclidean gradient and Hessian, and let $\mathbf1=(1,\ldots ,1)$. Since $u$ is invariant under complex scaling, for every $t\in \mathbb R$, 5DB0E5246A09 21.14.7  egin{equation}  F(x+t\mathbf1)=F(x)+kt. \end{equation} Proposition 21.14.8 . F23340CADBE0 On this locus, $k\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ if and only if $F$ is convex. If $F$ is convex, its gradient lies in \[  \Sigma _ k=\{ p\in \mathbb R^ n:p_ i\geq 0,\  	extstyle \sum _ i p_ i=k\} ,  \] and $D^2F\, \mathbf1=0$. If $k\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is positive definite on $\mathbb P^{n-1}$, the gradient induces a bijection from $\mathbb R^ n/\mathbb R\mathbf1$ onto the relative interior of $\Sigma _ k$. Proof. On the covering space, $k\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F$. In the coordinates $z_ i$, the Hermitian coefficient matrix of this form is a positive constant times \[  \left( rac{F_{ij}}{z_ i\overline z_ j}ight)_{i,j}.  \] This matrix is congruent to the real Hessian $(F_{ij})$ through the invertible diagonal matrix with entries $1/z_ i$, which proves the first equivalence. Differentiating ( 21.14.7 ) gives $\sum _ i F_ i=k$ and $D^2F\, \mathbf1=0$. Since $v$ is bounded on the compact base, there is a constant $C$ such that \[  \left|F(x)-k\log \sum _ i \mathrm{e}^{x_ i}ight|\leq C.  \] Fix $x$ and a coordinate vector $e_ i$. Since $n\geq 2$, the convex function $t\mapsto F(x+te_ i)$ is bounded above as $t	o -\infty $. Its derivative cannot be negative anywhere: otherwise the supporting line at such a point would tend to $+\infty $ as $t	o -\infty $. Thus $F_ i\geq 0$, which proves $
abla F\in \Sigma _ k$. Now assume that $k\sigma +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is positive definite. The kernel of the differential of the projection $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} 	o \mathbb P^{n-1}$ is exactly the complex scalar direction, so the Hessian of $F$ is positive definite transverse to $\mathbf1$. In particular $F$ is strictly convex on $H=\{ x:\sum _ i x_ i=0\} $. Along each line $x+te_ i$, the derivative of $F$ is strictly increasing and nonnegative everywhere, hence positive. Thus every gradient lies in the relative interior of $\Sigma _ k$. Conversely, take $p\in \mathbb R^ n$ with $p_ i>0$ and $\sum _ i p_ i=k$. The function $F(x)-p\cdot x$ is invariant under translation along $\mathbf1$, and we claim that it tends to $+\infty $ on $H$ as $|x|	o \infty $. Indeed, \[  k\max _ i x_ i-p\cdot x =\sum _ i p_ i(\max _ j x_ j-x_ i)  \] is strictly positive at every nonzero vector of $H$, and hence has a positive minimum on the unit sphere of $H$. Since $F$ differs from $k\log \sum _ i \mathrm{e}^{x_ i}$ by a bounded function and $\log \sum _ i \mathrm{e}^{x_ i}\geq \max _ i x_ i$, the claim follows. Hence $F(x)-p\cdot x$ has a unique minimizer on $H$. At this point $
abla F-p$ is a multiple of $\mathbf1$; both vectors have coordinate sum $k$, so the multiple is zero. This proves surjectivity, and strict convexity on $H$ proves injectivity. $\square$

title: 20.4 Divisorial currents on compact modifications
text: Let $X$ be a compact complex manifold and $Y\subset X$ a connected compact complex submanifold of dimension $r\geq 1$. Fix a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ and a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $X$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ have generic Lelong number $\nu (u,Y)=\inf _{y\in Y}\nu (u,y)=0$. The divisorial trace data of $u$ along $Y$ (section 20.3 ) assign a number to every prime divisor on every smooth compact modification of $Y$. A single model sees only part of these data, since blowing up can reveal vanishing that had higher codimension on $Y$. Summing the coefficients visible on one model gives a closed positive current, whose mass is controlled by a Gauduchon degree. These currents agree under pushforward, while their pullbacks acquire an effective exceptional correction. The trace envelope, which imposes the trace inequalities on all models at once, pulls back exactly. This discrepancy explains why the ordinary singularity type of the divisorial part on one model need not realize the full trace data. The divisorial currents are closed even when the background is not. In a closed restricted background, subtracting them gives residual Bott–Chern classes that are compatible between models. To identify the exceptional correction for an infinite divisorial sum, we need pullback to be continuous on closed positive currents; this continuity comes from choosing, in each Bott–Chern class, the representative of constant Gauduchon trace. Residual classes with a nonzero prescribed exterior derivative belong to the affine spaces of section 10.30 . Let $u_ m$ and $\epsilon _ m$ be the analytic approximants and curvature errors of corollary 5.36.2 : $u_ m$ has analytic singularities of type $(1/m,\mathcal I(mu))$, and $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ m\geq -\epsilon _ m\omega $ with $\epsilon _ m\to 0$. For a smooth compact modification $\pi :Z\to Y$, put \[  \theta _ Z=\pi ^*(\theta |_ Y),\qquad \omega _ Z^0=\pi ^*(\omega |_ Y),\qquad b_ m(E)=\operatorname {ord}_ E\bigl (\mathcal I(mu)\mathcal O_ Y\bigr ) \quad (m\in \mathbb Z_{\geq 1}).  \] Here $E$ is a prime divisor on $Z$, $[E]$ denotes its integration current, and $b_ m(E)$ is the vanishing order along $E$ of the image ideal $\mathfrak a_ m(u;Y)=\mathcal I(mu)\mathcal O_ Y$ pulled back to $Z$. By theorem 20.3.2 , the trace numbers satisfy \[  \frac{b_ m(E)}m\longrightarrow \tau _{Y,u}(E),\qquad \tau _{Y,u}(E)=\sup _{m\geq 1}\frac{b_ m(E)}m.  \] By corollary 5.43.26 , the restrictions $u_ m|_ Y$ are not identically $-\infty $, and the curvature bound pulls back to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((u_ m|_ Y)\circ \pi )\geq -\theta _ Z-\epsilon _ m\omega _ Z^0$.

title: 20.4.1 Divisorial trace currents
text: On a model $Z$, the curvature current of the pulled-back analytic approximant dominates the divisor of the image ideal of $\mathcal I(mu)$. Pairing with a Gauduchon metric removes the potential from this inequality, and the resulting bound passes to the limit in each coefficient and controls the sum of all trace coefficients. For a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ on $Z$, we call $\int _ ZT\wedge \gamma ^{r-1}$ the trace mass of a positive $(1,1)$-current $T$; when $r=1$, $\gamma ^{r-1}=1$ and $\gamma $ may be any Hermitian metric. For a positive integer $m$, with $E$ ranging over the prime divisors on $Z$, define the finite divisorial current \[  D_{m,Z}=\frac1m\sum _ E b_ m(E)[E].  \] The sum is finite: the pulled-back image ideal is a nonzero coherent ideal on the compact manifold $Z$, so its zero set has only finitely many components of codimension one. We also consider the possibly infinite sum \[  S_ Z(u;Y)=\sum _ E\tau _{Y,u}(E)[E],  \] which a priori is defined only through its finite subsums. Theorem 20.4.2 . A67FA9DFB4BC The sum $S_ Z(u;Y)$ defines a closed positive $(1,1)$-current of finite mass on $Z$. For every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ on $Z$, B7771456202C 20.4.3 \begin{equation}  \int _ Z S_ Z(u;Y)\wedge \gamma ^{r-1} \leq \int _ Z\theta _ Z\wedge \gamma ^{r-1}, \end{equation} where $\gamma ^{r-1}=1$ if $r=1$. Moreover, \[  0\leq D_{m,Z}\leq S_ Z(u;Y),\qquad \int _ Z\bigl (S_ Z(u;Y)-D_{m,Z}\bigr )\wedge \gamma ^{r-1} \longrightarrow 0.  \] In particular, $D_{m,Z}$ converges weakly to $S_ Z(u;Y)$ as currents, and the dyadic sequence $D_{2^ j,Z}$ is increasing. Proof. Set $w_ m=(u_ m|_ Y)\circ \pi $. By corollary 5.43.26 , these functions are not identically $-\infty $. Moreover, $u_ m|_ Y$ has analytic type $(1/m,\mathfrak a_ m(u;Y))$ by proposition 5.34.1 , as in the proof of that corollary, so its pullback $w_ m$ has generic Lelong number $b_ m(E)/m$ along $E$. Thus \[  T_ m=\theta _ Z+\epsilon _ m\omega _ Z^0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ m\geq 0, \qquad \nu (w_ m,E)=b_ m(E)/m.  \] Lemma 5.38.1 gives $D_{m,Z}\leq T_ m$. Integration by parts for currents and the Gauduchon condition therefore give \[  \int _ ZD_{m,Z}\wedge \gamma ^{r-1} \leq \int _ Z\theta _ Z\wedge \gamma ^{r-1} +\epsilon _ m\int _ Z\omega _ Z^0\wedge \gamma ^{r-1}.  \] For any fixed finite set of prime divisors, let $m\to \infty $ in the coefficients of these divisors, using theorem 20.3.2 , and then take the supremum over all finite sets. This proves ( 20.4.3 ) for every finite subsum. Every prime divisor has strictly positive $\gamma $-area. Hence at most countably many coefficients are positive: for each positive integer $k$, only finitely many terms can have trace mass at least $1/k$, and every positive term is among these for some $k$. Enumerate the corresponding divisors. The finite partial sums are increasing positive closed currents with uniformly bounded trace mass. They therefore converge, in the sense of coefficient measures and weakly as currents, to a positive current of finite mass, which is closed because differentiation is continuous on currents. This constructs $S_ Z(u;Y)$ and proves the integral inequality. The supremum formula for $\tau _{Y,u}(E)$ gives $b_ m(E)/m\leq \tau _{Y,u}(E)$ for every $m$ and $E$, and the limit along the integers gives coefficientwise convergence. Dominated convergence for the countable series with summable weights $\tau _{Y,u}(E)\int _ E\gamma ^{r-1}$ shows that the trace mass of $S_ Z-D_{m,Z}$ tends to zero. Since a fixed smooth test form is bounded in absolute value, on positive $(1,1)$-currents, by a constant times the trace mass, this gives weak convergence. Finally, $b_{2m}(E)\geq 2b_ m(E)$ gives $D_{2m,Z}\geq D_{m,Z}$. $\square$

title: Theorem 20.4.2
text: Theorem 20.4.2 . A67FA9DFB4BC The sum $S_ Z(u;Y)$ defines a closed positive $(1,1)$-current of finite mass on $Z$. For every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ on $Z$, B7771456202C 20.4.3 \begin{equation}  \int _ Z S_ Z(u;Y)\wedge \gamma ^{r-1} \leq \int _ Z\theta _ Z\wedge \gamma ^{r-1}, \end{equation} where $\gamma ^{r-1}=1$ if $r=1$. Thus \[  T_ m=\theta _ Z+\epsilon _ m\omega _ Z^0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ m\geq 0, \qquad \nu (w_ m,E)=b_ m(E)/m.  \] Lemma 5.38.1 gives $D_{m,Z}\leq T_ m$. title: 20.4.4 Compatibility between models
text: Under a further modification, a prime divisor and its strict transform define the same vanishing order on the image ideals, while exceptional divisors disappear under pushforward. Hence the trace currents are compatible with pushforward. Under pullback, exceptional divisors can carry additional vanishing, and divisibility of the pulled-back ideals shows that this additional vanishing is nonnegative. Theorem 20.4.5 . 76E7A41B366A Let $g:Z'\to Z$ be a smooth compact modification, and regard $Z'$ as a model over $Y$ through $\pi \circ g$. Then \[  g_*S_{Z'}(u;Y)=S_ Z(u;Y).  \] The current $S_ Z(u;Y)$ is additive and positively homogeneous in $u$. For every finite set $\mathcal F$ of prime divisors on $Z$, the finite effective real divisor \[  A_{\mathcal F}=\sum _{E\in \mathcal F}\tau _{Y,u}(E)E  \] satisfies \[  [g^*A_{\mathcal F}]\leq S_{Z'}(u;Y).  \] Proof. Every prime divisor on $Z'$ is either the strict transform of a prime divisor on $Z$ or exceptional for $g$. If $E'$ is the strict transform of a prime divisor $E\subset Z$, then $g$ is biholomorphic near generic points of $E'$. Hence $E'$ and $E$ define the same vanishing order on the image ideals from $Y$, so $\tau _{Y,u}(E')=\tau _{Y,u}(E)$, and $g_*[E']=[E]$. The image of an exceptional prime divisor $F$ has codimension at least two. The pullback of a smooth $(r-1,r-1)$ test form therefore restricts to zero on the regular locus of $F$, where the restriction of $g$ has complex rank at most $r-2$; thus $g_*[F]=0$. In dimension one, a modification between smooth compact curves is an isomorphism, and there are no exceptional divisors. Pushforward under the proper map $g$ is continuous on currents. Applying it to the increasing finite partial sums, or equivalently testing their summable positive coefficient measures, proves the displayed compatibility. Additivity and homogeneity follow coefficientwise from proposition 20.3.4 . For the inequality, fix a positive integer $m$ and let $\mathfrak a_{m,Z}=\mathcal I(mu)\mathcal O_ Z$ denote the image ideal on $Z$. Its divisorial vanishing gives \[  \mathfrak a_{m,Z}\subseteq \mathcal O_ Z\left(-\sum _{E\in \mathcal F}b_ m(E)E\right).  \] Indeed, on a manifold, a holomorphic function vanishing to the indicated generic orders is divisible by the corresponding powers of the local equations of the divisors. Pulling back this inclusion and taking the order along a prime divisor $F\subset Z'$ gives 55CA1CD82506 20.4.6 \begin{equation}  b_ m(F)\geq \sum _{E\in \mathcal F} b_ m(E)\operatorname {ord}_ F(g^*E). \end{equation} Divide by $m$ and let $m\to \infty $; the sum is finite. Thus every coefficient of $g^*A_{\mathcal F}$ is at most the corresponding coefficient $\tau _{Y,u}(F)$ of $S_{Z'}(u;Y)$. Since both sides are positive divisorial currents, this proves the asserted inequality of currents. $\square$

title: 20.4.7 The trace envelope as a common majorant
search_title: The trace envelope as a common majorant
text: The trace envelope of subsection 20.3.23 imposes the trace inequalities along all divisors over $Y$, including those that do not appear on a given model. It therefore gives a single potential on $Y$, in the original background $\theta |_ Y$, whose pulled-back curvature current dominates the trace current on every model. Proposition 20.4.8 . C592843AB1E3 There exists $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta |_ Y)$ such that, for every smooth compact modification $\pi :Z\to Y$, \[  \nu (v\circ \pi ,E)\geq \tau _{Y,u}(E) \quad \hbox{for every prime divisor }E\subset Z,  \] and \[  \pi ^*(\theta |_ Y)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ \pi )\geq S_ Z(u;Y).  \] Proof. Take for $v$ the trace envelope $\mathcal T_{\theta |_ Y}(u;Y)$ of ( 20.3.25 ). By theorem 20.3.27 , it belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta |_ Y)$ and satisfies every defining trace inequality. On a fixed model $Z$, lemma 5.38.1 therefore allows us to subtract every finite partial sum of $S_ Z(u;Y)$ from $\theta _ Z+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ \pi )$ while preserving positivity. Passing to the limit of these partial sums, constructed in theorem 20.4.2 , preserves positivity and proves the second assertion. $\square$ The potential in the proof is canonical: by theorem 20.3.30 , $v\circ \pi $ is the trace envelope on $Z$ in the background $\theta _ Z$ for the same trace data. Its generic Lelong numbers may nevertheless exceed the prescribed trace numbers. Exact realization of the trace data requires the reverse inequality, which section 20.3 establishes for analytic singularities, for Kähler $Y$ in sufficiently large closed backgrounds, and for pullbacks from curves. By contrast, the ordinary singularity type attached to $S_ Z$ by corollary 5.38.6 records only the divisorial part on the particular model $Z$.

title: 20.4.9 Bott–Chern classes and closed currents
text: Bott–Chern cohomology records a closed $(1,1)$-current modulo $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of global functions, and so separates the smooth background of the current from its potential. When $\theta $ is closed, subtracting the trace current from the pulled-back background gives a residual class on each model, and compatibility with pushforward organizes these classes into a b-divisor class in the sense of 20.1.1 The notion of b-divisors . For a complex manifold $Z$, let $\Lambda ^{1,1}_{\mathbb R}$ denote the bundle of real $(1,1)$-forms and define \[  H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(Z,\mathbb R) =\frac{\{ \beta \in C^\infty (Z,\Lambda ^{1,1}_{\mathbb R}):\mathrm{d}\beta =0\} }{\{ \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f:f\in C^\infty (Z,\mathbb R)\} }.  \] Lemma 20.4.10 . C288B8AF0D4E Replacing smooth forms and smooth functions in this quotient by real currents and real distributions gives the same space. In particular, every closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on $Z$ can be written \[  T=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w  \] with $\beta $ smooth and closed and $w$ a global quasi-plurisubharmonic function. Proof. The decomposition of lemma 5.38.4 shows that the natural map from the smooth quotient to the current quotient is surjective, and it gives a quasi-plurisubharmonic potential for positive currents. The same lemma shows that two distributional potentials in such decompositions differ by a smooth function; equivalently, a distribution whose $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ is smooth is itself smooth. Hence two smooth forms that are identified in the current quotient are already identified in the smooth quotient, and the map is injective. $\square$ From now on, $Z$ is connected and compact. By the lemma, every closed real $(1,1)$-current $T$ has a Bott–Chern class, written $\{ T\} _{\mathrm{BC}}$; the class is pseudoeffective if it contains a closed positive current. Pullback of classes is defined on smooth representatives. Pushforward of classes under a modification is defined on current representatives; it is well defined because pushforward commutes with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, and by the lemma the resulting class is again a smooth Bott–Chern class. For a modification $g$ and every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\beta $ on its target, $g_*g^*\beta =\beta $ as currents, by the change of variables formula for the degree-one map $g$. A Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ defines a linear functional on this cohomology: \[  \ell _\gamma (\{ T\} _{\mathrm{BC}})=\int _ ZT\wedge \gamma ^{\dim Z-1}.  \] Integration by parts for currents shows that it does not depend on the representative. On a positive representative it is nonnegative, and it vanishes only if that representative is zero, by the strict positivity of the metric. In particular, the pseudoeffective cone contains no line: if $T_1,T_2\geq 0$ represent opposite classes, their sum has zero Gauduchon pairing, hence $T_1=T_2=0$. Gauduchon pairings detect closed curvature information that is invisible in de Rham cohomology. Consider the Hopf manifold $X_ n$, $n\geq 2$, with its Gauduchon form $\omega $ and covering coordinates $z\in \mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $, as in subsection 19.8.12 . The form $\alpha =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |z|^2$ is exact as a de Rham form, because $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\log |z|^2$ descends to the quotient: the logarithm changes only by a constant under the contraction. Nevertheless, by the calculation in proposition 19.8.13 , \[  \ell _\omega (\{ \alpha \} _{\mathrm{BC}}) =\int _{X_ n}\alpha \wedge \omega ^{n-1}=2(n-1)>0,  \] so the Bott–Chern class of $\alpha $ is nonzero. We return to the smooth compact modifications of the manifold $Y$ fixed at the beginning of the chapter. Two such modifications $\pi :Z\to Y$ and $\pi ':Z'\to Y$ are compared through modifications $g:Z'\to Z$ with $\pi '=\pi \circ g$; we then say that $Z'$ dominates $Z$. Definition 20.4.11 . 6EC6FB71DCF4 A Bott–Chern b-divisor class over $Y$ is a family \[  \mathbb A=(\mathbb A_ Z)_{\pi :Z\to Y},\qquad \mathbb A_ Z\in H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(Z,\mathbb R),  \] indexed by the smooth compact modifications of $Y$ and compatible with pushforward: $g_*\mathbb A_{Z'}=\mathbb A_ Z$ whenever $g:Z'\to Z$ is a modification over $Y$. It is pseudoeffective if every $\mathbb A_ Z$ is pseudoeffective. It is Cartier if there are a model $Z$ and a class $a_ Z\in H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(Z,\mathbb R)$ such that $\mathbb A_{Z'}=g^*a_ Z$ for every model $g:Z'\to Z$ dominating $Z$; the pair $(Z,a_ Z)$ is then called a Cartier realization of $\mathbb A$. When the models are Kähler, the $\partial \bar\partial $-lemma identifies this cohomology with the real $(1,1)$-cohomology used in 20.1.1 The notion of b-divisors , and the definition agrees with the one given there. We now return to the trace data fixed at the beginning of the chapter. When $\theta $ is closed, the common majorant of proposition 20.4.8 provides positive representatives of the residual classes. Proposition 20.4.12 . E2830D0CF2C8 If the ambient background $\theta $ is closed, the classes \[  \mathbb A_ Z(u;Y,\theta ) =\{ \pi ^*(\theta |_ Y)-S_ Z(u;Y)\} _{\mathrm{BC}}  \] form a pseudoeffective Bott–Chern b-divisor class. They depend only on the ambient multiplier-ideal class of $u$ and the Bott–Chern class of $\theta |_ Y$. Proof. By proposition 20.4.8 , there is one $v$ on $Y$ such that \[  R_ Z=\pi ^*(\theta |_ Y)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ \pi )-S_ Z(u;Y)\geq 0  \] on every model. Since $\theta $ and $S_ Z$ are closed, $R_ Z$ is closed, and its class is the class in the statement. This proves pseudoeffectivity. Compatibility with pushforward follows from theorem 20.4.5 together with $g_*g^*(\theta _ Z)=\theta _ Z$. Finally, the trace data do not change under ambient multiplier-ideal equivalence, and replacing $\theta |_ Y$ by $\theta |_ Y+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ with $f$ smooth changes no class; this proves the last assertion. $\square$ If $\theta $ is not closed, the same expression $R_ Z$ is still a positive current, but \[  \mathrm{d}R_ Z=\pi ^*(\mathrm{d}\theta |_ Y).  \] It is therefore not closed in general and defines no Bott–Chern class. Classes whose representatives have a prescribed nonzero exterior derivative are treated in section 10.30 .

title: 20.4.16 Nef Cartier realizations
text: If $T$ has analytic singularities, a log resolution splits its pullback into a finite divisor and a current with bounded potentials. The bounded part acquires no divisorial component on higher models, so its class determines the whole b-divisor class there, and smooth regularization of its bounded potential shows that this class is nef. A class $a\in H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(Z,\mathbb R)$ is nef if, for one Hermitian metric $\gamma $, it has for every $\epsilon >0$ a smooth representative $\beta _\epsilon \geq -\epsilon \gamma $. Since any two Hermitian metrics are comparable, this does not depend on the metric. A Cartier b-divisor class is called nef if it has a Cartier realization $(Z,a_ Z)$ with $a_ Z$ nef. Lemma 20.4.17 . 6370BDE30D1B On a connected compact complex manifold $Z$, let $\beta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form and $v$ a bounded quasi-plurisubharmonic function. If $R=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq 0$ is closed, then $\{ R\} _{\mathrm{BC}}$ is nef. Proof. Since $R$ is closed, so is $\beta $. Fix a Hermitian metric $\gamma $. By proposition 5.31.2 , there are smooth functions $v_ j$ and numbers $\epsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ such that \[  \beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j\geq -\epsilon _ j\gamma .  \] These forms are closed representatives of $\{ R\} _{\mathrm{BC}}$. Given $\epsilon >0$, choosing $j$ with $\epsilon _ j\leq \epsilon $ gives the estimate required in the definition of nefness. $\square$ Theorem 20.4.18 . 0AD88DBD3706 If the closed positive current $T$ has analytic singularities, then $\mathbb D(T)$ is Cartier and has a nef Cartier realization on a smooth compact modification. Proof. Resolve the analytic singularity ideal, using the log-resolution theorem in [ section on analytic singularities, theorem on existence of log resolutions , SGPT ] . On a suitable smooth compact model $\pi :Z\to Y$, \[  \pi ^*T=[D]+R,  \] where $D$ is a finite effective rational divisor and $R$ is a closed positive current with locally bounded potentials. To obtain a global bounded potential, choose smooth metrics on the line bundles of the components of $D$ and subtract the corresponding logarithms of squared norms of the canonical sections from $w\circ \pi $. The remainder $v$ is globally bounded, and \[  R=\beta _ Z+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v  \] for a smooth closed form $\beta _ Z$. By the lemma, the class of $R$ is nef. On every further compact modification $g:Z'\to Z$, the current $g^*R$ still has bounded local potentials and therefore zero Lelong numbers. Hence the divisorial part of $g^*\pi ^*T$ is exactly $[g^*D]$, and its regular part is $g^*R$. It follows that $\mathbb D(T)_{Z'}=g^*\{ R\} _{\mathrm{BC}}$. Thus $(Z,\{ R\} _{\mathrm{BC}})$ is a nef Cartier realization. $\square$ For a general current, analytic regularization gives closed approximants bounded below by $-\epsilon _ m\gamma $. The approximation then takes place in the larger spaces of section 10.30 , and does not by itself approximate the original Bott–Chern b-divisor class by nef Cartier classes.

title: 20.4.19 Continuous representatives and pullback
text: A finite divisorial sum is pulled back through the local equations of its divisors. For an infinite sum we need pullback to be continuous on closed positive currents whose Bott–Chern classes vary. Solving a scalar equation for the Gauduchon trace selects a smooth representative in each class; the complementary normalized potentials then converge in $L^1$, and lemma 5.43.19 shows that their pullbacks converge as well. In this section, $Y$ denotes an arbitrary connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and $\gamma $ is a Gauduchon metric on $Y$; in dimension one, any Hermitian metric will do. Fix smooth norms on tensor fields induced by $\gamma $. Put $V_\gamma =\int _ Y\gamma ^ n$ and, for a real $(1,1)$-form or current $B$, define its scalar trace $\sigma _\gamma (B)$ by \[  \sigma _\gamma (B)\, \gamma ^ n=B\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}.  \] For a current this is an identity of distributions. As in the proof of theorem 11.4.2 , we use the classical elliptic Fredholm theorem, elliptic regularity, and the continuity on distributions of the normalized elliptic inverse. Lemma 20.4.20 . 721E66DF8C88 Every closed real $(1,1)$-current $T$ has a unique decomposition \[  T=B_\gamma (T)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\gamma (T),\qquad \int _ Yv_\gamma (T)\, \gamma ^ n=0,  \] where $v_\gamma (T)$ is a real distribution and $B_\gamma (T)$ is a smooth closed real form with constant scalar trace. Both assignments are linear and continuous from weak convergence of currents to convergence of distributions. The forms $B_\gamma (T)$ lie in a finite-dimensional space, and their convergence takes place in $C^\infty $. This space maps isomorphically onto $H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(Y,\mathbb R)$. If $T\geq 0$, then $v_\gamma (T)$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic. On the cone of positive closed currents, $v_\gamma (T)$ depends continuously on $T$ in $L^1$, and for every nonnegative integer $l$, 641BFD39D2E5 20.4.21 \begin{equation}  \| B_\gamma (T)\| _{C^ l}+\| v_\gamma (T)\| _{L^1(\gamma ^ n)} \leq C_ l\int _ YT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}, \end{equation} where the constants $C_ l$ depend only on the fixed metric and norms. Proof. Set $L_\gamma f=\sigma _\gamma (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)$. We use the inverse $G_\gamma $ of ( 11.31.3 ), normalized with the volume form $\gamma ^ n/V_\gamma $. It acts on top-degree distributions of total mass zero and is continuous by the elliptic estimates for the operator and its transpose. Step 1: construction. Define \[  c_ T=\frac{\int _ YT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{V_\gamma },\qquad v_\gamma (T)=G_\gamma \bigl ((\sigma _\gamma (T)-c_ T)\gamma ^ n\bigr ),\qquad B_\gamma (T)=T-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\gamma (T).  \] The current $B_\gamma (T)$ is closed and has scalar trace $c_ T$. We now prove its smoothness and the finite-dimensionality assertion without using any Kähler identity. Step 2: an elliptic system. Let $J$ be the complex structure acting on real covectors. On real $(1,1)$-forms consider the first-order operator \[  \mathscr P B=(\mathrm{d}B,\mathrm{d}\sigma _\gamma (B)).  \] Its principal symbol at a nonzero real covector $\xi $ is $B\mapsto (\xi \wedge B,\xi \, \sigma _\gamma (B))$, and we claim that it is injective. If $\xi \wedge B=0$, then the $(1,1)$ condition forces $B$ to be a real multiple of $\xi \wedge J\xi $. To check this, choose unitary real coordinates with $\xi =\mathrm{d}x_1$: every term of $B$ contains $\mathrm{d}x_1$, and invariance under $J$ forces every term to contain $\mathrm{d}y_1$ as well. If moreover $\xi \, \sigma _\gamma (B)=0$, then $\sigma _\gamma (B)=0$; since the scalar trace of $\xi \wedge J\xi $ is nonzero, the multiple is zero. Let $\mathscr P^*$ be the formal adjoint of $\mathscr P$ for the fixed metric and volume. Since the symbol of $\mathscr P$ is injective, $\mathscr P^*\mathscr P$ is elliptic. By elliptic regularity and compactness, its distributional kernel is a finite-dimensional space of smooth forms. Since $\mathscr P B_\gamma (T)=0$, the form $B_\gamma (T)$ belongs to this space. Conversely, the kernel consists exactly of the closed forms with constant scalar trace: integrating $\langle \mathscr P^*\mathscr P B,B\rangle $ gives $\mathscr P B=0$, and connectedness makes the trace constant. Denote this kernel by $\mathscr H_\gamma $. Step 3: Bott–Chern representatives. The construction is linear and continuous on distributions. Convergence of the components $B_\gamma (T)$ therefore takes place in the finite-dimensional space $\mathscr H_\gamma $, hence in every smooth norm. If $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ for a distribution $f$, then $c_ T=0$ and the inverse gives $v_\gamma (T)=f-V_\gamma ^{-1}\int _ Yf\gamma ^ n$, so $B_\gamma (T)=0$. Applied to smooth closed forms, this shows that $\mathscr H_\gamma $ contains exactly one representative of each Bott–Chern class. Uniqueness of the decomposition can also be seen directly: if two decompositions are given, $L_\gamma $ of the difference of the two potentials is a constant, integration forces this constant to be zero, and the normalized kernel of $L_\gamma $ is zero. Step 4: positive currents. Suppose now that $T\geq 0$. The inequality $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\gamma (T)\geq -B_\gamma (T)$ gives a quasi-plurisubharmonic representative of the distribution $v_\gamma (T)$. Let positive closed currents $T_ j$ converge weakly to $T$. Their components $B_\gamma (T_ j)$ converge smoothly, so the potentials $v_\gamma (T_ j)$ have a common smooth lower curvature bound. By theorem 5.25.2 , after subtracting their suprema they form an $L^1$-precompact family. If $a_ j=\sup _ Yv_\gamma (T_ j)$, the zero-mean normalization gives \[  0\leq a_ j V_\gamma =\int _ Y\bigl (a_ j-v_\gamma (T_ j)\bigr )\, \gamma ^ n,  \] and the right-hand side is uniformly bounded. Hence the potentials $v_\gamma (T_ j)$ themselves are $L^1$-precompact. Every cluster point equals their distributional limit $v_\gamma (T)$, so the whole sequence converges in $L^1$. Finally, the positive closed currents with trace mass $\int _ YT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=1$ form a weakly compact set: positivity bounds their coefficient measures, weak limits remain positive and closed, and testing with $\gamma ^{n-1}$ preserves the trace mass. The smooth and $L^1$ continuity just proved bounds both norms on this set, and positive homogeneity gives ( 20.4.21 ). A positive current of trace mass zero is zero, so this case is included. $\square$ The smooth representatives give a common curvature bound for converging normalized potentials. This is exactly the hypothesis needed to pull back their $L^1$ convergence. Proposition 20.4.22 . D7373D3639FA Let $g:Z\to Y$ be a smooth compact modification, and fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma '$ on $Z$. Pullback of positive closed $(1,1)$-currents, defined through their local potentials, is weakly continuous. Moreover, there is a constant $C_ g$, depending only on the modification and the fixed metrics, such that EBECC85902E6 20.4.23 \begin{equation}  \int _ Zg^*T\wedge (\gamma ')^{n-1} \leq C_ g\int _ YT\wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \qquad (T\geq 0,\  \mathrm{d}T=0). \end{equation} Proof. Write $T=B_\gamma (T)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\gamma (T)$. The pullback is \[  g^*T=g^*B_\gamma (T)+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_\gamma (T)\circ g).  \] This current is positive and closed, since it is locally $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of plurisubharmonic functions, and the composed potential is not identically $-\infty $ because $g$ is surjective. The formula agrees with the definition through local potentials, so it does not depend on the decomposition. If $T_ j\to T$, the smooth parts converge in $C^\infty $, and the potentials converge in $L^1(Y)$ with a common lower curvature bound. By lemma 5.43.19 , their compositions with $g$ converge in $L^1(Z)$, and taking $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ proves the weak convergence of the pullbacks. Integration by parts on $Z$ gives \[  \int _ Zg^*T\wedge (\gamma ')^{n-1} =\int _ Zg^*B_\gamma (T)\wedge (\gamma ')^{n-1}.  \] The absolute value of the right-hand side is at most a fixed constant times $\| B_\gamma (T)\| _{C^0}$. Since the left-hand side is nonnegative, ( 20.4.21 ) gives ( 20.4.23 ). $\square$ Corollary 20.4.24 . AC7947F570DB Let $g:Z\to Y$, $\gamma $ and $\gamma '$ be as in proposition 20.4.22 . Let $D_ j$ be prime divisors on $Y$, with integration currents $[D_ j]$, and let $c_ j>0$. If $S=\sum _ j c_ j[D_ j]$ is a positive closed current of finite mass, then \[  g^*S=\sum _ j c_ j[g^*D_ j]  \] as positive currents of finite mass. The trace masses on $Z$ of the positive tails of this series tend to zero. In particular, $g^*S$ is again purely divisorial. Proof. Apply the proposition to the increasing finite partial sums $S_ N$ and to their positive closed tails $S-S_ N$. Pullback is additive on positive closed currents, by addition of local potentials. Thus $g^*S-g^*S_ N=g^*(S-S_ N)\geq 0$, and its trace mass is at most $C_ g$ times the trace mass of $S-S_ N$, which tends to zero. The pullback of a finite divisor is the usual pullback of its local equations, which identifies $g^*S_ N$ with the corresponding partial sum of the series, and hence $g^*S$ with its limit. Its terms are integration currents of prime divisors with nonnegative coefficients, and regrouping this countable positive sum of finite mass does not change it. $\square$

title: 20.4.25 Exceptional divisors between trace models
text: We return to the trace data fixed at the beginning of the chapter, with $\dim Y=r$, and write $S_ Z=S_ Z(u;Y)$. By corollary 20.4.24 , the full trace current can now be pulled back under a modification $g:Z'\to Z$. The pullback is bounded above by the trace current on $Z'$, with equal coefficients along strict transforms, so the difference is a finite effective divisor supported on the exceptional locus. Its logarithmic potential measures the change in the ordinary singularity types of the divisorial parts. Theorem 20.4.26 . 400A4F39FD56 For a smooth compact modification $g:Z'\to Z$ over $Y$, there is a unique finite effective real divisor $E_ g$ supported on the exceptional locus of $g$ such that D5C95521E68E 20.4.27 \begin{equation}  S_{Z'}=g^*S_ Z+[E_ g]. \end{equation} For a further smooth compact modification $h:Z''\to Z'$, these divisors satisfy 398DC29813C5 20.4.28 \begin{equation}  E_{g\circ h}=E_ h+h^*E_ g. \end{equation} Their coefficients are additive and positively homogeneous in the ambient potential $u$. For every $m$, the analytic-ideal divisors on the two models differ by a finite effective divisor $E_{m,g}$ supported on the exceptional locus: \[  [E_{m,g}]=D_{m,Z'}-g^*D_{m,Z}.  \] For every Gauduchon metric $\gamma '$ on $Z'$, the measures \[  [E_{m,g}]\wedge (\gamma ')^{r-1} \longrightarrow [E_ g]\wedge (\gamma ')^{r-1}  \] converge in total variation. Proof. Step 1: the exceptional divisor. Enumerate the prime divisors on $Z$ with positive trace coefficient. By theorem 20.4.5 , the pullback of every finite partial sum of $S_ Z$ is at most $S_{Z'}$, and corollary 20.4.24 identifies the increasing limit of these pullbacks with $g^*S_ Z$. Thus $S_{Z'}-g^*S_ Z$ is a positive closed divisorial current. The two currents have equal coefficients along the strict transform of every prime divisor on $Z$, because these coefficients are computed by the same valuation. Every other prime divisor on $Z'$ is exceptional for $g$, and the exceptional analytic set has only finitely many irreducible components on the compact manifold $Z'$. Hence the difference is the integration current of a finite effective real divisor $E_ g$ supported on its divisorial components, and the coefficients of integration currents determine $E_ g$ uniquely. Step 2: the cocycle identity. Pullback of positive closed $(1,1)$-currents is functorial, since it is defined by composing local plurisubharmonic potentials. Using ( 20.4.27 ) for $h$ and for $g$ gives \[  S_{Z''}=h^*S_{Z'}+[E_ h] =(g\circ h)^*S_ Z+[h^*E_ g]+[E_ h],  \] and uniqueness gives ( 20.4.28 ). Additivity and positive homogeneity follow from the same properties of the trace coefficients and the linearity of pullback. Step 3: approximation. For fixed $m$, apply ( 20.4.6 ) to the finitely many prime divisors in the support of the image ideal on $Z$. After division by $m$, it gives $D_{m,Z'}-g^*D_{m,Z}\geq 0$. The coefficients along strict transforms vanish, so this difference is the integration current of an effective real divisor $E_{m,g}$ supported on the exceptional locus. Choose also a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ on $Z$. By theorem 20.4.2 , the currents $S_ Z-D_{m,Z}$ and $S_{Z'}-D_{m,Z'}$ are positive, and their trace masses tend to zero. Subtracting the two identities for the exceptional currents gives \[  [E_{m,g}]-[E_ g] =-(S_{Z'}-D_{m,Z'})+g^*(S_ Z-D_{m,Z}),  \] where both $S_{Z'}-D_{m,Z'}$ and $g^*(S_ Z-D_{m,Z})$ are positive. By ( 20.4.23 ), the total variation of the signed measure $([E_{m,g}]-[E_ g])\wedge (\gamma ')^{r-1}$ is therefore at most \[  \int _{Z'}(S_{Z'}-D_{m,Z'})\wedge (\gamma ')^{r-1} +C_ g\int _ Z(S_ Z-D_{m,Z})\wedge \gamma ^{r-1}.  \] Both terms tend to zero, which proves convergence in total variation. $\square$ For a modification $g:Z'\to Z$ as in the theorem, the coefficient of $E_ g$ along an exceptional prime divisor $F\subset Z'$ is 3A85C5091414 20.4.29 \begin{equation}  \tau _{Y,u}(F) -\sum _{D\subset Z}\tau _{Y,u}(D)\operatorname {ord}_ F(g^*D), \end{equation} where $D$ ranges over the prime divisors on $Z$ with positive trace coefficient. This countable sum converges: it is the coefficient of $g^*S_ Z$ along $F$ in the positive divisorial series of corollary 20.4.24 , and it is at most $\tau _{Y,u}(F)$. The same current identity compares the ordinary singularity types attached to $S_ Z$ and $S_{Z'}$ by corollary 5.38.6 . Corollary 20.4.30 . 74858EC68B34 Choose decompositions $S_ Z=B_ Z+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ Z$ and $S_{Z'}=B_{Z'}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_{Z'}$ with smooth closed forms $B_ Z,B_{Z'}$, as in corollary 5.38.6 . Let $\rho _{E_ g}$ be a global logarithmic potential of $E_ g$, that is, a quasi-plurisubharmonic function on $Z'$ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho _{E_ g}-[E_ g]$ is smooth. Then \[  v_{Z'}-(v_ Z\circ g)-\rho _{E_ g}  \] is represented by a smooth function. In particular, \[  v_{Z'}\preceq v_ Z\circ g  \] in the sense of definition 16.7.1 , and the two ordinary singularity types are equal if and only if $E_ g=0$. Proof. Global logarithmic potentials exist: choose smooth Hermitian metrics on the line bundles of the prime components of $E_ g$, let $\alpha _{E_ g}$ be the corresponding weighted sum of their curvature forms, and let $\rho _{E_ g}$ be the weighted sum of the logarithms of the squared norms of the canonical sections. Then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho _{E_ g}=[E_ g]-\alpha _{E_ g},  \] and any two global logarithmic potentials differ by a smooth function, by lemma 5.38.4 . We may therefore use this choice. The function $\rho _{E_ g}$ is quasi-plurisubharmonic and bounded above on the compact manifold $Z'$. The chosen decompositions and ( 20.4.27 ) give \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl (v_{Z'}-v_ Z\circ g-\rho _{E_ g}\bigr ) =g^*B_ Z+\alpha _{E_ g}-B_{Z'},  \] which is smooth. By lemma 5.38.4 , this difference of locally integrable functions is represented by a smooth function. The resulting equality of quasi-plurisubharmonic functions extends from almost everywhere to everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 . Since $\rho _{E_ g}$ is bounded above, this gives the ordinary domination. If $E_ g=0$, the smooth difference gives ordinary equivalence. Conversely, ordinary equivalence would give equal generic Lelong numbers along every prime divisor of $Z'$, whereas the identity just proved shows that along a prime component of $E_ g$ these numbers differ by its positive coefficient. Hence ordinary equivalence forces $E_ g=0$. $\square$ When $\theta $ is closed, the positive residual currents $R_ Z$ constructed in the proof of proposition 20.4.12 , and their Bott–Chern classes, satisfy \[  \begin{split}  R_{Z'}& =g^*R_ Z-[E_ g],\\  \mathbb A_{Z'}(u;Y,\theta ) & =g^*\mathbb A_ Z(u;Y,\theta )-\{ [E_ g]\} _{\mathrm{BC}}. \end{split}  \] Indeed, the smooth background and the common trace potential pull back, while ( 20.4.27 ) gives the change in the subtracted divisorial current. The correction $\{ [E_ g]\} _{\mathrm{BC}}$ accounts for the additional divisorial vanishing prescribed on the higher model. This is consistent with the exact pullback of the trace envelope in theorem 20.3.30 , since the envelope imposes the trace inequalities on all models at once. The following example shows that the correction can be nonzero even when the trace data are realized exactly by a potential. Example 20.4.31 . 74A0526E4030 Let $Y=\mathbb P^2$ with homogeneous coordinates $[t_0:t_1:t_2]$, let $\sigma $ be the Fubini–Study form normalized by $\int _ Y\sigma ^2=1$, and choose $a\in \mathbb Q_{>0}$. Put \[  u=a\log \frac{|t_1|^2+|t_2|^2}{|t_0|^2+|t_1|^2+|t_2|^2},  \] and take the ambient manifold to be $Y$ itself. Then $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,a\sigma )$. It has analytic singularities, with its only pole at $p=[1:0:0]$, and zero generic Lelong number on $Y$. By proposition 20.3.6 , its trace data are given by the generic Lelong numbers of its pullbacks: $\tau _{Y,u}(E)=\nu (u\circ \pi ,E)$ for every prime divisor $E$ on a smooth compact modification $\pi $ of $Y$. Since $u$ has no divisorial poles on $Y$, we have $S_ Y=0$, whose canonical ordinary type is that of a smooth function. If $\pi :\widetilde Y\to Y$ is the blowup at $p$ with exceptional curve $F$, then \[  S_{\widetilde Y}=a[F],\qquad E_\pi =aF.  \] Indeed, on either standard chart of the blowup, the numerator is the squared modulus of the exceptional coordinate times a smooth positive function, so the pole order is $a$ along $F$ and zero along every other prime divisor. Thus the trace data are realized exactly by $u$, although $E_\pi \neq 0$. The exceptional difference does not obstruct exact realization; it prevents the identification of the realizing potential with the canonical ordinary type of the divisorial part on the original model, which here is smooth. The same phenomenon occurs on a manifold without the bounded mass property. Let $(W,\omega _ W)$ be a compact Hermitian manifold of dimension $k$ that fails the bounded mass property, such as the Hopf threefold of theorem 23.1.1 , and pull $u$ back to $Y\times W$; take both the ambient manifold and the submanifold to be $Y\times W$. The pole set of the pullback is $\{ p\} \times W$, of codimension two, and the modification $\widetilde Y\times W\to Y\times W$ has exceptional coefficient $a$ along $F\times W$. Analytic restriction again shows that the trace data are realized exactly. Let $\operatorname {pr}_ Y$ and $\operatorname {pr}_ W$ be the two product projections. Choose smooth $\omega _ W$-plurisubharmonic functions $H_ j$ whose masses tend to infinity. For the Hermitian form $\Omega =\operatorname {pr}_ Y^*\sigma +\operatorname {pr}_ W^*\omega _ W$, the pullbacks of the $H_ j$ have masses \[  \binom {k+2}{2}\left(\int _ Y\sigma ^2\right) \left(\int _ W(\omega _ W+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ j)^ k\right)\longrightarrow +\infty ,  \] by the binomial expansion of smooth forms and the dimensions of the two factors. Hence the product also fails the bounded mass property. The pulled-back potential belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(Y\times W,C\Omega )$ for every $C\geq \max \{ a,1\} $, since its curvature is bounded below by $-a\operatorname {pr}_ Y^*\sigma $. Scaling the smooth functions $H_ j$ by $C$ shows that $C\Omega $ also has unbounded mass.

title: Theorem 20.4.26
text: Theorem 20.4.26 . 400A4F39FD56 For a smooth compact modification $g:Z'\to Z$ over $Y$, there is a unique finite effective real divisor $E_ g$ supported on the exceptional locus of $g$ such that D5C95521E68E 20.4.27 \begin{equation}  S_{Z'}=g^*S_ Z+[E_ g]. \end{equation} For a further smooth compact modification $h:Z''\to Z'$, these divisors satisfy 398DC29813C5 20.4.28 \begin{equation}  E_{g\circ h}=E_ h+h^*E_ g. \end{equation} Their coefficients are additive and positively homogeneous in the ambient potential $u$. For every $m$, the analytic-ideal divisors on the two models differ by a finite effective divisor $E_{m,g}$ supported on the exceptional locus: \[  [E_{m,g}]=D_{m,Z'}-g^*D_{m,Z}.  \] For every Gauduchon metric $\gamma '$ on $Z'$, the measures \[  [E_{m,g}]\wedge (\gamma ')^{r-1} \longrightarrow [E_ g]\wedge (\gamma ')^{r-1}  \] converge in total variation. Proof. Step 1: the exceptional divisor. Enumerate the prime divisors on $Z$ with positive trace coefficient. By theorem 20.4.5 , the pullback of every finite partial sum of $S_ Z$ is at most $S_{Z'}$, and corollary 20.4.24 identifies the increasing limit of these pullbacks with $g^*S_ Z$. Thus $S_{Z'}-g^*S_ Z$ is a positive closed divisorial current. The two currents have equal coefficients along the strict transform of every prime divisor on $Z$, because these coefficients are computed by the same valuation. Every other prime divisor on $Z'$ is exceptional for $g$, and the exceptional analytic set has only finitely many irreducible components on the compact manifold $Z'$. Hence the difference is the integration current of a finite effective real divisor $E_ g$ supported on its divisorial components, and the coefficients of integration currents determine $E_ g$ uniquely. Step 2: the cocycle identity. Pullback of positive closed $(1,1)$-currents is functorial, since it is defined by composing local plurisubharmonic potentials. Using ( 20.4.27 ) for $h$ and for $g$ gives \[  S_{Z''}=h^*S_{Z'}+[E_ h] =(g\circ h)^*S_ Z+[h^*E_ g]+[E_ h],  \] and uniqueness gives ( 20.4.28 ). Additivity and positive homogeneity follow from the same properties of the trace coefficients and the linearity of pullback. Step 3: approximation. For fixed $m$, apply ( 20.4.6 ) to the finitely many prime divisors in the support of the image ideal on $Z$. After division by $m$, it gives $D_{m,Z'}-g^*D_{m,Z}\geq 0$. The coefficients along strict transforms vanish, so this difference is the integration current of an effective real divisor $E_{m,g}$ supported on the exceptional locus. Choose also a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ on $Z$. By theorem 20.4.2 , the currents $S_ Z-D_{m,Z}$ and $S_{Z'}-D_{m,Z'}$ are positive, and their trace masses tend to zero. Subtracting the two identities for the exceptional currents gives \[  [E_{m,g}]-[E_ g] =-(S_{Z'}-D_{m,Z'})+g^*(S_ Z-D_{m,Z}),  \] where both $S_{Z'}-D_{m,Z'}$ and $g^*(S_ Z-D_{m,Z})$ are positive. By ( 20.4.23 ), the total variation of the signed measure $([E_{m,g}]-[E_ g])\wedge (\gamma ')^{r-1}$ is therefore at most \[  \int _{Z'}(S_{Z'}-D_{m,Z'})\wedge (\gamma ')^{r-1} +C_ g\int _ Z(S_ Z-D_{m,Z})\wedge \gamma ^{r-1}.  \] Both terms tend to zero, which proves convergence in total variation. $\square$

title: 10.30 Classes with a nonclosed background
text: Let $Y$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $Y$, and let $\pi :Z\to Y$ denote a smooth compact modification. When the background $\theta $ is not closed, subtracting a closed divisorial current from its pullback leaves the exterior derivative unchanged, so the residual currents of section 20.4 are not closed and define no Bott–Chern class. They do define classes in an affine space over Bott–Chern cohomology, since two representatives with the same exterior derivative differ by a closed current. The trace envelope still gives positive residual representatives, and the exceptional divisors of subsection 20.4.25 describe how the classes change between models. Analytic singularities give nef Cartier realizations in these affine spaces. For a general potential, analytic regularization gives such realizations in slightly larger backgrounds, and on each fixed model the positive residual currents converge weakly. The error in the background tends to zero smoothly, but removing it can destroy nefness. Nor does this linear convergence control Monge–Ampère mass: for a Hermitian background with unbounded upper mass, a potential of infinite mass can have the same residual classes as the zero potential, whose classes are realized by a smooth positive form.

title: 10.30.1 Affine classes with prescribed derivative
text: Two real $(1,1)$-currents on $Z$ with exterior derivative $\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta $ differ by a closed current, and modulo $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ of global distributions such differences are Bott–Chern classes. Let $\mathcal D'(Z,\mathbb R)$ denote the space of real distributions on $Z$, and set \[  \mathscr A_ Z(\theta )= \frac{\{ \pi ^*\theta +C:C\text{ is a closed real }(1,1)\text{-current on }Z\} }{\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\mathcal D'(Z,\mathbb R)}.  \] Write $\{ T\} $ for the class of $T$ in this space. By lemma 20.4.10 , every class has a smooth representative, and translation by Bott–Chern classes gives \[  \mathscr A_ Z(\theta )=\{ \pi ^*\theta \} +H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(Z,\mathbb R).  \] A smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\eta $ represents an element of $\mathscr A_ Z(\theta )$ exactly when $\mathrm{d}\eta =\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta $. As for Bott–Chern classes, pullback of a class is defined on a smooth representative and pushforward on current representatives. Proposition 10.30.2 . 5F6B6BF8B562 If $g:Z'\to Z$ is a compact modification over $Y$, pushforward and pullback induce maps \[  g_*:\mathscr A_{Z'}(\theta )\to \mathscr A_ Z(\theta ), \qquad g^*:\mathscr A_ Z(\theta )\to \mathscr A_{Z'}(\theta ), \qquad g_*g^*=\mathrm{id}.  \] Pushforward preserves classes with positive current representatives. Proof. Write $\pi '=\pi \circ g$. Translation by the pulled-back background identifies the required maps with the Bott–Chern maps of subsection 20.4.9 . Indeed, for a closed current $C'$ on $Z'$ and a smooth closed form $\beta $ on $Z$, \[  g_*(\pi '^*\theta +C')=\pi ^*\theta +g_*C',\qquad g^*(\pi ^*\theta +\beta )=\pi '^*\theta +g^*\beta ,  \] where the first equality uses the change of variables formula for the degree-one map $g$ on the smooth background. Since the Bott–Chern maps are well defined on the closed terms, these identities define the affine maps independently of the representatives. Their composition is the identity because $g_*g^*$ is the identity both on the background and on Bott–Chern classes. Finally, pushforward under a proper map preserves positive currents. $\square$ The prescribed derivative is essential for this pushforward: $g_*\pi '^*\mathrm{d}\theta =\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta $ is smooth, whereas the pushforward of an arbitrary smooth exact form can be a singular current. We call a family $(\mathbb A_ Z)$, with $\mathbb A_ Z\in \mathscr A_ Z(\theta )$ for every model $Z$ and compatible with pushforward, a b-divisor class over the background $\theta $ . Pseudoeffectivity and Cartier realizations are defined as in definition 20.4.11 , with affine classes in place of Bott–Chern classes. A class in $\mathscr A_ Z(\theta )$ is nef if, for a Hermitian form $\gamma $ on $Z$, it has for every $\epsilon >0$ a smooth representative bounded below by $-\epsilon \gamma $, as in subsection 20.4.16 .

title: Proposition 10.30.2
text: Proposition 10.30.2 . 5F6B6BF8B562 If $g:Z'\to Z$ is a compact modification over $Y$, pushforward and pullback induce maps \[  g_*:\mathscr A_{Z'}(\theta )\to \mathscr A_ Z(\theta ), \qquad g^*:\mathscr A_ Z(\theta )\to \mathscr A_{Z'}(\theta ), \qquad g_*g^*=\mathrm{id}.  \] Pushforward preserves classes with positive current representatives. Proof. Write $\pi '=\pi \circ g$. Translation by the pulled-back background identifies the required maps with the Bott–Chern maps of subsection 20.4.9 . Indeed, for a closed current $C'$ on $Z'$ and a smooth closed form $\beta $ on $Z$, \[  g_*(\pi '^*\theta +C')=\pi ^*\theta +g_*C',\qquad g^*(\pi ^*\theta +\beta )=\pi '^*\theta +g^*\beta ,  \] where the first equality uses the change of variables formula for the degree-one map $g$ on the smooth background. Since the Bott–Chern maps are well defined on the closed terms, these identities define the affine maps independently of the representatives. Their composition is the identity because $g_*g^*$ is the identity both on the background and on Bott–Chern classes. Finally, pushforward under a proper map preserves positive currents. $\square$

title: 10.30.3 Residual trace classes
text: Since the trace envelope dominates the trace currents on every model, subtracting them from its curvature current gives positive residual representatives, with exterior derivative $\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta $. The classes are determined by the prescribed trace currents, even when the envelope has larger Lelong numbers. In this section, $Y$ is a complex submanifold of a connected compact complex manifold $X$. Let $\Theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$ with $\Theta |_ Y=\theta $, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\Theta )$ have generic Lelong number $\nu (u,Y)=0$. We use the trace currents $S_ Z(u;Y)$ of subsection 20.4.1 , now with $\Theta $ in the role of the ambient background. Theorem 10.30.4 . 28C8F709D1CC The family defined by \[  \mathbb B_ Z(u;Y,\theta ) =\{ \pi ^*\theta -S_ Z(u;Y)\} \in \mathscr A_ Z(\theta )  \] is a pseudoeffective b-divisor class over $\theta $. It is unchanged by ambient multiplier-ideal equivalence and, after the resulting affine spaces are identified, by a smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ change of the restricted background. Proof. The currents $S_ Z$ are closed, so the classes belong to the indicated affine spaces, and their compatibility follows from theorem 20.4.5 , proposition 10.30.2 . Take $v=\mathcal T_\theta (u;Y)$, the trace envelope of ( 20.3.25 ). By proposition 20.4.8 , \[  \pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ \pi )-S_ Z(u;Y)\geq 0  \] on every model, which proves pseudoeffectivity in the original restricted background. The currents $S_ Z$ depend only on the ambient multiplier ideals. For a smooth real function $f$ on $Y$, the change $\theta \mapsto \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ adds $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(f\circ \pi )$ to every representative, which is zero in the quotient. This proves both invariances. $\square$ When $\theta $ is closed, this family is the Bott–Chern family of proposition 20.4.12 . On a higher model, the trace current can exceed the pullback of the trace current from a lower model. The effective exceptional difference of theorem 20.4.26 therefore translates the residual class, and the translation preserves the prescribed exterior derivative. Corollary 10.30.5 . 9157A5A52988 Let $g:Z'\to Z$ be a compact modification over $Y$, and let $E_ g$ be the effective exceptional divisor of theorem 20.4.26 . The trace classes of theorem 10.30.4 satisfy \[  \mathbb B_{Z'}(u;Y,\theta ) =g^*\mathbb B_ Z(u;Y,\theta )-\{ [E_ g]\} _{\mathrm{BC}},  \] where the Bott–Chern class on the right acts by translation on the affine space $\mathscr A_{Z'}(\theta )$. Proof. Let $\pi :Z\to Y$ be the structure map and put $\pi '=\pi \circ g$. Abbreviate $S_ Z=S_ Z(u;Y)$, and use lemma 5.38.4 to write $S_ Z=B_ Z+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ Z$ with $B_ Z$ smooth and closed and $v_ Z$ quasi-plurisubharmonic. The affine class $\mathbb B_ Z$ has the smooth representative $\pi ^*\theta -B_ Z$. Its pullback is therefore the class of $\pi '^*\theta -g^*S_ Z$, since the two representatives differ by $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ Z\circ g)$. Substituting $S_{Z'}=g^*S_ Z+[E_ g]$ gives the asserted identity. Both representatives have exterior derivative $\pi '^*\mathrm{d}\theta $, because the subtracted currents are closed, so the subtraction takes place within $\mathscr A_{Z'}(\theta )$. $\square$ The cocycle identity ( 20.4.28 ) makes these translations compatible with composition of modifications, and by theorem 20.4.26 their analytic-ideal approximants converge in total variation of the trace measures. On the other hand, theorem 20.3.30 identifies the trace envelopes on the models with pullbacks of the original trace envelope. The exceptional translation accounts for the additional divisorial subtraction on the higher model; it is consistent with this exact pullback of the envelope, and it can be nonzero even when the trace data are realized exactly, as in example 20.4.31 . For the rest of the chapter, the ambient manifold is $Y$ itself, and $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$. For a smooth compact modification $\pi :Z\to Y$, we write $N_ Z(u)$ for the divisorial current of $u\circ \pi $ and $\mathbb D_\theta (u)$ for the resulting residual family. By the self-trace identity of lemma 20.4.14 , \[  N_ Z(u)=\sum _ E\nu (u\circ \pi ,E)[E]=S_ Z(u;Y), \qquad \mathbb D_\theta (u)_ Z=\{ \pi ^*\theta -N_ Z(u)\} ,  \] where $E$ ranges over the prime divisors on $Z$. By theorem 10.30.4 , $\mathbb D_\theta (u)$ is pseudoeffective. In this case divisorial removal gives the positive representative $\pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi )-N_ Z(u)\geq 0$ directly, by lemma 5.38.1 and passage to the limit of increasing finite sums.

title: Theorem 10.30.4
text: Theorem 10.30.4 . 28C8F709D1CC The family defined by \[  \mathbb B_ Z(u;Y,\theta ) =\{ \pi ^*\theta -S_ Z(u;Y)\} \in \mathscr A_ Z(\theta )  \] is a pseudoeffective b-divisor class over $\theta $. It is unchanged by ambient multiplier-ideal equivalence and, after the resulting affine spaces are identified, by a smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ change of the restricted background. Proof. The currents $S_ Z$ are closed, so the classes belong to the indicated affine spaces, and their compatibility follows from theorem 20.4.5 , proposition 10.30.2 . The currents $S_ Z$ depend only on the ambient multiplier ideals. For a smooth real function $f$ on $Y$, the change $\theta \mapsto \theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ adds $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(f\circ \pi )$ to every representative, which is zero in the quotient. This proves both invariances. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.30.5
text: Corollary 10.30.5 . 9157A5A52988 Let $g:Z'\to Z$ be a compact modification over $Y$, and let $E_ g$ be the effective exceptional divisor of theorem 20.4.26 . The trace classes of theorem 10.30.4 satisfy \[  \mathbb B_{Z'}(u;Y,\theta ) =g^*\mathbb B_ Z(u;Y,\theta )-\{ [E_ g]\} _{\mathrm{BC}},  \] where the Bott–Chern class on the right acts by translation on the affine space $\mathscr A_{Z'}(\theta )$. Proof. Let $\pi :Z\to Y$ be the structure map and put $\pi '=\pi \circ g$. Abbreviate $S_ Z=S_ Z(u;Y)$, and use lemma 5.38.4 to write $S_ Z=B_ Z+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ Z$ with $B_ Z$ smooth and closed and $v_ Z$ quasi-plurisubharmonic. The affine class $\mathbb B_ Z$ has the smooth representative $\pi ^*\theta -B_ Z$. Its pullback is therefore the class of $\pi '^*\theta -g^*S_ Z$, since the two representatives differ by $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v_ Z\circ g)$. Substituting $S_{Z'}=g^*S_ Z+[E_ g]$ gives the asserted identity. Both representatives have exterior derivative $\pi '^*\mathrm{d}\theta $, because the subtracted currents are closed, so the subtraction takes place within $\mathscr A_{Z'}(\theta )$. $\square$

title: 10.30.6 Nef realizations and residual-current limits
text: On a resolution of an analytic singularity, the bounded residual potential has smooth approximants with arbitrarily small curvature error, and these prove nefness within the same affine class. Boundedness also prevents new divisorial terms on further modifications, which gives the Cartier realization. Proposition 10.30.7 . A8BE1F55208F If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$ has analytic singularities, then $\mathbb D_\theta (u)$ has a nef Cartier realization on a smooth compact modification. Proof. Resolve the analytic singularity ideal as in the proof of theorem 20.4.18 . On a suitable model $\pi :Z\to Y$ we obtain \[  \pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi )=[D]+R, \qquad R=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq 0,  \] where $D$ is a finite effective rational divisor, $\beta $ is smooth with $\mathrm{d}\beta =\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta $, and $v$ is globally bounded after the choice of metrics on the line bundles of the components of $D$. Positivity of $R$ follows from divisorial removal. Fix a Hermitian form $\gamma $ on $Z$ and apply proposition 5.31.2 to $v$ in the smooth background $\beta $. It gives smooth functions $v_ j$ with $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j\geq -\epsilon _ j\gamma $ and $\epsilon _ j\downarrow 0$. These forms represent the same affine class and have exterior derivative $\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta $, which proves nefness. On every further modification $g:Z'\to Z$, the current $g^*\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ g)$ is positive by lemma 5.43.2 . Its bounded potential has zero Lelong numbers, so the divisorial part of the full pullback is exactly $g^*D$. The residual affine class on $Z'$ is therefore $g^*\{ R\} $, which proves the Cartier realization. $\square$ For general $u$, add twice the curvature error of analytic regularization to the background. This gives positive currents with analytic singularities, to which the proposition applies, while the ideal orders identify the limiting residual family. Theorem 10.30.8 . 250F831D6E96 Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$ and fix a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $Y$. There are potentials $u_ m$ with analytic singularities, converging to $u$ in $L^1(Y)$, and positive numbers $\epsilon _ m\downarrow 0$, indexed by sufficiently large positive integers $m$, such that \[  \theta _ m=\theta +2\epsilon _ m\omega , \qquad \theta _ m+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ m\geq \epsilon _ m\omega .  \] For each $m$, the family $\mathbb D_{\theta _ m}(u_ m)$ has a nef Cartier realization. On every fixed compact model $\pi :Z\to Y$, its class has the current representative \[  C_{m,Z}=\pi ^*\theta +2\epsilon _ m\pi ^*\omega -D_{m,Z}, \qquad D_{m,Z}=\frac1m\sum _ E\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathcal I(mu)[E],  \] where $E$ ranges over the prime divisors on $Z$ and the order is computed after pulling the ideal back to $Z$. These representatives satisfy \[  C_{m,Z}\longrightarrow \pi ^*\theta -N_ Z(u) \quad \hbox{weakly as currents},  \] and the positive residual representatives satisfy \[  R_{m,Z}:=C_{m,Z}+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ m\circ \pi ) \longrightarrow \pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi )-N_ Z(u)\geq 0 \quad \hbox{weakly as currents}.  \] The exterior derivatives of both $C_{m,Z}$ and $R_{m,Z}$ converge smoothly to $\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta $. Proof. Take $u_ m$ from corollary 5.36.2 ; they converge to $u$ in $L^1$. If $e_ m\to 0$ are their curvature errors, put $\epsilon _ m=\sup _{\ell \geq m}e_\ell +1/m$. These numbers are positive and decrease to zero, and the indices $m$ are unchanged. Adding $2\epsilon _ m\omega $ to the background turns the lower bound $-\epsilon _ m\omega $ into $\epsilon _ m\omega $. Since each $u_ m$ has analytic type $(1/m,\mathcal I(mu))$, proposition 10.30.7 gives a nef Cartier realization in the background $\theta _ m$. On a fixed model, the generic divisorial Lelong numbers of $u_ m\circ \pi $ are exactly $m^{-1}\operatorname {ord}_ E\mathcal I(mu)$, so $N_ Z(u_ m)=D_{m,Z}$ and $C_{m,Z}=\pi ^*\theta _ m-N_ Z(u_ m)$ represents the class of $\mathbb D_{\theta _ m}(u_ m)$ on $Z$. The self-trace identity and theorem 20.4.2 give $D_{m,Z}\to N_ Z(u)$ in the trace mass of subsection 20.4.1 , hence weakly as currents. Since the smooth error $2\epsilon _ m\pi ^*\omega $ tends to zero with all its derivatives, $C_{m,Z}$ converges as stated. Divisorial removal gives $R_{m,Z}\geq 0$. All the $u_ m$ and $u$ have a common smooth lower curvature bound: choose $A>0$ with $\theta +\epsilon _ m\omega \leq A\omega $ for every index $m$ considered. By lemma 5.43.19 , the convergence in $L^1(Y)$ implies $u_ m\circ \pi \to u\circ \pi $ in $L^1(Z)$. Applying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ and adding the convergent currents $C_{m,Z}$ proves the convergence of the residual currents, and positivity persists in the weak limit. Finally, since each $D_{m,Z}$ is closed, \[  \mathrm{d}R_{m,Z}=\mathrm{d}C_{m,Z} =\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta +2\epsilon _ m\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\omega ,  \] which proves the smooth convergence of the exterior derivatives. $\square$ The classes $\mathbb D_{\theta _ m}(u_ m)_ Z$ lie in $\mathscr A_ Z(\theta _ m)$. Translation by $-2\epsilon _ m\pi ^*\omega $ identifies this space with $\mathscr A_ Z(\theta )$, but subtracting this form need not preserve nefness. Thus the convergence of currents above does not give an approximation by nef Cartier classes with exactly the prescribed exterior derivative.

title: Proposition 10.30.7
text: Proposition 10.30.7 . A8BE1F55208F If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\theta )$ has analytic singularities, then $\mathbb D_\theta (u)$ has a nef Cartier realization on a smooth compact modification. Proof. Resolve the analytic singularity ideal as in the proof of theorem 20.4.18 . On a suitable model $\pi :Z\to Y$ we obtain \[  \pi ^*\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ \pi )=[D]+R, \qquad R=\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq 0,  \] where $D$ is a finite effective rational divisor, $\beta $ is smooth with $\mathrm{d}\beta =\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta $, and $v$ is globally bounded after the choice of metrics on the line bundles of the components of $D$. Positivity of $R$ follows from divisorial removal. Fix a Hermitian form $\gamma $ on $Z$ and apply proposition 5.31.2 to $v$ in the smooth background $\beta $. It gives smooth functions $v_ j$ with $\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ j\geq -\epsilon _ j\gamma $ and $\epsilon _ j\downarrow 0$. These forms represent the same affine class and have exterior derivative $\pi ^*\mathrm{d}\theta $, which proves nefness. On every further modification $g:Z'\to Z$, the current $g^*\beta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(v\circ g)$ is positive by lemma 5.43.2 . Its bounded potential has zero Lelong numbers, so the divisorial part of the full pullback is exactly $g^*D$. The residual affine class on $Z'$ is therefore $g^*\{ R\} $, which proves the Cartier realization. $\square$

title: 10.30.9 Divisorial classes and infinite mass
text: Now let the background be a Hermitian form $\omega $ on $Y$, with upper mass $v_+(\omega )$ (definition 13.14.14 ) and extended Monge–Ampère measure $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega $ (theorem 13.14.3 ). When $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $, the potential of theorem 13.14.18 has the same multiplier ideals as a smooth potential. The two potentials therefore have the same residual classes on every model, while their extended masses differ. Proposition 10.30.10 . 6436A9863EBA If $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $, there is $U\in \mathrm{PSH}(Y,\omega )$ such that \[  \mathbb D_\omega (U)=\mathbb D_\omega (0),\qquad \int _ Y\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (U)=+\infty , \qquad \int _ Y\omega ^ n<+\infty .  \] The common family has the nef Cartier realization $(Y,\{ \omega \} )$. Proof. Take $U$ from theorem 13.14.18 . All its multiplier ideals at positive weights are trivial, so every divisorial order in $D_{m,Z}$ vanishes on every model. The self-trace identity gives $N_ Z(U)=0$, which is also the divisorial part of the zero potential. Both families therefore consist of the pullbacks of the class of $\omega $. Since $\omega $ is smooth and positive, its affine class is nef and realizes the family on $Y$ itself. The extended mass of $U$ is infinite by construction, whereas the smooth measure $\omega ^ n$ has finite mass because $Y$ is compact. $\square$

title: 16.29 Envelope systems over Hermitian perturbations
text: Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$, and fix real numbers $a<c$. For $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the multiplier-ideal envelope $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$ of definition 18.4.1 is the regularized supremum of the nonpositive $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions with the multiplier ideals of $u$. It depends on the background $\theta $. When $\theta $ is perturbed by Hermitian forms, the envelopes of one multiplier-ideal class in the perturbed backgrounds form a compatible family, and as the perturbation tends to zero these normalized representatives decrease to a potential in the original background. Projecting the limit back to the perturbed backgrounds recovers the family exactly when the limit keeps the multiplier ideals of the family; otherwise it gives the greatest family below it that comes from the original background. We apply this to test curves that are constant for parameters $\tau \leq a$ and have cutoff $c$. Recovery can fail even in a Kähler background: on a ruled surface, at zero volume, the limit acquires an additional divisorial pole. On the other hand, for big backgrounds on manifolds with the bounded mass property, recovery holds by theorem 13.21.7 when the lower volumes $\underline{\operatorname {vol}}$ of the initial slices (definition 16.28.58 ) have a positive limit. On the Hopf threefold, scalar invariance along the elliptic fibers instead allows recovery from positive lower volume on the projective base, by theorem 16.29.22 , even though ambient upper mass is unbounded. Smooth changes of the background commute with recovery, whereas the limiting Monge–Ampère mass can change when the background is not closed. We also use the ordinary singularity envelope $P_\theta [u]$ of definition 5.40.4 , the ordinary and multiplier-ideal singularity orders of section 5.33 , and the extended Monge–Ampère measure $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ of theorem 13.14.3 . A potential $u$ with $P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}=u$ is called $P_\theta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$-fixed.

title: 16.29.1 Curves constant on a left half-line
search_title: Curves constant on a left half-line
text: We restrict the envelope test curves of definition 17.17.2 by requiring that each slice be fixed by the multiplier-ideal envelope and that the curve be constant for $\tau \leq a$. Constancy identifies the initial potential explicitly as $\Gamma _ a$, and it confines the associated ray between the translates of this potential by $at$ and by $ct$. Definition 16.29.2 . F0A985779829 Let $\mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$ be the set of families $\Gamma =(\Gamma _\tau )_{\tau <c}$ such that $\Gamma _\tau \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$ and $P_\theta [\Gamma _\tau ]_{\mathcal I}=\Gamma _\tau $ for every $\tau <c$; the family is pointwise concave and decreasing in $\tau $; $\Gamma _\tau =\Gamma _ a$ for $\tau \leq a$. The cutoff of $\Gamma $ is $c$, and we extend $\Gamma $ by $\Gamma _ c=\lim _{\tau \uparrow c}\Gamma _\tau $ and $\Gamma _\tau =-\infty $ for $\tau >c$. Such curves are ordered by the pointwise order of their slices $\Gamma _\tau $, $\tau <c$. Every slice has supremum zero by theorem 18.4.2 . Hence, by theorem 5.25.2 , corollary 5.25.3 , the decreasing limit $\Gamma _ c$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$; in particular, it is not identically $-\infty $. It is also $P_\theta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$-fixed. Indeed, $\Gamma _ c\leq 0$ is a competitor for its own envelope, and $\Gamma _ c\leq \Gamma _\tau $, so the order preservation of proposition 18.4.6 gives \[  \Gamma _ c\leq P_\theta [\Gamma _ c]_{\mathcal I}\leq \Gamma _\tau \quad (\tau <c).  \] Taking the infimum over $\tau $ proves equality. Proposition 16.29.3 . 160B15BF08FE A curve $\Gamma \in \mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$ is an envelope test curve with initial potential $\varphi =\Gamma _ a$. Its Legendre transform \[  U_ t=\Bigl (\sup _{\tau <c}(\Gamma _\tau +t\tau )\Bigr )^*\qquad (t>0)  \] is an envelope ray with initial potential $\varphi $ and slope $c$, in the sense of definition 17.17.3 , and satisfies \[  \varphi +at\leq U_ t\leq \varphi +ct\qquad (t>0).  \] In particular $U_ t\sim \varphi $ for every $t>0$. Proof. By corollary 18.4.4 , a $P_\theta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$-fixed potential is also fixed by the ordinary envelope $P_\theta $. The regularized supremum of the curve is $\Gamma _ a$, since the curve is decreasing and constant for $\tau \leq a$. Hence all the conditions of definition 17.17.2 hold, and theorem 17.17.5 applies. The term $\tau =a$ in the transform gives the lower bound, and the inequalities $\Gamma _\tau \leq \varphi $ for $\tau <c$ give the upper bound. $\square$
