title: 16.29.4 Transition maps and envelope systems
text: Curves over different backgrounds are related by projecting each slice to the ideal envelope in the larger background. For these projections to form a consistent system, projecting in two steps must agree with projecting directly. This follows because each projection preserves multiplier ideals, while in each background a multiplier-ideal class has a unique representative fixed by the ideal envelope. The same fact gives injectivity: equal projected slices have equal multiplier ideals, hence come from equal fixed representatives. Proposition 16.29.5 . 7DD8E9433762 Let $\beta \geq \theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form on $X$. Slicewise projection, $\Gamma \mapsto (P_\beta [\Gamma _\tau ]_{\mathcal I})_{\tau <c}$, defines an injective and order-preserving map \[  P_\beta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}:\mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )\longrightarrow \mathscr T_{a,c}(\beta ).  \] For every smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\beta '$ with $\beta \geq \beta '\geq \theta $, these maps satisfy \[  P_\beta \bigl [P_{\beta '}[\Gamma ]_{\mathcal I}\bigr ]_{\mathcal I}=P_\beta [\Gamma ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] Proof. Since $\beta \geq \theta $, every slice is $\beta $-plurisubharmonic, and by theorem 18.4.2 its projection is a $\beta $-plurisubharmonic function fixed by $P_\beta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$. Decreasingness, constancy for $\tau \leq a$, and order preservation follow from proposition 18.4.6 . For concavity, let $r,t<c$ and $0<s<1$, and put $\tau =(1-s)r+s t$. By the same proposition and the concavity of the original curve, \[  \begin{split}  (1-s)P_\beta [\Gamma _ r]_{\mathcal I}+sP_\beta [\Gamma _ t]_{\mathcal I} & \leq P_\beta [(1-s)\Gamma _ r+s\Gamma _ t]_{\mathcal I}\\ & \leq P_\beta [\Gamma _\tau ]_{\mathcal I}. \end{split}  \] Here the first inequality follows by combining the scaling and addition formulas of that proposition, with backgrounds $(1-s)\beta $ and $s\beta $. Each projection preserves the multiplier ideals at every weight. Hence the two sides of the transition identity are $P_\beta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$-fixed representatives of the same multiplier-ideal class, and they are equal. If two projected curves agree, their original slices have the same multiplier ideals; since those slices are $P_\theta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$-fixed, they agree as well. This proves injectivity. $\square$ Let $\mathscr H(X)$ denote the set of Hermitian forms on $X$; for $\eta \in \mathscr H(X)$ we also write $\eta >0$. Definition 16.29.6 . 949E1D79FF19 An envelope system over $\theta $ , with parameters $a<c$, is a family \[  \boldsymbol \Gamma =(\Gamma ^\eta )_{\eta \in \mathscr H(X)}, \qquad \Gamma ^\eta \in \mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta +\eta ),  \] such that 101FB6DC67C6 16.29.7 \begin{equation}  \Gamma ^\eta =P_{\theta +\eta }[\Gamma ^{\eta '}]_{\mathcal I} \quad \hbox{whenever }\eta \geq \eta '. \end{equation} Write $\mathscr S_{a,c}(\theta )$ for the set of these systems, ordered componentwise. For $\Gamma \in \mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$, set \[  \mathsf E(\Gamma )^\eta =P_{\theta +\eta }[\Gamma ]_{\mathcal I} \qquad (\eta \in \mathscr H(X)).  \] A system is realized in the background $\theta $ if it equals $\mathsf E(\Gamma )$ for some $\Gamma \in \mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$. By the transition proposition, $\mathsf E(\Gamma )$ is an envelope system, and the map $\mathsf E$ is injective. All components of an envelope system have the same multiplier ideals at each $\tau <c$: compare two components $\Gamma ^\eta $ and $\Gamma ^{\eta '}$ with the component indexed by $\eta +\eta '$. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$, the constant family $\Gamma _\tau =P_\theta [u]_{\mathcal I}$, $\tau <c$, with cutoff $c$, lies in $\mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$, and its projections form the envelope system $\mathsf E(\Gamma )$.

title: 16.29.8 The limiting curve and recovery
text: Every Hermitian form dominates all sufficiently small multiples of a fixed Hermitian form. A single decreasing sequence of components therefore determines the limit of the whole system. Projecting the resulting curve back gives the greatest realized system below the original one, and strict inequality means that recovery fails. Theorem 16.29.9 . E94DE568F212 Fix a Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, and let $j$ range over the positive integers. For every $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(\theta )$ and every $\tau <c$, the sequence $\Gamma ^{h/j}_\tau $ decreases, and its limit \[  (\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )_\tau =\lim _{j\to \infty }\Gamma ^{h/j}_\tau  \] is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, in particular not identically $-\infty $. These limits define an element $\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma $ of $\mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$, which does not depend on $h$. The maps $\mathsf E$ and $\mathsf R$ satisfy \[  \mathsf R\mathsf E=\mathrm{id}, \qquad \mathsf E\mathsf R(\boldsymbol \Gamma ) \leq \boldsymbol \Gamma .  \] Both maps preserve order. More precisely, 44684C69B3B6 16.29.10 \begin{equation}  \mathsf E(\Gamma )\leq \boldsymbol \Gamma \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \Gamma \leq \mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma . \end{equation} Thus $\mathsf E\mathsf R(\boldsymbol \Gamma )$ is the greatest system below $\boldsymbol \Gamma $ that is realized in the original background. Proof. Step 1: the limit. Fix $\tau <c$ and put $q_ j=\Gamma ^{h/j}_\tau $. By compatibility, $q_ j=P_{\theta +h/j}[q_{j+1}]_{\mathcal I}$, and $q_{j+1}\leq 0$ is a competitor for this envelope; hence $q_ j\geq q_{j+1}$. The functions $q_ j$ have supremum zero and a common smooth lower curvature bound. By theorem 5.25.2 , corollary 5.25.3 , their decreasing limit $q$ is not identically $-\infty $ and has supremum zero. Passing to the limit in the distributional inequalities \[  \theta +h/j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_ j\geq 0  \] gives $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. The defining family of an ideal envelope grows when the background increases. Together with $q\leq q_ j$ and order preservation, this gives \[  q\leq P_\theta [q]_{\mathcal I} \leq P_{\theta +h/j}[q]_{\mathcal I} \leq P_{\theta +h/j}[q_ j]_{\mathcal I}=q_ j.  \] Taking the infimum over $j$ proves $P_\theta [q]_{\mathcal I}=q$. Concavity, decreasingness and constancy on the left half-line pass to the pointwise limits, so these limits form a curve in $\mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$. Step 2: independence of $h$. For every $\eta >0$ there is $j$ with $h/j\leq \eta $, and compatibility then gives $\Gamma ^\eta _\tau \geq \Gamma ^{h/j}_\tau $. Consequently \[  (\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )_\tau =\inf _{\eta \in \mathscr H(X)}\Gamma ^\eta _\tau ,  \] which proves that $\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma $ does not depend on $h$. This formula also shows that $\mathsf R$ preserves order. Step 3: the two compositions. Write $q=(\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )_\tau $. Since $q\leq \Gamma ^\eta _\tau $ and $\Gamma ^\eta _\tau $ is fixed by its envelope, order preservation gives $P_{\theta +\eta }[q]_{\mathcal I}\leq \Gamma ^\eta _\tau $. This proves $\mathsf E\mathsf R\leq \mathrm{id}$. Now start with a curve $\Gamma \in \mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$. Its slice $\Gamma _\tau $ is a competitor in every larger background, so \[  \Gamma _\tau \leq (\mathsf R\mathsf E\Gamma )_\tau \leq P_{\theta +\eta }[\Gamma _\tau ]_{\mathcal I} \quad (\eta >0).  \] The two outer terms have the same multiplier ideals, so the two ideal inclusions given by these inequalities show that the middle term has those ideals as well. Since both the middle term and $\Gamma _\tau $ are $P_\theta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$-fixed, they are equal. This proves $\mathsf R\mathsf E=\mathrm{id}$. Step 4: the adjunction. By the transition proposition, $\mathsf E$ preserves order. If $\mathsf E(\Gamma )\leq \boldsymbol \Gamma $, applying $\mathsf R$ gives $\Gamma =\mathsf R\mathsf E(\Gamma )\leq \mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma $. Conversely, if $\Gamma \leq \mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma $, applying $\mathsf E$ and using $\mathsf E\mathsf R\leq \mathrm{id}$ gives $\mathsf E(\Gamma )\leq \boldsymbol \Gamma $. This proves ( 16.29.10 ), and the final maximality assertion follows from it. $\square$ Proposition 16.29.11 . 93A1136C4F72 A system $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(\theta )$ is realized in $\theta $ if and only if, for every $\tau <c$, its limiting slice $(\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )_\tau $ is multiplier-ideal equivalent to one, and hence every, slice $\Gamma ^\eta _\tau $. Proof. For a realized system, this follows from $\mathsf R\mathsf E=\mathrm{id}$ and the preservation of multiplier ideals by each projection. Conversely, the assumed equivalence and the fact that $\Gamma ^\eta _\tau $ is fixed by its envelope in the larger background give \[  P_{\theta +\eta }[(\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )_\tau ]_{\mathcal I} =\Gamma ^\eta _\tau .  \] Thus the system equals $\mathsf E\mathsf R(\boldsymbol \Gamma )$. $\square$ By theorem 5.37.3 , multiplier-ideal equivalence means equality of all Lelong numbers on all local modifications. Recovery therefore holds exactly when the limiting slices keep these Lelong numbers. They are the same for all components of a system, whereas the limiting slice can have larger values: in the ruled-surface example of subsection 16.29.15 , one of them increases from zero to one. For big backgrounds on manifolds with the bounded mass property, theorem 13.21.7 excludes such an increase when the initial slices have positive limiting lower volume. When $X$ is Kähler, the Kähler forms are cofinal among the Hermitian forms: a sufficiently small positive multiple of a fixed Kähler form lies below any given Hermitian form. The compatibility condition therefore determines a system by its components indexed by Kähler forms. Conversely, every compatible family indexed by Kähler forms extends uniquely to a system: for $\eta >0$, choose a Kähler form $\kappa \leq \eta $ and set $\Gamma ^\eta =P_{\theta +\eta }[\Gamma ^\kappa ]_{\mathcal I}$. Two choices of $\kappa $ give the same result, as one sees by passing to a common smaller Kähler form and using the transition identity.

title: Theorem 16.29.9
text: Theorem 16.29.9 . E94DE568F212 Fix a Hermitian form $h$ on $X$, and let $j$ range over the positive integers. For every $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(\theta )$ and every $\tau <c$, the sequence $\Gamma ^{h/j}_\tau $ decreases, and its limit \[  (\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )_\tau =\lim _{j\to \infty }\Gamma ^{h/j}_\tau  \] is $\theta $-plurisubharmonic, in particular not identically $-\infty $. These limits define an element $\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma $ of $\mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$, which does not depend on $h$. The maps $\mathsf E$ and $\mathsf R$ satisfy \[  \mathsf R\mathsf E=\mathrm{id}, \qquad \mathsf E\mathsf R(\boldsymbol \Gamma ) \leq \boldsymbol \Gamma .  \] Both maps preserve order. More precisely, 44684C69B3B6 16.29.10 \begin{equation}  \mathsf E(\Gamma )\leq \boldsymbol \Gamma \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \Gamma \leq \mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma . \end{equation} Thus $\mathsf E\mathsf R(\boldsymbol \Gamma )$ is the greatest system below $\boldsymbol \Gamma $ that is realized in the original background. Proof. Step 1: the limit. Fix $\tau <c$ and put $q_ j=\Gamma ^{h/j}_\tau $. By compatibility, $q_ j=P_{\theta +h/j}[q_{j+1}]_{\mathcal I}$, and $q_{j+1}\leq 0$ is a competitor for this envelope; hence $q_ j\geq q_{j+1}$. The functions $q_ j$ have supremum zero and a common smooth lower curvature bound. By theorem 5.25.2 , corollary 5.25.3 , their decreasing limit $q$ is not identically $-\infty $ and has supremum zero. Passing to the limit in the distributional inequalities \[  \theta +h/j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q_ j\geq 0  \] gives $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. The defining family of an ideal envelope grows when the background increases. Together with $q\leq q_ j$ and order preservation, this gives \[  q\leq P_\theta [q]_{\mathcal I} \leq P_{\theta +h/j}[q]_{\mathcal I} \leq P_{\theta +h/j}[q_ j]_{\mathcal I}=q_ j.  \] Taking the infimum over $j$ proves $P_\theta [q]_{\mathcal I}=q$. Concavity, decreasingness and constancy on the left half-line pass to the pointwise limits, so these limits form a curve in $\mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$. Step 2: independence of $h$. For every $\eta >0$ there is $j$ with $h/j\leq \eta $, and compatibility then gives $\Gamma ^\eta _\tau \geq \Gamma ^{h/j}_\tau $. Consequently \[  (\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )_\tau =\inf _{\eta \in \mathscr H(X)}\Gamma ^\eta _\tau ,  \] which proves that $\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma $ does not depend on $h$. This formula also shows that $\mathsf R$ preserves order. Step 3: the two compositions. Write $q=(\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )_\tau $. Since $q\leq \Gamma ^\eta _\tau $ and $\Gamma ^\eta _\tau $ is fixed by its envelope, order preservation gives $P_{\theta +\eta }[q]_{\mathcal I}\leq \Gamma ^\eta _\tau $. This proves $\mathsf E\mathsf R\leq \mathrm{id}$. Now start with a curve $\Gamma \in \mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$. Its slice $\Gamma _\tau $ is a competitor in every larger background, so \[  \Gamma _\tau \leq (\mathsf R\mathsf E\Gamma )_\tau \leq P_{\theta +\eta }[\Gamma _\tau ]_{\mathcal I} \quad (\eta >0).  \] The two outer terms have the same multiplier ideals, so the two ideal inclusions given by these inequalities show that the middle term has those ideals as well. Since both the middle term and $\Gamma _\tau $ are $P_\theta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$-fixed, they are equal. This proves $\mathsf R\mathsf E=\mathrm{id}$. Step 4: the adjunction. By the transition proposition, $\mathsf E$ preserves order. If $\mathsf E(\Gamma )\leq \boldsymbol \Gamma $, applying $\mathsf R$ gives $\Gamma =\mathsf R\mathsf E(\Gamma )\leq \mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma $. Conversely, if $\Gamma \leq \mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma $, applying $\mathsf E$ and using $\mathsf E\mathsf R\leq \mathrm{id}$ gives $\mathsf E(\Gamma )\leq \boldsymbol \Gamma $. This proves ( 16.29.10 ), and the final maximality assertion follows from it. $\square$

title: 16.29.12 Changes of representative and limiting mass
search_title: Changes of representative and limiting mass
text: Subtracting a smooth function transports a curve to a new background, and projection restores the envelope normalization. The gauge estimate is uniform in the perturbation, so this transport also respects the limiting curve. The limiting Monge–Ampère mass behaves differently: in a nonclosed background, it can change even for the system all of whose slices are zero. Proposition 16.29.13 . 5B2E6F75BA98 Let $f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$ and $\theta '=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$. For $\Gamma \in \mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )$ and $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(\theta )$, the formulas \[  (\mathsf G_ f\Gamma )_\tau =P_{\theta '}[\Gamma _\tau -f]_{\mathcal I}, \qquad (\mathsf G_ f\boldsymbol \Gamma )^\eta _\tau =P_{\theta '+\eta }[\Gamma ^\eta _\tau -f]_{\mathcal I}  \] define bijections $\mathsf G_ f:\mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta )\to \mathscr T_{a,c}(\theta ')$ and $\mathsf G_ f:\mathscr S_{a,c}(\theta )\to \mathscr S_{a,c}(\theta ')$. They satisfy the cocycle law $\mathsf G_ g\mathsf G_ f=\mathsf G_{f+g}$, where $\mathsf G_ g$ is formed in the background $\theta '$, and they commute with $\mathsf E$ and $\mathsf R$. Proof. Subtracting $f$ changes the background from $\theta $ to $\theta '$ and preserves concavity, decreasingness and constancy on the left half-line. Slicewise projection preserves these properties by the argument of proposition 16.29.5 . Since $f$ is smooth, every new slice has the multiplier ideals of the original one. Applying the construction with $-f$ therefore gives a $P_\theta [\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$-fixed slice with the same ideals as the original slice, hence the original slice itself. This proves that $\mathsf G_{-f}$ is the inverse of $\mathsf G_ f$; the same uniqueness of fixed representatives proves the cocycle law. Compatibility of the transformed system and commutation with $\mathsf E$ follow by comparing multiplier ideals in the common final background. For commutation with $\mathsf R$, the gauge estimate of proposition 18.5.1 , applied in each background $\theta +\eta $, gives \[  \Gamma ^\eta _\tau +\min _ Xf \leq (\mathsf G_ f\boldsymbol \Gamma )^\eta _\tau +f \leq \Gamma ^\eta _\tau +\max _ Xf,  \] with constants independent of $\eta $. Pass to the decreasing limits along a cofinal sequence. The new limit has the same ordinary singularity type as the old limit minus $f$, and hence the same multiplier ideals. It is $P_{\theta '}[\cdot ]_{\mathcal I}$-fixed by theorem 16.29.9 , so it equals $P_{\theta '}[(\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )_\tau -f]_{\mathcal I}$. This proves commutation with $\mathsf R$. $\square$ For closed backgrounds on a compact Kähler manifold, 22.1.1 The definition of non-Archimedean metrics indexes such systems by Kähler perturbations, as above, and defines their volume as a limit of the masses of the initial potentials. Its components are general test curves fixed by the ideal envelope, with initial potentials of positive mass, whereas our curves are constant on a prescribed left half-line and our system spaces impose no mass condition. For nonclosed positive backgrounds, the corresponding limit of masses is not invariant under the gauge bijections. Proposition 16.29.14 . 3B3109886F9F There are a compact complex surface $X$, Hermitian forms $\omega ,h$ on $X$, and a smooth real function $f$ with $\omega '=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f>0$, with the following property. For every $a<c$ there is a system $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(\omega )$ such that the limits \[  \lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0} \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{\omega +\epsilon h} (\Gamma ^{\epsilon h}_ a), \qquad \lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0} \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{\omega '+\epsilon h} ((\mathsf G_ f\boldsymbol \Gamma )^{\epsilon h}_ a)  \] both exist and are different. Proof. Take the torus $X$ and the smooth perturbation of proposition 18.5.2 , so that $\omega '=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ is Hermitian and $\int _ X(\omega ')^2\neq \int _ X\omega ^2$, and fix any Hermitian form $h$. In every background $\omega +\eta $, let every slice with $\tau <c$ be zero. This is an envelope system for every $a<c$, since zero is the multiplier-ideal envelope of the unit-ideal class in a positive background. Its first limit is \[  \lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0}\int _ X(\omega +\epsilon h)^2 =\int _ X\omega ^2.  \] The gauge bijection sends every slice to $P_{\omega '+\eta }[-f]_{\mathcal I}=0$, since $f$ is smooth and the new background is positive. The second limit is therefore $\int _ X(\omega ')^2$, which is different. $\square$

title: 16.29.15 Failure of recovery in a positive background
search_title: Failure of recovery in a positive background
text:
We construct a Kähler background on a ruled surface over an elliptic curve and an envelope system that is not realized in this background. The obstruction is a section $D$ of the ruling whose class is nef but contains only one closed positive current, namely $[D]$. Prescribing a logarithmic pole along one fiber in the Kähler background leaves the class of $D$ as the residual class. In every positive perturbation of the background, this class has smooth positive representatives, so the perturbed envelopes have only the fiber pole. In the limit, however, the only positive representative left is $[D]$, so the limiting envelope acquires $D$ as an additional pole, and the residual volume tends to zero. In this section, $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\mathrm i\mathbb Z)$, and $X$ is the compact ruled surface \[  X=(\mathbb C_ z\times \mathbb P^1_ w)/\sim , \qquad (z,w)\sim (z+1,w),\qquad (z,w)\sim (z+\mathrm i,w+1).  \] These commuting transformations define a holomorphic $\mathbb P^1$-bundle $\pi :X\to E$. Let $D$ be its section $w=\infty $. The function $v=w-\operatorname {Im}z$ is invariant under both transformations and descends to a smooth function on $X\setminus D$. Lemma 16.29.16 . F6C7CDB99C6E Let $\sigma _0=(\mathrm i/2)\, \mathrm{d}z\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z$ be the flat probability form on $E$. There is a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form $\theta \in c_1(\mathcal O_ X(D))$ whose class is nef and for which \[  \kappa =\theta +\pi ^*\sigma _0  \] is a Kähler form. The only closed positive current of the form $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is $[D]$. Proof. Let $s_ D$ be the canonical section of $\mathcal O_ X(D)$, with zero divisor $D$. For a real parameter $t>0$, define a smooth Hermitian metric on this line bundle by prescribing the norm of $s_ D$: \[  |s_ D|_ t^2=(1+t|v|^2)^{-1}\quad \hbox{on }X\setminus D.  \] To check that it extends smoothly, use the coordinate $\xi =1/w$ near $D$. The squared norm of a local nonvanishing frame is \[  \bigl (|\xi |^2+t|1-(\operatorname {Im}z)\xi |^2\bigr )^{-1},  \] which is smooth and positive. The prescribed norm is invariant under the transformations on the complement of $D$, so these local extensions define a global metric. Its curvature form is \[  \theta _ t=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+t|v|^2) \quad \hbox{on }X\setminus D.  \] Set $\theta =\theta _1$, and let $\sigma =\sigma _0/\pi $ on $E$, where the denominator is the number $\pi $. We now estimate the curvature from below. Put $r=|v|^2$ and let $H$ be the complex Hessian of $\log (1+tr)$ in the coordinates $(z,w)$. Direct differentiation gives \[  \begin{split}  H_{w\bar w}& =\frac{t}{(1+tr)^2},\\  H_{z\bar w}& =\frac{\mathrm i t(1-tv^2)}{2(1+tr)^2},\\  H_{z\bar z}& =\frac{t}{2(1+tr)} -\frac{t^2(\operatorname {Re}v)^2}{(1+tr)^2}. \end{split}  \] Consequently \[  H_{z\bar z}-\frac{|H_{z\bar w}|^2}{H_{w\bar w}} =\frac{t(1-tr)}{4(1+tr)}\geq -\frac t4.  \] Completing the square gives $\theta _ t\geq -(t/4)\pi ^*\sigma $ on $X\setminus D$, and by continuity this inequality extends across $D$. The restriction of $\theta _ t$ to every fiber is a positive Fubini–Study form, including at infinity. Thus $\theta _ t+A\pi ^*\sigma $ is strictly positive off $D$ whenever $A>t/4$. At $\xi =0$, its coefficient matrix, with the common factor $\mathrm i/(2\pi )$ omitted, is \[  \begin{pmatrix}  A

& \mathrm i/2

\\ -\mathrm i/2

& 1/t

\end{pmatrix}.  \] Its vertical coefficient is positive and its Schur complement is $A-t/4>0$, so the form is strictly positive along $D$ as well. In particular, $\kappa =\theta +\pi ^*\sigma _0$ is Kähler. The function \[  f_ t=\log \frac{1+t|v|^2}{1+|v|^2}  \] extends smoothly across $D$ and satisfies $\theta _ t=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ t$. Letting $t\downarrow 0$ in the curvature lower bound shows that the class of $\theta $ is nef in the sense of subsection 20.4.16 . Write $\psi _ D=\log |s_ D|_1^2$. By the Poincaré–Lelong formula, $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ D=[D]$. Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then $u-\psi _ D$ is plurisubharmonic on $X\setminus D$. Its lift $\Phi (z,w)$ to $\mathbb C^2$ is invariant under the two deck transformations and, since $u$ is bounded above on the compact surface $X$, satisfies \[  \Phi (z,w)\leq C+\log \bigl (1+|w-\operatorname {Im}z|^2\bigr )  \] for some real constant $C$. For each fixed $w$, the function $z\mapsto \Phi (z,w)$ is either identically $-\infty $ or subharmonic. It is $1$-periodic and has logarithmic upper growth, so lemma 5.24.6 makes it constant. Thus $\Phi (z,w)=\phi (w)$, where $\phi $ is a subharmonic function of $w$, not identically $-\infty $. The second deck transformation gives $\phi (w+1)=\phi (w)$, and the bound at $z=0$ gives logarithmic growth, so the same lemma makes $\phi $ constant. Therefore $u=\psi _ D+C$ off $D$, and lemma 5.24.3 extends this equality across $D$. Hence $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=[D]$. $\square$ Fix a point $p\in E$ and let $F=\pi ^{-1}(p)$. The Green-kernel construction in the proof of theorem 20.3.10 gives a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $g$ on $E$ with $\sigma _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=\delta _ p$. Its pullback $\psi _ F=g\circ \pi $ has a logarithmic pole of coefficient one along $F$, and \[  \pi ^*\sigma _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ F=[F].  \] Theorem 16.29.17 . 761E4875D2B4 For the Kähler background $\kappa $ of lemma 16.29.16 and every $a<c$, there is a system $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(\kappa )$ for which \[  \mathsf E\mathsf R(\boldsymbol \Gamma ) \neq \boldsymbol \Gamma .  \] Every slice $\Gamma ^\eta _\tau $, $\tau <c$, of every component has multiplier ideals \[  \mathcal I(t\Gamma ^\eta _\tau ) =\mathcal O_ X(-\lfloor t\rfloor F)\qquad (t>0),  \] whereas its limiting slices have multiplier ideals \[  \mathcal I\bigl (t(\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )_\tau \bigr ) =\mathcal O_ X(-\lfloor t\rfloor (F+D)).  \] In particular, on the system space $\mathscr S_{a,c}(\kappa )$, which carries no mass condition, $\mathsf E$ is not surjective and $\mathsf R$ is not injective. Proof. For each Hermitian form $\eta $, the nef approximation of lemma 16.29.16 gives a smooth function $f_\eta $ such that $\theta +\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_\eta \geq 0$. Then \[  u_\eta =\psi _ F+f_\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa +\eta ).  \] Let every slice $\Gamma ^\eta _\tau $, $\tau <c$, of the component $\Gamma ^\eta $ be $q_\eta =P_{\kappa +\eta }[u_\eta ]_{\mathcal I}$, with cutoff $c$. The multiplier ideals of $q_\eta $ are those of $\psi _ F$ and do not depend on the smooth function $f_\eta $. Hence the compatibility condition follows by comparing these ideals in the larger background, and the constant curves form a system with the required parameters. Let $q$ be its limiting slice under $\mathsf R$, and let $\nu (q,F)$ be its generic Lelong number along $F$. Each $q_\eta $ has generic Lelong number one along $F$, so lemma 5.38.7 , applied to a decreasing cofinal sequence, gives $\nu (q,F)\geq 1$. By lemma 5.38.1 , \[  \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q-[F]\geq 0.  \] By the Poincaré–Lelong identity for $\psi _ F$, this current equals $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(q-\psi _ F)$, where the difference $q-\psi _ F$ is first taken as a locally integrable function. Since the current is positive, this difference has a canonical $\theta $-plurisubharmonic representative, and by lemma 16.29.16 it differs from $\psi _ D$ by a constant. Hence \[  q=\psi _ F+\psi _ D+C.  \] The divisors $F$ and $D$ are smooth and meet transversely, since one is a fiber and the other a section. A direct integrability calculation in local product coordinates therefore gives the stated ideals for every real $t>0$. In particular, the Lelong number at a generic point of $D$ has increased from zero to one, and proposition 16.29.11 shows that recovery fails. Finally, since $\mathsf R\mathsf E=\mathrm{id}$, the system $\boldsymbol \Gamma $ and the realized system $\mathsf E\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma \neq \boldsymbol \Gamma $ have the same image under $\mathsf R$. Thus $\mathsf R$ is not injective, and $\boldsymbol \Gamma $ is not in the image of $\mathsf E$. $\square$ Proposition 16.29.18 . 7F133849FE58 Let $q_\eta $ be the common slice of the component $\Gamma ^\eta $ constructed in the preceding proof. Along the closed perturbations $\eta =\epsilon \kappa $, with real $\epsilon >0$, \[  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{\kappa +\epsilon \kappa }(q_{\epsilon \kappa }) =2\epsilon \int _ X\theta \wedge \kappa +\epsilon ^2\int _ X\kappa ^2\longrightarrow 0.  \] The limiting slice has zero non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure. Proof. The potential $u_\eta =\psi _ F+f_\eta $ has analytic singularities, so proposition 18.4.8 gives $q_\eta \sim u_\eta \sim \psi _ F$. Removing the divisorial component $[F]$ gives a positive current in the background $\theta +\eta $, whose global potential $w_\eta =q_\eta -\psi _ F$ is bounded by this ordinary equivalence. Off $F$, plurifine locality identifies the Monge–Ampère measure of $q_\eta $ with $(\theta +\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\eta )^2$. This bounded product gives no mass to $F$ by proposition 5.28.2 . For closed $\eta =\epsilon \kappa $, Stokes' theorem gives its total mass as $\int _ X(\theta +\epsilon \kappa )^2$. The normal bundle of $D$ is trivial. Indeed, the transformation $w\mapsto w+1$ becomes $\xi \mapsto \xi /(1+\xi )$, whose derivative at $\xi =0$ is one, and the other transformation fixes $w$. Hence $\int _ X\theta ^2=D^2=0$, and expanding the square gives the formula. The limiting potential has curvature current $[F]+[D]$, which vanishes away from the pluripolar set $F\cup D$; its non-pluripolar measure is therefore zero. $\square$

Its curvature form is \[  \theta _ t=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+t|v|^2) \quad \hbox{on }X\setminus D.  \] Set $\theta =\theta _1$, and let $\sigma =\sigma _0/\pi $ on $E$, where the denominator is the number $\pi $. Direct differentiation gives \[  \begin{split}  H_{w\bar w}& =\frac{t}{(1+tr)^2},\\  H_{z\bar w}& =\frac{\mathrm i t(1-tv^2)}{2(1+tr)^2},\\  H_{z\bar z}& =\frac{t}{2(1+tr)} -\frac{t^2(\operatorname {Re}v)^2}{(1+tr)^2}. \end{split}  \] Consequently \[  H_{z\bar z}-\frac{|H_{z\bar w}|^2}{H_{w\bar w}} =\frac{t(1-tr)}{4(1+tr)}\geq -\frac t4.  \] Completing the square gives $\theta _ t\geq -(t/4)\pi ^*\sigma $ on $X\setminus D$, and by continuity this inequality extends across $D$. The restriction of $\theta _ t$ to every fiber is a positive Fubini–Study form, including at infinity. Thus $\theta _ t+A\pi ^*\sigma $ is strictly positive off $D$ whenever $A>t/4$. At $\xi =0$, its coefficient matrix, with the common factor $\mathrm i/(2\pi )$ omitted, is \[  \begin{pmatrix}  A

& \mathrm i/2

\\ -\mathrm i/2

& 1/t

\end{pmatrix}.  \] Its vertical coefficient is positive and its Schur complement is $A-t/4>0$, so the form is strictly positive along $D$ as well. In particular, $\kappa =\theta +\pi ^*\sigma _0$ is Kähler. The function \[  f_ t=\log \frac{1+t|v|^2}{1+|v|^2}  \] extends smoothly across $D$ and satisfies $\theta _ t=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_ t$. Letting $t\downarrow 0$ in the curvature lower bound shows that the class of $\theta $ is nef in the sense of subsection 20.4.16 . Write $\psi _ D=\log |s_ D|_1^2$. By the Poincaré–Lelong formula, $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ D=[D]$. Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. Then $u-\psi _ D$ is plurisubharmonic on $X\setminus D$. Its lift $\Phi (z,w)$ to $\mathbb C^2$ is invariant under the two deck transformations and, since $u$ is bounded above on the compact surface $X$, satisfies \[  \Phi (z,w)\leq C+\log \bigl (1+|w-\operatorname {Im}z|^2\bigr )  \] for some real constant $C$. For each fixed $w$, the function $z\mapsto \Phi (z,w)$ is either identically $-\infty $ or subharmonic. It is $1$-periodic and has logarithmic upper growth, so lemma 5.24.6 makes it constant. Thus $\Phi (z,w)=\phi (w)$, where $\phi $ is a subharmonic function of $w$, not identically $-\infty $. The second deck transformation gives $\phi (w+1)=\phi (w)$, and the bound at $z=0$ gives logarithmic growth, so the same lemma makes $\phi $ constant. Therefore $u=\psi _ D+C$ off $D$, and lemma 5.24.3 extends this equality across $D$. Hence $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=[D]$. $\square$

title: Theorem 16.29.17
text:
Theorem 16.29.17 . 761E4875D2B4 For the Kähler background $\kappa $ of lemma 16.29.16 and every $a<c$, there is a system $ oldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(\kappa )$ for which \[  \mathsf E\mathsf R( oldsymbol \Gamma ) 
eq  oldsymbol \Gamma .  \] Every slice $\Gamma ^\eta _	au $, $	au <c$, of every component has multiplier ideals \[  \mathcal I(t\Gamma ^\eta _	au ) =\mathcal O_ X(-\lfloor tfloor F)\qquad (t>0),  \] whereas its limiting slices have multiplier ideals \[  \mathcal I igl (t(\mathsf R oldsymbol \Gamma )_	au  igr ) =\mathcal O_ X(-\lfloor tfloor (F+D)).  \] In particular, on the system space $\mathscr S_{a,c}(\kappa )$, which carries no mass condition, $\mathsf E$ is not surjective and $\mathsf R$ is not injective. Proof. For each Hermitian form $\eta $, the nef approximation of lemma 16.29.16 gives a smooth function $f_\eta $ such that $	heta +\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_\eta \geq 0$. Then \[  u_\eta =\psi _ F+f_\eta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\kappa +\eta ).  \] Let every slice $\Gamma ^\eta _	au $, $	au <c$, of the component $\Gamma ^\eta $ be $q_\eta =P_{\kappa +\eta }[u_\eta ]_{\mathcal I}$, with cutoff $c$. The multiplier ideals of $q_\eta $ are those of $\psi _ F$ and do not depend on the smooth function $f_\eta $. Hence the compatibility condition follows by comparing these ideals in the larger background, and the constant curves form a system with the required parameters. Let $q$ be its limiting slice under $\mathsf R$, and let $
u (q,F)$ be its generic Lelong number along $F$. Each $q_\eta $ has generic Lelong number one along $F$, so lemma 5.38.7 , applied to a decreasing cofinal sequence, gives $
u (q,F)\geq 1$. By lemma 5.38.1 , \[  \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q-[F]\geq 0.  \] By the Poincaré–Lelong identity for $\psi _ F$, this current equals $	heta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(q-\psi _ F)$, where the difference $q-\psi _ F$ is first taken as a locally integrable function. Since the current is positive, this difference has a canonical $	heta $-plurisubharmonic representative, and by lemma 16.29.16 it differs from $\psi _ D$ by a constant. Hence \[  q=\psi _ F+\psi _ D+C.  \] The divisors $F$ and $D$ are smooth and meet transversely, since one is a fiber and the other a section. A direct integrability calculation in local product coordinates therefore gives the stated ideals for every real $t>0$. In particular, the Lelong number at a generic point of $D$ has increased from zero to one, and proposition 16.29.11 shows that recovery fails. Finally, since $\mathsf R\mathsf E=\mathrm{id}$, the system $ oldsymbol \Gamma $ and the realized system $\mathsf E\mathsf R oldsymbol \Gamma 
eq  oldsymbol \Gamma $ have the same image under $\mathsf R$. Thus $\mathsf R$ is not injective, and $ oldsymbol \Gamma $ is not in the image of $\mathsf E$. $\square$

title: Proposition 16.29.18
text: Proposition 16.29.18 . 7F133849FE58 Let $q_\eta $ be the common slice of the component $\Gamma ^\eta $ constructed in the preceding proof. Along the closed perturbations $\eta =\epsilon \kappa $, with real $\epsilon >0$, \[  \int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{\kappa +\epsilon \kappa }(q_{\epsilon \kappa }) =2\epsilon \int _ X\theta \wedge \kappa +\epsilon ^2\int _ X\kappa ^2\longrightarrow 0.  \] The limiting slice has zero non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure. Proof. The potential $u_\eta =\psi _ F+f_\eta $ has analytic singularities, so proposition 18.4.8 gives $q_\eta \sim u_\eta \sim \psi _ F$. Removing the divisorial component $[F]$ gives a positive current in the background $\theta +\eta $, whose global potential $w_\eta =q_\eta -\psi _ F$ is bounded by this ordinary equivalence. Off $F$, plurifine locality identifies the Monge–Ampère measure of $q_\eta $ with $(\theta +\eta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_\eta )^2$. This bounded product gives no mass to $F$ by proposition 5.28.2 . For closed $\eta =\epsilon \kappa $, Stokes' theorem gives its total mass as $\int _ X(\theta +\epsilon \kappa )^2$. The normal bundle of $D$ is trivial. Indeed, the transformation $w\mapsto w+1$ becomes $\xi \mapsto \xi /(1+\xi )$, whose derivative at $\xi =0$ is one, and the other transformation fixes $w$. Hence $\int _ X\theta ^2=D^2=0$, and expanding the square gives the formula. The limiting potential has curvature current $[F]+[D]$, which vanishes away from the pluripolar set $F\cup D$; its non-pluripolar measure is therefore zero. $\square$

title: 16.29.19 Recovery through the Hopf fibration
text: Positive lower volume on a closed base can force recovery even when the ambient manifold has unbounded upper mass. We now take \[  X=(\mathbb C^3\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle z\mapsto \mathrm e^{-1}z\rangle , \qquad B=\mathbb P^2,\qquad \pi :X\to B,  \] and use the geometry of section 23.1 . Write $\kappa =\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$, with $\int _ B\kappa ^2=1$, and put \[  s=\log |z|^2,\qquad \alpha =\pi ^*\kappa =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s,\qquad \beta =\mathrm ds\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}s,\qquad h=\alpha +\beta .  \] The derivatives of $s$ descend to $X$. Scalar multiplication gives an action of the elliptic group $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+2\pi \mathrm i\mathbb Z)$, transitive on each fiber of $\pi $ and preserving $h$. By theorem 23.1.1 , $h$ has unbounded upper mass. Invariant potentials nevertheless reduce to potentials on $B$ because the horizontal part of $h$ is the pullback of $\kappa $. Proposition 16.29.20 . D9BF9081FC38 For every $b>0$ and $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(B,b\kappa )$, \[  P_{bh}[\pi ^*v]_{\mathcal I} =\pi ^*P_{b\kappa }[v]_{\mathcal I}.  \] The envelope on the left uses all ambient competitors. Proof. First, an $E$-invariant $q\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,bh)$ descends to an upper semicontinuous function $w$ on $B$, since $\pi $ is proper and $q$ is constant on its fibers. In a product chart, Fubini gives $w\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$, and \[  bh+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q=\pi ^*(b\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)+b\beta .  \] Lift a smooth base vector to a vector annihilated by $\partial s$. Its pairing with $\beta $ is zero. Testing the positive current above against these lifts and a nonnegative smooth fiber density of integral one proves $b\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\geq 0$ distributionally. A local potential of $b\kappa $ gives its canonical plurisubharmonic representative. Its pullback agrees almost everywhere with $q$, hence everywhere by lemma 5.24.3 . Thus $w\in \mathrm{PSH}(B,b\kappa )$. Conversely, every such $w$ lifts to a $bh$-plurisubharmonic function by the displayed identity. Now set $q=P_{bh}[\pi ^*v]_{\mathcal I}$. Translation by any $g\in E$ preserves its complete competitor family: it preserves the background, the obstacle zero, and the ideals of the invariant input. The envelope is their greatest member, so $q\circ g=q$. Descend $q=\pi ^*w$ as above. By lemma 5.37.7 , its ideal equivalence to $\pi ^*v$ implies $w\sim _{\mathcal I}v$: a germ pulled back from the base is weighted-integrable in a product chart if and only if the base germ is, by Fubini. Hence $w$ is a base competitor. Every base competitor also lifts to an ambient competitor by the same lemma and the current identity. Taking the greatest members gives equality. $\square$ Fix real numbers $a<c$. For an envelope system $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(h)$, scalar invariance alone supplies the whole transverse system, including its components over nonclosed base perturbations. Lemma 16.29.21 . 2478F9CE0209 Suppose $\Gamma _\tau ^{\epsilon h}$ is $E$-invariant for every $\epsilon >0$ and $\tau <c$. There is a unique envelope system $\boldsymbol \Psi \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(\kappa )$ such that \[  \Gamma _\tau ^{\epsilon h}=\pi ^*\Psi _\tau ^{\epsilon \kappa } \quad (\epsilon >0,\  \tau <c).  \] Writing $\Gamma =\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma $ and $\psi =\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Psi $, we have $\Gamma _\tau =\pi ^*\psi _\tau $ for every $\tau <c$. Proof. The descent in proposition 16.29.20 gives $\Gamma _\tau ^{\epsilon h}=\pi ^*\phi _\tau ^\epsilon $ with $\phi _\tau ^\epsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,(1+\epsilon )\kappa )$. Normalization, decrease, concavity and constancy for $\tau \leq a$ descend pointwise. The fiber-envelope identity descends both ideal-model fixedness and scalar compatibility: \[  \phi _\tau ^{\epsilon _2} =P_{(1+\epsilon _2)\kappa } [\phi _\tau ^{\epsilon _1}]_{\mathcal I} \quad (\epsilon _2\geq \epsilon _1>0).  \] In particular, the positive scalar slices have the same ideals at every weight. For a Hermitian form $\xi >0$ on $B$, choose $\delta >0$ with $\delta \kappa \leq \xi $, fixed for the whole parameter interval, and define \[  \Psi _\tau ^\xi =P_{\kappa +\xi } [\phi _\tau ^\delta ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] The definition is independent of $\delta $ because the scalar inputs have the same ideals. It reproduces the scalar components, and proposition 16.29.5 proves that each component is a curve in $\mathscr T_{a,c}(\kappa +\xi )$. Projection preserves the ideals, so comparing the complete competitor families proves compatibility for $\xi \geq \xi '$. Thus $\boldsymbol \Psi $ is a full envelope system. Every possible extension is forced by this formula, which proves uniqueness. The retraction theorem applies to both systems. Taking their decreasing limits along $h/j$ and $\kappa /j$ in the scalar identity gives $\Gamma _\tau =\pi ^*\psi _\tau $. In particular the limits, including their values at poles, agree. For any other Hermitian metric $k$ on $B$, constants $0<l\leq r$ with $l\kappa \leq k\leq r\kappa $ give \[  \phi _\tau ^{l/j}\leq \Psi _\tau ^{k/j}\leq \phi _\tau ^{r/j}.  \] Both outer sequences decrease to $\psi _\tau $. This also identifies the transverse limit directly, without assuming that it keeps the ideals of the positive scalar slices. $\square$ Theorem 16.29.22 . 2DB4FF5FB5C1 Let $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(h)$ have $E$-invariant scalar components as in lemma 16.29.21 . Let $\psi =\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Psi $ be the transverse limiting curve. If \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\kappa (\psi _ a)>0,  \] then for every $\tau <c$ and every Hermitian form $\eta >0$ on $X$, \[  \Gamma _\tau ^\eta =P_{h+\eta }[\pi ^*\psi _\tau ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] Thus $\boldsymbol \Gamma =\mathsf E(\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )$. Proof. The closed Kähler background $\kappa $ is big and $B$ has the bounded mass property. Apply theorem 13.21.7 to the full transverse system. Its initial-volume hypothesis is exactly the displayed one, and it gives \[  \Psi _\tau ^{\epsilon \kappa } =P_{(1+\epsilon )\kappa }[\psi _\tau ]_{\mathcal I} \quad (\epsilon >0,\  \tau <c).  \] The fiber-envelope identity yields $\Gamma _\tau ^{\epsilon h}=P_{(1+\epsilon )h}[\pi ^*\psi _\tau ]_{\mathcal I}$. For a general $\eta >0$, choose $\epsilon h\leq \eta $. Compatibility and the nested-background identity of proposition 16.29.5 then give \[  \Gamma _\tau ^\eta =P_{h+\eta }[\Gamma _\tau ^{\epsilon h}]_{\mathcal I} =P_{h+\eta }[\pi ^*\psi _\tau ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] $\square$ The positivity condition is a lower ordinary-type volume on the closed base. It does not use an ambient upper-volume deficit or identify the ideals of the limit in advance. The conclusion holds at every finite $\tau <c$; it gives no uniform positive-volume bound as $\tau $ approaches $c$.

title: Theorem 16.29.22
text: Theorem 16.29.22 . 2DB4FF5FB5C1 Let $\boldsymbol \Gamma \in \mathscr S_{a,c}(h)$ have $E$-invariant scalar components as in lemma 16.29.21 . Let $\psi =\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Psi $ be the transverse limiting curve. If \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\kappa (\psi _ a)>0,  \] then for every $\tau <c$ and every Hermitian form $\eta >0$ on $X$, \[  \Gamma _\tau ^\eta =P_{h+\eta }[\pi ^*\psi _\tau ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] Thus $\boldsymbol \Gamma =\mathsf E(\mathsf R\boldsymbol \Gamma )$. Proof. The closed Kähler background $\kappa $ is big and $B$ has the bounded mass property. Apply theorem 13.21.7 to the full transverse system. Its initial-volume hypothesis is exactly the displayed one, and it gives \[  \Psi _\tau ^{\epsilon \kappa } =P_{(1+\epsilon )\kappa }[\psi _\tau ]_{\mathcal I} \quad (\epsilon >0,\  \tau <c).  \] The fiber-envelope identity yields $\Gamma _\tau ^{\epsilon h}=P_{(1+\epsilon )h}[\pi ^*\psi _\tau ]_{\mathcal I}$. title: 16.29.23 A nonanalytic family
text: The countable hyperplane series of 13.24.7 , 13.24.8 supplies an explicit family satisfying the transverse condition. Choose infinitely many distinct hyperplanes $H_ j\subset B$, positive coefficients $q_ j$ with $\sum _ jq_ j=1$, and their standard logarithms $\ell _ j\leq 0$. Put \[  u_0=\sum _{j\geq 1}q_ j\ell _ j -\sup _ B\sum _{j\geq 1}q_ j\ell _ j.  \] Then $u_0\leq 0$ is $\kappa $-plurisubharmonic and $\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0=\sum _ jq_ j[H_ j]$. Example 16.29.24 . 0631D73C4C88 Fix $0<\lambda _0<\lambda _*<1$ and $r>0$ with $r(c-a)<\lambda _*-\lambda _0$. For $\tau <c$, set \[  \lambda (\tau )=\lambda _0+r\max (\tau -a,0),\qquad u_\tau =\lambda (\tau )u_0,  \] and, for every Hermitian form $\eta >0$ on $X$, define \[  \Gamma _\tau ^\eta =P_{h+\eta }[\pi ^*u_\tau ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] These components form an envelope system with $E$-invariant scalar slices. Its transverse limiting curve is $\psi _\tau =P_\kappa [u_\tau ]_{\mathcal I}$, and \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\kappa (\psi _\tau ) =\overline{\operatorname {vol}}_\kappa (\psi _\tau ) =(1-\lambda (\tau ))^2>0.  \] The system is recovered from its limit. Its ideal data cannot be represented by analytic singularities. Proof. The function $\lambda $ is positive, increasing and convex, and $u_0\leq 0$, so $u_\tau $ decreases, is pointwise concave and is constant for $\tau \leq a$. Moreover, \[  \kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\tau =(1-\lambda (\tau ))\kappa +\lambda (\tau )\sum _ jq_ j[H_ j]>0, \qquad h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\pi ^*u_\tau \geq (1-\lambda _*)h.  \] Set $q_\tau =P_\kappa [u_\tau ]_{\mathcal I}$. The order, scaling and addition inequalities of proposition 18.4.6 show that $q_\tau $ remains decreasing and concave; it is constant on the same left half-line. Thus $q\in \mathscr T_{a,c}(\kappa )$. Apply the same argument upstairs to $Q_\tau =P_ h[\pi ^*u_\tau ]_{\mathcal I}$. The fiber-envelope identity gives $Q_\tau =\pi ^*q_\tau $, and the nested-background identity identifies the displayed family with $\mathsf E(Q)$. It is therefore an envelope system, its limit is $Q$ by $\mathsf R\mathsf E=\mathrm{id}$, and its scalar slices are invariant. Apply 13.24.8 with background $\kappa $, coefficients $a_ j=\lambda (\tau )q_ j$ and residual $(1-\lambda (\tau ))\kappa $. It gives the asserted exact lower and upper volumes of $q_\tau $. The transverse recovery theorem applies, also confirming recovery directly. For every $j$, the divisorial coefficient of $u_\tau $ along $H_ j$ is positive. Projection preserves all ideals and hence these coefficients. Analytic singularities on a compact manifold have only finitely many divisorial components, since their defining coherent ideals have this property. Thus no analytic singularity type has the same all-weight ideals. The same conclusion holds upstairs along the distinct divisors $\pi ^{-1}(H_ j)$, by submersion pullback. $\square$

title: 16.29.25 Exact pullback and smooth changes of background
search_title: Exact pullback and smooth changes of background
text:
Let $\mu :Y	o X$ be a modification and let $ oldsymbol \Gamma $ satisfy theorem 16.29.22 . By proposition 18.4.3 , its recovery identity pulls back to \[  \Gamma _	au ^\eta \circ \mu =P_{\mu ^*(h+\eta )}[\Gamma _	au \circ \mu ]_{\mathcal I}.  \] This concerns the exact pulled backgrounds. The form $\mu ^*\eta $ may be degenerate, so these identities do not define a full system indexed by every Hermitian form on $Y$. For a modification $
u :\widetilde B	o B$, proposition 16.28.59 gives \[  \underline{\operatorname {vol}}_{
u ^*\kappa } (\psi _ a\circ 
u ) =\underline{\operatorname {vol}}_\kappa (\psi _ a)>0,  \] so the transverse positivity test survives exact pullback. The same proposition also preserves ambient singularity volumes in an exact pulled background; it makes no comparison with an independent positive background upstairs. Finally, the smooth transport $\mathsf G_ f$ of proposition 16.29.13 commutes with both $\mathsf E$ and $\mathsf R$. Therefore recovery survives the change from $h$ to $h+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ for every smooth real $f$. The transported scalar slices need not remain invariant under $E$, and no invariance of the raw masses of independently normalized nonclosed-background representatives is inferred. The general recovery problem without the scalar symmetry or transverse positive-volume condition remains open.

title: 12.1 A Gauduchon variational volume
text: Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, let $\theta $ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, which we call the background , and let $\mu $ be a smooth strictly positive probability form on $X$. If $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$ for some smooth real function $v$, there is exactly one constant $c>0$ for which the Monge–Ampère equation $(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=c\mu $ has a smooth solution $u$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. When $\theta $ is closed, Stokes' theorem gives $c=\int _ X\theta ^ n$, independently of $\mu $. For a nonclosed background the total mass $\int _ X(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ can depend on the potential, and the constant $c$ is the one number that the equation attaches to the pair $(\theta ,\mu )$. This chapter studies it as a function of the background. The starting point is a dual formula. Integrating the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality against the $(n-1)$st power of a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, that is, of a Hermitian form with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\gamma ^{n-1})=0$, shows that $c^{1/n}$ is the infimum of a quotient whose numerator $\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ is linear in $\theta $ and unchanged by smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ changes of $\theta $. Taking this infimum for every pseudoeffective background defines the root of the Gauduchon variational volume. The root volume is concave. On the positive cone, a minimizing Gauduchon metric computes its derivative, and the Hessian of its negative logarithm defines a Riemannian metric on background classes in each finite-dimensional family. Invariant forms on compact quotients of complex Lie groups and warped products with a curve show that the unit-volume hypersurface of this metric may be complete or may acquire a boundary at finite distance. For $n\geq 2$, the same quotient computes the subsolution threshold $b_\omega (f)$ for a Hermitian background $\omega $ and an integrable density $f$. Allowing positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed currents as tests makes this dual problem compact. For continuous densities the maximizing currents represent exactly the supporting probabilities of the normalization functional; for integrable densities, a uniform tail condition passes the determinant integral to weak limits and again gives a maximizing current. A maximizing test that is a smooth strictly positive form gives more: equality in the trace inequality determines the solution current and forces an exact smooth equation. The exact equation persists when the maximizing form degenerates along a proper analytic set, whereas a threshold solution with a point pole can admit no smooth maximizing test at all. The last part of the chapter concerns the boundary of the positive cone and the dependence on $\mu $. At a nef background the variational volume is the limit of the smooth equation constants of nearby positive backgrounds. A projective radial model gives positive variational volume without bigness, even at the finite maximal time of a Chern–Ricci flow. Varying $\mu $ recovers the upper and lower Monge–Ampère masses. A threefold with zero lower mass shows that positivity for each smooth density need not be uniform over densities, whereas on an elliptic threefold a nonnegative sum of curvature squares gives a bounded cubic energy identity and hence a positive lower bound for every potential, even when the manifold admits no pluriclosed metric. Finally, nef degeneration gives a further contrast with closed Kähler classes: intersection polynomials are replaced by fractional, logarithmic or oscillating decay, and a single blowup can change its order. Throughout the chapter, a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ is called pseudoeffective if $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )\ne \varnothing $, that is, if $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ for some quasi-plurisubharmonic $u$; by theorem 11.6.1 this holds exactly when $\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\geq 0$ for every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $. Bigness is defined in section 5.40 , and $\theta $ is nef if, for a Hermitian form $h$ and every $\epsilon >0$, there is a smooth real $f_\epsilon $ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f_\epsilon \geq -\epsilon h$; this is the condition of subsection 20.4.16 for the affine class of $\theta $ in subsection 10.30.1 . None of these notions requires $\theta $ to be closed, and each is unchanged by a smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ change of $\theta $.

section: 12.2 The quotient and the smooth equation
text: For a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, Stokes' theorem shows that the pairing $\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ is unchanged by a smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ change of $\theta $; this pairing will be the numerator of our quotient. For the denominator, put \[  D_\mu (\gamma )=\int _ X \left(\frac{\mu }{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n.  \] This number is positive. Like the numerator, it is multiplied by $r^{n-1}$ when $\gamma $ is multiplied by a positive constant $r$, so the quotient below depends only on the ray of $\gamma $. Definition 12.2.1 . 0C4AF7E2CEBB For a pseudoeffective smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$, define \[  \lambda _\mu (\theta )= \inf _{\gamma \text{ Gauduchon}} \frac{\displaystyle \int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{D_\mu (\gamma )}, \qquad \mathcal V_\mu (\theta )=\lambda _\mu (\theta )^ n.  \] We call $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )$ the Gauduchon variational volume of $\theta $ with respect to $\mu $, and $\lambda _\mu (\theta )$ its root volume . In dimension one every Hermitian metric is Gauduchon, and every quotient equals $\int _ X\theta $. Proposition 12.2.2 . 4AF37F3C8091 For a pseudoeffective $\theta $, the number $\lambda _\mu (\theta )$ is finite and nonnegative. It is unchanged by a smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ change of $\theta $, positively homogeneous of degree one, and concave on the cone of pseudoeffective forms. If $\beta $ is a smooth real $(1,1)$-form and $\beta -\theta $ is pseudoeffective, then \[  \lambda _\mu (\beta )\geq \lambda _\mu (\theta ).  \] Finally, $\lambda _\mu $ is upper semicontinuous under smooth convergence within this cone. Proof. Choose $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\theta )$. For every Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, Stokes' theorem for currents and the Gauduchon condition give \[  \int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\int _ X(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\geq 0.  \] Thus every quotient is nonnegative, and testing one fixed Gauduchon metric gives a finite upper bound. The same identity shows that each quotient is unchanged by a smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ change of the background, and, applied to $\beta -\theta $, it proves the monotonicity. Each quotient is a linear function of the background, so their infimum is concave and positively homogeneous. Each individual quotient is also continuous in the smooth topology. Given a smoothly converging sequence, we bound the infimum by any one quotient, take the upper limit, and finally take the infimum over the test metric. This proves upper semicontinuity. $\square$ The smooth equation identifies both the value of the quotient and every minimizing metric. Let $\mathscr P$ be the set of backgrounds $\theta $ admitting a smooth real function $u$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$. Choosing such a Hermitian representative of $\theta $ and writing $\mu $ as a smooth positive density relative to its volume form, we may apply theorem 14.2.1 . It gives, for each $\theta \in \mathscr P$, a unique positive form $\Omega _\theta $, which we call the solution form , and a unique constant $c_\theta (\mu )>0$ such that \[  \Omega _\theta =\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\theta , \qquad \Omega _\theta ^ n=c_\theta (\mu )\mu .  \] The potential $u_\theta $ is unique after any fixed additive normalization. Theorem 12.2.3 . 2DB664A6EFDF For every $\theta \in \mathscr P$, \[  \lambda _\mu (\theta )=c_\theta (\mu )^{1/n}, \qquad \mathcal V_\mu (\theta )=c_\theta (\mu ).  \] The infimum in definition 12.2.1 is attained. When $n\geq 2$, its minimizing Gauduchon metrics are precisely the constant multiples of the Gauduchon metric conformal to $\Omega _\theta $. Proof. For any Hermitian metric $\gamma $, the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality for the eigenvalues of $\Omega _\theta $ relative to $\gamma $ gives the pointwise inequality \[  \Omega _\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \geq \left(\frac{\Omega _\theta ^ n}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n =c_\theta (\mu )^{1/n} \left(\frac{\mu }{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n.  \] If $\gamma $ is Gauduchon, integration and Stokes' theorem replace $\Omega _\theta $ in the numerator by $\theta $. Every test quotient is therefore at least $c_\theta (\mu )^{1/n}$. For $n\geq 2$, take the Gauduchon metric $\gamma =\mathrm{e}^ g\Omega _\theta $ conformal to $\Omega _\theta $, given by theorem 11.4.2 , where $g$ is a smooth real function. Since all eigenvalues of $\Omega _\theta $ relative to $\gamma $ are equal at every point, equality holds pointwise and hence in the quotient. This proves the formula and attainment. Conversely, if a Gauduchon metric attains the infimum, the nonnegative smooth difference of the two sides of the pointwise inequality has zero integral. It therefore vanishes everywhere, and the equality case of the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality makes $\gamma $ conformal to $\Omega _\theta $. Since the Gauduchon metric in a conformal class is unique up to a constant factor, this proves the last assertion. For $n=1$, we integrate the equation and use $\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\theta =0$. This gives $c_\theta (\mu )=\int _ X\theta $, which equals every quotient in the definition. $\square$ For a Hermitian background $\omega $, a smooth positive probability volume $\mathrm{d}V$ and a nonzero nonnegative density $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, the analogous quotient, with $\mu $ replaced by $f\, \mathrm{d}V$, computes the subsolution threshold $b_\omega (f)$ of section 15.28 ; see theorem 15.29.1 . Attainment in this extremal problem, and the regularity of the extremal tests, are studied from section 12.7 on. Corollary 12.2.4 . A486E36565B6 If $\theta $ is big, then $\lambda _\mu (\theta )>0$. Proof. By the definition of bigness, there are a Hermitian form $h$ and $\delta >0$ such that $\theta -\delta h$ is pseudoeffective. Monotonicity, homogeneity and the theorem, applied to $h\in \mathscr P$, give $\lambda _\mu (\theta )\geq \delta \lambda _\mu (h)>0$. $\square$ The converse fails for nef nonclosed backgrounds: theorem 12.14.6 gives, on a projective manifold, a nef background of positive volume that is not big.

title: 12.3 The equality case of concavity and the first variation

section: 12.3 The equality case of concavity and the first variation
text: Since $\lambda _\mu $ is an infimum of linear functions, each minimizing Gauduchon metric at $\theta $ defines a linear functional that supports $\lambda _\mu $ at $\theta $. If equality holds in the concavity inequality along a segment, a metric minimizing at an interior point must minimize at both endpoints, and theorem 12.2.3 then makes the two endpoint solution forms proportional. Differentiating the smooth equation shows that the supporting functional is the derivative of $\lambda _\mu $. For $\theta \in \mathscr P$ we write $\gamma _\theta $ for a minimizing Gauduchon metric, which exists by theorem 12.2.3 ; variation directions are smooth real $(1,1)$-forms. Theorem 12.3.1 . 2220E0C47510 Let $\theta _0,\theta _1\in \mathscr P$ and $0<s<1$. Then \[  \lambda _\mu ((1-s)\theta _0+s\theta _1) \geq (1-s)\lambda _\mu (\theta _0)+s\lambda _\mu (\theta _1).  \] Equality holds if and only if, for some $r>0$ and some smooth real $f$, \[  \theta _1=r\theta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f.  \] Proof. Concavity was proved in proposition 12.2.2 . Suppose first that $n\geq 2$ and that equality holds. Take a minimizing Gauduchon metric for the middle background $(1-s)\theta _0+s\theta _1$. Its quotient at the middle background is the same convex combination of its quotients at $\theta _0$ and $\theta _1$, and each of these is at least the corresponding infimum. Equality therefore forces this metric to minimize both endpoint quotients. By theorem 12.2.3 , the solution forms $\Omega _ i=\Omega _{\theta _ i}$, with constants $c_ i=c_{\theta _ i}(\mu )$ for $i=0,1$, are then both conformal to this metric. Their volume forms are $c_0\mu $ and $c_1\mu $, so their pointwise proportionality factor is the constant $r=(c_1/c_0)^{1/n}$. Hence $\Omega _1=r\Omega _0$, which gives the stated smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ relation. Conversely, if that relation holds, invariance under smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ changes and homogeneity give equality. When $n=1$, the function is $\theta \mapsto \int _ X\theta $. Take $r=\int _ X\theta _1/\int _ X\theta _0$. The difference $\theta _1-r\theta _0$ has integral zero, so the Green operator of the compact curve writes it as $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ with $f$ smooth. Thus the same equivalence holds. $\square$ Proposition 12.3.2 . 94AFD9E43DE0 The function $\lambda _\mu $ is smooth along smooth finite-dimensional families in $\mathscr P$. For a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\chi $ and $n\geq 2$, its derivative at $\theta $ is \[  (\mathrm{d}\lambda _\mu )_\theta (\chi ) =\frac{\displaystyle \int _ X\chi \wedge \gamma _\theta ^{n-1}}{D_\mu (\gamma _\theta )},  \] where $\gamma _\theta $ is any minimizing Gauduchon metric. In dimension one the derivative is $\int _ X\chi $. Proof. Choose a smooth potential $u_*$ with $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_*>0$. Backgrounds $\theta _ t$ near $\theta $ then have the positive representatives $\theta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_*$. The implicit-function argument in the proof of proposition 11.40.4 applies to this family and shows that the solution and its constant depend smoothly on the parameters. Adding $u_*$ to these solution potentials and fixing the mean gives the normalized solutions for $\theta _ t$, so $\lambda _\mu (\theta _ t)=c_{\theta _ t}(\mu )^{1/n}$ is smooth. To compute the derivative, write $\lambda =\lambda _\mu (\theta )$ and $\Omega =\Omega _\theta $, and write the minimizing metric as $\gamma _\theta =\mathrm{e}^ g\Omega $ with $g$ smooth and real, as theorem 12.2.3 permits. Along $\theta _ t=\theta +t\chi $ for small real $t$, put $\Omega _ t=\theta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ t$ and $\lambda _ t=\lambda _\mu (\theta _ t)$, and let dots denote derivatives at $t=0$. Differentiating $\Omega _ t^ n=\lambda _ t^ n\mu $ gives \[  (\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\dot u)\wedge \Omega ^{n-1} =\lambda ^{n-1}\dot\lambda \, \mu .  \] We multiply by $\mathrm{e}^{(n-1)g}$, so that $\Omega ^{n-1}$ becomes $\gamma _\theta ^{n-1}$, and integrate. The term with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\dot u$ vanishes by the Gauduchon condition, and $\int _ X\chi \wedge \gamma _\theta ^{n-1}=\lambda ^{n-1}\dot\lambda \int _ X\mathrm{e}^{(n-1)g}\mu $. On the other hand, $\gamma _\theta ^ n=\mathrm{e}^{ng}\lambda ^ n\mu $, so that \[  D_\mu (\gamma _\theta ) =\lambda ^{n-1}\int _ X \mathrm{e}^{(n-1)g}\mu .  \] Dividing the two identities proves the derivative formula. In dimension one the formula follows directly from the definition. $\square$

title: 12.5 Recovering a positive class from its Gauduchon derivative
search_title: Recovering a positive class from its Gauduchon derivative
section: 12.5 Recovering a positive class from its Gauduchon derivative
text: By proposition 12.3.2 , the derivative of $\lambda _\mu $ at $\theta \in \mathscr P$ is represented by a minimizing Gauduchon metric, which is determined up to a constant factor. The solution form is conformal to this metric and has a prescribed volume form, so the value and the derivative of $\lambda _\mu $ together reconstruct the solution form, and hence the background class. Fix $\theta \in \mathscr P$ and a minimizing metric $\gamma _\theta $. For $n\geq 2$ define the smooth positive $(n-1,n-1)$-form \[  \Xi _\theta =\frac{\gamma _\theta ^{n-1}}{D_\mu (\gamma _\theta )}.  \] Since numerator and denominator are both homogeneous of degree $n-1$ in $\gamma _\theta $, this form does not depend on the choice of the minimizing metric. It is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed, and by proposition 12.3.2 it represents the derivative in every smooth real $(1,1)$-direction $\chi $: \[  (\mathrm{d}\lambda _\mu )_\theta (\chi )=\int _ X\chi \wedge \Xi _\theta .  \] Proposition 12.5.1 . 4BBB232A044C Let $n\geq 2$ and $\theta \in \mathscr P$. The value $\lambda _\mu (\theta )$ and the derivative of $\lambda _\mu $ at $\theta $ on all smooth real $(1,1)$-forms together determine the background class of $\theta $, and the derivative alone determines this class up to multiplication by a positive constant. More precisely, if $\widehat\gamma $ is the positive $(1,1)$-form with $\widehat\gamma ^{n-1}=\Xi _\theta $, then \[  D_\mu (\widehat\gamma )=1, \qquad \Omega _\theta = \lambda _\mu (\theta ) \left(\frac{\mu }{\widehat\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n} \widehat\gamma .  \] Moreover, assigning to a background class in $\mathscr P$ with $\lambda _\mu =1$ the ray of its minimizing Gauduchon metrics is a bijection onto the set of rays of Gauduchon metrics. Proof. The values of the derivative on all smooth $(1,1)$-forms determine the smooth form $\Xi _\theta $. Its positive root exists and is unique by the positive-root construction preceding the proof of theorem 11.6.1 . If $D=D_\mu (\gamma _\theta )$, this root is $\widehat\gamma =D^{-1/(n-1)}\gamma _\theta $, and the homogeneity of $D_\mu $ gives $D_\mu (\widehat\gamma )=1$. By theorem 12.2.3 , the solution form $\Omega _\theta $ is conformal to $\widehat\gamma $, and its volume form is $\lambda _\mu (\theta )^ n\mu $. These two requirements determine the conformal factor pointwise and give the formula for $\Omega _\theta $. Thus the value and the derivative recover $\Omega _\theta $, a representative of the class of $\theta $. Without the value, the same formula recovers $\Omega _\theta $ up to a positive constant factor. Conversely, multiplying the class by a positive constant multiplies $\Omega _\theta $ by the same constant and leaves its minimizing Gauduchon ray, and hence $\Xi _\theta $, unchanged; so the derivative cannot determine more than the ray of the class. For the surjectivity in the last assertion, take any Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ and set \[  \Omega _\gamma =\left(\frac\mu {\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma .  \] This Hermitian form is unchanged by constant rescaling of $\gamma $ and satisfies $\Omega _\gamma ^ n=\mu $. The zero potential therefore solves the equation for the background $\Omega _\gamma $ with constant one, so its class has $\lambda _\mu =1$, and $\gamma $ is a minimizing Gauduchon metric by theorem 12.2.3 . Injectivity follows from the recovery formula: two classes with $\lambda _\mu =1$ and the same Gauduchon ray have the same solution form. This proves the bijection. $\square$ In dimension one, a background class is determined by its integral, by the Green operator of the curve. The derivative is then the fixed functional $\chi \mapsto \int _ X\chi $, and the value alone determines the class.

title: Proposition 12.5.1
section: 12.5 Recovering a positive class from its Gauduchon derivative
text: Proposition 12.5.1 . 4BBB232A044C Let $n\geq 2$ and $\theta \in \mathscr P$. The value $\lambda _\mu (\theta )$ and the derivative of $\lambda _\mu $ at $\theta $ on all smooth real $(1,1)$-forms together determine the background class of $\theta $, and the derivative alone determines this class up to multiplication by a positive constant. More precisely, if $\widehat\gamma $ is the positive $(1,1)$-form with $\widehat\gamma ^{n-1}=\Xi _\theta $, then \[  D_\mu (\widehat\gamma )=1, \qquad \Omega _\theta = \lambda _\mu (\theta ) \left(\frac{\mu }{\widehat\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n} \widehat\gamma .  \] Moreover, assigning to a background class in $\mathscr P$ with $\lambda _\mu =1$ the ray of its minimizing Gauduchon metrics is a bijection onto the set of rays of Gauduchon metrics. Proof. The values of the derivative on all smooth $(1,1)$-forms determine the smooth form $\Xi _\theta $. Its positive root exists and is unique by the positive-root construction preceding the proof of theorem 11.6.1 . If $D=D_\mu (\gamma _\theta )$, this root is $\widehat\gamma =D^{-1/(n-1)}\gamma _\theta $, and the homogeneity of $D_\mu $ gives $D_\mu (\widehat\gamma )=1$. By theorem 12.2.3 , the solution form $\Omega _\theta $ is conformal to $\widehat\gamma $, and its volume form is $\lambda _\mu (\theta )^ n\mu $. These two requirements determine the conformal factor pointwise and give the formula for $\Omega _\theta $. Thus the value and the derivative recover $\Omega _\theta $, a representative of the class of $\theta $. Without the value, the same formula recovers $\Omega _\theta $ up to a positive constant factor. Conversely, multiplying the class by a positive constant multiplies $\Omega _\theta $ by the same constant and leaves its minimizing Gauduchon ray, and hence $\Xi _\theta $, unchanged; so the derivative cannot determine more than the ray of the class. For the surjectivity in the last assertion, take any Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ and set \[  \Omega _\gamma =\left(\frac\mu {\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma .  \] This Hermitian form is unchanged by constant rescaling of $\gamma $ and satisfies $\Omega _\gamma ^ n=\mu $. The zero potential therefore solves the equation for the background $\Omega _\gamma $ with constant one, so its class has $\lambda _\mu =1$, and $\gamma $ is a minimizing Gauduchon metric by theorem 12.2.3 . Injectivity follows from the recovery formula: two classes with $\lambda _\mu =1$ and the same Gauduchon ray have the same solution form. This proves the bijection. $\square$

title: 12.6 The Hessian metric and its completion

section: 12.6 The Hessian metric and its completion
text: We now study the metric $\mathfrak g$ of ( 12.4.4 ) on finite-dimensional cones of backgrounds, where it defines an ordinary Riemannian path distance. Homogeneity of $\lambda _\mu $ separates the scale of a positive class from its position on a level set of $\lambda _\mu $, and the logarithm of this scale turns out to be a Euclidean coordinate orthogonal to the level sets. The metric is therefore a product, and its completeness reduces to that of the unit-volume hypersurface. Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space of smooth real $(1,1)$-forms such that \[  V\cap \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)=\{ 0\} , \qquad \mathscr C=V\cap \mathscr P\ne \varnothing .  \] Then $\mathscr C$ is an open convex cone in $V$. Write $\lambda =\lambda _\mu |_{\mathscr C}$, and let $g=-D^2\log \lambda $ be the restriction to $\mathscr C$ of the metric ( 12.4.4 ); it is a smooth Riemannian metric on $\mathscr C$ because $V$ meets $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)$ only in zero. Put \[  \mathscr S=\{ \theta \in \mathscr C:\lambda (\theta )=1\} ,  \] and equip this smooth hypersurface with the induced metric $g_{\mathscr S}$. Proposition 12.6.1 . 88C1708A920C The map \[  \Phi :\mathbb R\times \mathscr S\longrightarrow \mathscr C, \qquad (r,q)\longmapsto \mathrm{e}^ r q  \] is an isometry from the product metric $\mathrm{d}r^2+g_{\mathscr S}$ onto $g$. In particular, if $d_ g$ and $d_{\mathscr S}$ are the intrinsic distances, then \[  d_ g(\mathrm{e}^{r_0}q_0,\mathrm{e}^{r_1}q_1)^2 =|r_1-r_0|^2+d_{\mathscr S}(q_0,q_1)^2.  \] The metric on $\mathscr C$ is complete if and only if the induced metric on $\mathscr S$ is complete. Every path for which $\lambda $ tends to zero or to infinity has infinite length. Proof. Homogeneity gives $\lambda (s\theta )=s\lambda (\theta )$ for $s>0$. Hence $r=\log \lambda (\theta )$ and $q=\theta /\lambda (\theta )$ define the smooth inverse of $\Phi $. The level set is smooth because the Euler identity gives $D\lambda _\theta (\theta )=\lambda (\theta )>0$. Differentiating the Euler identity $D\log \lambda _\theta (\theta )=1$ in a direction $\chi \in V$ gives \[  g_\theta (\theta ,\chi )=D\log \lambda _\theta (\chi ), \qquad g_\theta (\theta ,\theta )=1.  \] For directions $\chi ,\eta \in V$, differentiating homogeneity twice also gives \[  g_{s\theta }(s\chi ,s\eta )=g_\theta (\chi ,\eta ).  \] Let $q\in \mathscr S$, let $\xi ,\eta \in T_ q\mathscr S$, and let $a,b,r$ be real numbers. Since $\xi $ and $\eta $ are tangent to a level set of $\lambda $, the first of these identities shows that both are $g_ q$-orthogonal to the radial vector $q$. Using also the second identity and the scaling rule, we obtain \[  g_{\mathrm{e}^ rq}\bigl (\mathrm{e}^ r(aq+\xi ),\mathrm{e}^ r(bq+\eta )\bigr ) =ab+g_ q(\xi ,\eta ),  \] which proves the metric identity. It remains to prove the distance formula and its consequences. A path $(r(t),q(t))$ in the product has length $\int \sqrt{|r'|^2+|q'|_{g_{\mathscr S}}^2}\, \mathrm{d}t$. The triangle inequality in $\mathbb R^2$ (applied to the integral of the vector $(|r'|,|q'|_{g_{\mathscr S}})$) bounds this below by the square root of the sum of the squared endpoint difference in $r$ and the squared length of the projected path in $\mathscr S$. For the opposite bound, choose a path in $\mathscr S$ of length within $\epsilon $ of the distance of its endpoints, parametrize it with constant speed, and let $r$ vary linearly; then let $\epsilon $ decrease to zero. This proves the distance formula. It identifies Cauchy sequences in $\mathscr C$ with pairs of Cauchy sequences in the two factors; since $\mathbb R$ is complete, the completeness assertion follows. Finally, the length of any path is at least the total change of $\log \lambda $ along it, and this change is infinite when $\lambda $ tends to zero or to infinity. $\square$

title: 12.6.2 Product and blowup examples
section: 12.6 The Hessian metric and its completion
text: The following two examples of closed classes show that the unit-volume hypersurface may be complete or may have a boundary at finite distance. The first also shows why the derivative is needed in proposition 12.5.1 : knowing the volume for every smooth probability measure need not identify the class. For the first example take $X=\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1$, and let $\alpha ,\beta $ be the pulled-back Fubini–Study forms of integral one on their respective factors. They satisfy \[  \alpha ^2=\beta ^2=0,\qquad \int _ X\alpha \wedge \beta =1.  \] For $a,b>0$ the form $\theta _{a,b}=a\alpha +b\beta $ is Kähler. Since it is closed, integrating the smooth equation gives, for every smooth positive probability measure $\mu $, \[  \mathcal V_\mu (\theta _{a,b})=2ab, \qquad \lambda _\mu (\theta _{a,b})=\sqrt{2ab}.  \] Consequently, for real $t$, all the forms $\theta _{\mathrm{e}^ t,\mathrm{e}^{-t}}$ have volume $2$ for every $\mu $. Their background classes are nevertheless distinct: for any fixed point $p$ of the second factor, integration over $\mathbb P^1\times \{ p\} $ gives $\mathrm{e}^ t$, and this integral is unchanged by the addition of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$. By direct differentiation, the restriction of ( 12.4.4 ) to this two-dimensional cone is \[  \mathfrak g=\frac12\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}a^2}{a^2}+\frac{\mathrm{d}b^2}{b^2}\right).  \] The coordinates $((\log a)/\sqrt2,(\log b)/\sqrt2)$ identify this metric with the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb R^2$, so the metric on this family is complete. The curve $a=\mathrm{e}^ t$, $b=\mathrm{e}^{-t}$ has unit speed. All distances here are intrinsic to this two-dimensional family. In the second example, the blowup of $\mathbb P^2$ at a point, the cone is incomplete, and the boundary added by the completion consists of classes of positive volume. Example 12.6.3 . 316E7687E1CC Let $\pi :X\to \mathbb P^2$ be the blowup at one point. Write $H$ for the pullback of the hyperplane class and $E$ for the exceptional divisor class. In the two-dimensional space they span, the cone of classes with a positive smooth representative is \[  \mathscr C=\{ aH-bE:a>b>0\} .  \] These are closed classes, and we represent them by fixed smooth forms in order to apply proposition 12.6.1 . Their intersection numbers are $H^2=1$, $H\cdot E=0$, $E^2=-1$. Consequently, for every smooth positive probability measure $\mu $, \[  \lambda _\mu (aH-bE)=\sqrt{a^2-b^2}.  \] In the coordinates \[  a=\mathrm{e}^ r\cosh s,\qquad b=\mathrm{e}^ r\sinh s, \qquad r\in \mathbb R,\quad s>0,  \] the Hessian metric is $\mathrm{d}r^2+\mathrm{d}s^2$. Its completion is therefore the Euclidean closed half-plane. The added boundary $s=0$ consists of the nef classes $\mathrm{e}^ rH$, each of positive volume $\mathrm{e}^{2r}$. Proof. The projection from the blown-up point extends to a morphism $f:X\to \mathbb P^1$ with class $L=H-E$. The incidence map $(\pi ,f):X\to \mathbb P^2\times \mathbb P^1$ is an embedding. If $h$ and $\ell $ are pullbacks of Fubini–Study forms of integral one, then \[  (a-b)h+b\ell  \] is positive for $a>b>0$, by the product embedding. Conversely, a positive representative has positive integrals over the exceptional curve and the strict transform of a line through the blown-up point. These integrals are respectively $b$ and $a-b$, proving the cone description. The same curves show that no nonzero linear combination in this two-dimensional space is smoothly $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. The intersection numbers follow from the hyperplane pullback and the normal bundle $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1)$ of the exceptional curve; equivalently $H^2=H\cdot L=1$ and $L^2=0$. Since the classes are closed, integrating the smooth equation gives $\mathcal V_\mu =a^2-b^2$, independently of $\mu $. Direct differentiation of $-\log \sqrt{a^2-b^2}$ gives \[  g=\frac{(a^2+b^2)(\mathrm{d}a^2+\mathrm{d}b^2)-4ab\, \mathrm{d}a\, \mathrm{d}b}{(a^2-b^2)^2}.  \] Substituting the stated coordinates gives $\mathrm{d}r^2+\mathrm{d}s^2$. The coordinate domain is exactly $\mathbb R\times (0,\infty )$, so the intrinsic distance and completion are those of that Euclidean half-plane. Finally, $H$ has a semipositive pullback representative and is a limit of positive classes, hence is nef. Its square is one, but its integral over $E$ is zero, so it has no positive representative. This proves all assertions about the added boundary. $\square$
