text:
On a compact quotient of a complex Lie group, the backgrounds with constant coefficients in an invariant coframe form a cone of nonclosed backgrounds on which everything can be computed explicitly. With respect to the normalized invariant volume, the root volume is the $n$th root of a determinant, the minimizing metric is the background itself, and the Hessian metric is the trace metric on positive Hermitian matrices. Its unit-volume hypersurface is complete, so the boundary of the cone of coefficient matrices lies at infinite distance after normalization. Let $G$ be a connected complex Lie group of dimension $n\geq 2$, and let $X=\Gamma  ackslash G$ be compact, where the discrete subgroup $\Gamma $ acts on the left. Choose a left-invariant holomorphic coframe $\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ n$, which descends to $X$. For a Hermitian matrix $A$ put \[   egin{gathered} 	heta _ A= rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\sum _{j,k}A_{jk}\alpha _ j\wedge  ar\alpha _ k, \qquad h_0=	heta _ I,\ H=\int _ Xh_0^ n,\qquad \mu = rac{h_0^ n}{H}. \end{gathered}  \] Here $\operatorname {Herm}(n)$ is the real vector space of Hermitian $n	imes n$ matrices, and $A>0$ (respectively $A\geq 0$) means that $A$ is positive definite (respectively semidefinite). Fix a real linear subspace $W\subset \operatorname {Herm}(n)$ containing a positive matrix, and write $V_ W=\{ 	heta _ A:A\in W\} $. Throughout this subsection, the probability form is the normalized invariant volume $\mu $ just defined. Proposition 12.6.5 . 47DDBF953B9C The backgrounds in $V_ W\cap \mathscr P$ are exactly the forms $	heta _ A$ with $A\in W$ and $A>0$. Moreover, \[  V_ W\cap \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)=\{ 0\} .  \] Every positive $	heta _ A$ is balanced, and its unique minimizing Gauduchon metric normalized by $D_\mu =1$ is 684C5D55AF27 12.6.6  egin{equation}  \lambda _\mu (	heta _ A)=(H\det A)^{1/n},\qquad \gamma _ A= rac{	heta _ A}{\lambda _\mu (	heta _ A)},\qquad \gamma _ A^ n=\mu . \end{equation} On this coefficient cone the Hessian metric is 85B17908B21F 12.6.7  egin{equation}  g_ A(U,Z)= rac1n\operatorname {tr}(A^{-1}UA^{-1}Z), \qquad U,Z\in W. \end{equation} For $A\in W$, there is a real distribution $u$ with $	heta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ exactly when $A\geq 0$. The closure of $\{ A\in W:A>0\} $ is $W\cap \{ A\geq 0\} $, and each of its points $A$ is represented by the smooth semipositive form $	heta _ A$. For $A=0$, the only positive current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is zero. If $G$ is nonabelian, every positive background in this cone is nonclosed, and adding a smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ term never makes it closed. Proof. Invariant averages and balancedness. Let $Z_1,\ldots ,Z_ n$ be the invariant holomorphic vector fields dual to $\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ n$, and set $\Upsilon =\alpha _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \alpha _ n$. This holomorphic top-degree form and its conjugate are closed. For an invariant holomorphic vector field $Z$, evaluation on the invariant frame gives \[  \mathcal L_ Z\Upsilon =-\operatorname {tr}(\operatorname {ad}Z)\Upsilon , \qquad \mathcal L_ Z ar\Upsilon =0.  \] The second identity also follows from Cartan's formula. Since $h_0^ n$ is a positive constant multiple of the appropriately oriented form $\Upsilon \wedge  ar\Upsilon $, Stokes' theorem on compact $X$ gives \[  0=\int _ X\mathcal L_ Zh_0^ n=-H\operatorname {tr}(\operatorname {ad}Z).  \] Thus the fields $Z_ j$ and their conjugates have zero divergence with respect to $\mu $. In particular, 8E5F08796F4E 12.6.8  egin{equation}  \int _ XZ_ jf\, \mu =\int _ X ar Z_ jf\, \mu =0 \qquad (f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb C)). \end{equation} Cartan's formula also gives $\mathrm d(\iota _{Z_ j}\Upsilon )=0$. These contractions span the invariant $(n-1,0)$-forms. The form $	heta _ A^{n-1}$ is a constant linear combination of their wedges with conjugates, so $\mathrm d	heta _ A^{n-1}=0$. The holomorphic fields commute with the antiholomorphic fields, and $\mathrm d\alpha _ j$ has type $(2,0)$. The coefficient matrix of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is therefore $(Z_ j ar Z_ k u)$. For smooth $u$ its entries have $\mu $-mean zero by ( 12.6.8 ), so the matrix of $\mu $-means of the coefficients of $	heta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is $A$. If $	heta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$, averaging the positive coefficient matrix gives $A>0$. The converse follows by taking $u=0$. The same average shows that $V_ W$ contains no nonzero smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ direction. For a distribution $u$, the adjoints of $Z_ j$ and $ ar Z_ k$ with respect to $\mu $ annihilate constants, so the mean of each $Z_ j ar Z_ k u$ is still zero. The coefficients of a positive current in this global frame form a positive matrix of measures, whose matrix of total masses is semipositive; for $	heta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ this gives $A\geq 0$. Conversely, $	heta _ A$ itself is a positive current when $A\geq 0$. Finally, for a fixed positive $A_+\in W$, the matrices $A+\varepsilon A_+$ with $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ approximate every semipositive $A\in W$ from the positive cone. This proves the unique minimizer and its volume identity. Differentiating $-\log \lambda _\mu (	heta _ A)=-(\log H+\log \det A)/n$ twice gives ( 12.6.7 ). The corresponding squared norm of $U$ is $\| A^{-1/2}UA^{-1/2}\| _{\mathrm F}^2/n$, which is positive for $U
e 0$; here $\| B\| _{\mathrm F}^2=\operatorname {tr}(B^*B)$ denotes the squared Frobenius norm. Finally, \[  \partial 	heta _ A= rac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\sum _{j,k}A_{jk}\, \mathrm d\alpha _ j\wedge  ar\alpha _ k.  \] For invertible $A$, the vanishing of this form forces every $\mathrm d\alpha _ j=0$, by independence of the conjugate coframe, and the Lie algebra would then be abelian. Since adding $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ does not change $\mathrm d	heta _ A$, this proves the last assertion. $\square$ Lemma 12.6.9 . 81EECB4E9700 On the cone of all positive definite Hermitian $n	imes n$ matrices, the Riemannian distance of the metric ( 12.6.7 ) is C6F155F53713 12.6.10  egin{equation}  d_{\mathrm{full}}(A,B)= rac1{\sqrt n} \| \log (A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2})\| _{\mathrm F}. \end{equation} For endpoints with equal determinant, this is also the intrinsic distance in the hypersurface of all positive definite matrices with that determinant. Proof. By the trace formula, the congruence $M\mapsto P^*MP$ by a fixed invertible matrix $P$ is an isometry. Taking $P=A^{-1/2}$, we may assume that the endpoints are $I$ and $C=A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2}>0$. The curve $\exp (t\log C)$, $0\leq t\leq 1$, has constant speed $\| \log C\| _{\mathrm F}/\sqrt n$, which gives the upper bound for the distance. For the reverse inequality, diagonalization gives the convergent resolvent formula for the matrix logarithm and its derivative  egin{align*}  \log M& =\int _0^\infty  igl ((1+s)^{-1}I-(M+sI)^{-1} igr )\, \mathrm ds,\  D\log _ M[U]& =\int _0^\infty (M+sI)^{-1}U(M+sI)^{-1}\, \mathrm ds. \end{align*} On a neighborhood of $M$ where the spectrum is bounded below by a positive constant, differentiation under the integral sign is justified by an integrable bound. e d_ j), \qquad c_{ij}= rac1{d_ i}\quad (d_ i=d_ j).  \] Writing $d_ i/d_ j=\mathrm e^{2s}$ gives $\sqrt{d_ id_ j}|c_{ij}|=|s/\sinh s|\leq 1$, including the limiting value at $s=0$. Hence \[  \| D\log _ M[U]\| _{\mathrm F} \leq \| M^{-1/2}UM^{-1/2}\| _{\mathrm F}.  \] Applying this along a piecewise $C^1$ path of positive matrices from $I$ to $C$ and integrating, we bound its length below by $\| \log C\| _{\mathrm F}/\sqrt n$. This proves the distance formula. title: Proposition 12.6.5
section: 12.6 The Hessian metric and its completion
text: Proposition 12.6.5 . 47DDBF953B9C The backgrounds in $V_ W\cap \mathscr P$ are exactly the forms $\theta _ A$ with $A\in W$ and $A>0$. Moreover, \[  V_ W\cap \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}C^\infty (X,\mathbb R)=\{ 0\} .  \] Every positive $\theta _ A$ is balanced, and its unique minimizing Gauduchon metric normalized by $D_\mu =1$ is 684C5D55AF27 12.6.6 \begin{equation}  \lambda _\mu (\theta _ A)=(H\det A)^{1/n},\qquad \gamma _ A=\frac{\theta _ A}{\lambda _\mu (\theta _ A)},\qquad \gamma _ A^ n=\mu . \end{equation} On this coefficient cone the Hessian metric is 85B17908B21F 12.6.7 \begin{equation}  g_ A(U,Z)=\frac1n\operatorname {tr}(A^{-1}UA^{-1}Z), \qquad U,Z\in W. \end{equation} For $A\in W$, there is a real distribution $u$ with $\theta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ exactly when $A\geq 0$. The closure of $\{ A\in W:A>0\} $ is $W\cap \{ A\geq 0\} $, and each of its points $A$ is represented by the smooth semipositive form $\theta _ A$. For $A=0$, the only positive current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is zero. If $G$ is nonabelian, every positive background in this cone is nonclosed, and adding a smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ term never makes it closed. Proof. Invariant averages and balancedness. Let $Z_1,\ldots ,Z_ n$ be the invariant holomorphic vector fields dual to $\alpha _1,\ldots ,\alpha _ n$, and set $\Upsilon =\alpha _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \alpha _ n$. This holomorphic top-degree form and its conjugate are closed. For an invariant holomorphic vector field $Z$, evaluation on the invariant frame gives \[  \mathcal L_ Z\Upsilon =-\operatorname {tr}(\operatorname {ad}Z)\Upsilon , \qquad \mathcal L_ Z\bar\Upsilon =0.  \] The second identity also follows from Cartan's formula. Since $h_0^ n$ is a positive constant multiple of the appropriately oriented form $\Upsilon \wedge \bar\Upsilon $, Stokes' theorem on compact $X$ gives \[  0=\int _ X\mathcal L_ Zh_0^ n=-H\operatorname {tr}(\operatorname {ad}Z).  \] Thus the fields $Z_ j$ and their conjugates have zero divergence with respect to $\mu $. In particular, 8E5F08796F4E 12.6.8 \begin{equation}  \int _ XZ_ jf\, \mu =\int _ X\bar Z_ jf\, \mu =0 \qquad (f\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb C)). \end{equation} Cartan's formula also gives $\mathrm d(\iota _{Z_ j}\Upsilon )=0$. These contractions span the invariant $(n-1,0)$-forms. The form $\theta _ A^{n-1}$ is a constant linear combination of their wedges with conjugates, so $\mathrm d\theta _ A^{n-1}=0$. The holomorphic fields commute with the antiholomorphic fields, and $\mathrm d\alpha _ j$ has type $(2,0)$. The coefficient matrix of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is therefore $(Z_ j\bar Z_ k u)$. For smooth $u$ its entries have $\mu $-mean zero by ( 12.6.8 ), so the matrix of $\mu $-means of the coefficients of $\theta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is $A$. If $\theta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$, averaging the positive coefficient matrix gives $A>0$. The converse follows by taking $u=0$. The same average shows that $V_ W$ contains no nonzero smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ direction. For a distribution $u$, the adjoints of $Z_ j$ and $\bar Z_ k$ with respect to $\mu $ annihilate constants, so the mean of each $Z_ j\bar Z_ k u$ is still zero. The coefficients of a positive current in this global frame form a positive matrix of measures, whose matrix of total masses is semipositive; for $\theta _ A+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ this gives $A\geq 0$. Conversely, $\theta _ A$ itself is a positive current when $A\geq 0$. If $A=0$, the positive trace measure of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ has total mass zero, and polarization then makes the entire current zero. Finally, for a fixed positive $A_+\in W$, the matrices $A+\varepsilon A_+$ with $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ approximate every semipositive $A\in W$ from the positive cone. This proves the closure assertion. The quotient and its equality case. Put $Q=H\det A$, so that $\theta _ A^ n=Q\mu $. For every smooth positive Hermitian form $\gamma $, the matrix arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives \[  \frac{\theta _ A\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{\gamma ^ n} =\frac1n\operatorname {tr}_\gamma \theta _ A \geq \left(\frac{\theta _ A^ n}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}.  \] Integration yields $\int _ X\theta _ A\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}\geq Q^{1/n}D_\mu (\gamma )$, which bounds every Gauduchon quotient in definition 12.2.1 from below. The balanced, hence Gauduchon, metric $\gamma =\theta _ A$ has $D_\mu (\theta _ A)=Q^{(n-1)/n}$ and attains equality. This proves the formula for $\lambda _\mu (\theta _ A)$. For a minimizing Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, the continuous nonnegative difference of the two sides of the pointwise inequality has integral zero. Pointwise equality then forces $\gamma =f\theta _ A$ for a smooth positive function $f$. Set $q=f^{n-1}$ and $T=\theta _ A^{n-1}$. Since $\mathrm dT=0$, the Gauduchon equation becomes $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\wedge T=0$, and \[  0=\int _ Xq\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\wedge T=-\int _ X\mathrm dq\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}q\wedge T.  \] The last integrand is nonnegative and vanishes exactly where $\mathrm dq=0$. Thus $f$ is constant. As $n\geq 2$ and \[  D_\mu (c\theta _ A)=c^{n-1}\lambda _\mu (\theta _ A)^{n-1},  \] normalization determines $c=\lambda _\mu (\theta _ A)^{-1}$. This proves the unique minimizer and its volume identity. Differentiating $-\log \lambda _\mu (\theta _ A)=-(\log H+\log \det A)/n$ twice gives ( 12.6.7 ). The corresponding squared norm of $U$ is $\| A^{-1/2}UA^{-1/2}\| _{\mathrm F}^2/n$, which is positive for $U\ne 0$; here $\| B\| _{\mathrm F}^2=\operatorname {tr}(B^*B)$ denotes the squared Frobenius norm. Finally, \[  \partial \theta _ A=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\sum _{j,k}A_{jk}\, \mathrm d\alpha _ j\wedge \bar\alpha _ k.  \] For invertible $A$, the vanishing of this form forces every $\mathrm d\alpha _ j=0$, by independence of the conjugate coframe, and the Lie algebra would then be abelian. Since adding $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ does not change $\mathrm d\theta _ A$, this proves the last assertion. $\square$

text: Lemma 12.6.9 . 81EECB4E9700 On the cone of all positive definite Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices, the Riemannian distance of the metric ( 12.6.7 ) is C6F155F53713 12.6.10 \begin{equation}  d_{\mathrm{full}}(A,B)=\frac1{\sqrt n} \| \log (A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2})\| _{\mathrm F}. \end{equation} For endpoints with equal determinant, this is also the intrinsic distance in the hypersurface of all positive definite matrices with that determinant. Proof. By the trace formula, the congruence $M\mapsto P^*MP$ by a fixed invertible matrix $P$ is an isometry. Taking $P=A^{-1/2}$, we may assume that the endpoints are $I$ and $C=A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2}>0$. The curve $\exp (t\log C)$, $0\leq t\leq 1$, has constant speed $\| \log C\| _{\mathrm F}/\sqrt n$, which gives the upper bound for the distance. For the reverse inequality, diagonalization gives the convergent resolvent formula for the matrix logarithm and its derivative \begin{align*}  \log M& =\int _0^\infty \bigl ((1+s)^{-1}I-(M+sI)^{-1}\bigr )\, \mathrm ds,\\  D\log _ M[U]& =\int _0^\infty (M+sI)^{-1}U(M+sI)^{-1}\, \mathrm ds. \end{align*} On a neighborhood of $M$ where the spectrum is bounded below by a positive constant, differentiation under the integral sign is justified by an integrable bound. In a unitary basis diagonalizing $M$, with eigenvalues $d_ i>0$, the derivative has entries $c_{ij}U_{ij}$, where \[  c_{ij}=\frac{\log d_ i-\log d_ j}{d_ i-d_ j}\quad (d_ i\ne d_ j), \qquad c_{ij}=\frac1{d_ i}\quad (d_ i=d_ j).  \] Writing $d_ i/d_ j=\mathrm e^{2s}$ gives $\sqrt{d_ id_ j}|c_{ij}|=|s/\sinh s|\leq 1$, including the limiting value at $s=0$. Hence \[  \| D\log _ M[U]\| _{\mathrm F} \leq \| M^{-1/2}UM^{-1/2}\| _{\mathrm F}.  \] Applying this along a piecewise $C^1$ path of positive matrices from $I$ to $C$ and integrating, we bound its length below by $\| \log C\| _{\mathrm F}/\sqrt n$. This proves the distance formula. In terms of the original endpoints, the length-minimizing curve is 3C044D127EF7 12.6.11 \begin{equation}  M(t)=A^{1/2}(A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2})^ tA^{1/2}. \end{equation} Its determinant is $(\det A)^{1-t}(\det B)^ t$, so for endpoints with equal determinant it stays in the fixed-determinant hypersurface. $\square$

title: Example 12.6.18
section: 12.6 The Hessian metric and its completion
text: Example 12.6.18 . 704C3B45EDAF On $G=\mathbb C^3$ take the multiplication \[  z\cdot w=(z_1+w_1,z_2+w_2,z_3+w_3+z_1w_2),  \] the Gaussian lattice $\Gamma =\mathbb Z[\mathrm i]^3$, and $X=\Gamma \backslash G$. This is a compact non-Kähler manifold of dimension three, with invariant coframe \[  \alpha _1=\mathrm dz_1,\qquad \alpha _2=\mathrm dz_2,\qquad \alpha _3=\mathrm dz_3-z_1\mathrm dz_2.  \] For its full nine-dimensional cone $W=\operatorname {Herm}(3)$ and the normalized invariant probability, \[  H=\frac6{\pi ^3},\qquad \mathcal V_\mu (\theta _ A)=\frac6{\pi ^3}\det A,\qquad S=\{ A>0:\det A=\pi ^3/6\} .  \] Every positive background is nonclosed. The eight-dimensional unit-volume hypersurface is complete and proper, and its intrinsic distance is 8B7DB948FBBB 12.6.19 \begin{equation}  d_ S(A,B)=\frac1{\sqrt3}\| \log (A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2})\| _{\mathrm F}. \end{equation} Proof. The bilinear cross term makes the multiplication associative, with identity zero and inverse $(-z_1,-z_2,-z_3+z_1z_2)$. These operations preserve the Gaussian lattice. Its action by left multiplication is free and properly discontinuous: for a compact set $K\subset G$, elements $\gamma $ with $\gamma K\cap K\ne \varnothing $ belong to the compact set $KK^{-1}$, containing only finitely many lattice elements. Choose Gaussian integers $\gamma _1,\gamma _2$ that move $z_1,z_2$ into the half-open unit square, and then $\gamma _3$ that moves $z_3+\gamma _1z_2$ into it. This gives a representative in the real six-dimensional unit cube. If two points of the half-open cube are equivalent, then $\gamma _1=\gamma _2=0$ and then $\gamma _3=0$. The cube is therefore a measurable fundamental domain, and $X$ is compact, being the image of its closure. This coframe is left-invariant, descends to $X$, and has \[  \mathrm d\alpha _3=-\alpha _1\wedge \alpha _2,\qquad \alpha _1\wedge \alpha _2\wedge \alpha _3 =\mathrm dz_1\wedge \mathrm dz_2\wedge \mathrm dz_3.  \] The density of $h_0^3$ is $6/\pi ^3$ times real Lebesgue volume on the fundamental cube, giving the stated $H$. The coefficient of $\alpha _1\wedge \alpha _2\wedge \bar\alpha _3$ in $\partial \theta _ A$ is $-\mathrm iA_{33}/(2\pi )$, so positivity makes every such background nonclosed. To see that $X$ admits no Kähler metric at all, suppose that a positive closed $(1,1)$-form $\kappa $ existed, and average its coefficient functions in this coframe against $\mu $. Their mean is a positive matrix $A$. In the coefficients of $\partial \kappa $, derivative terms have mean zero by ( 12.6.8 ); the remaining means are exactly the coefficients of $\partial \theta _ A$. Closedness would force them to vanish, contradicting $A_{33}>0$. Thus $X$ is non-Kähler. The assertions about the volume, the minimizers and completeness follow from proposition 12.6.5 , theorem 12.6.12 . As $W$ is the full matrix space, the equal-determinant exponential path stays in $S$, and lemma 12.6.9 gives ( 12.6.19 ). For $A_\star =aI$, $a=(\pi ^3/6)^{1/3}$, this becomes \[  d_ S(A_\star ,A)^2=\frac13\sum _{j=1}^3 \left(\log \frac{\lambda _ j(A)}a\right)^2.  \] The three logarithms sum to zero. For a concrete degeneration, take $A_\varepsilon =\operatorname {diag}(1,1,\varepsilon )$, $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$. As $\varepsilon \to 0$, the coefficients converge to the nonzero smooth semipositive form $\theta _{\operatorname {diag}(1,1,0)}$. The normalized matrices and their distances, on the other hand, are 269EE4BAAD07 12.6.20 \begin{equation}  \begin{gathered} \widehat A_\varepsilon =a\operatorname {diag}(\varepsilon ^{-1/3},\varepsilon ^{-1/3},\varepsilon ^{2/3}),\\ d_ S(A_\star ,\widehat A_\varepsilon )=\frac{\sqrt2}{3}|\log \varepsilon |. \end{gathered} \end{equation} Thus, after normalization, the boundary form $\theta _{\operatorname {diag}(1,1,0)}$ lies at infinite distance. $\square$

title: Theorem 12.6.32

text: Theorem 12.6.32 . 40DF235D735C This span contains no nonzero smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ direction, and its intersection with $\mathscr P$ is the cone \[  \mathscr C=\{ b>0,\  e>0,\  e+cM>0\} .  \] For $\theta =\theta _{b,c,e}\in \mathscr C$, let $H(c,e)=\int _ B\sigma /L$. Then 49FA03FEEBDF 12.6.33 \begin{equation}  \mathcal V_\mu (\theta )=\frac{nb^ m}{H(c,e)}. \end{equation} A minimizing Gauduchon metric is \[  \gamma =L^{-1/m}(A+Lw),\qquad A=b\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi >0,\qquad A^ m=\frac{b^ m}{H}\frac{\sigma }{L},  \] where $\phi $ is a smooth real function on $B$. This metric is balanced. Backgrounds with $c\ne 0$ are nonclosed. Proof. Pairing a smooth positive representative $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ with the closed semipositive form $\kappa ^{m-1}\wedge w$ gives $b>0$, and its integral over the compact fiber $\{ y\} \times C$ is $L(y)>0$, by Stokes' theorem. These are exactly the stated inequalities; conversely, they make $\theta $ itself positive. The same tests applied to a smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ direction give $b=0$ and $ca+e=0$ everywhere, and since $a$ is nonconstant, $c=e=0$. Also $\mathrm{d}\theta =c\, \mathrm{d}a\wedge w$, which is not identically zero when $c\ne 0$. Next we apply theorem 14.2.1 on $B$ to the closed positive background $b\kappa $ and the density $(b^ m/H)\sigma /L$. Since this density has integral $b^ m=\int _ B(b\kappa )^ m$, Stokes' theorem forces the constant in the equation to be one, and we obtain $A$. Put $\Omega =A+Lw$. Since $A^{m+1}=0$ and $(Lw)^2=0$, the binomial expansion gives 0989D826EF96 12.6.34 \begin{equation}  \Omega ^ n=\frac{nb^ m}{H}\mu ,\qquad \gamma ^ m=L^{-1}A^ m+mA^{m-1}\wedge w. \end{equation} The first summand is the pullback of a top-degree form on $B$, and the second is closed. Hence $\gamma $ is balanced, and in particular Gauduchon. For every Gauduchon metric $\eta $ on $X$, Stokes' theorem and the pointwise arithmetic–geometric mean inequality give \[  \int _ X\theta \wedge \eta ^ m =\int _ X\Omega \wedge \eta ^ m \geq \left(\frac{nb^ m}{H}\right)^{1/n}D_\mu (\eta ).  \] For $\eta =\gamma $ the numerator is $nb^ m$, while $D_\mu (\gamma )=(nb^ m/H)^{m/n}H$. The quotient of $\gamma $ therefore attains the lower bound, which proves ( 12.6.33 ) and the minimizing property of $\gamma $. $\square$

title: Theorem 12.6.41
section: 12.6 The Hessian metric and its completion
text: Theorem 12.6.41 . 72BDB634BD0E Under the hypotheses of lemma 12.6.39 on the extreme sets, the metric completion of $\mathscr S$ is a closed Euclidean strip if $r_0,r_ M>1$, a closed Euclidean half-plane if exactly one of them exceeds one, and the whole Euclidean plane otherwise. Each boundary line of the completion is parametrized by $b>0$, and its points are represented by the forms \begin{align*}  \theta _+(b)& =b\kappa +\frac{H_ a}{nb^ m}a w, & H_ a& =\int _ B\frac{\sigma }{a}\quad (r_0>1),\\  \theta _-(b)& =b\kappa +\frac{H_-}{nb^ m}(1-a/M)w, & H_-& =\int _ B\frac{\sigma }{1-a/M}\quad (r_ M>1). \end{align*} These forms are smooth, semipositive, nef, nonclosed and not big, and their variational volume is one. The completion has no other boundary points. Proof. The completion of the convex product $\mathbb R\times I$ of proposition 12.6.36 is its Euclidean closure. Along a Cauchy sequence, $Y$ converges, so $b$ has a finite positive limit, and $R$ converges to a point of $I$ or to a finite endpoint of $I$. Lemma 12.6.39 decides which endpoints are finite and gives the three alternatives. On $\mathscr S$ we have $e=Q(v)/(nb^ m)$ and $c=ve$. At the end $v\to \infty $, $vQ(v)\to H_ a$ by monotone convergence, which gives the coefficient limit $\theta _+(b)$. At the end $v\to -1/M$, write $1+va=1-a/M+(v+1/M)a$; dominated convergence gives $Q(v)\to H_-$, and hence the limit $\theta _-(b)$. These are the coefficient limits at all finite ends. The forms are semipositive, hence nef, and they are nonclosed. Increasing their fiber coefficient by $\epsilon >0$ makes them positive, and ( 12.6.33 ) shows that the resulting volumes tend to one as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. Monotonicity bounds the root volume of the limit form by this limit. Conversely, each fixed Gauduchon quotient is continuous in $\epsilon $, so the limit of the root volumes is at most every quotient of the limit form, hence at most its root volume. Thus the variational volume of $\theta _\pm (b)$ is one. Suppose that some quasi-plurisubharmonic $u$ satisfied \[  \theta _\pm +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \delta (\kappa +w),\qquad \delta >0.  \] For every smooth nonnegative top-degree form $\eta $ on $B$, its pullback is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed for degree reasons, and $\kappa \wedge \eta =0$. Stokes' theorem for currents therefore gives \[  \int _ B(L_\pm -\delta )\eta \geq 0.  \] where $L_\pm $ is the fiber coefficient of $\theta _\pm $. But $L_\pm $ vanishes somewhere, and a nonzero $\eta $ supported where $L_\pm <\delta $ contradicts this inequality. Thus $\theta _\pm $ is not big. $\square$

title: 12.6.42 Current cones and endpoint equations
section: 12.6 The Hessian metric and its completion
text: We keep the product $X=B\times C$, the backgrounds $\theta =b\kappa +(ca+e)w$ with real parameters $b,c,e$, and the probability $\mu =\sigma \wedge w$ of subsection 12.6.31 , and write $h=\kappa +w$ for the product Hermitian form. Pullbacks of nonnegative top-degree forms on $B$ are closed, and testing against them determines which backgrounds have positive current representatives, not only which have smooth positive ones. At a finite end of the unit-volume hypersurface, the reciprocal of the fiber coefficient is integrable with an exponent greater than one, so the equation on the base still has a continuous solution. Proposition 12.6.43 . 67B12ACF7773 In this real span, the pseudoeffective and nef cones both equal \[  \{ b\geq 0,\  e\geq 0,\  e+cM\geq 0\} .  \] A background in this span is big, that is, admits a representative $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \delta h$ with $\delta >0$, if and only if $b>0$, $e>0$ and $e+cM>0$. Thus the big backgrounds in this span form exactly the cone $\mathscr C$ of theorem 12.6.32 . Proof. Put $L=ca+e$, and suppose that a quasi-plurisubharmonic $u$ satisfies $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \delta h$ for some $\delta \geq 0$. Pairing with the closed semipositive form $\kappa ^{m-1}\wedge w$ and using Stokes' theorem for currents gives $b\geq \delta $. For every smooth nonnegative top-degree form $\eta $ on $B$, its pullback to $X$ is closed for degree reasons, and \[  \int _ X(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-\delta h)\wedge \eta =\int _ B(L-\delta )\eta \geq 0.  \] If $L<\delta $ at some point, a nonzero form $\eta $ supported in the open set where $L<\delta $ contradicts this inequality. Hence $L\geq \delta $ everywhere. For $\delta =0$ these conditions are exactly $b\geq 0$, $e\geq 0$ and $e+cM\geq 0$; conversely, they make $\theta $ semipositive, and such forms are nef because $\theta +\varepsilon h>0$ for every $\varepsilon >0$. Conversely, if $\theta $ is nef, applying the same tests to smooth positive representatives of $\theta +\varepsilon h$ and letting $\varepsilon $ tend to zero gives these inequalities. For $\delta >0$ the conditions force the three strict inequalities, and conversely these make $\theta $ itself strictly positive. $\square$ Proposition 12.6.44 . 10BD5355ECF4 Under the hypotheses of lemma 12.6.39 on the extreme sets, let $\theta =b\kappa +L_0w$, with $b>0$, be one of the boundary forms $\theta _+(b)$ or $\theta _-(b)$ of theorem 12.6.41 at a finite end. There is a continuous $\theta $-plurisubharmonic function $u$, pulled back from $B$, such that ED7129134319 12.6.45 \begin{equation}  (\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mu . \end{equation} Here the product is the usual product of bounded potentials. No solution of this equation is of class $C^{1,1}$ on $X$. Proof. Let $f=a$ for $\theta _+(b)$ and $f=1-a/M$ for $\theta _-(b)$, and let $r>1$ be the corresponding ratio $r_0$ or $r_ M$. The coefficient $L_0$ is a positive constant multiple of $f$. In each tube around an extreme component, the integral of $f^{-p}$ converges exactly when \[  \int _0^{s_0}s^{\operatorname {codim}_{\mathbb R}Z_ i-1-k_ ip}\, \mathrm{d}s  \] converges, where $s$ is the normal radius and $s_0>0$ is small. Thus $1/L_0\in L^ p(B,\sigma )$ for every $1<p<r$. The zero set of $L_0$ has volume zero, so the value assigned to the density there is irrelevant. The formulas for $\theta _\pm (b)$ give \[  H_0:=\int _ B\frac{\sigma }{L_0}=nb^ m.  \] We apply theorem 14.19.2 on $B$ to the positive closed background $b\kappa $ and obtain a continuous $\phi $ with $A=b\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi \geq 0$ and $A^ m=c_0\sigma /L_0$ for a constant $c_0>0$. Since $b\kappa $ is closed, bounded potentials do not change its mass, by theorem 11.1.7 ; hence $\int _ BA^ m=b^ m$ and $c_0=b^ m/H_0$. Set $u=\phi \circ p_ B$, where $p_ B:X\to B$ is the projection. Then $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=A+L_0w\geq 0$. The pullback identity of lemma 5.28.4 gives $A^{m+1}=0$ on $X$, and $(L_0w)^2=0$. The multilinear expansion of proposition 5.28.2 therefore gives \[  (A+L_0w)^ n=nL_0 A^ m\wedge w =\frac{nb^ m}{H_0}\sigma \wedge w=\mu .  \] The cancellation $L_0(\sigma /L_0)=\sigma $ holds as measures, since the zero set of $L_0$ has volume zero and $A^ m$ is absolutely continuous with density $c_0/L_0$ relative to $\sigma $. Suppose that some solution $q$, not necessarily pulled back from $B$, were of class $C^{1,1}$ on $X$. Since $\mu /h^ n$ is smooth and strictly positive on compact $X$, proposition 5.28.6 would give $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}q\geq \delta h$ for some $\delta >0$. This contradicts proposition 12.6.43 , because $L_0$ vanishes somewhere. $\square$

title: 12.6.46 Limits of the base potentials
section: 12.6 The Hessian metric and its completion
text: The base potentials used in theorem 12.6.32 to construct the minimizing balanced metrics converge uniformly at each finite end, and the limit solves the endpoint equation ( 12.6.45 ). Both the compactness and the uniqueness needed here concern only the equation on $B$, whose background is closed. Proposition 12.6.47 . C7D8502937F2 Under the hypotheses of theorem 12.6.41 , let $\theta _ j=b_ j\kappa +L_ jw\in \mathscr S$ converge in coefficients to a boundary form $\theta _0=b\kappa +L_0w$ at a finite end. Normalize the smooth base potentials $\phi _ j$ of theorem 12.6.32 by $\sup _ B\phi _ j=0$ and put $u_ j=\phi _ j\circ p_ B$. Then the $u_ j$ converge uniformly on $X$ to a continuous solution $u_0$ of ( 12.6.45 ) pulled back from $B$. For every $1\leq k\leq n$, \[  (\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ k\rightharpoonup (\theta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0)^ k.  \] Moreover, $u_0$ is the unique bounded solution of ( 12.6.45 ) that is pulled back from $B$ and has supremum zero. Proof. Write $v_ j=c_ j/e_ j$ and $\psi _ j=\phi _ j/b_ j$. On $\mathscr S$ the equation for $\phi _ j$ on $B$ becomes \[  (\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _ j)^ m=F_{v_ j}\sigma , \qquad F_ v=\frac1{Q(v)(1+va)},\qquad \sup _ B\psi _ j=0.  \] At the end where $\theta _0=\theta _+(b)$, $v_ j\to \infty $. Set $\epsilon =1/v$ and $H_\epsilon =\int _ B\sigma /(a+\epsilon )$. Then $F_ v=[H_\epsilon (a+\epsilon )]^{-1}$ and $H_\epsilon \to H_ a$. At the end where $\theta _0=\theta _-(b)$, $v_ j\to -1/M$. With $f=1-a/M$ and $t=v+1/M>0$, the denominator of $F_ v$ is $Q(v)(f+ta)$, and $Q(v)\to H_-$. Thus the respective limits of $F_{v_ j}$ are \[  F_+=\frac1{H_ a a},\qquad F_-=\frac1{H_-(1-a/M)}.  \] Choose $1<p<r$, where $r>1$ is the ratio $r_0$ or $r_ M$ of that end. Integration over tubes as in the proof of proposition 12.6.44 gives $a^{-1}\in L^ p(B,\sigma )$, respectively $f^{-1}\in L^ p(B,\sigma )$. Near the first end $F_ v\leq C/a$, and near the second $F_ v\leq C/f$. Since the extreme sets have volume zero, dominated convergence gives $F_{v_ j}\to F_\pm $ in $L^ p(B,\sigma )$, and each limiting density has integral one. Since $\sigma /\kappa ^ m$ is smooth and strictly positive on compact $B$, the densities of the equations also have a common bound in $L^ p(B,\kappa ^ m)$. We apply theorem 14.19.21 to the fixed background $\kappa $: every subsequence of $(\psi _ j)$ has a uniformly convergent further subsequence. Continuity of bounded products under uniform convergence identifies its limit with a normalized solution of $(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _0)^ m=F_\pm \sigma $. Since $\kappa $ is closed, it satisfies the Guan–Li condition, so 14.25.2 makes this solution unique. Every cluster limit is consequently the same, which proves uniform convergence of the whole sequence. Since $b_ j\to b>0$, we obtain $u_ j\to u_0=(b\psi _0)\circ p_ B$ uniformly. To prove convergence of the products, note that on each coordinate ball the convergence of the background coefficients provides a common smooth function $q$, a quadratic polynomial, such that all $u_ j+q$ are plurisubharmonic. These corrected potentials are uniformly bounded and converge uniformly. The continuity of bounded products under convergence in capacity (section 5.27 ) gives weak convergence of all their products, with uniform local mass bounds. Expanding the products as in ( 5.28.1 ), and using smooth convergence of the remaining background factors, we obtain the asserted convergence of currents. In top degree, $(\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ n=\mu $ for all $j$, so the limit solves the endpoint equation. For uniqueness, let $v=\chi \circ p_ B$ be a bounded solution pulled back from $B$, with $\sup _ B\chi =0$. The current $A_\chi =b\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi $ on $B$ is positive, as one sees by pairing the pulled-back current $\theta _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ with $w$ and with pullbacks of positive forms on $B$. The product expansion gives $nL_0A_\chi ^ m\wedge w=\sigma \wedge w$, which determines $A_\chi ^ m=\sigma /(nL_0)$ off the extreme set. That density already has total mass $H_0/n=b^ m$, whereas mass invariance for the closed background $b\kappa $ gives $\int _ BA_\chi ^ m=b^ m$. Positivity therefore excludes any mass of $A_\chi ^ m$ on the extreme set. Thus $\chi /b$ satisfies the same normalized equation on $B$ as $\psi _0$, and 14.25.2 proves the asserted uniqueness. $\square$ The proposition concerns the limit of the base potentials constructed above. It does not describe solutions of the endpoint equation that are not pulled back from $B$, nor does it give a pointwise limit of the balanced metrics $\gamma _ j=L_ j^{-1/m}(b_ j\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ j+L_ jw)$.

We apply theorem 14.19.21 to the fixed background $\kappa $: every subsequence of $(\psi _ j)$ has a uniformly convergent further subsequence. Continuity of bounded products under uniform convergence identifies its limit with a normalized solution of $(\kappa +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi _0)^ m=F_\pm \sigma $. Since $\kappa $ is closed, it satisfies the Guan–Li condition, so 14.25.2 makes this solution unique. To prove convergence of the products, note that on each coordinate ball the convergence of the background coefficients provides a common smooth function $q$, a quadratic polynomial, such that all $u_ j+q$ are plurisubharmonic. These corrected potentials are uniformly bounded and converge uniformly. The continuity of bounded products under convergence in capacity (section 5.27 ) gives weak convergence of all their products, with uniform local mass bounds. Expanding the products as in ( 5.28.1 ), and using smooth convergence of the remaining background factors, we obtain the asserted convergence of currents. In top degree, $(\theta _ j+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ n=\mu $ for all $j$, so the limit solves the endpoint equation. For uniqueness, let $v=\chi \circ p_ B$ be a bounded solution pulled back from $B$, with $\sup _ B\chi =0$. The product expansion gives $nL_0A_\chi ^ m\wedge w=\sigma \wedge w$, which determines $A_\chi ^ m=\sigma /(nL_0)$ off the extreme set. That density already has total mass $H_0/n=b^ m$, whereas mass invariance for the closed background $b\kappa $ gives $\int _ BA_\chi ^ m=b^ m$. Positivity therefore excludes any mass of $A_\chi ^ m$ on the extreme set. Thus $\chi /b$ satisfies the same normalized equation on $B$ as $\psi _0$, and 14.25.2 proves the asserted uniqueness. $\square$

title: 12.6.52 Projective and torus examples
section: 12.6 The Hessian metric and its completion
text: Example 12.6.53 . 27A22321E298 On $B=\mathbb P^2$, take normalized Fubini–Study $\kappa $, $\sigma =\kappa ^2$, $C=\mathbb P^1$, and \[  a([Z])=\frac{|Z_1|^2/2+|Z_2|^2}{|Z_0|^2+|Z_1|^2+|Z_2|^2}.  \] Then $M=1$, $r_0=r_ M=2$, and the completion is a closed strip with finite faces \[  b\kappa +\frac{4\log 2}{3b^2}a w,\qquad b\kappa +\frac{4\log 2}{3b^2}(1-a)w.  \] For $v\ne 0$, \[  Q(v)=\frac4{v^2}\bigl [(v+1)\log (1+v) -(v+2)\log (1+v/2)\bigr ], \qquad Q(0)=1.  \] The width of the strip is the finite positive integral \[  \int _{-1}^{\infty } \sqrt{\frac{Q''/Q-2(Q'/Q)^2}{3}}\, \mathrm{d}v.  \] Proof. The extreme sets are the points $[1:0:0]$ and $[0:0:1]$. In affine coordinates, $a$ and $1-a$ vanish there to exactly second order, so both real codimensions are four and both orders are two. To compute the law of $a$ under $\sigma $, polar integration in the chart $Z_0=1$ gives $2\, \mathrm{d}s_1\mathrm{d}s_2/(1+s_1+s_2)^3$, where $s_ j=|z_ j|^2$. The transformation $u_ j=s_ j/(1+s_1+s_2)$ gives the uniform density two on the triangle $u_1,u_2\geq 0$, $u_1+u_2\leq 1$, and $a=u_1/2+u_2$. For $0\leq s\leq 1/2$, the triangle $u_1/2+u_2\leq s$ has area $s^2$, so the law of $a$ has density $4s$ on $[0,1/2]$. With $u_0=1-u_1-u_2$, exchanging $u_0$ and $u_2$ preserves the uniform measure and replaces $a$ by $1-a$; hence the law has density $4(1-s)$ on $[1/2,1]$. Integrating against these two densities gives $H_ a=H_-=4\log 2$ and the formula for $Q$, and the integral definition of $Q$ shows that $Q(0)=1$ is its continuous extension. Theorem 12.6.41 gives the boundary lines and the finite width, with Euclidean coordinates $Y=\sqrt2\log b$ and $R(v)$. $\square$ Example 12.6.54 . CD9181602A11 Let $E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)$, $B=E^ m$, and write $z_ j=u_ j+i\tau _ j$. Put \[  \eta _ j=\frac i2\mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ j, \qquad s=(m!)^{-1/m},\qquad \kappa =s\sum _ j\eta _ j,\qquad \sigma =\kappa ^ m.  \] For $a=\sin ^2(\pi u_1)$, the unit-volume hypersurface is itself a complete Euclidean plane, with Euclidean coordinates \[  Y=\sqrt m\log b,\qquad R=\frac{\log (1+v)}{2\sqrt n},\qquad v>-1.  \] Its minimizing balanced metrics can be written down by integrating a periodic function twice. Proof. The forms descend to $B$, and $\sigma =\eta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \eta _ m$ is a probability form. Both extreme sets are real hypersurfaces along which $a$, respectively $1-a$, vanishes to second order, so $r_0=r_ M=1/2$. Splitting the period and substituting $t=\tan (\pi u)$ gives \begin{align*}  Q(v)& =\int _0^1\frac{\mathrm{d}u}{1+v\sin ^2(\pi u)}\\ & =\frac2\pi \int _0^\infty \frac{\mathrm{d}t}{1+(1+v)t^2} =\frac1{\sqrt{1+v}}. \end{align*} Let $F_ v(u)=[Q(v)(1+v\sin ^2(\pi u))]^{-1}$, which has mean one over a period. Integrating the equation \[  \phi _ v''=4\pi bs(F_ v-1)  \] twice, whose right side has mean zero, gives a smooth periodic potential $\phi _ v$ of $u=u_1$; the first integration constant is chosen so that $\phi _ v'$ has mean zero. In our normalization $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _ v=\phi _ v''\eta _1/(4\pi )$, hence \[  A=bs\left(F_ v\eta _1+\sum _{j=2}^ m\eta _ j\right)>0, \qquad A^ m=b^ mF_ v\sigma =\frac{b^ m}{H}\frac{\sigma }{L}.  \] Thus the minimizer of theorem 12.6.32 , with its cofactor formula ( 12.6.34 ), is explicit in this example, without an appeal to theorem 14.2.1 . Differentiating $Q$ gives \[  \rho (v)=\frac1{4n(1+v)^2},\qquad g_{\mathscr S}=m\, \mathrm{d}U^2+ \frac1{4n}\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{1+v}\right)^2.  \] As $U$ and $v$ range over $\mathbb R$ and $(-1,\infty )$, the coordinates $(Y,R)$ range over all of $\mathbb R^2$. Both boundary faces of the coefficient cone are therefore at infinite distance on the unit-volume hypersurface. $\square$ These distances are those of the fixed three-parameter cone with the product probability $\mu =\sigma \wedge w$. The endpoint criterion of lemma 12.6.39 uses the hypothesis that the extreme sets are disjoint unions of submanifolds along which $a$ vanishes to finite power order; intersecting extreme strata or vanishing of infinite order would require further estimates. The variances are computed from the minimizing metrics, but we do not assert that these metrics have a pointwise limit at a finite end.

title: 12.7 A compact dual problem over Gauduchon currents
search_title: A compact dual problem over Gauduchon currents
section: 12.7 A compact dual problem over Gauduchon currents
text: We now fix a Hermitian background and vary the density. For a smooth positive density, theorem 12.2.3 provides a minimizing Gauduchon metric; for a density that is only continuous or integrable, there is no smooth equation to produce one. The extremal problem becomes compact when positive $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed $(n-1,n-1)$-currents are allowed as tests, provided the denominator $D_\mu $ is extended to currents. For this we take the determinant of the matrix density of a current relative to its trace measure. The integral of its $n$th root is an infimum of continuous linear functionals, hence upper semicontinuous under weak convergence, and its maximum over normalized currents is attained. The smooth equation identifies this maximum with the supremum over smooth tests. From here until section 12.11 , we assume $n\geq 2$, and we fix a Hermitian form $\omega $ and a smooth positive probability volume form $\mathrm{d}V$ on $X$; integrability and convergence in measure refer to $\mathrm{d}V$. As in section 13.14 , $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ for bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, and $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)$ is the extended non-pluripolar Monge–Ampère measure of theorem 13.14.3 . Let $\mathscr G_\omega $ be the compact convex set of normalized Gauduchon currents of section 11.7 , that is, of positive $(n-1,n-1)$-currents $T$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ and $\int _ X\omega \wedge T=1$. Finally, let $F\in C(X,\mathbb R)$. For $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $, the trace measure $\sigma _ T=\omega \wedge T$ is a probability measure, and all coefficient measures of $T$ are absolutely continuous with respect to it. In a unitary frame for $\omega $, let $B$ be the matrix of a smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\beta $ relative to $\omega $. The coefficient densities of $T$ form a measurable positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix $P_ T$, determined $\sigma _ T$-almost everywhere by \[  \beta \wedge T=\frac1n\operatorname {tr}(B P_ T)\, \mathrm{d}\sigma _ T, \qquad \operatorname {tr}P_ T=n\quad \sigma _ T\text{-almost everywhere}.  \] The matrix $P_ T$ transforms by unitary conjugation when the frame changes, so its determinant is well defined. Define A99038CD10B4 12.7.1 \begin{equation}  f_ F=\left(\frac{\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V}{\omega ^ n}\right)^{1/n},\qquad \Gamma _ F(T)=f_ F(\det P_ T)^{1/n}\sigma _ T,\qquad \mathfrak D_ F(T)=\Gamma _ F(T)(X). \end{equation} These quantities are finite, since the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives $(\det P_ T)^{1/n}\leq 1$; the measure $\Gamma _ F(T)$ may vanish for some currents. The same definitions apply to every positive $(n-1,n-1)$-current $T$ of finite mass, with the finite measure $\sigma _ T=\omega \wedge T$ and $\operatorname {tr}P_ T=n$, and $\Gamma _ F$ is positively homogeneous of degree one in $T$. If the coefficient measures of $T$ are written instead as a matrix density $P'$ relative to another positive measure $\sigma '$ with respect to which they are absolutely continuous, then $(\det P_ T)^{1/n}\sigma _ T=(\det P')^{1/n}\sigma '$, by homogeneity of the determinant. For a smooth positive $T=\gamma ^{n-1}$, we may therefore use the reference measure $\omega ^ n$. The coefficient matrix of $T$ relative to $\omega ^ n$ is the cofactor matrix of the matrix of $\gamma $, and its determinant is $(\gamma ^ n/\omega ^ n)^{n-1}$. The definition therefore gives \[  \mathfrak D_ F(\gamma ^{n-1}) =\int _ X\left(\frac{\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n.  \] Thus $\mathfrak D_ F$ extends the denominator $D_\mu $ of definition 12.2.1 to currents, with $\mu $ replaced by the possibly unnormalized density $\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V$. Lemma 12.7.2 . FB6C2382E066 For every positive $(n-1,n-1)$-current $T$ of finite mass on $X$, \[  \mathfrak D_ F(T) =\inf _{\substack {\beta >0\  \mathrm{continuous}\\ \beta ^ n=\mathrm{e}^ F\mathrm{d}V}} \int _ X\beta \wedge T.  \] In particular, $\mathfrak D_ F$ is concave, positively homogeneous and weakly upper semicontinuous on $\mathscr G_\omega $, and its value does not depend on the auxiliary frame or on the metric used to express the matrix density. Proof. Let $I$ be the identity matrix of size $n$. For any positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix $P$ of that size, \[  (\det P)^{1/n} =\inf _{Q>0,\  \det Q=1}\frac1n\operatorname {tr}(QP).  \] The inequality $\leq $ is the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality. For the reverse inequality, take, for real $\varepsilon >0$, \[  Q_\varepsilon = \det (P+\varepsilon I)^{1/n}(P+\varepsilon I)^{-1}.  \] Its determinant is one. If $P$ is positive definite, the trace expression $\frac1n\operatorname {tr}(Q_\varepsilon P)$ converges to $(\det P)^{1/n}$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. If $P$ is singular, it converges to zero: each ratio of an eigenvalue of $P$ to that eigenvalue plus $\varepsilon $ is bounded, while the prefactor tends to zero. When $\operatorname {tr}P=n$, the trace expression is at most $1+\varepsilon $. We apply this formula to $P_ T$ and multiply by $f_ F$. Every continuous positive $\beta $ in the asserted infimum has matrix $f_ FQ$ with $\det Q=1$, so it gives an upper bound for $\mathfrak D_ F(T)$. Conversely, for fixed $\varepsilon >0$ the measurable field $Q_\varepsilon $ formed with $P=P_ T$ is bounded above and below by positive constants. It can be approximated in $L^1(\sigma _ T)$ by continuous positive definite Hermitian fields with bounds of the same type. One way to construct them is to apply Lusin's theorem in finitely many bundle charts, extend the continuous fields from the resulting compact sets, and glue with a partition of unity; spectral truncation to a fixed positive interval preserves the bounds. Finally we divide each approximating field by the $n$th root of its determinant. This normalization is uniformly continuous on fields with spectrum in a fixed compact positive interval, so the normalized fields still converge in $L^1(\sigma _ T)$ and have determinant one. Their trace integrals converge to that of $Q_\varepsilon $. Now let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. The bound $1+\varepsilon $ permits dominated convergence, and we obtain equality of the infimum and the integral. For a current of arbitrary positive finite trace mass we use homogeneity, and the zero current is immediate. The infimum is taken over functionals $T\mapsto \int _ X\beta \wedge T$ that are linear and weakly continuous, which proves concavity and upper semicontinuity. It also expresses $\mathfrak D_ F(T)$ without a matrix frame or an auxiliary metric, which proves the final assertion. $\square$ Let $B_0(F)$ be the normalization scalar of section 11.33 for the background $\omega $ and the reference potential zero. Thus the equation $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=\mathrm{e}^{B_0(F)+F}\mathrm{d}V$ has a bounded solution $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, and $B_0(F)$ is the only constant with this property. Theorem 12.7.3 . 0537569F9F52 For every $F\in C(X,\mathbb R)$, 053F006B114F 12.7.4 \begin{equation}  M(F):=\max _{T\in \mathscr G_\omega }\mathfrak D_ F(T) =\mathrm{e}^{-B_0(F)/n}>0. \end{equation} The maximum equals the supremum over the smooth strictly positive members of $\mathscr G_\omega $. The set $\mathscr M(F)$ of maximizing currents is nonempty, compact and convex. If $F$ is smooth, there is exactly one maximizing current, namely the normalized $(n-1)$st power of the Gauduchon metric conformal to the smooth solution form $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=\mathrm{e}^{B_0(F)+F}\mathrm{d}V$. Proof. Upper semicontinuity of $\mathfrak D_ F$ on the compact set $\mathscr G_\omega $ gives attainment, and testing a smooth positive member gives a positive value. Concavity makes the set of maximizers convex, and upper semicontinuity makes it closed. Suppose first that $F$ is smooth, and let $\Omega =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$ be the smooth solution form with $\Omega ^ n=\mathrm{e}^{B_0(F)+F}\mathrm{d}V$. The form $\beta =\mathrm{e}^{-B_0(F)/n}\Omega $ is an admissible test in the preceding lemma, so Stokes' theorem for currents gives, for every $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $, \[  \mathfrak D_ F(T)\leq \int _ X\beta \wedge T =\mathrm{e}^{-B_0(F)/n}\int _ X\omega \wedge T=\mathrm{e}^{-B_0(F)/n}.  \] If $\gamma $ is the Gauduchon metric conformal to $\Omega $, equality holds in the pointwise matrix inequality for $T$ proportional to $\gamma ^{n-1}$; normalizing $T$ so that $\int _ X\omega \wedge T=1$, we obtain the formula and its attainment by a smooth test. For uniqueness, let $T$ be a maximizer. Equality in the integrated inequalities forces equality in the matrix arithmetic–geometric mean inequality $\sigma _ T$-almost everywhere. Since the matrix of $\beta $ is positive definite and $\operatorname {tr}P_ T=n$, this means that the coefficient measures of $T$ are a nonnegative scalar measure times the smooth coefficients of $\gamma ^{n-1}$. Thus $T=a\gamma ^{n-1}$, where $a$ is a positive measure, regarded as a distribution. The equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(a\gamma ^{n-1})=0$ is the adjoint of a scalar elliptic equation, so elliptic regularity makes $a$ smooth. Since $\gamma $ is Gauduchon, proposition 11.23.2 identifies the kernel of this adjoint operator with the constants: the trace operator $v\mapsto n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}/\gamma ^ n$ has the constants as kernel and index zero, and integration against $\gamma ^ n$ annihilates its range. Thus $a$ is constant, and the normalization fixes the constant. This proves uniqueness. For continuous $F,G$, the pointwise definition gives \[  \mathrm{e}^{-\| F-G\| _\infty /n}\mathfrak D_ G(T) \leq \mathfrak D_ F(T) \leq \mathrm{e}^{\| F-G\| _\infty /n}\mathfrak D_ G(T).  \] The same bounds hold for the maxima, and for the suprema over smooth positive members. We approximate $F$ uniformly by smooth functions. Since $B_0$ is $1$-Lipschitz for the uniform norm by proposition 11.33.2 , the formula just proved for smooth data gives ( 12.7.4 ) in the limit, including the equality with the smooth supremum. Note that only $F$ is approximated here: some normalized Gauduchon currents are not limits of smooth positive ones, as example 10.18.3 shows. $\square$

title: Lemma 12.8.1
section: 12.8 Supporting probabilities represented by maximizing currents
text: Lemma 12.8.1 . 47843166E777 Suppose $T_ j\to T$ weakly in $\mathscr G_\omega $ and $\mathfrak D_ F(T_ j)\to M(F)$. Then $T\in \mathscr M(F)$ and $\Gamma _ F(T_ j)\rightharpoonup \Gamma _ F(T)$. On $\mathscr M(F)$ the map $T\mapsto \Gamma _ F(T)$ is affine and continuous. Proof. Upper semicontinuity gives $\mathfrak D_ F(T)\geq M(F)$, hence equality. The measures $\Gamma _ F(T_ j)$ have bounded mass; let $\Gamma '$ be a weak cluster point, whose mass is $M(F)$. For a continuous real function $h$, choose $\varepsilon >0$ with $1\pm \varepsilon h>0$. Since $\Gamma _{F+n\log (1\pm \varepsilon h)}=(1\pm \varepsilon h)\Gamma _ F$, upper semicontinuity of $\mathfrak D$ for these two continuous logarithmic densities gives \[  \int _ X(1\pm \varepsilon h)\, \mathrm{d}\Gamma ' \leq \int _ X(1\pm \varepsilon h)\, \mathrm{d}\Gamma _ F(T).  \] Since both measures have mass $M(F)$, the two signs give equality of the integrals of $h$. Thus every cluster point equals $\Gamma _ F(T)$, which proves the convergence. For affineness, take $T_1,T_2\in \mathscr G_\omega $ and $t\in [0,1]$, and express the coefficient measures of both currents through densities with respect to the sum of their trace measures. Concavity and homogeneity of the $n$th root of the determinant, applied to these matrix densities, give \[  \Gamma _ F(tT_1+(1-t)T_2) \geq t\Gamma _ F(T_1)+(1-t)\Gamma _ F(T_2),\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1.  \] If $T_1$ and $T_2$ maximize, so does the current on the left, by concavity of $\mathfrak D_ F$. Both measures in the inequality then have mass $M(F)$, so equality holds. This proves affineness, and continuity is the special case of the first assertion in which every $T_ j$ is a maximizer. $\square$

title: 12.9 Integrability of Gauduchon determinant measures
text:
A lower bound for the constants of smooth equations in terms of an $L^ p$ norm of the density gives, by duality, a uniform $L^ q$ bound for the determinant measures of all normalized Gauduchon currents, for every exponent $q<n/(n-1)$. At the endpoint $q=n/(n-1)$, the optimal constant is exactly $v_-(\omega )^{-1/n}$, where $v_-(\omega )$ is the lower Monge–Ampère mass of definition 13.14.14 . Thus integrability of the dual tests at the critical exponent is equivalent to positive lower mass of the background. Write $\Gamma _0(T)$ for the determinant measure $\Gamma _ F(T)$ of ( 12.7.1 ) with $F=0$. Theorem 12.9.1 . BF52D98B114F For every $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $, the measure $\Gamma _0(T)$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mathrm{d}V$; we write $\Gamma _0(T)=k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V$ and call $k_ T\geq 0$ the determinant density of $T$. For every $1<q<n/(n-1)$ there is $C_ q>0$ such that \[  \| k_ T\| _{L^ q(\mathrm{d}V)}\leq C_ q \qquad (T\in \mathscr G_\omega ).  \] Proof. Fix $p>1$ and a smooth strictly positive function $h$. By theorem 14.2.1 there are a smooth form $\Omega _ h=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ h>0$ and a constant $c_ h>0$ such that \[  \Omega _ h^ n=c_ hh^ n\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The lower-density estimate of theorem 14.19.19 gives a constant $c_ p>0$, independent of $h$, such that \[  c_ h\| h^ n\| _{L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)}\geq c_ p.  \] The pointwise matrix arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, applied to $\Omega _ h$ and the coefficient density of $T$, gives the inequality of measures \[  c_ h^{1/n}h\, \Gamma _0(T)\leq \Omega _ h\wedge T.  \] Integrating and using $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ yields \[  \int _ Xh\, \mathrm{d}\Gamma _0(T) \leq c_ h^{-1/n}\int _ X\Omega _ h\wedge T =c_ h^{-1/n} \leq c_ p^{-1/n}\| h\| _{L^{np}(\mathrm{d}V)}.  \] Approximation by smooth strictly positive functions extends this bound to every continuous nonnegative $h$, and applied to $|h|$ it bounds the integral of every continuous function against $\Gamma _0(T)$ by its $L^{np}$ norm. Since continuous functions are dense in $L^{np}$, the duality between $L^{np}$ and $L^{np/(np-1)}$ shows that $\Gamma _0(T)$ has a density in $L^{np/(np-1)}$, with norm at most $c_ p^{-1/n}$. As $p$ ranges over $(1,+\infty )$, the exponent $np/(np-1)$ ranges over $(1,n/(n-1))$. This proves the theorem. $\square$ In particular, the determinant of the matrix density vanishes on the singular part of the trace measure: if $\sigma _ T=\sigma _{T,\mathrm{ac}}+\sigma _{T,\mathrm{s}}$ is its Lebesgue decomposition with respect to $\mathrm{d}V$, then \[  \det P_ T=0\quad \sigma _{T,\mathrm{s}}	ext{-almost everywhere}.  \] Indeed, $f_0=(\mathrm{d}V/\omega ^ n)^{1/n}$ is everywhere positive and $\Gamma _0(T)=f_0(\det P_ T)^{1/n}\sigma _ T$ is absolutely continuous. This says nothing about a possible singular part of the current $T$ itself. Theorem 12.9.2 . E7F890105D42 With the extended value $+\infty $ allowed, one has \[  \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_\omega } \| k_ T\| _{L^{n/(n-1)}(\mathrm{d}V)}=v_-(\omega )^{-1/n},  \] where the right side is interpreted as $+\infty $ when $v_-(\omega )=0$. The supremum does not change if $T$ is restricted to the smooth strictly positive members of $\mathscr G_\omega $. Thus a uniform estimate at the endpoint exponent holds if and only if $v_-(\omega )>0$. Proof. Suppose first that $v_-(\omega )>0$. For the smooth equation in the preceding proof, the definition of $v_-$ gives \[  c_ h\int _ Xh^ n\, \mathrm{d}V=\int _ X\Omega _ h^ n\geq v_-(\omega ).  \] The same pointwise inequality and Stokes' theorem therefore give \[  \int _ Xh\, \mathrm{d}\Gamma _0(T) \leq v_-(\omega )^{-1/n}\| h\| _{L^ n(\mathrm{d}V)}.  \] By duality, $\| k_ T\| _{L^{n/(n-1)}}\leq v_-(\omega )^{-1/n}$ for every $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $. For the reverse bound, let $g$ be any smooth positive probability density relative to $\mathrm{d}V$, and solve \[  \Omega _ g^ n=c(g)g\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Let $T_ g$ be the trace-normalized $(n-1)$st power of the Gauduchon metric conformal to $\Omega _ g$. Equality in the pointwise matrix inequality gives \[  \int _ Xg^{1/n}\, \mathrm{d}\Gamma _0(T_ g)=c(g)^{-1/n}.  \] Since $\| g^{1/n}\| _{L^ n}=1$, Hölder's inequality gives $\| k_{T_ g}\| _{L^{n/(n-1)}}\geq c(g)^{-1/n}$. By theorem 12.15.4 , theorem 12.2.3 , \[  \inf _{g>0\  \mathrm{smooth},\  \int _ Xg\, \mathrm{d}V=1}c(g)=v_-(\omega ).  \] Taking the supremum over these smooth currents $T_ g$ proves the matching lower bound; if $v_-(\omega )=0$, the same argument makes this supremum infinite. Since the currents $T_ g$ are smooth, this also proves that allowing nonsmooth currents does not change the supremum. $\square$ The formula shows that the optimal endpoint constant does not depend on the choice of $\mathrm{d}V$, whereas the subcritical constants $C_ q$ may depend on it. Corollary 12.9.3 . 893A41D78AF5 For every $R>0$ and $1<q<n/(n-1)$ there is a constant $C_{R,q}$ with the following property. If $F\in C(X)$ and $\| F\| _\infty \leq R$, every supporting probability $
u \in \mathcal A_0(F)$ of theorem 12.8.2 has a density $a$ satisfying \[  
u =a\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad \| a\| _{L^ q(\mathrm{d}V)}\leq C_{R,q}.  \] If $v_-(\omega )>0$, this holds also for $q=n/(n-1)$. Proof. Recall that $M(F)=\exp (-B_0(F)/n)$, and represent $
u $ by a maximizing current $T\in \mathscr M(F)$, using theorem 12.8.2 . Since $\Gamma _ F(T)=\mathrm{e}^{F/n}\Gamma _0(T)$ and $B_0$ is $1$-Lipschitz, \[  
u = rac{\mathrm{e}^{F/n}k_ T}{M(F)}\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad M(F)\geq \mathrm{e}^{-R/n}M(0)>0.  \] Theorem 12.9.1 therefore gives the subcritical bound with constant $\mathrm{e}^{2R/n}M(0)^{-1}C_ q$. When $v_-(\omega )>0$, the same argument with the endpoint constant $v_-(\omega )^{-1/n}$ of theorem 12.9.2 gives the case $q=n/(n-1)$. $\square$ On the threefold of theorem 12.19.1 , every Hermitian form has zero lower mass, so the endpoint estimate fails for the whole family $\mathscr G_\omega $, while all the subcritical estimates above remain valid. For a fixed smooth density, theorem 12.7.3 gives a unique smooth maximizing current, and its determinant density is bounded. Sequences of currents whose values approach the maximum need not, however, have uniformly bounded higher moments, as proposition 12.18.2 shows. On the other hand, the endpoint estimate can hold on a manifold with infinite upper mass. On the Hopf threefold of section 23.1 , take the Gauduchon metric $\omega $ of that chapter, for which $v_-(\omega )=6$ and $v_+(\omega )=+\infty $, and set $\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^3/6$. The normalized Gauduchon form $T_0=\omega ^2/6$ has $\sigma _{T_0}=\mathrm{d}V$ and $P_{T_0}=I$. Hence $k_{T_0}=6^{-1/3}$, and \[  \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_\omega }\| k_ T\| _{L^{3/2}(\mathrm{d}V)}=6^{-1/3}.  \] Thus an endpoint determinant estimate, with its optimal constant attained, can coexist with infinite upper Monge–Ampère mass.

BF52D98B114F For every $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $, the measure $\Gamma _0(T)$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mathrm{d}V$; we write $\Gamma _0(T)=k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V$ and call $k_ T\geq 0$ the determinant density of $T$. For every $1<q<n/(n-1)$ there is $C_ q>0$ such that \[  \| k_ T\| _{L^ q(\mathrm{d}V)}\leq C_ q \qquad (T\in \mathscr G_\omega ).  \] Proof. Fix $p>1$ and a smooth strictly positive function $h$. By theorem 14.2.1 there are a smooth form $\Omega _ h=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ h>0$ and a constant $c_ h>0$ such that \[  \Omega _ h^ n=c_ hh^ n\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The lower-density estimate of theorem 14.19.19 gives a constant $c_ p>0$, independent of $h$, such that \[  c_ h\| h^ n\| _{L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)}\geq c_ p.  \] The pointwise matrix arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, applied to $\Omega _ h$ and the coefficient density of $T$, gives the inequality of measures \[  c_ h^{1/n}h\, \Gamma _0(T)\leq \Omega _ h\wedge T.  \] Integrating and using $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ yields \[  \int _ Xh\, \mathrm{d}\Gamma _0(T) \leq c_ h^{-1/n}\int _ X\Omega _ h\wedge T =c_ h^{-1/n} \leq c_ p^{-1/n}\| h\| _{L^{np}(\mathrm{d}V)}.  \] Approximation by smooth strictly positive functions extends this bound to every continuous nonnegative $h$, and applied to $|h|$ it bounds the integral of every continuous function against $\Gamma _0(T)$ by its $L^{np}$ norm. Since continuous functions are dense in $L^{np}$, the duality between $L^{np}$ and $L^{np/(np-1)}$ shows that $\Gamma _0(T)$ has a density in $L^{np/(np-1)}$, with norm at most $c_ p^{-1/n}$. As $p$ ranges over $(1,+\infty )$, the exponent $np/(np-1)$ ranges over $(1,n/(n-1))$. This proves the theorem. $\square$

title: Theorem 12.9.2
text: Theorem 12.9.2 . E7F890105D42 With the extended value $+\infty $ allowed, one has \[  \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_\omega } \| k_ T\| _{L^{n/(n-1)}(\mathrm{d}V)}=v_-(\omega )^{-1/n},  \] where the right side is interpreted as $+\infty $ when $v_-(\omega )=0$. The supremum does not change if $T$ is restricted to the smooth strictly positive members of $\mathscr G_\omega $. Thus a uniform estimate at the endpoint exponent holds if and only if $v_-(\omega )>0$. Proof. Suppose first that $v_-(\omega )>0$. For the smooth equation in the preceding proof, the definition of $v_-$ gives \[  c_ h\int _ Xh^ n\, \mathrm{d}V=\int _ X\Omega _ h^ n\geq v_-(\omega ).  \] The same pointwise inequality and Stokes' theorem therefore give \[  \int _ Xh\, \mathrm{d}\Gamma _0(T) \leq v_-(\omega )^{-1/n}\| h\| _{L^ n(\mathrm{d}V)}.  \] By duality, $\| k_ T\| _{L^{n/(n-1)}}\leq v_-(\omega )^{-1/n}$ for every $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $. For the reverse bound, let $g$ be any smooth positive probability density relative to $\mathrm{d}V$, and solve \[  \Omega _ g^ n=c(g)g\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Let $T_ g$ be the trace-normalized $(n-1)$st power of the Gauduchon metric conformal to $\Omega _ g$. Equality in the pointwise matrix inequality gives \[  \int _ Xg^{1/n}\, \mathrm{d}\Gamma _0(T_ g)=c(g)^{-1/n}.  \] Since $\| g^{1/n}\| _{L^ n}=1$, Hölder's inequality gives $\| k_{T_ g}\| _{L^{n/(n-1)}}\geq c(g)^{-1/n}$. By theorem 12.15.4 , theorem 12.2.3 , \[  \inf _{g>0\  \mathrm{smooth},\  \int _ Xg\, \mathrm{d}V=1}c(g)=v_-(\omega ).  \] Taking the supremum over these smooth currents $T_ g$ proves the matching lower bound; if $v_-(\omega )=0$, the same argument makes this supremum infinite. Since the currents $T_ g$ are smooth, this also proves that allowing nonsmooth currents does not change the supremum. $\square$

title: Corollary 12.9.3
text:
Corollary 12.9.3 . 893A41D78AF5 For every $R>0$ and $1<q<n/(n-1)$ there is a constant $C_{R,q}$ with the following property. If $F\in C(X)$ and $\| F\| _\infty \leq R$, every supporting probability $
u \in \mathcal A_0(F)$ of theorem 12.8.2 has a density $a$ satisfying \[  
u =a\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad \| a\| _{L^ q(\mathrm{d}V)}\leq C_{R,q}.  \] If $v_-(\omega )>0$, this holds also for $q=n/(n-1)$. Proof. Recall that $M(F)=\exp (-B_0(F)/n)$, and represent $
u $ by a maximizing current $T\in \mathscr M(F)$, using theorem 12.8.2 . Since $\Gamma _ F(T)=\mathrm{e}^{F/n}\Gamma _0(T)$ and $B_0$ is $1$-Lipschitz, \[  
u = rac{\mathrm{e}^{F/n}k_ T}{M(F)}\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad M(F)\geq \mathrm{e}^{-R/n}M(0)>0.  \] Theorem 12.9.1 therefore gives the subcritical bound with constant $\mathrm{e}^{2R/n}M(0)^{-1}C_ q$. When $v_-(\omega )>0$, the same argument with the endpoint constant $v_-(\omega )^{-1/n}$ of theorem 12.9.2 gives the case $q=n/(n-1)$. $\square$

title: 12.9.4 Uniform bounds near a smooth density
search_title: Uniform bounds near a smooth density

The endpoint estimate can fail for the family of all tests while the maximizing tests for a family of densities remain uniformly controlled. For smooth densities close in $C^{2,\alpha }$ to the normalized volume form $\omega ^ n/\int _ X\omega ^ n$ of the background, a fixed-point argument keeps the solution forms close to $\omega $ and their Gauduchon factors close to that of $\omega $. This gives uniform bounds for both the determinant density of the maximizing current and the density of the supporting probability. In this subsection we assume $n\geq 3$ and fix $0<\alpha <1$. All Hölder norms are defined using a fixed finite atlas and fixed smooth connections. Put \[  H= rac{\omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V},\qquad V=\int _ X\omega ^ n,\qquad F_*=\log (H/V).  \] Thus $\mathrm{e}^{F_*}\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^ n/V$ is a probability measure. By theorem 11.4.2 , there is a unique smooth positive function $\chi _0$, the normalized Gauduchon factor of $\omega $, such that \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi _0\omega ^{n-1})=0,\qquad \int _ X\chi _0\omega ^ n=1.  \] Write $m=\min _ X\chi _0$, $a=\max _ X\chi _0$ and $C_0=\| \chi _0\| _{C^{2,\alpha }}$. We first specify the constants that determine the size of the neighborhood. For a smooth positive $(1,1)$-form $\Omega $, set \[  L_\omega v= rac{n\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\wedge \omega ^{n-1}}{\omega ^ n}, \qquad A_\Omega \eta = rac{\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\eta \Omega ^{n-1})}{\mathrm{d}V}.  \] The compatibility argument of proposition 11.23.2 , proposition 14.4.1 shows that \[  \mathcal L(v,c)=L_\omega v-c, \qquad \int _ Xv\, \mathrm{d}V=0,  \] is an isomorphism from the space of pairs $(v,c)\in C^{4,\alpha }	imes \mathbb R$ with this normalization onto $C^{2,\alpha }$. Let $K\geq 1$ bound its inverse for the norm $\| v\| _{C^{4,\alpha }}+|c|$. The formal adjoint of $A_\omega $ with respect to $\mathrm{d}V$ is $(H/n)L_\omega $, whose kernel consists of the constants and whose index is zero. Consequently $A_\omega $ has kernel $\mathbb R\chi _0$ and range \[  Z_0=\left\{ g\in C^{0,\alpha }:\int _ Xg\, \mathrm{d}V=0ight\} .  \] Its restriction to \[  E_\chi =\left\{ \eta \in C^{2,\alpha }:\int _ X\eta \omega ^ n=0ight\}   \] has a bounded inverse $\mathcal R:Z_0	o E_\chi $. Fix $G\geq 1$ bounding this inverse. We normalize the Hölder norms of forms and of endomorphism fields so that they dominate pointwise operator norms and are submultiplicative under composition of endomorphisms; the subscript $\mathrm{alg}$ below refers to this norm on endomorphism fields. Choose $D\geq 1$ so that \[  \| \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\| _{C^{2,\alpha }}\leq D\| v\| _{C^{4,\alpha }},\qquad \| \omega ^{-1}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\| _{C^{2,\alpha },\mathrm{alg}} \leq D\| v\| _{C^{4,\alpha }}.  \] Let $C_{\mathrm{tr}}\geq 1$ be a bound for the trace map on endomorphism fields, and put $Q=2C_{\mathrm{tr}}D^2$. Expanding $\Omega ^{n-1}-\omega ^{n-1}$ gives a constant $C_ A\geq 1$ such that \[  \| A_\Omega -A_\omega \| _{C^{2,\alpha }	o C^{0,\alpha }} \leq C_ A\| \Omega -\omega \| _{C^{2,\alpha }} \quad 	ext{if }\| \Omega -\omega \| _{C^{2,\alpha }}\leq 1.  \] Only two derivatives of $\Omega $ enter this polynomial estimate. Define A7F3B3DF78D5 12.9.5  egin{equation}  r=\min \left\{  rac1{2D}, rac1{4KQ},  rac{m}{4GC_ ADC_0}ight\} , \qquad \varepsilon = rac r{2K}. \end{equation} These constants depend only on $\omega $, $\mathrm{d}V$, $\alpha $ and the chosen norms. Lemma 12.9.6 . 9F57BA26805A Let $F$ be smooth with $\| F-F_*\| _{C^{2,\alpha }}\leq \varepsilon $. The solution form $\Omega _ F=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ F$ of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_ F)=\mathrm{e}^{B_0(F)+F}\mathrm{d}V$ and its Gauduchon factor $\chi _ F$, normalized as below, satisfy  egin{gather*}  	frac 12\omega \leq \Omega _ F\leq 	frac 32\omega , \qquad  rac m2\leq \chi _ F\leq  rac{3a}2,\  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi _ F\Omega _ F^{n-1})=0, \qquad \int _ X\chi _ F\omega ^ n=1. \end{gather*} The potential can be normalized by $\int _ Xu_ F\, \mathrm{d}V=0$ with $\| u_ F\| _{C^{4,\alpha }}+|B_0(F)-\log V|\leq r$. Its fixed point obeys \[  \| \eta \| _{C^{2,\alpha }} \leq  rac{\kappa C_0}{1-\kappa } \leq 2\kappa C_0\leq m/2.  \] Since $A_\omega \chi _0=0$ and $A_\omega \mathcal R$ is the identity on $Z_0$, the function $\chi _ F=\chi _0+\eta $ satisfies $A_{\Omega _ F}\chi _ F=0$, and it has the stated normalization and bounds. Elliptic regularity makes it smooth. Every Gauduchon factor of $\Omega _ F$ with the same normalization satisfies the same affine fixed-point equation, so this factor is the one given by theorem 11.4.2 . $\square$ Theorem 12.9.7 . 6A30AAE398CD For every smooth $F$ in the ball of lemma 12.9.6 , let $T_ F$ be the maximizing current of theorem 12.7.3 and $
u _ F$ the supporting probability of $B_0$ at $F$; both are unique. With \[  H_{\max }=\max _ XH,\qquad C_

u _ F=q_ F\, \mathrm{d}V,\qquad \| q_ F\| _{L^\infty }\leq C_
u ,\qquad \| k_{T_ F}\| _{L^\infty }\leq C_ k.  \] In particular, for $p=n/(n-1)$, \[  \| q_ F\| _{L^ p}\leq C_
u ^{1/n},\qquad \| k_{T_ F}\| _{L^ p}\leq C_ k.  \] The constants do not involve $v_-(\omega )$; in particular, these bounds hold also when $v_-(\omega )=0$. Proof. Set $\Omega =\Omega _ F$, $\chi =\chi _ F$ and \[  Z=\int _ X\chi \omega \wedge \Omega ^{n-1}.  \] The form comparison and $\int _ X\chi \omega ^ n=1$ give 8926A66CEBEF 12.9.8  egin{equation}  2^{-(n-1)}\leq Z\leq (3/2)^{n-1}. \end{equation} Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi \Omega ^{n-1})=0$, Stokes' theorem also gives $Z=\int _ X\chi \Omega ^ n$. u _ F=\Omega \wedge T_ F$, and hence CED2026424BD 12.9.9  egin{equation}   egin{aligned}  T_ F& = rac\chi Z\Omega ^{n-1},\  
u _ F& =\Omega \wedge T_ F= rac\chi Z\Omega ^ n,\  q_ F& = rac\chi Z rac{\Omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V},\  k_{T_ F}& = rac\chi Z \left( rac{\Omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V}ight)^{(n-1)/n}. \end{aligned} \end{equation} The last identity uses the positive root $\gamma =(\chi /Z)^{1/(n-1)}\Omega $, for which $T_ F=\gamma ^{n-1}$. Uniqueness of the supporting probability follows from theorem 12.8.2 . Now $\chi /Z\leq (3a/2)2^{n-1}$ and $\Omega ^ n/\mathrm{d}V\leq (3/2)^ nH_{\max }$, and multiplying gives exactly $q_ F\leq C_
u $ and $k_{T_ F}\leq C_ k$. Since $\int _ Xq_ F\, \mathrm{d}V=1$, we have $\int _ Xq_ F^ p\, \mathrm{d}V\leq C_
u ^{p-1}$, which gives the sharper $L^ p$ estimate for $q_ F$. It also contains a smooth path of such data whose maximizing currents are pairwise distinct. Proof. For a small smooth function $f$, put \[  F(f)=F_*+f-\log \int _ X\mathrm{e}^{F_*+f}\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] If $F(f)=F(g)$, then $f-g$ is constant, so the map $f\mapsto F(f)$ is injective on functions of zero $\mathrm{d}V$-mean. By its continuity in $C^{2,\alpha }$, it maps a sufficiently small neighborhood of zero in any fixed finite-dimensional space of such smooth functions into the ball, and these spaces can have arbitrary dimension. For the path, choose a smooth real $\psi $ of zero $\mathrm{d}V$-mean whose complex Hessian at some point $x_0$ has, in an $\omega $-unitary frame, a matrix $Q_0$ that is not a multiple of the identity. A cutoff of $|z_1|^2-|z_2|^2$ in local coordinates, minus its mean, is such a function. For small real $t$ put \[  \Omega _ t=\omega +t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi ,\qquad V_ t=\int _ X\Omega _ t^ n,\qquad F_ t=\log  rac{\Omega _ t^ n}{V_ t\, \mathrm{d}V}.  \] These normalized data tend to $F_*$ in $C^{2,\alpha }$ as $t	o 0$, and by uniqueness in theorem 14.2.1 their solution forms are the forms $\Omega _ t$. If $F_ s=F_ t$, then $\log (\Omega _ s^ n/\Omega _ t^ n)$ is the constant $\log (V_ s/V_ t)$. The signs of the complex Hessian of $(s-t)\psi $ at a maximum and at a minimum force this constant to be zero. Integrating the derivative of $\log \det $ along the segment between $\Omega _ t$ and $\Omega _ s$ then gives a uniformly elliptic equation for $(s-t)\psi $ without zeroth-order term, and the maximum principle forces $(s-t)\psi $ to be constant. Since $\psi $ is not constant, $s=t$. If the maximizing currents for $F_ s$ and $F_ t$ agree, ( 12.9.9 ) makes $\Omega _ s^{n-1}$ and $\Omega _ t^{n-1}$ proportional at $x_0$. Positive cofactor matrices determine positive forms up to scale, so $I+sQ_0$ and $I+tQ_0$ are proportional. Since $I$ and $Q_0$ are linearly independent, comparing coefficients gives $s=t$. $\square$ The small $C^{2,\alpha }$ neighborhood gives a condition directly on the prescribed density. The next estimate instead assumes uniform bounds for the solution forms and covers a larger smooth family without derivative bounds on its densities. The question for arbitrary bounded families of continuous densities remains open when $v_-(\omega )=0$. The concentrating sequences of proposition 12.18.2 consist of near-maximizers, so these estimates do not apply to them.

The signs of the complex Hessian of $(s-t)\psi $ at a maximum and at a minimum force this constant to be zero. Integrating the derivative of $\log \det $ along the segment between $\Omega _ t$ and $\Omega _ s$ then gives a uniformly elliptic equation for $(s-t)\psi $ without zeroth-order term, and the maximum principle forces $(s-t)\psi $ to be constant. Since $\psi $ is not constant, $s=t$. If the maximizing currents for $F_ s$ and $F_ t$ agree, ( 12.9.9 ) makes $\Omega _ s^{n-1}$ and $\Omega _ t^{n-1}$ proportional at $x_0$. Positive cofactor matrices determine positive forms up to scale, so $I+sQ_0$ and $I+tQ_0$ are proportional. Since $I$ and $Q_0$ are linearly independent, comparing coefficients gives $s=t$. $\square$

title: 12.9.11 Uniformly controlled complex Hessians
text:
The preceding construction bounds the solution form and its Gauduchon factor by controlling derivatives of the logarithmic density. A bound on the solution form itself leads to a different estimate. If $\Omega =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$, then $d\Omega =d\omega $, so the divergence of its cofactor depends only on the fixed torsion and the size of $\Omega $. This permits uniform bounds for the factor even when derivatives of the varying complex Hessian are unbounded. We continue to assume $n\geq 3$ and that $\mathrm{d}V$ is a probability volume form. We first give the real elliptic estimate used below. A cube denoted by $tQ$ has the same center as $Q$ and $t$ times its side length, and $ int _ Q$ denotes its Euclidean average. Lemma 12.9.12 . F7130F1BDC30 Let $Q\subset \mathbb R^ m$, $m>2$, be a cube. Suppose that $u$ is a smooth strictly positive solution on a neighborhood of $3Q$ of \[  \operatorname {div}(A
abla u+Bu)=0, \qquad \lambda I\leq A\leq \Lambda I,\qquad |B|\leq K,  \] where $A$ is a smooth symmetric matrix field and $B$ is a smooth vector field. Their total measure is at most $|Q|/a$. The parent of each selected cube has average at most $aK_0$, hence $|f_ S-f_ Q|\leq 2^ maK_0$. Outside their union, differentiation of dyadic averages gives $|f-f_ Q|\leq aK_0$ almost everywhere. Repeat this selection inside each chosen cube, subtracting its own mean. For every smooth real $v$ with \[  \delta \omega \leq \Omega _ v:=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\leq \Lambda \omega ,  \] let $ho _ v$ be its Gauduchon factor normalized by \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(ho _ v\Omega _ v^{n-1})=0, \qquad \int _ Xho _ v\, \mathrm{d}V=1.  \] There is $C_ H\geq 1$, depending only on $X,\omega ,\mathrm{d}V,\delta ,\Lambda $, such that $C_ H^{-1}\leq ho _ v\leq C_ H$ on $X$ for every such $v$. Proof. Existence and uniqueness of $ho _ v$ follow from theorem 11.4.2 . Fix a real reference metric on $X$, and put $Q_ v=\Omega _ v^{n-1}$ and $J_ v=\Omega _ v^ n/\mathrm{d}V$. Since $d\Omega _ v=d\omega $, 82DFE47055F1 12.9.16  egin{equation}  dQ_ v=(n-1)d\omega \wedge \Omega _ v^{n-2}. \end{equation} Both $Q_ v$ and $dQ_ v$ have uniformly bounded coefficients in fixed charts. The normalization and $\mathrm{d}V(X)=1$ imply the claimed two-sided bound. $\square$ For a fixed $0<\varepsilon <1$, consider the full family BB82503DF712 12.9.17  egin{equation}  \mathcal V_\varepsilon = \{ v\in C^\infty (X,\mathbb R):\sup _ Xv=0, -\varepsilon \omega \leq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\leq \varepsilon \omega \} . \end{equation} Set $c_ v=\int _ X\Omega _ v^ n$ and $F_ v=\log (J_ v/c_ v)$, so that $\int _ X\mathrm e^{F_ v}\mathrm{d}V=1$. AD62F7DA0E68 Let \[  j_-=(1-\varepsilon )^ n\min _ X rac{\omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V}, \qquad j_+=(1+\varepsilon )^ n\max _ X rac{\omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V},  \] and take $C_ H$ from proposition 12.9.15 with $\delta =1-\varepsilon $ and $\Lambda =1+\varepsilon $. u _{T_ v,F_ v}/\mathrm{d}V$ satisfy FEAB45A97679 12.9.19  egin{equation}   rac{j_-}{C_ Hj_+}\leq r_ v\leq  rac{C_ Hj_+}{j_-}, \qquad j_+^{-1/n} rac{j_-}{C_ Hj_+} \leq k_{T_ v}\leq j_-^{-1/n} rac{C_ Hj_+}{j_-}. \end{equation} In particular both densities are uniformly bounded at the critical exponent $n/(n-1)$, without an assumption on the lower mass. Use the normalization of proposition 12.9.15 and put \[  N_ v=\int _ XJ_ vho _ v\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad T_ v= rac{ho _ v}{N_ v}\Omega _ v^{n-1}.  \] The factor equation and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-Stokes give \[  \int _ X\omega \wedge ho _ v\Omega _ v^{n-1} =\int _ X\Omega _ v\wedge ho _ v\Omega _ v^{n-1}=N_ v.  \] Hence $T_ v\in \mathscr G_\omega $. CAEF64468276 For every fixed $0<\varepsilon <1$, there are $v_ j\in \mathcal V_\varepsilon $ with $\| v_ j\| _{C^0}	o 0$ such that their normalized densities $F_{v_ j}$ are pairwise distinct, bounded in $C^0$, and unbounded in $C^1$. Choose holomorphic coordinates centered at a point $p$, put $x=\operatorname {Re}z_1$, and take a smooth real cutoff $\zeta $ supported in the chart and equal to one near $p$. Thus a fixed $C>0$ bounds the operator norm of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j$ relative to $\omega $ by $aC$ for every $j\geq 1$. Choose $a$ so small that $aC\leq \varepsilon /2$. Then $v_ j\in \mathcal V_\varepsilon $, and $\| v_ j\| _{C^0}\leq 2a/j^2$. Write $s=\operatorname {tr}_{\omega (p)} eta >0$. Hence the densities are pairwise distinct and their $C^1$ norms are unbounded. Their uniform $C^0$ bound is part of theorem 12.9.18 . To check failure of equicontinuity, take points $p_ j^\pm $ with $x=\pm \pi /(2j)$ and all other real coordinates zero. For large $j$ they lie where $\zeta =1$, and $\Omega _{v_ j}(p_ j^\pm )=\omega (p_ j^\pm )\mp a eta $. The integral normalizing $F_{v_ j}$ cancels from the difference, so \[  F_{v_ j}(p_ j^-)-F_{v_ j}(p_ j^+) \longrightarrow \log  rac{1+as}{1-as}>0.  \] Indeed, $ eta ^2=0$ gives $(\omega (p)\pm a eta )^ n=(1\pm as)\omega (p)^ n$, and $as<1$ by the chosen form comparison. Both points tend to $p$, which proves the failure of equicontinuity. The exact-adjoint bounds still apply because the entire sequence lies in $\mathcal V_\varepsilon $. $\square$ The same estimate applies to the family with $\delta \omega \leq \Omega _ v\leq \Lambda \omega $ by replacing $j_-$ and $j_+$ with $\delta ^ n\min _ X(\omega ^ n/\mathrm{d}V)$ and $\Lambda ^ n\max _ X(\omega ^ n/\mathrm{d}V)$. Applying the estimate to a prescribed family of densities requires uniformly comparable solution forms. Thus this construction provides critical estimates when $v_-(\omega )=0$ for a larger smooth family, but leaves the question for arbitrary bounded families of continuous densities open.
