title: Proposition 12.9.15
text: Proposition 12.9.15 . 9D81484FC945 Fix $0<\delta \leq \Lambda $. For every smooth real $v$ with \[  \delta \omega \leq \Omega _ v:=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\leq \Lambda \omega ,  \] let $\rho _ v$ be its Gauduchon factor normalized by \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\rho _ v\Omega _ v^{n-1})=0, \qquad \int _ X\rho _ v\, \mathrm{d}V=1.  \] There is $C_ H\geq 1$, depending only on $X,\omega ,\mathrm{d}V,\delta ,\Lambda $, such that $C_ H^{-1}\leq \rho _ v\leq C_ H$ on $X$ for every such $v$. Proof. Existence and uniqueness of $\rho _ v$ follow from theorem 11.4.2 . Fix a real reference metric on $X$, and put $Q_ v=\Omega _ v^{n-1}$ and $J_ v=\Omega _ v^ n/\mathrm{d}V$. Since $d\Omega _ v=d\omega $, 82DFE47055F1 12.9.16 \begin{equation}  dQ_ v=(n-1)d\omega \wedge \Omega _ v^{n-2}. \end{equation} Both $Q_ v$ and $dQ_ v$ have uniformly bounded coefficients in fixed charts. Define a real tensor $A_ v$ and vector field $b_ v$ by \[  \langle A_ vd\phi ,d\psi \rangle \, \mathrm{d}V =n\, d\psi \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi \wedge Q_ v, \qquad (b_ v\cdot d\phi )\, \mathrm{d}V =-n\, \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi \wedge dQ_ v.  \] Only the $(1,1)$ part of $d\psi \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\phi $ contributes to the first identity; it is \[  \frac{\mathrm i}{4\pi } (\partial \psi \wedge \bar\partial \phi +\partial \phi \wedge \bar\partial \psi ).  \] Thus $A_ v$ is symmetric and uniformly positive definite, with a uniform upper bound. text: Theorem 12.9.18 . AD62F7DA0E68 Let \[  j_-=(1-\varepsilon )^ n\min _ X\frac{\omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V}, \qquad j_+=(1+\varepsilon )^ n\max _ X\frac{\omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V},  \] and take $C_ H$ from proposition 12.9.15 with $\delta =1-\varepsilon $ and $\Lambda =1+\varepsilon $. For every $v\in \mathcal V_\varepsilon $, the exact maximizing current $T_ v\in \mathscr G_\omega $ for $F_ v$ is unique. Its determinant density $k_{T_ v}$ and the probability density $r_ v=\mathrm d\nu _{T_ v,F_ v}/\mathrm{d}V$ satisfy FEAB45A97679 12.9.19 \begin{equation}  \frac{j_-}{C_ Hj_+}\leq r_ v\leq \frac{C_ Hj_+}{j_-}, \qquad j_+^{-1/n}\frac{j_-}{C_ Hj_+} \leq k_{T_ v}\leq j_-^{-1/n}\frac{C_ Hj_+}{j_-}. \end{equation} In particular both densities are uniformly bounded at the critical exponent $n/(n-1)$, without an assumption on the lower mass. Moreover, \[  \| F_ v-F_0\| _\infty \leq n\log \frac{1+\varepsilon }{1-\varepsilon },  \] and this normalized family contains infinitely many distinct nonconstant densities on the fixed manifold $X$. Proof. Use the normalization of proposition 12.9.15 and put \[  N_ v=\int _ XJ_ v\rho _ v\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad T_ v=\frac{\rho _ v}{N_ v}\Omega _ v^{n-1}.  \] The factor equation and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-Stokes give \[  \int _ X\omega \wedge \rho _ v\Omega _ v^{n-1} =\int _ X\Omega _ v\wedge \rho _ v\Omega _ v^{n-1}=N_ v.  \] Hence $T_ v\in \mathscr G_\omega $. It is the $(n-1)$st power of the Gauduchon metric $\gamma _ v=(\rho _ v/N_ v)^{1/(n-1)}\Omega _ v$. The equation $\Omega _ v^ n=c_ v\mathrm e^{F_ v}\mathrm{d}V$ gives $B_0(F_ v)=\log c_ v$. Thus theorem 12.7.3 identifies $T_ v$ as the unique exact maximizer, and $M(F_ v)=c_ v^{-1/n}$. The determinant and probability normalizations are therefore 2B0B40A18948 12.9.20 \begin{equation}  k_{T_ v}=\frac{\rho _ v}{N_ v}J_ v^{(n-1)/n}, \qquad \Gamma _{F_ v}(T_ v)=c_ v^{-1/n}\frac{J_ v\rho _ v}{N_ v}\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad r_ v=\frac{J_ v\rho _ v}{N_ v}. \end{equation} Here $j_-\leq J_ v\leq j_+$ and, since $\int _ X\rho _ v\, \mathrm{d}V=1$, also $j_-\leq N_ v\leq j_+$. The factor bound gives the first pair of inequalities in ( 12.9.19 ); the identity $k_{T_ v}=J_ v^{-1/n}r_ v$ gives the second. The critical norms are bounded by the respective upper constants because $\mathrm{d}V$ is a probability volume. The inequalities \[  (1-\varepsilon )^ n\leq \frac{J_ v}{J_0}\leq (1+\varepsilon )^ n, \qquad (1-\varepsilon )^ n\leq \frac{c_ v}{c_0}\leq (1+\varepsilon )^ n  \] give the bound for $F_ v-F_0$ by subtracting logarithms. To prove nontriviality, choose a nonconstant smooth real $\phi $. For small $t$, the potential $t\phi -\sup _ X(t\phi )$ belongs to $\mathcal V_\varepsilon $ and gives the same density as $t\phi $. Differentiation at zero gives \[  \left.\frac{d}{dt}F_{t\phi }\right|_{t=0} =L_\omega \phi - \frac{\int _ XJ_0L_\omega \phi \, \mathrm{d}V}{\int _ XJ_0\, \mathrm{d}V}.  \] This function is nonconstant: otherwise $L_\omega \phi $ would be constant, its values at a maximum and a minimum would force that constant to be zero, and the strong maximum principle would make $\phi $ constant. Choose two points where the displayed derivative differs. The difference of the densities at these points is strictly monotone for $t$ in a small interval. These give infinitely many distinct densities, with at most one parameter having equal values at the chosen points. Discarding that parameter gives the nonconstant family. $\square$

title: Example 12.9.21
text: Example 12.9.21 . CAEF64468276 For every fixed $0<\varepsilon <1$, there are $v_ j\in \mathcal V_\varepsilon $ with $\| v_ j\| _{C^0}\to 0$ such that their normalized densities $F_{v_ j}$ are pairwise distinct, bounded in $C^0$, and unbounded in $C^1$. This family is not equicontinuous. Nevertheless, both densities of its exact maximizers satisfy the uniform bounds of theorem 12.9.18 . Proof. Choose holomorphic coordinates centered at a point $p$, put $x=\operatorname {Re}z_1$, and take a smooth real cutoff $\zeta $ supported in the chart and equal to one near $p$. We may assume $0\leq \zeta \leq 1$. On the chart set \[  \beta =dx\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}x=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(x^2/2) =\frac{\mathrm i}{8\pi }dz_1\wedge d\bar z_1.  \] This is a nonzero semipositive form of rank one. For a constant $a>0$ to be chosen, extend \[  w_ j=\frac a{j^2}\zeta \sin (jx)  \] by zero outside the chart, and put $v_ j=w_ j-\sup _ Xw_ j$. The product rule gives \begin{align*}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j={}& -a\zeta \sin (jx)\beta +\frac aj\cos (jx) (d\zeta \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}x+dx\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\zeta )\\ & +\frac a{j^2}\sin (jx)\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\zeta . \end{align*} All fixed forms in this expression have compact support after multiplication by the indicated cutoff or its derivatives. Thus a fixed $C>0$ bounds the operator norm of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j$ relative to $\omega $ by $aC$ for every $j\geq 1$. Choose $a$ so small that $aC\leq \varepsilon /2$. Then $v_ j\in \mathcal V_\varepsilon $, and $\| v_ j\| _{C^0}\leq 2a/j^2$. Write $s=\operatorname {tr}_{\omega (p)}\beta >0$. Since $x(p)=0$ and $\zeta =1$ near $p$, we have $\Omega _{v_ j}(p)=\omega (p)$ and \[  \partial _ x\Omega _{v_ j}(p)=\partial _ x\omega (p)-aj\beta .  \] Differentiating the logarithmic determinant, and observing that its normalizing integral is constant in the spatial variable, gives the exact identity \[  \partial _ xF_{v_ j}(p) =\partial _ x\log \frac{\omega ^ n}{\mathrm{d}V}(p)-ajs.  \] These derivatives are pairwise different and their absolute values tend to infinity. Hence the densities are pairwise distinct and their $C^1$ norms are unbounded. Their uniform $C^0$ bound is part of theorem 12.9.18 . To check failure of equicontinuity, take points $p_ j^\pm $ with $x=\pm \pi /(2j)$ and all other real coordinates zero. For large $j$ they lie where $\zeta =1$, and $\Omega _{v_ j}(p_ j^\pm )=\omega (p_ j^\pm )\mp a\beta $. The integral normalizing $F_{v_ j}$ cancels from the difference, so \[  F_{v_ j}(p_ j^-)-F_{v_ j}(p_ j^+) \longrightarrow \log \frac{1+as}{1-as}>0.  \] Indeed, $\beta ^2=0$ gives $(\omega (p)\pm a\beta )^ n=(1\pm as)\omega (p)^ n$, and $as<1$ by the chosen form comparison. Both points tend to $p$, which proves the failure of equicontinuity. The exact-adjoint bounds still apply because the entire sequence lies in $\mathcal V_\varepsilon $. $\square$

title: 12.10 Integrable densities in the compact Gauduchon problem

section: 12.10 Integrable densities in the compact Gauduchon problem
text: We keep the Hermitian background $\omega $ and replace the continuous logarithmic density by an integrable density. For an unbounded density, weak compactness of the test currents alone does not pass the determinant integral to the limit; uniform control of the weighted tails provides the missing upper semicontinuity. We use the following notation from section 15.28 , section 15.29 , with $\omega $ in place of $h$. For a nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, the subsolution threshold $b_\omega (f)\geq 0$ is, by theorem 15.28.4 , the largest $b\geq 0$ for which some $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$. For $p\in L^ n$, the root norm is $\rho _\omega (p)=b_\omega (|p|^ n)^{-1/n}$ if $p\ne 0$, and $\rho _\omega (0)=0$. The space $\mathcal D_\omega $ of proposition 15.32.5 consists of the $p\in L^ n$ with $\rho _\omega (p)<+\infty $, and $\mathcal D_\omega ^0$ is the closure of the bounded functions in $\mathcal D_\omega $, characterized by vanishing tails in proposition 15.32.9 . For a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, $L_{\omega ,\gamma }(p)$ denotes the test quotient of section 15.29 , and theorem 15.29.1 gives $\rho _\omega (p)=\sup _\gamma L_{\omega ,\gamma }(|p|)$. Finally, $k_ T$ is the determinant density of $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ from theorem 12.9.1 . If $p\geq 0$ is measurable, define \[  D_ p(T)=\int _ Xp k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V\qquad (T\in \mathscr G_\omega ),  \] allowing the value $+\infty $. If $T=\gamma ^{n-1}/\int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ for a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, then $D_ p(T)=L_{\omega ,\gamma }(p)$. Theorem 12.10.1 . 41D17749328B For every nonnegative $p\in L^ n$, 025E3287544B 12.10.2 \begin{equation}  \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_\omega }D_ p(T)=\rho _\omega (p), \end{equation} with the value $+\infty $ allowed. If $p\in \mathcal D_\omega ^0$, the functional $D_ p$ is finite, concave and weakly upper semicontinuous on $\mathscr G_\omega $, its maximum is attained, and the densities $p k_ T$, for $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $, are uniformly integrable. Proof. For a smooth strictly positive $p$, we have $D_ p=\mathfrak D_{n\log p}$ and $\mathrm{e}^{-B_0(n\log p)/n}=\rho _\omega (p)$, so theorem 12.7.3 , applied to $F=n\log p$, proves ( 12.10.2 ). By Hölder's inequality and theorem 12.9.1 , for every real $r>n$ there is a constant $C_ r$ such that, for every $q\in L^ r$, B5DC9A4ABEEC 12.10.3 \begin{equation}  \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_\omega }\int _ X|q| k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V \leq C_ r\| q\| _{L^ r}. \end{equation} Next, approximate a bounded nonnegative $p$ in $L^{2n}$ by smooth strictly positive functions. This estimate and ( 15.32.8 ) give uniform convergence on $\mathscr G_\omega $ of the corresponding functionals $D$ and convergence of the root norms, so the supremum formula holds for bounded $p$. For such $p$, the functional $D_ p$ is also upper semicontinuous and concave, by lemma 12.7.2 and uniform convergence. For general $p\in L^ n$, we use the truncations $\min (p,K)$ at positive integer levels $K$. Monotone convergence and the definition of $b_\omega $ through truncations give \[  \sup _ T D_ p(T)=\sup _ T\sup _ K D_{\min (p,K)}(T) =\sup _ K\rho _\omega (\min (p,K))=\rho _\omega (p).  \] This step only interchanges two suprema and gives no attainment. Now suppose $p\in \mathcal D_\omega ^0$. The supremum formula applied to the tail gives \[  0\leq D_ p(T)-D_{\min (p,K)}(T) \leq \rho _\omega (p\mathbf1_{\{ p>K\} })\longrightarrow 0  \] uniformly in $T$, by proposition 15.32.9 . Hence $D_ p$ is finite and is a uniform limit of upper semicontinuous concave functionals, and compactness of $\mathscr G_\omega $ gives a maximizer. Finally, fix $1<q<n/(n-1)$. By Hölder's inequality and theorem 12.9.1 , for every measurable set $E$, \[  \sup _ T\int _ Ep k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \rho _\omega (p\mathbf1_{\{ p>K\} }) +K C_ q\, \mathrm{d}V(E)^{1-1/q}.  \] Choosing first $K$ large and then the volume of $E$ small proves uniform absolute continuity. Since the total masses are bounded by $\rho _\omega (p)$, the densities are uniformly integrable. $\square$ For a nonzero density, a maximizing current gives a supporting probability for the threshold, as we show below. Whether the threshold is attained by an exact equation depends on the regularity of the maximizing current, which enters through the trace inequalities of 12.10.10 .

title: 12.10.4 The tail condition and perturbations of the density

section: 12.10 Integrable densities in the compact Gauduchon problem
text: Vanishing tails are equivalent to continuity of the threshold under uniformly bounded multiplicative perturbations of the density that converge in measure. This explains the role of the tail condition: if it fails, a perturbation supported on sets of shrinking volume can lower the threshold by a fixed factor. Proposition 12.10.5 . 249445C21482 Let $0\leq p\in \mathcal D_\omega $ be nonzero. The following are equivalent: $p\in \mathcal D_\omega ^0$; the densities $p k_ T$, for $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $, are uniformly integrable; whenever $F_ j$ are smooth real functions, uniformly bounded and tending to zero in measure, one has \[  b_\omega (\mathrm{e}^{F_ j}p^ n)\longrightarrow b_\omega (p^ n).  \] If the first condition holds, the convergence in the third also holds for bounded measurable $F_ j$ with the same uniform bound and convergence in measure. If it fails, there are smooth $F_ j\geq 0$, uniformly bounded and tending to zero in measure, such that \[  \mathrm{e}^{F_ j}p^ n\longrightarrow p^ n\quad \text{in }L^1, \qquad b_\omega (\mathrm{e}^{F_ j}p^ n)\leq 2^{-n}b_\omega (p^ n).  \] Proof. The first condition implies the second by theorem 12.10.1 . Conversely, $\mathrm{d}V(\{ p>K\} )\to 0$ as $K\to \infty $, so uniform integrability and ( 12.10.2 ) give \[  \rho _\omega (p\mathbf1_{\{ p>K\} }) =\sup _{T\in \mathscr G_\omega }\int _{\{ p>K\} }p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V \longrightarrow 0.  \] This is the first condition by proposition 15.32.9 . If $p\in \mathcal D_\omega ^0$ and $|F_ j|\leq A$, then $p(\mathrm{e}^{F_ j/n}-1)$ tends to zero in measure and its absolute value is at most $(\mathrm{e}^{A/n}+1)p$. The dominated-convergence criterion of proposition 15.32.9 makes its root norm tend to zero, and the triangle inequality gives $\rho _\omega (p\mathrm{e}^{F_ j/n})\to \rho _\omega (p)>0$. Taking negative $n$th powers proves the third condition, also for bounded measurable $F_ j$. Suppose now that the tails do not tend to zero, and put $R=\rho _\omega (p)>0$. The formula of theorem 15.29.1 , which uses only smooth tests, yields $\delta >0$, numbers $K_ j\to \infty $ and smooth strictly positive $T_ j\in \mathscr G_\omega $ such that \[  \int _{\{ p>K_ j\} }p k_{T_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V>\delta .  \] Since the finite measure $p k_{T_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V$ is regular, we can choose a compact set $C_ j\subset \{ p>K_ j\} $ of mass greater than $\delta /2$ for this measure. By outer regularity of $\mathrm{d}V$, choose an open set $O_ j\supset \{ p>K_ j\} $ with $\mathrm{d}V(O_ j)\leq \mathrm{d}V(\{ p>K_ j\} )+1/j$, and a smooth cutoff $0\leq \chi _ j\leq 1$ that equals one on $C_ j$ and has support in $O_ j$. Fix $A>0$ with $\mathrm{e}^{A/n}\delta /2>2R$, and set $F_ j=A\chi _ j$. Then $F_ j\to 0$ in measure, while \[  \rho _\omega (p\mathrm{e}^{F_ j/n}) \geq \int _ Xp\mathrm{e}^{F_ j/n}k_{T_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V >2R.  \] Since $b_\omega (\mathrm{e}^{F_ j}p^ n)=\rho _\omega (p\mathrm{e}^{F_ j/n})^{-n}$, this gives the asserted uniform gap. Finally, $|\mathrm{e}^{F_ j}-1|p^ n\leq (\mathrm{e}^ A-1)p^ n\mathbf1_{O_ j}$, whose integral tends to zero by absolute continuity of the integral. This proves the last assertion and the converse to the third condition. $\square$ For $f=p^ n$, the perturbed densities satisfy $\mathrm{e}^{-A}f\leq \mathrm{e}^{F_ j}f\leq \mathrm{e}^ Af$ with a fixed $A$, so the continuity statement concerns only such order intervals. The instability under general $L^1$ approximation in section 15.32 involves approximations without these bounds. For attainment at one density, uniform integrability along a single maximizing sequence is enough, and this weaker condition also identifies the limit of its weighted measures. Proposition 12.10.6 . B62E802ED631 Let $0\leq p\in \mathcal D_\omega $ be nonzero and put $R=\rho _\omega (p)$. Suppose $T_ j\in \mathscr G_\omega $ converge weakly to $T$ and satisfy $D_ p(T_ j)\to R$. If the densities $p k_{T_ j}$ are uniformly integrable, then \[  D_ p(T)=R,\qquad p k_{T_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V\rightharpoonup p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Consequently, a maximizing sequence for $D_ p$ with uniformly integrable densities $pk_{T_ j}$ has a maximizing current among its weak cluster limits. Proof. For positive integers $K$, put $p_ K=\min (p,K)$. Since $p$ is finite almost everywhere, uniform integrability gives \[  \varepsilon _ K:=\sup _ j\int _{\{ p>K\} }p k_{T_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V \longrightarrow 0.  \] For every nonnegative continuous function $h$, the weight $hp_ K$ is bounded and measurable, so the upper semicontinuity of $D_{hp_ K}$ proved in theorem 12.10.1 gives \[  \limsup _ j\int _ Xhp k_{T_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V \leq \int _ Xhp_ K k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V +\| h\| _\infty \varepsilon _ K.  \] Now let $K\to \infty $. For $h=1$ this yields $R\leq D_ p(T)$, and the supremum formula ( 12.10.2 ) gives the reverse inequality. If $\Lambda $ is a weak cluster limit of the measures $p k_{T_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V$, the same estimate for all nonnegative continuous $h$ gives $\Lambda \leq p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V$. Both measures have mass $R$, so they agree. Since these measures have bounded masses, they form a weakly relatively compact family, and every cluster limit has now been identified. The final assertion follows from the compactness of $\mathscr G_\omega $. $\square$

Both measures have mass $R$, so they agree. Since these measures have bounded masses, they form a weakly relatively compact family, and every cluster limit has now been identified. The final assertion follows from the compactness of $\mathscr G_\omega $. $\square$

text: Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ be nonzero with $b=b_\omega (f)>0$. Recall from section 15.28 that a threshold subsolution is a function $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$, and a threshold solution is one for which equality holds; threshold subsolutions exist by theorem 15.28.4 . A smooth Gauduchon test can be paired with the full current $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ of a threshold subsolution, and by lemma 13.14.12 the resulting trace measure is bounded below by the determinant-weighted density. The nonnegative difference has a mass that depends only on the test. Along a maximizing sequence this mass tends to zero, uniformly over all threshold subsolutions. We write $\| \cdot \| _{\mathrm{TV}}$ for the total variation of a finite signed measure. Proposition 12.10.11 . 08C2A578ACE2 Let $0\leq f\in L^1$ be nonzero and $b=b_\omega (f)>0$, and write $p=f^{1/n}$. Suppose $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)\geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V$. For every smooth strictly positive $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $, the measure \[  R_{u,T}=(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge T-b^{1/n}p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V  \] is positive and has mass \[  R_{u,T}(X)=1-b^{1/n}D_ p(T).  \] In particular, if $(T_ j)$ is a sequence of smooth strictly positive members of $\mathscr G_\omega $ with $D_ p(T_ j)\to \rho _\omega (p)$, then $\| R_{u,T_ j}\| _{\mathrm{TV}}\to 0$, uniformly over all threshold subsolutions $u$. If also $p\in \mathcal D_\omega ^0$ and $T_ j\to T$ as currents, then $T$ maximizes $D_ p$ and \[  (\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge T_ j \rightharpoonup b^{1/n}p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] In particular, for a fixed sequence $(T_ j)$ with limit $T$, this limiting probability is the same for all threshold subsolutions $u$. Proof. A smooth strictly positive $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ is $\gamma ^{n-1}$ for a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ normalized by $\int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=1$. Lemma 13.14.12 proves positivity of $R_{u,T}$, and Stokes' theorem for currents gives $((\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge T)(X)=\int _ X\omega \wedge T=1$. This proves the mass formula. Since $\rho _\omega (p)=b^{-1/n}$, the nonnegative mass tends to zero along a maximizing sequence; it equals the total variation norm and does not depend on $u$. Under the tail hypothesis, theorem 12.10.1 gives uniform integrability of the densities $p k_{T_ j}$. Thus proposition 12.10.6 makes $T$ a maximizer and gives $p k_{T_ j}\, \mathrm{d}V\rightharpoonup p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V$. Adding the error measures $R_{u,T_ j}$, which tend to zero in total variation, proves the limit formula. $\square$ The limit formula concerns smooth maximizing sequences. It does not define the product $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)\wedge T$ for a singular current $T$, nor does it show that the limit is the same for different maximizing currents. If a maximizing test is itself a smooth strictly positive form, the trace inequality becomes an equality of currents, and since $n\geq 2$ this forces an exact smooth equation. The local regularity needed for this comes from lemma 5.22.4 . Corollary 12.10.12 . F5E70269636C Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ be nonzero with $b=b_\omega (f)>0$. If $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth strictly positive maximizer $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $, then $f^{1/n}$ agrees almost everywhere with a smooth nonnegative function, and every threshold subsolution $u$ is smooth and satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u)=bf\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] In particular a smooth threshold solution exists, and any two threshold subsolutions differ by a constant. Proof. Let $u$ be any threshold subsolution; one exists by theorem 15.28.4 . Write $T=\gamma ^{n-1}$, where $\gamma $ is the smooth Gauduchon metric given by the positive $(n-1)$st root of $T$, and set \[  a=\left(\frac{bf\, \mathrm{d}V}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}.  \] Put $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. Since $T$ maximizes, the positive measure $R_{u,T}$ of proposition 12.10.11 has mass zero, which gives the equality \[  A\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=a\gamma ^ n.  \] The coefficient measures of the positive current $A$ are controlled by this trace measure, which is absolutely continuous. Thus $A$ has a matrix density that is positive semidefinite almost everywhere, with coefficients in $L^ n$ because $a\in L^ n$. For every smooth Hermitian form $\beta $, lemma 13.14.12 also gives \[  A\wedge \beta ^{n-1} \geq \left(\frac{bf\, \mathrm{d}V}{\beta ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\beta ^ n.  \] The resulting pointwise matrix inequalities hold almost everywhere, simultaneously for all positive definite matrices: on each coordinate chart, first use a countable dense family of constant positive matrices, realized on smaller charts by global smooth Hermitian forms, and then use continuity in the matrix. The variational formula for $(\det P)^{1/n}$ in the proof of lemma 12.7.2 therefore yields \[  \left(\frac{A^ n}{\gamma ^ n}\right)^{1/n}\geq a \quad \text{almost everywhere}.  \] Here $A^ n$ denotes only the determinant of the measurable coefficient matrix of $A$; no nonlinear product of currents is used. The trace equality gives the reverse inequality, by the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality. Equality then forces all eigenvalues of $A$ relative to $\gamma $ to equal $a$, also where $a=0$. Consequently $A=a\gamma $ as currents. By lemma 5.22.4 , applied with $\theta =\omega $, both $a$ and $u$ are smooth, and $f^{1/n}=b^{-1/n}a(\gamma ^ n/\mathrm{d}V)^{1/n}$ has a smooth nonnegative representative. Since $u$ is smooth, we may now take the top power: $(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=a^ n\gamma ^ n=bf\, \mathrm{d}V$. Finally, the function $a$ was defined from $f$, $b$ and $\gamma $ alone, so two threshold subsolutions $u_1,u_2$ satisfy $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1=a\gamma =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2$. Their smooth difference is therefore pluriharmonic, hence constant on the connected compact manifold $X$. $\square$ If $f$ is smooth and strictly positive, theorem 12.2.3 provides a smooth strictly positive maximizing Gauduchon form, obtained from the smooth equation. The corollary therefore applies, and shows in particular that all threshold subsolutions, bounded or not, differ from the smooth solution by constants. Corollary 12.10.13 . 2C73D81273C0 Under the hypotheses of corollary 12.10.12 , let $u$ be the threshold solution with $\sup _ Xu=0$. If $u_\lambda $ is the unique bounded solution of \[  \mathrm{MA}_\omega (u_\lambda )=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda }f\, \mathrm{d}V, \qquad \lambda >0,  \] then $u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda \to u$ uniformly as $\lambda \downarrow 0$. Proof. By corollary 12.10.12 , $f$ agrees almost everywhere with a smooth function, so it belongs to $L^ p$ for every finite $p$. By proposition 15.28.7 , the constant $c$ for which $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (v)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ has a bounded solution is $b_\omega (f)$. Thus proposition 15.20.1 , with the trivial symmetry group, shows that the normalized family $u_\lambda -\sup _ Xu_\lambda $ is uniformly precompact as $\lambda \downarrow 0$ and that every cluster limit is a normalized solution with this constant. Each cluster limit is therefore a normalized threshold subsolution and equals $u$ by corollary 12.10.12 . If the whole family did not converge uniformly, a sequence staying at a fixed positive uniform distance from $u$ would have a uniformly convergent subsequence, a contradiction. $\square$ Corollary 12.10.14 . 6362B224AE69 Suppose $\omega $ is Kähler. For a nonzero nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, the functional $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth strictly positive maximizer in $\mathscr G_\omega $ if and only if $f$ agrees almost everywhere with a smooth strictly positive function. Proof. The Kähler formula in proposition 15.28.7 gives $b_\omega (f)>0$. If a smooth strictly positive maximizer exists, the proof of corollary 12.10.12 gives \[  \omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=a\gamma , \qquad a\geq 0,  \] with $a,u$ smooth and $a\not\equiv 0$. Since $\mathrm{d}\omega =0$, the first-order equation in lemma 5.22.4 becomes $\mathrm{d}a=-aC$ for a smooth one-form $C$. Along any smooth path $\sigma $, this is the linear scalar equation \[  (a\circ \sigma )'=-(a\circ \sigma )C(\dot\sigma ).  \] whose solution is the initial value multiplied by a positive exponential. Since $X$ is connected and $a\not\equiv 0$, it follows that $a>0$ everywhere, and $f=b_\omega (f)^{-1}a^ n\gamma ^ n/\mathrm{d}V$ is smooth and strictly positive. Conversely, if $f$ is smooth and strictly positive, the smooth equation and theorem 12.2.3 provide the maximizing Gauduchon form. $\square$ For a nonclosed background, the strict positivity of $f$ in corollary 12.10.14 fails, on every compact complex manifold of dimension at least two, including Kähler manifolds. Example 12.10.15 . 36B0532E29A1 On every connected compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n\geq 2$, with a fixed smooth strictly positive probability volume $\mathrm{d}V$, there is a nonclosed Hermitian form $\omega $ and a nonzero smooth nonnegative density $f$ vanishing on an open set such that $b_\omega (f)=1$ and $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth strictly positive maximizer. Proof. Fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ and a point $x$. Choose a smooth real function $\psi $ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi \leq -\gamma $ on a coordinate neighborhood $U$ of $x$; in holomorphic coordinates $z=(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)$ centered at $x$, such a function is obtained by multiplying $-M|z|^2$, with $M$ large enough, by a cutoff that equals one near $x$, and then shrinking $U$. Choose a smooth function $\chi $ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ that vanishes on a smaller neighborhood of $x$ and equals one outside $U$. Put \[  a=L\chi ,\qquad \omega =a\gamma -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi .  \] Since $X$ is compact, $\omega $ is strictly positive for sufficiently large $L>0$: on $U$ the term $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $ is at least $\gamma $, and outside $U$ the term $L\gamma $ dominates $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $. Set $f=a^ n\gamma ^ n/\mathrm{d}V$. The smooth function $\psi $ satisfies $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =a\gamma \geq 0$ and $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (\psi )=f\, \mathrm{d}V$, so $b_\omega (f)\geq 1$. Stokes' theorem and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\gamma ^{n-1}=0$ give \[  \int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\int _ Xa\gamma ^ n =\int _ X(f\, \mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n.  \] Testing ( 15.29.3 ) with $\gamma $ therefore gives the opposite inequality $b_\omega (f)\leq 1$. Hence $b_\omega (f)=1$, the metric $\gamma $ attains the infimum, and the normalized current $\gamma ^{n-1}/\int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ is a smooth strictly positive maximizer of $D_{f^{1/n}}$. If $\omega $ were closed, corollary 12.10.14 would force $f$ to be strictly positive, contrary to its vanishing on an open set. Thus $\omega $ is nonclosed. $\square$ In example 12.10.15 , corollary 12.10.12 , corollary 12.10.13 show that every threshold subsolution is a constant translate of $\psi $ and that the normalized solutions of the exponential equations converge uniformly to $\psi -\sup _ X\psi $. Thus vanishing of the density on an open set does not by itself force nonuniqueness or the failure of this approximation. The restriction $n\geq 2$ in corollary 12.10.12 is necessary. On a compact connected Riemann surface $X$ with a Hermitian form $\omega $, a normalized Gauduchon current has bidegree $(0,0)$, and the equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ makes it a harmonic function, hence the constant $(\int _ X\omega )^{-1}$. This single smooth strictly positive current maximizes for every nonzero nonnegative $L^1$ density, which need not have a smooth representative.

text: Example 12.10.15 . 36B0532E29A1 On every connected compact complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n\geq 2$, with a fixed smooth strictly positive probability volume $\mathrm{d}V$, there is a nonclosed Hermitian form $\omega $ and a nonzero smooth nonnegative density $f$ vanishing on an open set such that $b_\omega (f)=1$ and $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth strictly positive maximizer. Proof. Fix a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ and a point $x$. Choose a smooth real function $\psi $ such that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi \leq -\gamma $ on a coordinate neighborhood $U$ of $x$; in holomorphic coordinates $z=(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)$ centered at $x$, such a function is obtained by multiplying $-M|z|^2$, with $M$ large enough, by a cutoff that equals one near $x$, and then shrinking $U$. Choose a smooth function $\chi $ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ that vanishes on a smaller neighborhood of $x$ and equals one outside $U$. Put \[  a=L\chi ,\qquad \omega =a\gamma -\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi .  \] Since $X$ is compact, $\omega $ is strictly positive for sufficiently large $L>0$: on $U$ the term $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $ is at least $\gamma $, and outside $U$ the term $L\gamma $ dominates $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi $. Set $f=a^ n\gamma ^ n/\mathrm{d}V$. The smooth function $\psi $ satisfies $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =a\gamma \geq 0$ and $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (\psi )=f\, \mathrm{d}V$, so $b_\omega (f)\geq 1$. Stokes' theorem and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\gamma ^{n-1}=0$ give \[  \int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} =\int _ Xa\gamma ^ n =\int _ X(f\, \mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n.  \] Testing ( 15.29.3 ) with $\gamma $ therefore gives the opposite inequality $b_\omega (f)\leq 1$. title: 12.10.16 A smooth maximizing form with an analytic degeneracy set
search_title: A smooth maximizing form with an analytic degeneracy set
section: 12.10 Integrable densities in the compact Gauduchon problem
text: We now allow the smooth maximizing form to degenerate. Where it is strictly positive, the argument of corollary 12.10.12 still determines the solution current and gives the equation. If the degeneracy set is a proper analytic subset, neither side of the equation charges it, so the equation holds on all of $X$. Uniqueness follows by passing to the maximum of two threshold subsolutions and applying lemma 5.38.2 . Theorem 12.10.17 . 51F452E9F8D1 Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ be nonzero, and assume $b=b_\omega (f)>0$. Suppose that $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth semipositive maximizer $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ that is strictly positive on $X\setminus Z$, where $Z$ is a proper analytic subset of $X$. Then every threshold subsolution $u$ is smooth on $X\setminus Z$ and satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)=bf\, \mathrm{d}V  \] on $X$. In particular a threshold solution exists, and it has finite mass. The function $f^{1/n}$ has a smooth nonnegative representative on $X\setminus Z$. Any two threshold subsolutions differ by a constant. Proof. Put $p=f^{1/n}$ and $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, where $u$ is any threshold subsolution; one exists by theorem 15.28.4 . Fix a smooth strictly positive $T_0\in \mathscr G_\omega $, and for real $\varepsilon >0$ set $T_\varepsilon =(T+\varepsilon T_0)/(1+\varepsilon )$. Each $T_\varepsilon $ is a smooth strictly positive member of $\mathscr G_\omega $, so proposition 12.10.11 gives \[  A\wedge T_\varepsilon \geq b^{1/n}p k_{T_\varepsilon }\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] For a smooth semipositive form $T$ with coefficient matrix $P'$ relative to $\omega ^ n$, ( 12.7.1 ) gives $k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V=f_0(\det P')^{1/n}\omega ^ n$, so that $k_ T=f_0^{1-n}(\det P')^{1/n}$ is a continuous function of that matrix. Thus $k_{T_\varepsilon }\to k_ T$ uniformly on the compact manifold $X$. Since $p\in L^1$, passing to the limit gives \[  A\wedge T\geq b^{1/n}p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The left side has mass one by Stokes' theorem and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$, and the right side has mass $b^{1/n}D_ p(T)=1$ because $T$ maximizes. Their difference is positive and has mass zero, hence E32DBBA007AF 12.10.18 \begin{equation}  A\wedge T=b^{1/n}p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V. \end{equation} On $U=X\setminus Z$ write $T=\gamma ^{n-1}$, where $\gamma $ is smooth and strictly positive, and set $a=(bf\, \mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}$. The trace equality becomes $A\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=a\gamma ^ n$ on $U$. On relatively compact subsets of $U$, it controls every coefficient measure of $A$ by an $L^ n$ density. The trace inequalities for all Hermitian forms and the matrix arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, used exactly as in the proof of corollary 12.10.12 , force $A=a\gamma $ on $U$. This step uses only the positivity of $\gamma $ on $U$, since the Hermitian test forms needed there can be taken to be global forms obtained by extension from smaller coordinate charts. The local regularity lemma lemma 5.22.4 makes $u$ and $a$ smooth on $U$. Taking the top power proves the equation on $U$, and $f^{1/n}=b^{-1/n}a(\gamma ^ n/\mathrm{d}V)^{1/n}$ is smooth and nonnegative there. Both $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)$ and $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ put no mass on the pluripolar set $Z$. Hence the equality holds on $X$, and its total mass is $b\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V<+\infty $. It remains to prove uniqueness. Let $v$ be another threshold subsolution and put $w=\max (u,v)$. By proposition 13.14.6 , \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (w)\geq \mathbf1_{\{ u\geq v\} }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u) +\mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (v) \geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Here the pole sets carry no mass for any of the measures involved. Thus $w$ is also a threshold subsolution, and the preceding argument gives the same smooth current $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=a\gamma $ on $U$. We apply lemma 5.38.2 to $u\leq w$ and to $v\leq w$: their complex Hessians agree on $X\setminus Z$, so $w-u$ and $w-v$ are constant. Hence $u-v$ is constant. $\square$

title: Theorem 12.10.17

text: Theorem 12.10.17 . 51F452E9F8D1 Let $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ be nonzero, and assume $b=b_\omega (f)>0$. Suppose that $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth semipositive maximizer $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ that is strictly positive on $X\setminus Z$, where $Z$ is a proper analytic subset of $X$. Then every threshold subsolution $u$ is smooth on $X\setminus Z$ and satisfies \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)=bf\, \mathrm{d}V  \] on $X$. In particular a threshold solution exists, and it has finite mass. The function $f^{1/n}$ has a smooth nonnegative representative on $X\setminus Z$. Any two threshold subsolutions differ by a constant. Proof. Put $p=f^{1/n}$ and $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, where $u$ is any threshold subsolution; one exists by theorem 15.28.4 . Fix a smooth strictly positive $T_0\in \mathscr G_\omega $, and for real $\varepsilon >0$ set $T_\varepsilon =(T+\varepsilon T_0)/(1+\varepsilon )$. Each $T_\varepsilon $ is a smooth strictly positive member of $\mathscr G_\omega $, so proposition 12.10.11 gives \[  A\wedge T_\varepsilon \geq b^{1/n}p k_{T_\varepsilon }\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] For a smooth semipositive form $T$ with coefficient matrix $P'$ relative to $\omega ^ n$, ( 12.7.1 ) gives $k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V=f_0(\det P')^{1/n}\omega ^ n$, so that $k_ T=f_0^{1-n}(\det P')^{1/n}$ is a continuous function of that matrix. Thus $k_{T_\varepsilon }\to k_ T$ uniformly on the compact manifold $X$. Since $p\in L^1$, passing to the limit gives \[  A\wedge T\geq b^{1/n}p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The left side has mass one by Stokes' theorem and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$, and the right side has mass $b^{1/n}D_ p(T)=1$ because $T$ maximizes. Their difference is positive and has mass zero, hence E32DBBA007AF 12.10.18 \begin{equation}  A\wedge T=b^{1/n}p k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V. \end{equation} On $U=X\setminus Z$ write $T=\gamma ^{n-1}$, where $\gamma $ is smooth and strictly positive, and set $a=(bf\, \mathrm{d}V/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}$. The trace equality becomes $A\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=a\gamma ^ n$ on $U$. On relatively compact subsets of $U$, it controls every coefficient measure of $A$ by an $L^ n$ density. The trace inequalities for all Hermitian forms and the matrix arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, used exactly as in the proof of corollary 12.10.12 , force $A=a\gamma $ on $U$. This step uses only the positivity of $\gamma $ on $U$, since the Hermitian test forms needed there can be taken to be global forms obtained by extension from smaller coordinate charts. The local regularity lemma lemma 5.22.4 makes $u$ and $a$ smooth on $U$. Taking the top power proves the equation on $U$, and $f^{1/n}=b^{-1/n}a(\gamma ^ n/\mathrm{d}V)^{1/n}$ is smooth and nonnegative there. Both $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)$ and $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ put no mass on the pluripolar set $Z$. Hence the equality holds on $X$, and its total mass is $b\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V<+\infty $. It remains to prove uniqueness. Let $v$ be another threshold subsolution and put $w=\max (u,v)$. By proposition 13.14.6 , \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (w)\geq \mathbf1_{\{ u\geq v\} }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u) +\mathbf1_{\{ u<v\} }\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (v) \geq bf\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] Here the pole sets carry no mass for any of the measures involved. Thus $w$ is also a threshold subsolution, and the preceding argument gives the same smooth current $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w=a\gamma $ on $U$. We apply lemma 5.38.2 to $u\leq w$ and to $v\leq w$: their complex Hessians agree on $X\setminus Z$, so $w-u$ and $w-v$ are constant. Hence $u-v$ is constant. $\square$

D179EF5E5E25 Under the hypotheses of proposition 12.10.20 , suppose in addition that the obstacle envelope $P_{\delta \omega }(u_0)$ of section 5.40 is not identically $-\infty $ for some real $0<\delta <1$. Then $v_\lambda \to u_0$ in capacity as $\lambda \downarrow 0$. In particular this holds if the threshold solution $u_0$ is bounded. Proof. Fix a sequence $\lambda _ j\downarrow 0$. Proposition 12.10.20 gives $u_0-C\leq v_{\lambda _ j}\leq 0$ and $v_{\lambda _ j}\to u_0$ in $L^1$. For all $j$ with $\lambda _ j\leq 1$, \[  \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (v_{\lambda _ j}) =c_{\lambda _ j}\mathrm{e}^{\lambda _ jv_{\lambda _ j}}f\, \mathrm{d}V \leq b\mathrm{e}^{C}f\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The bounded functions $|\mathrm{e}^{v_{\lambda _ j}}-\mathrm{e}^{u_0}|$ tend to zero in $\mathrm{d}V$-measure. Since $f\in L^1$, their integrals against $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ tend to zero, so the error term in ( 15.9.2 ) tends to zero. We apply proposition 15.9.3 with $\theta =\omega $ and $\varphi =u_0$; its additional hypothesis that the $L^1$ limit $u$ satisfies $u\preceq \varphi $, in the notation of definition 16.7.1 , holds trivially, since $u=u_0$. This proves convergence in capacity along every sequence, and hence for the family. Finally, if $u_0$ is bounded, a constant below it is a competitor for $P_{\delta \omega }(u_0)$, so this envelope is not identically $-\infty $. $\square$

The capacity criterion above requires the obstacle envelope of $u_0$ in a smaller background $\delta \omega $ not to be identically $-\infty $. We give two sufficient conditions of different origin: invariance of the Monge–Ampère mass controls the contact measures of envelopes of stretched truncations, while a sublinear bound on the singularity provides explicit competitors. Both conditions also give zero Lelong numbers. In the setting of theorem 12.10.17 , if the maximizing form has a globally smooth root of rank at least two, zero Lelong numbers then allow the threshold solution to be extended smoothly across the analytic degeneracy set. The setting is unchanged: $X$ has dimension $n\geq 2$, $\omega $ is a Hermitian form and $\mathrm{d}V$ a smooth positive probability volume form. Inequalities between quasi-plurisubharmonic functions refer to their canonical representatives, and $
u (u,x)$ denotes the Lelong number of $u$ at $x$. We will use the following consequence of lemma 5.38.8 , where $C_\omega $ is the bound for the Lelong numbers of $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions given there: if $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ and, for every $0<\delta <1$, some $v_\delta \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\delta \omega )$ satisfies $v_\delta \leq u$, then \[  0\leq

For every nonzero $0\leq f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$, with $M=\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V$, one has \[  b_\omega (f)= rac VM.  \] Every threshold subsolution $u$ satisfies $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)=(V/M)f\, \mathrm{d}V$ and has mass $V$. More generally, these last two conclusions hold for every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ with $\int _ X\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)=V$. Proof. By theorem 11.1.7 , every bounded $\omega $-plurisubharmonic function has mass $V$, and truncation therefore bounds every extended mass by $V$. section: 12.10 Integrable densities in the compact Gauduchon problem
text: Theorem 12.10.26 . 7449627F15EC Assume the hypotheses of theorem 12.10.17 , with analytic degeneracy set $Z$, and let $\Phi _ f$ be the greatest threshold subsolution with supremum zero, from proposition 15.28.6 ; by that theorem it is the threshold solution with supremum zero. Suppose that the maximizing form is $T=\gamma ^{n-1}$ for a globally smooth semipositive $(1,1)$-form $\gamma $ whose rank is at least two everywhere. If $\Phi _ f$ has zero Lelong numbers, then it is smooth on $X$; by theorem 12.10.23 , proposition 12.10.24 , this applies under either of the conditions above. Every threshold subsolution is then smooth, since these subsolutions differ by constants. Proof. Put $U=X\setminus Z$ and $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ f$. By theorem 12.10.17 , $A$ is smooth on $U$ and $\Phi _ f$ satisfies the equation on $X$; the root $\gamma $ is positive on $U$. Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ XA\wedge T=1$, while attainment gives \[  \int _ U(A^ n)^{1/n}(\gamma ^ n)^{(n-1)/n} =b_\omega (f)^{1/n}D_{f^{1/n}}(T)=1.  \] The difference $A\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}-(A^ n/\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n$ is nonnegative and continuous on $U$ by the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, and its integral vanishes. The equality case gives $A=r\gamma $ on $U$ with the smooth function $r=\operatorname {tr}_\gamma A/n\geq 0$; where $A^ n=0$, equality forces $A=0$ and $r=0$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ f$ is closed, \[  \mathrm dr\wedge \gamma +r\, \mathrm d\gamma =\mathrm d\omega \quad \hbox{on }U.  \] For a semipositive form $\gamma $ of rank at least two, the real-linear map $W_\gamma :\xi \mapsto \xi \wedge \gamma $ from real one-forms to three-forms is injective at every point. Indeed, write $\gamma =\sum _ k\lambda _ k\, \mathrm dx_ k\wedge \mathrm dy_ k$ at the point in suitable real coordinates $z_ k=x_ k+\mathrm iy_ k$, with $\lambda _ k\geq 0$ and at least two $\lambda _ k$ positive. For each index $j$ choose $k\neq j$ with $\lambda _ k>0$. The coefficient of $\mathrm dx_ j\wedge \mathrm dx_ k\wedge \mathrm dy_ k$ in $\xi \wedge \gamma $ is $\lambda _ k$ times the coefficient of $\mathrm dx_ j$ in $\xi $, and similarly for $\mathrm dy_ j$. Hence $\xi \wedge \gamma =0$ forces $\xi =0$. Choose an auxiliary Riemannian metric. The left inverse $L_\gamma =(W_\gamma ^*W_\gamma )^{-1}W_\gamma ^*$ is smooth and uniformly bounded on compact $X$. Thus BD4046661AE4 12.10.27 \begin{equation}  \mathrm dr=\alpha -r\beta ,\qquad \alpha =L_\gamma (\mathrm d\omega ),\quad \beta =L_\gamma (\mathrm d\gamma ), \end{equation} with smooth one-forms on $X$. In particular $|\mathrm d\log (1+r)|\leq C$ on $U$. Points of $U$ can be joined by short paths avoiding $Z$. In a coordinate ball, stratify $Z$ into countably many smooth strata of real dimension at most $2n-2$. For a fixed point outside $Z$, the endpoints of segments from it that meet one stratum lie in a cone of dimension at most $2n-1$, which is Lebesgue-null. Given two nearby points outside $Z$, choose a generic intermediate point in a ball of radius comparable to their distance; both connecting segments then avoid $Z$, and their combined length is bounded by a fixed multiple of that distance. Using a finite connected cover by coordinate balls, with intermediate points chosen in the overlaps, we also obtain a uniform bound for the lengths of connecting paths in $U$. The bound on $\mathrm d\log (1+r)$ now bounds $r$ on $U$, and ( 12.10.27 ) bounds its derivative. The short paths therefore give a unique locally Lipschitz extension of $r$ across $Z$. Since $Z$ is Lebesgue-null, the weak derivative of the extension satisfies ( 12.10.27 ) on $X$. The right side is continuous, so $r$ is $C^1$, and iterating makes it smooth. Set $S=r\gamma $. It is smooth and semipositive, and $\mathrm dS=\mathrm d\omega $ on $X$ by density of $U$. The current $R=A-S$ is therefore closed, and it is supported on $Z$. It is also positive: since $A=S$ off $Z$ and $S$ puts no mass on $Z$, the current $R$ is the restriction of the positive current $A$ to $Z$. The support theorem recalled in section 5.38 expresses $R$ as a nonnegative combination of currents of integration along the components of $Z$ of codimension one. Locally $S-\omega $ is smooth and closed, so it has a smooth local $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-potential, and the coefficients of $R$ are the generic Lelong numbers of $\Phi _ f$ along these components. All of them vanish, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ f=S-\omega $ is smooth. Taking a Euclidean trace and applying elliptic regularity gives a smooth function equal to $\Phi _ f$ almost everywhere, and hence everywhere, since $\Phi _ f$ is its canonical representative. $\square$ The smooth root and its rank bound are hypotheses of the theorem: a smooth semipositive $(n-1,n-1)$-form need not have a smooth $(1,1)$-root across its degeneracy set. On a surface the rank condition already forces $\gamma >0$ everywhere.

It is smooth and semipositive, and $\mathrm dS=\mathrm d\omega $ on $X$ by density of $U$. The current $R=A-S$ is therefore closed, and it is supported on $Z$. It is also positive: since $A=S$ off $Z$ and $S$ puts no mass on $Z$, the current $R$ is the restriction of the positive current $A$ to $Z$. The support theorem recalled in section 5.38 expresses $R$ as a nonnegative combination of currents of integration along the components of $Z$ of codimension one. Locally $S-\omega $ is smooth and closed, so it has a smooth local $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-potential, and the coefficients of $R$ are the generic Lelong numbers of $\Phi _ f$ along these components. All of them vanish, so $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Phi _ f=S-\omega $ is smooth. Taking a Euclidean trace and applying elliptic regularity gives a smooth function equal to $\Phi _ f$ almost everywhere, and hence everywhere, since $\Phi _ f$ is its canonical representative. $\square$

title: 12.10.28 Two attained instances
section: 12.10 Integrable densities in the compact Gauduchon problem
text: Example 12.10.29 . E97964925666 On the Hopf surface $X=(\mathbb C^2\setminus \{ 0\} )/\langle z\mapsto 2z\rangle $, the background $\omega =|z|^{-2}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2$ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =0$, so its Monge–Ampère mass is invariant. There are smooth densities whose threshold solutions are smooth and nonconstant and whose maximizing tests are smooth strictly positive forms. Proof. The form is invariant under $z\mapsto 2z$, so it descends to $X$, and it is positive. For $s=|z|^2$ and $F(s)=s^{-1}$, the identity $sF''+2F'=0$ gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(s^{-1})\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s=0$, while $\omega $ is not closed. Choose a nonconstant smooth real $q$ and small nonzero $\varepsilon $ such that $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\varepsilon q)>0$. Put $V=\int _ X\omega ^2$, $\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^2/V$, $f=A^2/\mathrm{d}V$ and $u=\varepsilon q-\sup _ X\varepsilon q$. Invariance of the mass gives $\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V=\int _ XA^2=V$, hence $b_\omega (f)=1$ by theorem 12.10.23 . The form $T=A/V$ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$, $\int _ X\omega \wedge T=1$ and $D_{\sqrt f}(T)=1$. For every smooth strictly positive $Q\in \mathscr G_\omega $, the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality and Stokes' theorem give $D_{\sqrt f}(Q)\leq \int _ XA\wedge Q=1$. Thus $T$ is a smooth strictly positive maximizer, and since $u$ is a threshold solution with supremum zero, corollary 12.10.12 gives $\Phi _ f=u$. This is a bounded nonconstant example. $\square$ Example 12.10.30 . 4C03E42B184D Let $n\geq 3$, and view the smooth quadric of dimension $n$ as a double cover of $\mathbb P^ n$. For the restricted Fubini–Study form and a suitable smooth density, the maximizing test is a smooth semipositive form whose smooth root has rank at least two everywhere and degenerates along the ramification divisor. Proof. Let \[  X=\{ [w:z_0:\cdots :z_ n]:w^2=\textstyle \sum _{i=0}^ nz_ i^2\}  \subset \mathbb P^{n+1},\qquad F([w:z])=[z].  \] The quadratic form is nonsingular, and $F$ is finite of degree two, with smooth ramification divisor $Z=\{ w=0\} $. Local branch coordinates show that $\mathrm dF$ has rank $n-1$ on $Z$ and $n$ elsewhere. Let $\omega $ be the restriction to $X$ of the normalized Fubini–Study form of $\mathbb P^{n+1}$, and let $A=F^*\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$, where $\omega _{\mathrm{FS}}$ is the normalized Fubini–Study form of $\mathbb P^ n$. Then \[  u=\log \frac{\sum _ i|z_ i|^2}{|w|^2+\sum _ i|z_ i|^2}  \] is a smooth function on $X$ with $-\log 2\leq u\leq 0$, $\sup _ Xu=0$ and $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. The change of variables for the branched cover gives $\int _ XA^ n=2$, and Stokes' theorem gives $V=\int _ X\omega ^ n=2$. Set $\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^ n/V$, $f=A^ n/\mathrm{d}V$, $T=A^{n-1}/V$ and $\gamma =A/V^{1/(n-1)}$. Since $\omega $ is closed, theorem 12.10.23 gives $b_\omega (f)=V/\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V=1$. Stokes' theorem gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ and $\int _ X\omega \wedge T=1$, and computing the determinant density gives $D_{f^{1/n}}(T)=1$. The arithmetic–geometric mean inequality, which remains valid for semipositive $A$, bounds $D_{f^{1/n}}(Q)$ by $\int _ XA\wedge Q=1$ for every smooth strictly positive $Q\in \mathscr G_\omega $. Thus $T$ is a maximizer, strictly positive off the proper analytic set $Z$, and theorem 12.10.17 gives $\Phi _ f=u$. Its root $\gamma $ has rank $n-1\geq 2$ on $Z$ and is positive elsewhere, as required. $\square$ The invariant-mass and sublinear conditions settle the envelope condition only in special situations. We do not know whether general moment or entropy bounds imply either of them, or the hypothesis on the smooth root. Corollary 12.10.31 . 2A3A58A80CB4 Under the hypotheses of theorem 12.10.17 , suppose in addition that $f\in L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ for some $p>1$. Then the normalized threshold solution $u_0$ is continuous, and the normalized greatest exponential solutions converge uniformly to $u_0$ as the exponent tends to zero. Proof. By proposition 15.28.7 , the constant $c$ for which $\mathrm{MA}_\omega (v)=cf\, \mathrm{d}V$ has a continuous solution is $b_\omega (f)$. The continuous normalized solution is therefore a threshold solution, and it equals $u_0$ by the uniqueness in theorem 12.10.17 . For $L^ p$ data the greatest exponential solution coincides with the bounded solution, as explained after theorem 15.35.2 . By proposition 15.20.1 , applied with the trivial group, the normalized family is uniformly precompact, and every cluster limit solves the threshold equation. Uniqueness identifies every cluster limit with $u_0$, which proves uniform convergence of the whole family. $\square$

section: 12.10 Integrable densities in the compact Gauduchon problem
text: The envelope criteria above do not require $L^ p$ integrability of the density. In the following example on projective space, with a closed background, the threshold solution is unbounded, while its envelopes $P_{\delta \omega }(u)$ in smaller backgrounds are not identically $-\infty $. The dual supremum is approached by smooth tests but attained by no smooth semipositive test. Proposition 12.10.33 . DB722F1D363A Let $X=\mathbb P^ n$, $n\geq 2$, and let $\omega $ be the normalized Fubini–Study form, with $\int _ X\omega ^ n=1$ and $\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^ n$. For $0<\alpha <1$ put \[  \psi =\log \frac{\sum _{i=1}^ n|z_ i|^2}{\sum _{i=0}^ n|z_ i|^2}, \qquad u=1-(1-\psi )^\alpha , \qquad o=[1:0:\cdots :0].  \] The function $u$ belongs to $\mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, satisfies $\sup _ Xu=0$, has $o$ as its only pole, and has extended mass one. For every $0<\delta <1$, the envelope $P_{\delta \omega }(u)$ is not identically $-\infty $. The measure $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (u)$ is $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ with $f\in L^1(\mathrm{d}V)$ and $f\notin L^ p(\mathrm{d}V)$ for every $p>1$. Moreover, $b_\omega (f)=1$ and $\rho _\omega (f^{1/n})=1$, so $u$ is a threshold solution for $f$. No smooth semipositive $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ attains $D_{f^{1/n}}(T)=1$. Proof. The numerator in the definition of $\psi $ vanishes only at $o$, and locally $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log \sum _{i=1}^ n|z_ i|^2\geq 0$. The function $\chi (t)=1-(1-t)^\alpha $ is increasing and convex on $t\leq 0$, with $0\leq \chi '\leq \alpha $. Applying the chain inequality to bounded truncations of $\psi $ and taking the decreasing limit, we obtain $u=\chi \circ \psi \in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$, with \[  A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq (1-\alpha )\omega .  \] The function $u$ is smooth off $o$, and it attains its supremum zero on $\{ z_0=0\} $. Since $u=-(1-\psi )^\alpha +1$, proposition 12.10.24 shows that all the envelopes $P_{\delta \omega }(u)$ are not identically $-\infty $. To compute the mass, use the chart $z_0=1$ and write $s=\sum _{i=1}^ n|z_ i|^2$. A local potential $F$ for $A$, as a function of $s$, and the function $q=sF'$ are 33BC8E188D93 12.10.34 \begin{equation}  \begin{aligned}  F(s)& =\log (1+s)+1-\left(1-\log \frac{s}{1+s}\right)^\alpha ,\\  q(s)& =sF'(s)=\frac{s+\alpha (1-\log (s/(1+s)))^{\alpha -1}}{1+s}. \end{aligned} \end{equation} The eigenvalues of $A$ are $q/s$ in the tangential directions and $q'$ in the radial direction. Polar integration gives the radial top-degree measure $nq^{n-1}q'\, \mathrm{d}s$, where the angular normalization follows from the Fubini–Study case $q=s/(1+s)$, whose radial density is $ns^{n-1}(1+s)^{-n-1}\, \mathrm{d}s$ and whose total mass is one. Consequently, for $0<s_1<s_2$, \[  \int _{\{ s_1<|z|^2<s_2\} }A^ n=q(s_2)^ n-q(s_1)^ n.  \] Here $q(s)\to 0$ as $s\downarrow 0$ and $q(s)\to 1$ as $s\to \infty $. On each compact annulus the extended measure equals the smooth top power, and it puts no mass on $o$ or on the hyperplane at infinity, since both are pluripolar. Exhausting the affine chart by annuli therefore gives extended mass exactly one. (This computation does not use the vanishing of the Lelong numbers.) Near $o$ write $L=1-\log s$. Differentiating ( 12.10.34 ) gives \[  \begin{gathered} \frac qs\sim \alpha s^{-1}L^{\alpha -1},\qquad q'\sim \alpha (1-\alpha )s^{-1}L^{\alpha -2},\\ f(s)\asymp s^{-n}L^{-1-n(1-\alpha )}. \end{gathered}  \] The smooth volume form, written in terms of $s$, is comparable to $s^{n-1}\, \mathrm{d}s$, so the contribution of a neighborhood of $o$ to $\int _ Xf\, \mathrm{d}V$ is comparable to $\int ^\infty L^{-1-n(1-\alpha )}\, \mathrm{d}L$, which is finite. For every $p>1$, the corresponding integral of $f^ p$ contains an exponentially growing factor $\exp (n(p-1)L)$ and diverges. The measure is smooth off $o$ and puts no mass on $o$, so it is $f\, \mathrm{d}V$ on all of $X$. Since its total mass is one and $\omega $ is closed, theorem 12.10.23 gives $b_\omega (f)=1$, and hence $\rho _\omega (f^{1/n})=b_\omega (f)^{-1/n}=1$. Suppose that a smooth semipositive $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $ attained this value. The positive current $A$ satisfies $\int _ XA\wedge T=1$ by Stokes' theorem for currents. On $X\setminus \{ o\} $, the matrix arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives \[  A\wedge T\geq f^{1/n}k_ T\, \mathrm{d}V.  \] The right side has total mass one by attainment, so the nonnegative difference of the two sides vanishes off $o$. Since $A$ is smooth and strictly positive there, the equality case gives $T=tA^{n-1}$ on $X\setminus \{ o\} $, also at points where $T=0$: applying the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality to the positive semidefinite coefficient matrix of $T$ conjugated by $A^{1/2}$ shows that all its eigenvalues agree, possibly at zero. The function $t=(T\wedge A)/A^ n$ is smooth and nonnegative on $X\setminus \{ o\} $. Since $A$ is closed, the equation $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$ becomes $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}t\wedge A^{n-1}=0$, a locally strictly elliptic scalar equation on $X\setminus \{ o\} $. All eigenvalues of $A$ tend to infinity at $o$, and since $n\geq 2$, so do all eigenvalues of $A^{n-1}$, which are products of $n-1$ eigenvalues of $A$. Since the coefficient matrix of the smooth form $T$ is bounded, it follows that $t\to 0$ at $o$. Set $t(o)=0$. The resulting continuous nonnegative function on compact $X$ is not identically zero, by the normalization of $T$, so it attains a positive maximum away from $o$. The strong maximum principle on the connected manifold $X\setminus \{ o\} $ forces it to be constant there, contrary to its zero limit at $o$. This excludes every smooth semipositive maximizing test; no assumption on the degeneracy set of $T$ was needed. $\square$ Corollary 12.10.35 . D0692BB5EDD8 For the density and potential of proposition 12.10.33 , \[  \int _ X f\log f\, \mathrm{d}V<+\infty \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \alpha <1-\frac1n.  \] For every real $r>0$, \[  \int _ X(-u)^ r f\, \mathrm{d}V<+\infty \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \alpha r<n(1-\alpha ).  \] In particular, finite entropy of the density can coexist with an unbounded threshold solution of full mass and with the absence of a smooth semipositive maximizing test. Proof. Only a neighborhood of $o$ can contribute a divergence. There the preceding estimates give $f\, \mathrm{d}V\asymp L^{-1-n(1-\alpha )}\, \mathrm{d}L$, $\log f\sim nL$ and $-u\asymp L^\alpha $. Hence the entropy integral converges exactly when $n(1-\alpha )>1$, and the weighted integral exactly when $\alpha r<n(1-\alpha )$. In the equality cases both integrals are comparable to $\int ^\infty L^{-1}\, \mathrm{d}L$ and diverge. The negative part of $f\log f$ is bounded, hence integrable for the probability volume, so the entropy criterion is unambiguous. $\square$ These are integrals of the single density $f$. They should be distinguished from uniform moment or entropy bounds for the determinant-weighted probabilities of a maximizing sequence, as in theorem 12.10.43 ; since the present example has no smooth semipositive maximizer, it lies outside the setting of theorem 12.10.17 . The proposition concerns the explicit threshold solution $u$; identifying it with the greatest normalized threshold subsolution $\Phi _ f$ would require a separate uniqueness argument.

In the equality cases both integrals are comparable to $\int ^\infty L^{-1}\, \mathrm{d}L$ and diverge. The negative part of $f\log f$ is bounded, hence integrable for the probability volume, so the entropy criterion is unambiguous. $\square$

u (u,D)$ for the generic Lelong number of $u$ along $D$. Corollary 12.10.39 . 1E2D5DAE5C6C Under the hypotheses of theorem 12.10.17 , let $u$ be a threshold solution and let $D_1,\ldots ,D_ k$ be the prime divisors with $
u (u,D_ j)>0$. Then the classes $\{ D_ j\} $ are linearly independent in $H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)$. In particular their number is at most $\dim _{\mathbb R}H^{1,1}_{\mathrm{BC}}(X,\mathbb R)$. Proof. Since $u$ is smooth off $Z$, these divisors are among the finitely many components of $Z$ of codimension one. Put $a_ j=
u (u,D_ j)>0$. By lemma 5.38.1 , \[  R=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-\sum _ j a_ j[D_ j]\geq 0.  \] Suppose that real numbers $c_1,\ldots ,c_ k$ satisfy $\sum _ j c_ j\{ D_ j\} =0$. Since the smooth representative in that lemma depends linearly on the Bott–Chern class, we obtain \[  h=\sum _ j c_ j v_\eta ([D_ j])\in L^1(X),\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}h=\sum _ j c_ j[D_ j].  \] Choose $t
e 0$ sufficiently small that $a_ j+tc_ j\geq 0$ for every $j$. title: 12.10.40 A branched projective example
section: 12.10 Integrable densities in the compact Gauduchon problem
text: The squaring map of projective space gives a smooth threshold solution whose maximizing form degenerates along the coordinate hyperplanes. The density is smooth, but its $n$th root is not differentiable along these hyperplanes. For this example take $X=\mathbb P^ n$, $n\geq 2$, with homogeneous coordinates $[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ n]$, and let $\omega $ be the Fubini–Study form normalized by $\int _ X\omega ^ n=1$. Set $\mathrm{d}V=\omega ^ n$. Example 12.10.41 . 2A68BBAE5086 For every $n\geq 2$, there is a smooth nonnegative density $f$ on $\mathbb P^ n$, vanishing precisely on the coordinate hyperplanes, such that $b_\omega (f)=1$ and $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth semipositive maximizer strictly positive off those hyperplanes. The threshold solution is smooth, but $f^{1/n}$ is not differentiable at a general point of any coordinate hyperplane. There is no smooth strictly positive maximizing form. The normalized greatest exponential solutions converge uniformly to the normalized threshold solution. Proof. Define the holomorphic map $F:\mathbb P^ n\to \mathbb P^ n$ and the semipositive form $A$ by \[  F[Z_0:\cdots :Z_ n]=[Z_0^2:\cdots :Z_ n^2],\qquad A=\tfrac 12F^*\omega .  \] The homogeneous formula \[  u=\tfrac 12\log \! \left(\sum _{i=0}^ n|Z_ i|^4\right) -\log \! \left(\sum _{i=0}^ n|Z_ i|^2\right)  \] defines a smooth function on projective space, and $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. The form $A$ is semipositive, and it is strictly positive exactly where every homogeneous coordinate is nonzero. Define \[  f=A^ n/\omega ^ n,\qquad T=A^{n-1}.  \] Since $\omega $ and $A$ are closed and cohomologous, Stokes' theorem gives $\int _ X f\omega ^ n=\int _ X\omega \wedge T=1$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=0$; thus $T\in \mathscr G_\omega $. Every $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )$ has extended mass at most one: each bounded truncation $\max (v,-k)$ has mass one, and restricting its Monge–Ampère measure to $\{ v>-k\} $ can only decrease that mass. Consequently an inequality $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega (v)\geq c f\omega ^ n$ forces $c\leq 1$. The smooth solution $u$ gives the reverse bound, so $b_\omega (f)=1$. The determinant formula for smooth semipositive forms gives \[  k_ T=f^{(n-1)/n},\qquad D_{f^{1/n}}(T)=\int _{\mathbb P^ n}f\omega ^ n=1.  \] By ( 12.10.2 ) and $\rho _\omega (f^{1/n})=b_\omega (f)^{-1/n}=1$, the form $T$ is a maximizer. It is strictly positive away from the coordinate hyperplanes because $A$ is; on these hyperplanes $A$ has deficient rank, and hence so does the coefficient matrix of $T=A^{n-1}$. For the density root, use the chart $Z_0=1$ with coordinates $z_1,\ldots ,z_ n$. Pulling back the Fubini–Study volume by $(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)\mapsto (z_1^2,\ldots ,z_ n^2)$ and including the factor $2^{-n}$ gives \[  f(z)=2^ n\left(\prod _{i=1}^ n|z_ i|^2\right) \frac{(1+\sum _ i|z_ i|^2)^{n+1}}{(1+\sum _ i|z_ i|^4)^{n+1}}.  \] Near a point of $\{ z_1=0\} $ at which all the other coordinates are nonzero, $f^{1/n}$ is $|z_1|^{2/n}$ times a smooth strictly positive function. Restricting to a real line transverse to that hyperplane proves nondifferentiability, also in the case $n=2$, where $|z_1|^{2/n}=|z_1|$. By symmetry of the coordinates, the same holds on every coordinate hyperplane. The absence of a smooth strictly positive maximizer follows from corollary 12.10.14 , since $f$ has zeros. Finally, $f$ is bounded, so corollary 12.10.31 gives the uniform convergence of the normalized exponential solutions. $\square$

title: 12.11 Nef limits and nonattainment
text: We return to arbitrary dimension $n\geq 1$. If $\theta $ is nef and $h$ is a Hermitian form, then the backgrounds $\theta +\epsilon h$ lie in $\mathscr P$ for every $\epsilon >0$, directly from the definition of nefness; their volumes are therefore scalars of smooth equations. As $\epsilon $ decreases to zero, the infimum over Gauduchon metrics commutes with the decreasing limit of the background. Thus the boundary value is determined by smooth equations, even when no metric attains it. Theorem 12.11.1 . 9ECB2B21B601 For every nef background $\theta $ and every Hermitian form $h$, \[  \lambda _\mu (\theta ) =\lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0}\lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h), \qquad \mathcal V_\mu (\theta ) =\lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0}c_{\theta +\epsilon h}(\mu ).  \] Both quantities on the right decrease as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, and their limits do not depend on $h$. Proof. For $0<\epsilon '<\epsilon $ the difference of the two backgrounds is the positive form $(\epsilon -\epsilon ')h$, so the monotonicity in proposition 12.2.2 shows that $\lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)$ decreases as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. Its limit is therefore the infimum over $\epsilon >0$. Infima over $\epsilon >0$ and over Gauduchon metrics commute, and for a fixed metric the quotient is affine in $\epsilon $. Hence \[  \begin{split}  \inf _{\epsilon >0}\lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h) & =\inf _\gamma \inf _{\epsilon >0} \frac{\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} +\epsilon \int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{D_\mu (\gamma )}\\ & =\lambda _\mu (\theta ). \end{split}  \] Here the second equality holds because the coefficient of $\epsilon $ is positive, so the inner infimum is the value at $\epsilon =0$. This proves the first identity, and its right side is the definition of $\lambda _\mu (\theta )$, which does not involve $h$. The second identity follows by raising the first to the $n$th power, since $\lambda _\mu (\theta +\epsilon h)^ n=c_{\theta +\epsilon h}(\mu )$ by theorem 12.2.3 . $\square$ If $X$ is Kähler and $\theta $ is closed and nef, choose $h$ Kähler. Each perturbed solution form is then closed and cohomologous to $\theta +\epsilon h$, so integrating its equation and applying Stokes' theorem gives \[  c_{\theta +\epsilon h}(\mu )=\int _ X(\theta +\epsilon h)^ n.  \] Letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, we obtain $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta )=\int _ X\theta ^ n$ for every closed nef $\theta $ on a compact Kähler manifold and every $\mu $. We refer to this as the closed nef formula . Proposition 12.11.2 . 854AAD5CF1CA Suppose $\theta $ is pseudoeffective and $\lambda _\mu (\theta )=0$. The infimum in definition 12.2.1 is attained if and only if $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$ for a smooth real function $f$. Proof. Since $D_\mu (\gamma )>0$, a metric $\gamma $ attaining the value zero satisfies $\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}=0$. By lemma 11.6.3 , including its dimension-one case, $\theta $ is then smoothly $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact. Conversely, if $\theta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f$, Stokes' theorem makes every quotient zero, so every admissible metric attains the infimum. $\square$ For example, let $X$ be the ruled surface and $D$ the section of lemma 16.29.16 . The class $c_1(\mathcal O_ X(D))$ is nef, has zero square, and contains the nonzero positive current $[D]$. By the closed nef formula its volume is zero. A smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact representative would make $[D]$ itself $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-exact, which is impossible because $\int _ D\kappa >0$ for a Kähler form $\kappa $. By proposition 12.11.2 , no Gauduchon metric minimizes the defining quotient.

title: 12.12 Subtraction with a closed nef core

section: 12.12 Subtraction with a closed nef core
text:
Consider a path of backgrounds that starts in $\mathscr P$ and reaches its boundary at a nef point. If the path contains a closed nef class of positive top intersection, this closed core keeps the root volume positive up to and including the boundary, and adding a semipositive form, closed or not, preserves this lower bound. By proposition 12.3.2 , the total decrease of the root volume along the path is the integral of an explicit ratio formed with the minimizing Gauduchon metrics; we call it the subtraction cost. Two test metrics chosen at the initial point bound this cost from above, with explicit dependence on the density and on the derivatives of the added form. Throughout this section, $X$ is a compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$ and $\Omega $ is a fixed Kähler form on $X$. Let $\alpha $ be a smooth closed nef real $(1,1)$-form, let $B\geq 0$ be a smooth real $(1,1)$-form, and let $t>0$. For real $s$, put \[  a_ s=\alpha +(t-s)\Omega ,\qquad 	heta _ s=a_ s+B,\qquad V_ s=\int _ Xa_ s^ n.  \] The class of $a_0$ is Kähler. Choose a Kähler representative $\kappa _0$ of $[a_0]$, and let $u_0$ be the smooth solution of the Calabi–Yau equation $\gamma _0=\kappa _0+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0>0$, $\gamma _0^ n=V_0\mu $. Define the fixed quantities 3B788E18394E 12.12.1  egin{equation}   egin{gathered} I_ B=\int _ XB\wedge \kappa _0^{n-1},\qquad U_\mu = rac{V_0+I_ B}{D_\mu (\kappa _0)},\ \Delta _\mu (B)=V_0^{-(n-1)/n}\int _ XB\wedge \gamma _0^{n-1}. \end{gathered} \end{equation} Theorem 12.12.2 . 026E84610646 Suppose that $V:=V_ t>0$ and that there is a smooth compact complex curve $C\subset X$ with $\int _ C\alpha =\int _ CB=0$. Then $	heta _ s$ has a smooth positive representative for $s<t$, $	heta _ t$ is nef but has no smooth positive representative, and $	heta _ s$ is not nef for $s>t$. Moreover, \[  \lambda _\mu (a_ s)=V_ s^{1/n}\quad (0\leq s\leq t), \qquad \lambda _\mu (	heta _ t)\geq V^{1/n}>0.  \] For every choice of minimizing Gauduchon metrics $g_ s$ for $	heta _ s$, $0\leq s<t$, the ratio $\int _ X\Omega \wedge g_ s^{n-1}/D_\mu (g_ s)$ is a continuous function of $s$, and the subtraction cost satisfies 2FB723BB4645 12.12.3  egin{equation}   egin{split}  0\leq \mathcal C & :=\int _0^ t rac{\int _ X\Omega \wedge g_ s^{n-1}}{D_\mu (g_ s)}\, \mathrm{d}s =\lambda _\mu (	heta _0)-\lambda _\mu (	heta _ t)\ & \leq \min \{ U_\mu ,V_0^{1/n}+\Delta _\mu (B)\} -V^{1/n}<\infty , \end{split} \end{equation} where the integral is improper at $t$. If $B\leq M\kappa _0$ for a constant $M\geq 0$, then \[  \Delta _\mu (B)\leq MV_0^{1/n},\qquad \mathcal C\leq (1+M)V_0^{1/n}-V^{1/n}.  \] Finally, there are a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $ho $ and a constant $\varepsilon >0$ with $\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho \geq \varepsilon \Omega $ and $	heta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho \geq \varepsilon \Omega $. Proof. We first locate the boundary of $\mathscr P$ along the path. Let $s<t$. Since $\alpha $ is nef, for every $\delta >0$ there is a smooth function $v_\delta $ with $\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\delta \geq -\delta \Omega $. Taking $\delta <t-s$ makes $a_ s+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\delta $ Kähler, and adding $B\geq 0$ gives a positive representative of $	heta _ s$. The same approximations show that $	heta _ t$ is nef. On the other hand, the hypotheses on $C$ and Stokes' theorem on the compact curve give \[  \int _ C(	heta _ s+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)=(t-s)\int _ C\Omega  \] for every smooth $v$. At $s=t$ the right side vanishes, which excludes a positive representative of $	heta _ t$. For $s>t$, a representative with $	heta _ s+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq -\delta \Omega $ and $\delta <s-t$ would contradict this identity, so $	heta _ s$ is not nef. Since every $a_ s$ with $s\leq t$ is closed and nef, the closed nef formula following theorem 12.11.1 gives $\lambda _\mu (a_ s)=V_ s^{1/n}$, including at $s=t$. The difference $	heta _ t-a_ t=B$ is semipositive, so monotonicity gives $\lambda _\mu (	heta _ t)\geq V^{1/n}$, while any fixed Gauduchon test bounds $\lambda _\mu (	heta _ t)$ from above. Since $	heta _ s=	heta _ t+(t-s)\Omega $, theorem 12.11.1 with the Hermitian form $\Omega $ identifies $\lambda _\mu (	heta _ t)$ with the limit of $\lambda _\mu (	heta _ s)$ as $s\uparrow t$. Write $f(s)=\lambda _\mu (	heta _ s)$ for $s<t$. The path has constant velocity $-\Omega $, so proposition 12.3.2 shows that $f$ is smooth and \[  H(s):= rac{\int _ X\Omega \wedge g_ s^{n-1}}{D_\mu (g_ s)}=-f'(s).  \] In particular, the ratio $H$ is continuous and independent of the choice of minimizing metrics. For $r<t$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \[  \int _0^ rH(s)\, \mathrm{d}s=f(0)-f(r).  \] Since $H\geq 0$, letting $r\uparrow t$ and using the limit just established yields the identity in ( 12.12.3 ). It remains to bound $f(0)=\lambda _\mu (	heta _0)$ from above by two test metrics. The Kähler form $\kappa _0$ is Gauduchon, and since $\kappa _0$ is cohomologous to $a_0$, closed Stokes gives $\int _ X	heta _0\wedge \kappa _0^{n-1}=V_0+I_ B$; hence $\lambda _\mu (	heta _0)\leq U_\mu $. For the second test $\gamma _0$, the equation $\gamma _0^ n=V_0\mu $ and the cohomology class of $\gamma _0$ give \[  D_\mu (\gamma _0)=V_0^{(n-1)/n},\qquad \int _ Xa_0\wedge \gamma _0^{n-1}=V_0,  \] so its quotient for $	heta _0$ is $V_0^{1/n}+\Delta _\mu (B)$. Combined with the lower bound $\lambda _\mu (	heta _ t)\geq V^{1/n}$, these two tests prove the upper bound in ( 12.12.3 ). If $B\leq M\kappa _0$, closed Stokes yields $\int _ XB\wedge \gamma _0^{n-1}\leq M\int _ X\kappa _0\wedge \gamma _0^{n-1}=MV_0$, which gives the remaining cost bounds. Finally, $V=\int _ X\alpha ^ n>0$, so the closed nef class of $\alpha $ is big by the nef-and-big criterion on compact Kähler manifolds recalled in [ SGPT ] . Hence it contains a Kähler current $\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho \geq \varepsilon \Omega $. Adding $B\geq 0$ gives the last assertion. Unlike the first current, the second is not closed when $\mathrm dB
eq 0$, since its exterior derivative is $\mathrm{d}B$. $\square$ Such data arise from a bimeromorphic holomorphic map $p:X	o Y$ onto a compact Kähler manifold $Y$ that contracts a smooth curve $C$ to a point. Take $\alpha =p^*\omega _ Y$, with $\omega _ Y$ Kähler, and any smooth $B\geq 0$ vanishing on $TC$. Since $p$ has degree one, $\int _ X\alpha ^ n=\int _ Y\omega _ Y^ n>0$, while both curve integrals vanish. The second initial test separates the closed intersection number $I_ B$ from a correction that involves only $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}B$. Proposition 12.12.4 . FBFFC53EC40F Set $S=\sum _{j=0}^{n-2}\gamma _0^ j\wedge \kappa _0^{n-2-j}$. Then 91D85F52923D 12.12.5  egin{equation}  \Delta _\mu (B)=V_0^{-(n-1)/n} \left(I_ B+\int _ Xu_0\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}B\wedge Sight). \end{equation} If $-C_ B\kappa _0^2\leq \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}B\leq C_ B\kappa _0^2$ in the sense of weak positivity of $(2,2)$-forms, then \[  \Delta _\mu (B)\leq V_0^{-(n-1)/n}I_ B +(n-1)C_ B\operatorname {osc}_ X(u_0)V_0^{1/n}.  \] Such a finite constant $C_ B$ exists for every fixed smooth $B$. eq 0$, \[  \lambda _\mu (	heta _1)\geq  rac32,\qquad 0\leq \mathcal C\leq  rac{11}{\sqrt8}- rac32,  \] and an explicit current $	heta _1+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}ho \geq  rac12\Omega $ at the nef endpoint. e 0$, the form $L$ is symplectic, and wedging with $L$ is injective on real one-forms in real dimension four. Hence $\mathrm{d}B=	frac 12\mathrm{d}f\wedge L
e 0$. At the endpoint $	heta _1=(2+f/2)L\geq 3L/2$, and $\lambda _\mu (L)=1$ by the closed nef formula; this gives the lower bound for $\lambda _\mu (	heta _1)$.
