title: Theorem 12.12.2
section: 12.12 Subtraction with a closed nef core
text: Theorem 12.12.2 . 026E84610646 Suppose that $V:=V_ t>0$ and that there is a smooth compact complex curve $C\subset X$ with $\int _ C\alpha =\int _ CB=0$. Then $\theta _ s$ has a smooth positive representative for $s<t$, $\theta _ t$ is nef but has no smooth positive representative, and $\theta _ s$ is not nef for $s>t$. Moreover, \[  \lambda _\mu (a_ s)=V_ s^{1/n}\quad (0\leq s\leq t), \qquad \lambda _\mu (\theta _ t)\geq V^{1/n}>0.  \] For every choice of minimizing Gauduchon metrics $g_ s$ for $\theta _ s$, $0\leq s<t$, the ratio $\int _ X\Omega \wedge g_ s^{n-1}/D_\mu (g_ s)$ is a continuous function of $s$, and the subtraction cost satisfies 2FB723BB4645 12.12.3 \begin{equation}  \begin{split}  0\leq \mathcal C & :=\int _0^ t\frac{\int _ X\Omega \wedge g_ s^{n-1}}{D_\mu (g_ s)}\, \mathrm{d}s =\lambda _\mu (\theta _0)-\lambda _\mu (\theta _ t)\\ & \leq \min \{ U_\mu ,V_0^{1/n}+\Delta _\mu (B)\} -V^{1/n}<\infty , \end{split} \end{equation} where the integral is improper at $t$. If $B\leq M\kappa _0$ for a constant $M\geq 0$, then \[  \Delta _\mu (B)\leq MV_0^{1/n},\qquad \mathcal C\leq (1+M)V_0^{1/n}-V^{1/n}.  \] Finally, there are a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $\rho $ and a constant $\varepsilon >0$ with $\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \varepsilon \Omega $ and $\theta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \varepsilon \Omega $. Proof. We first locate the boundary of $\mathscr P$ along the path. Let $s<t$. Since $\alpha $ is nef, for every $\delta >0$ there is a smooth function $v_\delta $ with $\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\delta \geq -\delta \Omega $. Taking $\delta <t-s$ makes $a_ s+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\delta $ Kähler, and adding $B\geq 0$ gives a positive representative of $\theta _ s$. The same approximations show that $\theta _ t$ is nef. On the other hand, the hypotheses on $C$ and Stokes' theorem on the compact curve give \[  \int _ C(\theta _ s+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)=(t-s)\int _ C\Omega  \] for every smooth $v$. At $s=t$ the right side vanishes, which excludes a positive representative of $\theta _ t$. For $s>t$, a representative with $\theta _ s+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq -\delta \Omega $ and $\delta <s-t$ would contradict this identity, so $\theta _ s$ is not nef. Since every $a_ s$ with $s\leq t$ is closed and nef, the closed nef formula following theorem 12.11.1 gives $\lambda _\mu (a_ s)=V_ s^{1/n}$, including at $s=t$. The difference $\theta _ t-a_ t=B$ is semipositive, so monotonicity gives $\lambda _\mu (\theta _ t)\geq V^{1/n}$, while any fixed Gauduchon test bounds $\lambda _\mu (\theta _ t)$ from above. Since $\theta _ s=\theta _ t+(t-s)\Omega $, theorem 12.11.1 with the Hermitian form $\Omega $ identifies $\lambda _\mu (\theta _ t)$ with the limit of $\lambda _\mu (\theta _ s)$ as $s\uparrow t$. Write $f(s)=\lambda _\mu (\theta _ s)$ for $s<t$. The path has constant velocity $-\Omega $, so proposition 12.3.2 shows that $f$ is smooth and \[  H(s):=\frac{\int _ X\Omega \wedge g_ s^{n-1}}{D_\mu (g_ s)}=-f'(s).  \] In particular, the ratio $H$ is continuous and independent of the choice of minimizing metrics. For $r<t$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \[  \int _0^ rH(s)\, \mathrm{d}s=f(0)-f(r).  \] Since $H\geq 0$, letting $r\uparrow t$ and using the limit just established yields the identity in ( 12.12.3 ). It remains to bound $f(0)=\lambda _\mu (\theta _0)$ from above by two test metrics. The Kähler form $\kappa _0$ is Gauduchon, and since $\kappa _0$ is cohomologous to $a_0$, closed Stokes gives $\int _ X\theta _0\wedge \kappa _0^{n-1}=V_0+I_ B$; hence $\lambda _\mu (\theta _0)\leq U_\mu $. For the second test $\gamma _0$, the equation $\gamma _0^ n=V_0\mu $ and the cohomology class of $\gamma _0$ give \[  D_\mu (\gamma _0)=V_0^{(n-1)/n},\qquad \int _ Xa_0\wedge \gamma _0^{n-1}=V_0,  \] so its quotient for $\theta _0$ is $V_0^{1/n}+\Delta _\mu (B)$. Combined with the lower bound $\lambda _\mu (\theta _ t)\geq V^{1/n}$, these two tests prove the upper bound in ( 12.12.3 ). If $B\leq M\kappa _0$, closed Stokes yields $\int _ XB\wedge \gamma _0^{n-1}\leq M\int _ X\kappa _0\wedge \gamma _0^{n-1}=MV_0$, which gives the remaining cost bounds. Finally, $V=\int _ X\alpha ^ n>0$, so the closed nef class of $\alpha $ is big by the nef-and-big criterion on compact Kähler manifolds recalled in [ SGPT ] . Hence it contains a Kähler current $\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\rho \geq \varepsilon \Omega $. Adding $B\geq 0$ gives the last assertion. Unlike the first current, the second is not closed when $\mathrm dB\neq 0$, since its exterior derivative is $\mathrm{d}B$. $\square$

title: 12.13 Subtraction on warped products
text: The closed core in section 12.12 keeps the endpoint big. On a warped product, the subtraction cost can instead be computed all the way to an endpoint that is not big. Its rate is determined by two inverse moments of the fiber coefficient, while its total integral remains finite even when the endpoint volume vanishes. Let $(B,\alpha )$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $m\geq 2$, put $W=\int _ B\alpha ^ m$, and let $C$ be a connected compact complex curve. Fix smooth strictly positive probability forms $\sigma $ on $B$ and $w$ on $C$. On $X=B\times C$, of dimension $n=m+1$, use $\mu =\sigma \wedge w$ and omit pullbacks. For a smooth function $a\geq 0$ on $B$ and a real number $t>0$, set \[  \theta _ s=\alpha +(a+t-s)w\quad (s<t),\qquad \theta _ t=\alpha +aw.  \] The endpoint is semipositive, hence nef. For $\epsilon >0$, write \[  H(\epsilon )=\int _ B\frac{\sigma }{a+\epsilon },\qquad J(\epsilon )=\int _ B\frac{\sigma }{(a+\epsilon )^2},\qquad H(0)=\int _ B\frac{\sigma }{a},  \] allowing $H(0)=+\infty $, with $1/a=+\infty $ at a zero of $a$. Theorem 12.13.1 . B5C9469E9BB3 For $s<t$, the full Gauduchon infimum is attained by a balanced metric and \[  \mathcal V_\mu (\theta _ s)=\frac{nW}{H(t-s)},\qquad \mathcal V_\mu (\theta _ t)=\frac{nW}{H(0)},  \] where the last value is zero if $H(0)=+\infty $. Every minimizing Gauduchon metric $g_ s$ at $s$ has the same subtraction cost 503F3EDAE05A 12.13.2 \begin{equation}  \frac{\int _ Xw\wedge g_ s^{n-1}}{D_\mu (g_ s)} =\mathcal C(s) :=n^{-(n-1)/n}W^{1/n} H(t-s)^{-(n+1)/n}J(t-s). \end{equation} For every selection of these metrics, the improper integral satisfies C0A4C9A1103C 12.13.3 \begin{equation}  \int _0^ t\mathcal C(s)\, \mathrm{d}s =\lambda _\mu (\theta _0)-\lambda _\mu (\theta _ t)<\infty . \end{equation} Proof. Put $\epsilon =t-s$ and $L=a+\epsilon $. Apply theorem 14.2.1 on the closed positive base to obtain \[  A_\epsilon =\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _\epsilon >0,\qquad A_\epsilon ^ m=\frac{W}{H(\epsilon )}\frac{\sigma }{L}.  \] The target has total mass $W$, so closed Stokes fixes its scalar. The construction of theorem 12.6.32 , now without a normalization of $W$ or a nonconstancy requirement on $a$, gives \[  \Omega _\epsilon =A_\epsilon +Lw,\qquad \Omega _\epsilon ^ n=\frac{nW}{H(\epsilon )}\mu , \qquad \gamma _ s=L^{-1/m}\Omega _\epsilon .  \] Indeed, \[  \gamma _ s^ m=L^{-1}A_\epsilon ^ m +mA_\epsilon ^{m-1}\wedge w  \] is closed: its first summand has top degree on the base, and its second has closed factors. Thus $\gamma _ s$ is balanced. Gauduchon Stokes and the matrix arithmetic–geometric mean inequality give \[  \int _ X\theta _ s\wedge \xi ^ m \geq \left(\frac{nW}{H(\epsilon )}\right)^{1/n}D_\mu (\xi )  \] for every Gauduchon metric $\xi $. The metric $\gamma _ s$ attains equality, with numerator $nW$ and denominator $(nW/H)^{m/n}H$. This proves the full volume formula. For every fixed test, its quotient at $\theta _ t+\epsilon w$ decreases to its quotient at $\theta _ t$. The two infima, over $\epsilon >0$ and over the tests, commute, as in theorem 12.11.1 . Hence the endpoint value is the limit of the strict values. Monotone convergence of $H(\epsilon )$ gives the asserted value, including when the integral is infinite. The cost numerator for the displayed balanced metric is $WJ/H$. Dividing by its denominator gives ( 12.13.2 ). Also $\mathrm{d}H(t-s)/\mathrm{d}s=J(t-s)$, so differentiation of the volume formula gives $-\mathrm{d}\lambda _\mu (\theta _ s)/\mathrm{d}s=\mathcal C(s)$. By proposition 12.3.2 this is the cost of every minimizing metric, regardless of the regularity of the selection. On each interval $[0,r]$ with $r<t$, integrate this identity. Since $\mathcal C\geq 0$ and the root volume has the finite endpoint limit just proved, letting $r\uparrow t$ gives ( 12.13.3 ). $\square$ The identity applies to every smooth nonnegative coefficient, including coefficients with flat zeros. Finite-order zeros give more precise rates. Fix a Riemannian metric on $B$ for the following distance comparisons. Proposition 12.13.4 . 6E8682D7FD89 Suppose that $Z=\{ a=0\} $ is a nonempty smooth compact real submanifold of positive codimension $d$, that $a\asymp \operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,Z)^ k$ in a fixed tube for a real number $k>0$, and that $a$ is bounded below by a positive constant outside that tube. Put $r=d/k$. Then, as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, F4721C1DF1D8 12.13.5 \begin{equation}  \mathcal C(t-\epsilon )\asymp \begin{cases}  \epsilon ^{(1-r)/n-1},& r<1,\\  \epsilon ^{-1}(\log (1/\epsilon ))^{-(n+1)/n},& r=1,\\  \epsilon ^{r-2},& 1<r<2,\\  \log (1/\epsilon ),& r=2,\\  1,& r>2. \end{cases} \end{equation} Each rate is integrable, and the endpoint volume is positive exactly when $d>k$. For $r>2$, the cost tends to \[  n^{-(n-1)/n}W^{1/n}H(0)^{-(n+1)/n}J(0)>0, \qquad J(0)=\int _ B\frac{\sigma }{a^2}.  \] For finitely many disjoint zero components satisfying these hypotheses with codimensions $d_ i$ and orders $k_ i$, the same assertions hold with $r=\min _ i d_ i/k_ i$. Proof. The positive density and the tubular Jacobians are bounded above and below by positive constants. For $p=1,2$, radial integration therefore gives \[  \int _ B\frac{\sigma }{(a+\epsilon )^ p} \asymp 1+\int _0^ R\frac{u^{d-1}}{(u^ k+\epsilon )^ p}\, \mathrm{d}u =1+\frac{\epsilon ^{r-p}}k \int _0^{R^ k/\epsilon }\frac{v^{r-1}}{(1+v)^ p}\, \mathrm{d}v,  \] with the equality applying to the radial expression. For $r<p$ the last integral tends to a finite positive constant; for $r=p$ it grows logarithmically; for $r>p$ the unregularized moment is finite, and monotone convergence gives its positive limit. Applying this to $H$ and $J$ in ( 12.13.2 ) proves the five rates and the criterion $H(0)<\infty $ exactly when $r>1$. The power $(1-r)/n-1$ exceeds $-1$ for $r<1$, as does $r-2$ for $1<r<2$. At $r=1$, substitution of $\log (1/\epsilon )$ gives an integrable tail because $(n+1)/n>1$. The logarithmic and bounded rates are also integrable. When $r>2$, both inverse moments have finite positive limits, which gives the displayed limit. With finitely many disjoint components, the moments are finite sums of positive tube contributions and a bounded complement term; their smallest ratio determines the divergence, without cancellation. $\square$ Proposition 12.13.6 . 172CF285DEA0 The endpoint $\theta _ t$ is big exactly when $a$ is positive everywhere. If $a$ has a zero, there is no decomposition \[  \theta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=\chi +\beta  \] with $f$ smooth and real, $\chi $ smooth and closed with nef class and $\int _ X\chi ^ n>0$, and $\beta \geq 0$ smooth. Proof. Suppose that $\theta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \delta (\alpha +w)$ for a quasi-plurisubharmonic $u$ and $\delta >0$. Pull back an arbitrary smooth nonnegative top-degree form $\zeta $ on $B$. It is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed by dimension, so Stokes' theorem for distributions gives \[  0\leq \int _ X(\theta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-\delta (\alpha +w))\wedge \zeta =\int _ B(a-\delta )\zeta .  \] A nonzero $\zeta $ supported where $a<\delta $ contradicts this inequality. Thus a zero excludes every strict current representative; no singular potential has been restricted to its zero fiber. Conversely, if $a>0$ everywhere, compactness makes $\theta _ t$ itself Hermitian, so it is big. For a proposed decomposition, the closed nef-and-big criterion used in theorem 12.12.2 supplies a global quasi-plurisubharmonic $v$ with $\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq \delta (\alpha +w)$ for some $\delta >0$. Then \[  \theta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(f+v)=\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v+\beta \geq \delta (\alpha +w),  \] contradicting the first part. This excludes any such closed core, including after a smooth change of gauge. $\square$ In the closed case $a\equiv a_0\geq 0$, put $P=\alpha +(a_0+t)w$ and $Q=tw$. These closed nef forms satisfy 1B46207D92EB 12.13.7 \begin{equation}  \int _ XP^ n-n\int _ XP^{n-1}\wedge Q =nWa_0=\mathcal V_\mu (\theta _ t). \end{equation} This is the expression on the right of the closed Morse inequality discussed in section 25.22 ; the equality follows from $w^2=0$, $\alpha ^{m+1}=0$ and $\int _ Cw=1$. For nonconstant $a$, the exterior derivative $\mathrm{d}\theta _ s=\mathrm{d}a\wedge w$ is not identically zero, and the endpoint formula retains the specified probability $\sigma $ through $H(0)$. The comparison in ( 12.13.7 ) therefore concerns the constant closed case. For example, take $B=\mathbb P^ m$, normalized Fubini–Study $\alpha $, $\sigma =\alpha ^ m$, and $a([Z])=\sum _{j=1}^ m|Z_ j|^2/\sum _{j=0}^ m|Z_ j|^2$. Its law under $\sigma $ is $m x^{m-1}\, \mathrm{d}x$ on $[0,1]$, by the radial integration used in theorem 12.14.6 . Hence $W=1$, $H(0)=m/(m-1)$ and $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta _ t)=(m+1)(m-1)/m>0$, while the endpoint is not big and admits no closed nef core of positive top intersection. Its sole zero has real codimension $2m$ and order two. The cost is therefore logarithmic when $m=2$ and tends to a positive finite value when $m>2$, by proposition 12.13.4 .

title: Theorem 12.13.1
text: Theorem 12.13.1 . B5C9469E9BB3 For $s<t$, the full Gauduchon infimum is attained by a balanced metric and \[  \mathcal V_\mu (\theta _ s)=\frac{nW}{H(t-s)},\qquad \mathcal V_\mu (\theta _ t)=\frac{nW}{H(0)},  \] where the last value is zero if $H(0)=+\infty $. Every minimizing Gauduchon metric $g_ s$ at $s$ has the same subtraction cost 503F3EDAE05A 12.13.2 \begin{equation}  \frac{\int _ Xw\wedge g_ s^{n-1}}{D_\mu (g_ s)} =\mathcal C(s) :=n^{-(n-1)/n}W^{1/n} H(t-s)^{-(n+1)/n}J(t-s). \end{equation} For every selection of these metrics, the improper integral satisfies C0A4C9A1103C 12.13.3 \begin{equation}  \int _0^ t\mathcal C(s)\, \mathrm{d}s =\lambda _\mu (\theta _0)-\lambda _\mu (\theta _ t)<\infty . \end{equation} Proof. Put $\epsilon =t-s$ and $L=a+\epsilon $. Apply theorem 14.2.1 on the closed positive base to obtain \[  A_\epsilon =\alpha +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi _\epsilon >0,\qquad A_\epsilon ^ m=\frac{W}{H(\epsilon )}\frac{\sigma }{L}.  \] The target has total mass $W$, so closed Stokes fixes its scalar. The construction of theorem 12.6.32 , now without a normalization of $W$ or a nonconstancy requirement on $a$, gives \[  \Omega _\epsilon =A_\epsilon +Lw,\qquad \Omega _\epsilon ^ n=\frac{nW}{H(\epsilon )}\mu , \qquad \gamma _ s=L^{-1/m}\Omega _\epsilon .  \] Indeed, \[  \gamma _ s^ m=L^{-1}A_\epsilon ^ m +mA_\epsilon ^{m-1}\wedge w  \] is closed: its first summand has top degree on the base, and its second has closed factors. Thus $\gamma _ s$ is balanced. Gauduchon Stokes and the matrix arithmetic–geometric mean inequality give \[  \int _ X\theta _ s\wedge \xi ^ m \geq \left(\frac{nW}{H(\epsilon )}\right)^{1/n}D_\mu (\xi )  \] for every Gauduchon metric $\xi $. The metric $\gamma _ s$ attains equality, with numerator $nW$ and denominator $(nW/H)^{m/n}H$. This proves the full volume formula. For every fixed test, its quotient at $\theta _ t+\epsilon w$ decreases to its quotient at $\theta _ t$. The two infima, over $\epsilon >0$ and over the tests, commute, as in theorem 12.11.1 . Hence the endpoint value is the limit of the strict values. Monotone convergence of $H(\epsilon )$ gives the asserted value, including when the integral is infinite. The cost numerator for the displayed balanced metric is $WJ/H$. Dividing by its denominator gives ( 12.13.2 ). Also $\mathrm{d}H(t-s)/\mathrm{d}s=J(t-s)$, so differentiation of the volume formula gives $-\mathrm{d}\lambda _\mu (\theta _ s)/\mathrm{d}s=\mathcal C(s)$. By proposition 12.3.2 this is the cost of every minimizing metric, regardless of the regularity of the selection. On each interval $[0,r]$ with $r<t$, integrate this identity. Since $\mathcal C\geq 0$ and the root volume has the finite endpoint limit just proved, letting $r\uparrow t$ gives ( 12.13.3 ). $\square$

title: Proposition 12.13.4
text: Proposition 12.13.4 . 6E8682D7FD89 Suppose that $Z=\{ a=0\} $ is a nonempty smooth compact real submanifold of positive codimension $d$, that $a\asymp \operatorname {dist}(\cdot ,Z)^ k$ in a fixed tube for a real number $k>0$, and that $a$ is bounded below by a positive constant outside that tube. Put $r=d/k$. Then, as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, F4721C1DF1D8 12.13.5 \begin{equation}  \mathcal C(t-\epsilon )\asymp \begin{cases}  \epsilon ^{(1-r)/n-1},& r<1,\\  \epsilon ^{-1}(\log (1/\epsilon ))^{-(n+1)/n},& r=1,\\  \epsilon ^{r-2},& 1<r<2,\\  \log (1/\epsilon ),& r=2,\\  1,& r>2. \end{cases} \end{equation} Each rate is integrable, and the endpoint volume is positive exactly when $d>k$. For $r>2$, the cost tends to \[  n^{-(n-1)/n}W^{1/n}H(0)^{-(n+1)/n}J(0)>0, \qquad J(0)=\int _ B\frac{\sigma }{a^2}.  \] For finitely many disjoint zero components satisfying these hypotheses with codimensions $d_ i$ and orders $k_ i$, the same assertions hold with $r=\min _ i d_ i/k_ i$. Proof. The positive density and the tubular Jacobians are bounded above and below by positive constants. For $p=1,2$, radial integration therefore gives \[  \int _ B\frac{\sigma }{(a+\epsilon )^ p} \asymp 1+\int _0^ R\frac{u^{d-1}}{(u^ k+\epsilon )^ p}\, \mathrm{d}u =1+\frac{\epsilon ^{r-p}}k \int _0^{R^ k/\epsilon }\frac{v^{r-1}}{(1+v)^ p}\, \mathrm{d}v,  \] with the equality applying to the radial expression. For $r<p$ the last integral tends to a finite positive constant; for $r=p$ it grows logarithmically; for $r>p$ the unregularized moment is finite, and monotone convergence gives its positive limit. Applying this to $H$ and $J$ in ( 12.13.2 ) proves the five rates and the criterion $H(0)<\infty $ exactly when $r>1$. The power $(1-r)/n-1$ exceeds $-1$ for $r<1$, as does $r-2$ for $1<r<2$. At $r=1$, substitution of $\log (1/\epsilon )$ gives an integrable tail because $(n+1)/n>1$. The logarithmic and bounded rates are also integrable. When $r>2$, both inverse moments have finite positive limits, which gives the displayed limit. With finitely many disjoint components, the moments are finite sums of positive tube contributions and a bounded complement term; their smallest ratio determines the divergence, without cancellation. $\square$

title: Proposition 12.13.6
text: Proposition 12.13.6 . 172CF285DEA0 The endpoint $\theta _ t$ is big exactly when $a$ is positive everywhere. If $a$ has a zero, there is no decomposition \[  \theta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f=\chi +\beta  \] with $f$ smooth and real, $\chi $ smooth and closed with nef class and $\int _ X\chi ^ n>0$, and $\beta \geq 0$ smooth. Proof. Suppose that $\theta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq \delta (\alpha +w)$ for a quasi-plurisubharmonic $u$ and $\delta >0$. Pull back an arbitrary smooth nonnegative top-degree form $\zeta $ on $B$. It is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed by dimension, so Stokes' theorem for distributions gives \[  0\leq \int _ X(\theta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u-\delta (\alpha +w))\wedge \zeta =\int _ B(a-\delta )\zeta .  \] A nonzero $\zeta $ supported where $a<\delta $ contradicts this inequality. Thus a zero excludes every strict current representative; no singular potential has been restricted to its zero fiber. Conversely, if $a>0$ everywhere, compactness makes $\theta _ t$ itself Hermitian, so it is big. For a proposed decomposition, the closed nef-and-big criterion used in theorem 12.12.2 supplies a global quasi-plurisubharmonic $v$ with $\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq \delta (\alpha +w)$ for some $\delta >0$. Then \[  \theta _ t+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(f+v)=\chi +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v+\beta \geq \delta (\alpha +w),  \] contradicting the first part. This excludes any such closed core, including after a smooth change of gauge. $\square$

title: 12.14 Positive volume without bigness
text: By corollary 12.2.4 , every big background has positive volume. For a closed nef class on a compact Kähler manifold the converse also holds: the volume is then $\int _ X\theta ^ n$, and a closed nef class with positive top self-intersection is big. We now show that the converse fails for nonclosed nef backgrounds, even on a projective manifold: such a background can have positive volume without containing a Kähler current. In the example, the coefficient of a fiber direction vanishes at one point of the base. A radial potential on the base compensates for this vanishing, and the determinant of the resulting current bounds every Gauduchon quotient from below. Bigness, on the other hand, is excluded by pairing with a closed semipositive form concentrated near the vanishing point. Throughout this section fix an integer $m\geq 2$, and put $n=m+1$, $t=(m-1)/m$ and $B=\mathbb P^ m$. Give $B$ and $\mathbb P^1$ their Fubini–Study forms $\omega $ and $w$, normalized by $\int _ B\omega ^ m=\int _{\mathbb P^1}w=1$. On $B$ define \[  x([Z_0:\cdots :Z_ m])= \frac{\sum _{j=1}^ m|Z_ j|^2}{\sum _{j=0}^ m|Z_ j|^2}, \qquad a=x/t,\qquad p=[1:0:\cdots :0].  \] Thus $x$ is a smooth function on $B$ with values in $[0,1]$; it vanishes only at $p$ and equals one on the hyperplane $\{ Z_0=0\} $. On $X=B\times \mathbb P^1$, with pullbacks understood, set \[  h=\omega +w,\qquad \mu =\omega ^ m\wedge w, \qquad \theta =\omega +a w.  \] For $\epsilon >0$ put 71973446DB97 12.14.1 \begin{equation}  H_\epsilon =m\int _0^1\frac{y^{m-1}}{y/t+\epsilon }\, \mathrm{d}y. \end{equation} Lemma 12.14.2 . C0A6E438A11D There are smooth real functions $\varphi _\epsilon $ on $B$ such that $A_\epsilon =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _\epsilon >0$ and 471F6FE31EB0 12.14.3 \begin{equation}  A_\epsilon ^ m=\frac{\omega ^ m}{H_\epsilon (a+\epsilon )}. \end{equation} As $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ they converge uniformly to a bounded continuous function $\varphi \in \mathrm{PSH}(B,\omega )$ that is smooth on $B\setminus \{ p\} $. On $B\setminus \{ p\} $ the current $A=\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is a smooth strictly positive form satisfying C34D8558189E 12.14.4 \begin{equation}  A^ m=a^{-1}\omega ^ m. \end{equation} Moreover $H_\epsilon \to 1$ as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. Proof. In the affine chart $Z_0=1$, write $s=|z|^2$. Then $x=s/(1+s)$ and $\omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log (1+s)$. Polar integration gives 8523C0528005 12.14.5 \begin{equation}  \int _ B b(x)\omega ^ m=m\int _0^1 b(y)y^{m-1}\, \mathrm{d}y \end{equation} for every integrable function $b$ on $[0,1]$, since the normalized radial density of $\omega ^ m$ in the variable $s$ is $m s^{m-1}(1+s)^{-m-1}\, \mathrm{d}s$. In particular $\int _ B a^{-1}\omega ^ m=mt/(m-1)=1$, and monotone convergence in ( 12.14.1 ) gives $H_\epsilon \to 1$. Define $q_\epsilon \geq 0$ and $\varphi _\epsilon $ on $[0,1]$ by \[  q_\epsilon (x)^ m=\frac m{H_\epsilon } \int _0^ x\frac{y^{m-1}}{y/t+\epsilon }\, \mathrm{d}y, \qquad \varphi _\epsilon (x)=\int _0^ x \frac{q_\epsilon (y)-y}{y(1-y)}\, \mathrm{d}y.  \] Near zero, \[  q_\epsilon (x)=x\left(\frac m{H_\epsilon } \int _0^1\frac{u^{m-1}}{xu/t+\epsilon }\, \mathrm{d}u\right)^{1/m},  \] so $q_\epsilon $ is $x$ times a smooth positive function; moreover $q_\epsilon (1)=1$. Hence both apparent singularities of $\varphi _\epsilon '$, at $0$ and at $1$, are removable, and $\varphi _\epsilon $ is smooth on $[0,1]$. Composing with the smooth function $x$ gives a smooth function on $B$, again denoted $\varphi _\epsilon $. To compute $A_\epsilon $, recall that for a local potential of the form $F(s)$, with $q=sF'(s)$, the complex Hessian has the tangential eigenvalue $q/s$, of multiplicity $m-1$, and the radial eigenvalue $\mathrm{d}q/\mathrm{d}s$. For $F_\epsilon =\log (1+s)+\varphi _\epsilon (x)$ one finds $sF_\epsilon '=q_\epsilon (x)$. Differentiating the integral defining $q_\epsilon $ shows that both eigenvalues are positive, also at $s=0$ by the smooth factorization above. Their product relative to the Fubini–Study determinant is \[  \frac{A_\epsilon ^ m}{\omega ^ m} =\frac{q_\epsilon ^{m-1}q_\epsilon '}{x^{m-1}} =\frac1{H_\epsilon (a+\epsilon )}.  \] At a point of the hyperplane $\{ Z_0=0\} $, the smooth form $A_\epsilon $ is semipositive, as a limit of the positive matrices in the affine chart. Since the determinant just computed extends there with a strictly positive value, every eigenvalue is positive. This proves strict positivity on all of $B$ and ( 12.14.3 ). We now pass to the limit. For $x>0$, $q_\epsilon (x)$ tends to $x^ t$. To bound $q_\epsilon $ uniformly, note that $q_\epsilon ^ m$ is the distribution function of the probability density $\frac{m}{H_\epsilon }\frac{y^{m-1}}{y/t+\epsilon }$ on $[0,1]$. Relative to the probability density $my^{m-1}$, this density has a decreasing weight; relative to $(m-1)y^{m-2}$, its weight is proportional to $y/(y+t\epsilon )$ and hence increasing. If one probability density on $[0,1]$ has a decreasing weight relative to another, its average weight on $[0,x]$ is at least one and its distribution function is the larger of the two; an increasing weight reverses the inequality. Consequently \[  x^ m\leq q_\epsilon (x)^ m\leq x^{m-1}, \qquad \text{that is,}\qquad x\leq q_\epsilon (x)\leq x^ t.  \] The function \[  \varphi (x)=\int _0^ x\frac{y^ t-y}{y(1-y)}\, \mathrm{d}y  \] is bounded and continuous on $[0,1]$, since $t>0$, and smooth on $(0,1]$; its derivative extends smoothly at one. The integrable function $(y^ t-y)/[y(1-y)]$ dominates the derivatives of the functions $\varphi _\epsilon $, so dominated convergence gives uniform convergence $\varphi _\epsilon \to \varphi $ on $B$. Distributional convergence shows that $A$ is a closed positive current. On each coordinate chart, a smooth local potential of $\omega $ plus $\varphi $ is a uniform limit of the corresponding plurisubharmonic functions built with $\varphi _\epsilon $, including at $p$. Hence $\varphi $ is $\omega $-plurisubharmonic. Off $p$, the limit $q=x^ t$ gives \[  \frac{A^ m}{\omega ^ m} =\frac{(x^ t)^{m-1}t x^{t-1}}{x^{m-1}}=\frac tx=\frac1a.  \] Smoothness of $\varphi $ off $p$ and the same determinant argument at the hyperplane $\{ Z_0=0\} $ prove ( 12.14.4 ). $\square$ Theorem 12.14.6 . ECAB6BFB33FD The background $\theta $ on $X$ is smooth, semipositive, nef and nonclosed. It is not big, but 3D231D52B18A 12.14.7 \begin{equation}  \lambda _\mu (\theta )=n^{1/n},\qquad \mathcal V_\mu (\theta )=n. \end{equation} For $\theta _\epsilon =\omega +(a+\epsilon )w$, one has \[  \mathcal V_\mu (\theta _\epsilon )=\frac n{H_\epsilon },  \] and the smooth positive metrics F9FEC7FAC55E 12.14.8 \begin{equation}  \gamma _\epsilon =(a+\epsilon )^{-1/m} \bigl (A_\epsilon +(a+\epsilon )w\bigr ) \end{equation} are balanced and minimize the defining quotient at $\theta _\epsilon $. Proof. The coefficient $a$ is nonnegative, and $\theta +\eta h>0$ for every $\eta >0$; this proves semipositivity and nefness. Since $a$ is nonconstant, $\mathrm{d}\theta =\mathrm{d}a\wedge w\ne 0$. Suppose that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq \delta h$ for a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $v$ and some $\delta >0$. Choose a nonzero smooth function $f\geq 0$ on $B$ supported in $\{ a<\delta \} $. Its pullback $S=f\omega ^ m$ is a smooth semipositive $(m,m)$-form, closed because it has top degree on the base. Positivity and distributional Stokes would give \[  0\leq \int _ X(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v-\delta h)\wedge S =\int _ B f(a-\delta )\omega ^ m<0.  \] This contradiction shows that $\theta $ is not big, since every Hermitian form on $X$ dominates a positive multiple of $h$. For the lower bound on the volume, pull back the bounded potential $\varphi $ of lemma 12.14.2 . The positive current $\Omega =A+a w=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is a smooth strictly positive form off $Z=\{ p\} \times \mathbb P^1$, where \[  \Omega ^ n=n a A^ m\wedge w=n\mu .  \] Let $\gamma $ be a Gauduchon metric. Since $\varphi $ is bounded, distributional Stokes lets us replace $\theta $ by $\Omega $ in the numerator of its quotient. The set $Z$ has zero smooth volume and $\Omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ is a positive measure, so the pointwise arithmetic–geometric mean inequality off $Z$ gives \[  \int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \geq n^{1/n}\int _ X (\mu /\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n =n^{1/n}D_\mu (\gamma ).  \] This lower bound holds for every test in definition 12.2.1 ; no power of the current $\Omega $ along $Z$ is needed. For the upper bound, put $c_\epsilon =n/H_\epsilon $ and $\Omega _\epsilon =A_\epsilon +(a+\epsilon )w=\theta _\epsilon +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _\epsilon $. Then $\Omega _\epsilon ^ n=c_\epsilon \mu $. The metrics in ( 12.14.8 ) satisfy \[  T_\epsilon =\gamma _\epsilon ^ m =(a+\epsilon )^{-1}A_\epsilon ^ m +m A_\epsilon ^{m-1}\wedge w.  \] The first term has top degree on the base and the second is a product of closed forms, so $T_\epsilon $ is closed; that is, $\gamma _\epsilon $ is balanced, and in particular Gauduchon. Smooth Stokes and ( 12.14.5 ) give \[  \int _ X\theta _\epsilon \wedge T_\epsilon =c_\epsilon \int _ X(a+\epsilon )^{-1}\mu =n, \qquad D_\mu (\gamma _\epsilon )=c_\epsilon ^{m/n}H_\epsilon ,  \] so the quotient of $\gamma _\epsilon $ at $\theta _\epsilon $ equals $c_\epsilon ^{1/n}$. The same arithmetic–geometric mean argument, applied to the smooth representative $\Omega _\epsilon $, bounds every Gauduchon quotient at $\theta _\epsilon $ below by $c_\epsilon ^{1/n}$. This proves that $\gamma _\epsilon $ minimizes, and gives the formula for $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta _\epsilon )$. Since $\theta \leq \theta _\epsilon $, the metrics $\gamma _\epsilon $, used as tests for $\theta $, also give $\lambda _\mu (\theta )\leq c_\epsilon ^{1/n}$. Letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ proves ( 12.14.7 ). By theorem 12.11.1 , this value is also the limit of the volumes of the Hermitian perturbations $\theta +\epsilon h$. $\square$ The value $n$ refers to the probability measure $\mu $ fixed above, but positivity holds for every smooth positive probability measure by proposition 12.15.1 . Thus positive volume does not characterize bigness for nonclosed nef backgrounds, even on a projective manifold. The construction needs $m\geq 2$, so that $t>0$ and the endpoint potential is bounded; it says nothing about surfaces, or about closed nef classes on general compact complex manifolds.

title: Theorem 12.14.6
text: Theorem 12.14.6 . ECAB6BFB33FD The background $\theta $ on $X$ is smooth, semipositive, nef and nonclosed. It is not big, but 3D231D52B18A 12.14.7 \begin{equation}  \lambda _\mu (\theta )=n^{1/n},\qquad \mathcal V_\mu (\theta )=n. \end{equation} For $\theta _\epsilon =\omega +(a+\epsilon )w$, one has \[  \mathcal V_\mu (\theta _\epsilon )=\frac n{H_\epsilon },  \] and the smooth positive metrics F9FEC7FAC55E 12.14.8 \begin{equation}  \gamma _\epsilon =(a+\epsilon )^{-1/m} \bigl (A_\epsilon +(a+\epsilon )w\bigr ) \end{equation} are balanced and minimize the defining quotient at $\theta _\epsilon $. Proof. The coefficient $a$ is nonnegative, and $\theta +\eta h>0$ for every $\eta >0$; this proves semipositivity and nefness. Since $a$ is nonconstant, $\mathrm{d}\theta =\mathrm{d}a\wedge w\ne 0$. Suppose that $\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq \delta h$ for a quasi-plurisubharmonic function $v$ and some $\delta >0$. Choose a nonzero smooth function $f\geq 0$ on $B$ supported in $\{ a<\delta \} $. Its pullback $S=f\omega ^ m$ is a smooth semipositive $(m,m)$-form, closed because it has top degree on the base. Positivity and distributional Stokes would give \[  0\leq \int _ X(\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v-\delta h)\wedge S =\int _ B f(a-\delta )\omega ^ m<0.  \] This contradiction shows that $\theta $ is not big, since every Hermitian form on $X$ dominates a positive multiple of $h$. For the lower bound on the volume, pull back the bounded potential $\varphi $ of lemma 12.14.2 . The positive current $\Omega =A+a w=\theta +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ is a smooth strictly positive form off $Z=\{ p\} \times \mathbb P^1$, where \[  \Omega ^ n=n a A^ m\wedge w=n\mu .  \] Let $\gamma $ be a Gauduchon metric. Since $\varphi $ is bounded, distributional Stokes lets us replace $\theta $ by $\Omega $ in the numerator of its quotient. The set $Z$ has zero smooth volume and $\Omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ is a positive measure, so the pointwise arithmetic–geometric mean inequality off $Z$ gives \[  \int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1} \geq n^{1/n}\int _ X (\mu /\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n =n^{1/n}D_\mu (\gamma ).  \] This lower bound holds for every test in definition 12.2.1 ; no power of the current $\Omega $ along $Z$ is needed. For the upper bound, put $c_\epsilon =n/H_\epsilon $ and $\Omega _\epsilon =A_\epsilon +(a+\epsilon )w=\theta _\epsilon +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi _\epsilon $. Then $\Omega _\epsilon ^ n=c_\epsilon \mu $. The metrics in ( 12.14.8 ) satisfy \[  T_\epsilon =\gamma _\epsilon ^ m =(a+\epsilon )^{-1}A_\epsilon ^ m +m A_\epsilon ^{m-1}\wedge w.  \] The first term has top degree on the base and the second is a product of closed forms, so $T_\epsilon $ is closed; that is, $\gamma _\epsilon $ is balanced, and in particular Gauduchon. Smooth Stokes and ( 12.14.5 ) give \[  \int _ X\theta _\epsilon \wedge T_\epsilon =c_\epsilon \int _ X(a+\epsilon )^{-1}\mu =n, \qquad D_\mu (\gamma _\epsilon )=c_\epsilon ^{m/n}H_\epsilon ,  \] so the quotient of $\gamma _\epsilon $ at $\theta _\epsilon $ equals $c_\epsilon ^{1/n}$. The same arithmetic–geometric mean argument, applied to the smooth representative $\Omega _\epsilon $, bounds every Gauduchon quotient at $\theta _\epsilon $ below by $c_\epsilon ^{1/n}$. This proves that $\gamma _\epsilon $ minimizes, and gives the formula for $\mathcal V_\mu (\theta _\epsilon )$. Since $\theta \leq \theta _\epsilon $, the metrics $\gamma _\epsilon $, used as tests for $\theta $, also give $\lambda _\mu (\theta )\leq c_\epsilon ^{1/n}$. Letting $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ proves ( 12.14.7 ). By theorem 12.11.1 , this value is also the limit of the volumes of the Hermitian perturbations $\theta +\epsilon h$. $\square$

title: 12.14.9 Volume tests and threshold tests
text: Two quotients are formed from the same pairing $\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$. The volume quotient divides it by the determinant integral $D_\mu (\gamma )$, whereas the linear threshold $\kappa _ h(\theta )$ of corollary 11.6.2 divides it by the trace $\int _ Xh\wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$. This threshold is positive exactly when $\theta $ is big, and we call it the bigness threshold; for the pseudoeffective but nonbig background $\theta $ of theorem 12.14.6 it vanishes. The same metrics can approach both infima, but need not do so. In the radial model, the volume-minimizing metrics approach the bigness threshold only in dimension three, while a second family of smooth balanced metrics approaches it in every dimension by concentrating on the fiber over $p$. Keep the data of theorem 12.14.6 , and put \[  T_\epsilon =\gamma _\epsilon ^ m,\qquad I_\epsilon =\int _ B(a+\epsilon )^{-2}\omega ^ m, \qquad M_\epsilon =m+I_\epsilon /H_\epsilon , \qquad g_\epsilon =M_\epsilon ^{-1/m}\gamma _\epsilon .  \] Write $Z=\{ p\} \times \mathbb P^1$. Its integration current $[Z]$ satisfies $\int _ Zh=1$ and annihilates $\theta $, since $\theta |_ Z=a(p)w=0$. Proposition 12.14.10 . 0E9506DB4E70 The metrics $g_\epsilon $ are balanced, satisfy $\int _ Xh\wedge g_\epsilon ^ m=1$, and 662BE6BF9C61 12.14.11 \begin{equation}  \int _ X\theta \wedge g_\epsilon ^ m =\frac{n-\epsilon I_\epsilon /H_\epsilon }{M_\epsilon }, \qquad D_\mu (g_\epsilon ) =\frac{(n/H_\epsilon )^{m/n}H_\epsilon }{M_\epsilon }. \end{equation} Their volume quotients tend to $n^{1/n}$ as $\epsilon \downarrow 0$. If $n=3$, then $g_\epsilon ^2$ converges weakly to $[Z]$, and F4D7155E150D 12.14.12 \begin{equation}  \int _ X\theta \wedge g_\epsilon ^2 \sim \frac6{\log (1/\epsilon )}, \qquad D_\mu (g_\epsilon ) \sim \frac{2\, 3^{2/3}}{\log (1/\epsilon )}. \end{equation} If $n\geq 4$, put $M_0=m+(m-1)^2/[m(m-2)]$. Then \[  \int _ X\theta \wedge g_\epsilon ^ m\longrightarrow \frac n{M_0}>0, \qquad D_\mu (g_\epsilon )\longrightarrow \frac{n^{m/n}}{M_0}>0.  \] Thus this family approaches the bigness threshold, which is zero, exactly when $n=3$. Proof. By the power formula in the proof of theorem 12.14.6 and ( 12.14.3 ), \[  T_\epsilon =\frac{\omega ^ m}{H_\epsilon (a+\epsilon )^2} +mA_\epsilon ^{m-1}\wedge w.  \] Since $A_\epsilon $ is cohomologous to $\omega $, closed Stokes gives $\int _ B\omega \wedge A_\epsilon ^{m-1}=1$. Consequently the two terms have $h$-traces $I_\epsilon /H_\epsilon $ and $m$, which proves the trace normalization of $g_\epsilon ^ m=T_\epsilon /M_\epsilon $. Subtracting $\epsilon w$ from $\theta _\epsilon $ subtracts $\epsilon I_\epsilon /H_\epsilon $ from the pairing $\int _ X\theta _\epsilon \wedge T_\epsilon =n$. Rescaling $\gamma _\epsilon $ by $M_\epsilon ^{-1/m}$ divides both the linear pairing and $D_\mu $ by $M_\epsilon $, proving ( 12.14.11 ). Polar integration gives \[  I_\epsilon =m t^2\int _0^1 \frac{x^{m-1}}{(x+t\epsilon )^2}\, \mathrm{d}x.  \] When $m=2$, put $q=\epsilon /2$. Direct integration yields \[  I_\epsilon =\tfrac 12\left(\log \frac{1+q}{q} +\frac q{1+q}-1\right), \qquad H_\epsilon =1-q\log \frac{1+q}{q}.  \] Hence $I_\epsilon \sim \tfrac 12\log (1/\epsilon )$ and $\epsilon I_\epsilon \to 0$. Since $H_\epsilon \to 1$, the asymptotics in ( 12.14.12 ) follow from ( 12.14.11 ). For the weak limit when $n=3$, note that the mixed positive term $2A_\epsilon \wedge w$ has $h$-trace two; divided by $M_\epsilon \to \infty $, it tends weakly to zero. The horizontal probability measure \[  I_\epsilon ^{-1}(a+\epsilon )^{-2}\omega ^2  \] on $B$ concentrates at $p$: outside any fixed neighborhood of $p$ its unnormalized density stays bounded, while $I_\epsilon \to \infty $. For a smooth $(1,1)$-test form on $X$, integration along the fibers $\{ b\} \times \mathbb P^1$ gives a smooth function on $B$. The convergence of these probability measures to the Dirac mass at $p$ therefore shows that the horizontal term of $g_\epsilon ^2$ converges to $[Z]$, because its coefficient $I_\epsilon /(H_\epsilon M_\epsilon )$ tends to one. For $m\geq 3$, monotone convergence instead gives \[  I_\epsilon \longrightarrow m t^2\int _0^1x^{m-3}\, \mathrm{d}x =\frac{(m-1)^2}{m(m-2)}.  \] In both cases $\epsilon I_\epsilon \to 0$. Using $H_\epsilon \to 1$ in ( 12.14.11 ) proves the remaining limits, including that of the volume quotients. $\square$ For $n\geq 4$ the metrics $g_\epsilon $ still minimize the perturbed volumes, and their quotients converge to $\lambda _\mu (\theta )$, but their normalized pairings with $\theta $ stay bounded away from zero. This does not contradict nonbigness: the bigness threshold is approached by a different family. Proposition 12.14.13 . F8EA88FD522E For every $n\geq 3$ there are smooth balanced metrics $b_\rho $, $0<\rho <1$, with \[  \int _ Xh\wedge b_\rho ^ m=1,\qquad b_\rho ^ m\rightharpoonup [Z],\qquad \int _ X\theta \wedge b_\rho ^ m\longrightarrow 0, \qquad D_\mu (b_\rho )\longrightarrow 0  \] as $\rho \downarrow 0$. Proof. Choose a nonzero smooth function $f_\rho \geq 0$ on $B$, supported in $\{ x<\rho \} $ and normalized by $\int _ Bf_\rho \omega ^ m=1$. The form F8E2395BD557 12.14.14 \begin{equation}  \Gamma _\rho =\frac{f_\rho \omega ^ m+\rho h^ m}{1+n\rho } \end{equation} is smooth, strictly positive and closed: the first summand has top degree on the base, and $h$ is Kähler. The positive-root construction in the proof of theorem 11.6.1 gives a unique smooth metric $b_\rho $ with $b_\rho ^ m=\Gamma _\rho $, and $b_\rho $ is balanced because $\Gamma _\rho $ is closed. Since $\int _ Xh^{m+1}=n$, its $h$-trace is one. Put $C_\theta =\int _ X\theta \wedge h^ m$. Since $a<\rho /t$ on the support of $f_\rho $, \[  0\leq \int _ X\theta \wedge \Gamma _\rho \leq \frac{\rho /t+\rho C_\theta }{1+n\rho }\longrightarrow 0.  \] The lower bound in the proof of theorem 12.14.6 gives $D_\mu (b_\rho )\leq n^{-1/n}\int _ X\theta \wedge \Gamma _\rho $, so the determinant integrals also tend to zero. The probability measures $f_\rho \omega ^ m$ converge to the Dirac mass at $p$ because their supports shrink to that point. Fiber integration, as in the preceding proof, gives the current limit $[Z]$, while the term $\rho h^ m$ tends to zero. $\square$ Thus the normalized current $[Z]$ is a weak limit of smooth balanced metrics normalized by their $h$-traces. It annihilates $\theta $, and its determinant-weighted measure vanishes by proposition 12.34.2 . The two families give explicit instances of the separation between the volume and threshold denominators described in proposition 24.3.2 , without any general smoothing result for Gauduchon currents.

title: 12.15 Varying the probability measure
text:
From now on $X$ is again an arbitrary connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$. Changing the smooth positive probability measure $\mu $ multiplies each denominator $D_\mu (\gamma )$ by a factor bounded above and below independently of $\gamma $. The value of the volume may therefore change, but its vanishing and positivity do not. Moreover, every smooth strictly positive potential solves the normalized equation for a suitable measure. Consequently, on $\mathscr P$ the volume is independent of the measure exactly when the total Monge–Ampère mass is independent of the potential. Proposition 12.15.1 . 37E6FFC01EDB For smooth positive probability measures $\mu ,
u $, choose constants $m,M>0$ such that $m\mu \leq 
u \leq M\mu $. Then for every pseudoeffective $	heta $, \[  M^{-1/n}\lambda _\mu (	heta ) \leq \lambda _
u (	heta ) \leq m^{-1/n}\lambda _\mu (	heta ).  \] In particular, whether $\lambda _\mu (	heta )$ vanishes does not depend on the smooth positive probability measure $\mu $. Proof. Since $D_
u (\gamma )=\int _ X(
u /\mu )^{1/n}(\mu /\gamma ^ n)^{1/n}\gamma ^ n$, the inequalities $m\mu \leq 
u \leq M\mu $ give \[  m^{1/n}D_\mu (\gamma )\leq D_
u (\gamma )\leq M^{1/n}D_\mu (\gamma )  \] for every admissible metric $\gamma $. The numerators of the quotients are nonnegative and do not involve the measure. Dividing and taking infima proves the assertion. $\square$ Proposition 12.15.2 . D26C76DEC922 Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form on $X$. The value $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )$ is the same for all smooth positive probability measures $\mu $ if and only if \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n  \] is independent of the smooth potential $v$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$. Proof. For a smooth potential $v$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$, put \[  M_ v=\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n, \qquad \mu _ v= rac{(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n}{M_ v}.  \] Then $\mu _ v$ is a smooth positive probability measure, and $v$ solves the normalized equation for $\mu _ v$ with scalar $M_ v$. Uniqueness of the scalar and theorem 12.2.3 give $\mathcal V_{\mu _ v}(\omega )=M_ v$. Hence, if the volume does not depend on the measure, neither does the mass. Conversely, suppose that all these masses equal one constant $M$. For an arbitrary smooth positive probability measure $\mu $, integrating the normalized equation gives $c_\omega (\mu )=M$, so $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )=M$ for every $\mu $. $\square$ For instance, the nonclosed torus metric of example 11.1.12 has volumes that depend on the measure. If $n=2$ and $\omega $ is Gauduchon, Stokes' theorem shows that the smooth masses are all equal to $\int _ X\omega ^2$, so $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )=\int _ X\omega ^2$ for every $\mu $. On the Hopf threefold of section 23.1 , each $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )$ is finite and positive, although the upper mass $v_+(\omega )$ is infinite.

title: Proposition 12.15.2
text: Proposition 12.15.2 . D26C76DEC922 Let $\omega $ be a Hermitian form on $X$. The value $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )$ is the same for all smooth positive probability measures $\mu $ if and only if \[  \int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n  \] is independent of the smooth potential $v$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$. Proof. For a smooth potential $v$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$, put \[  M_ v=\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n, \qquad \mu _ v=\frac{(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n}{M_ v}.  \] Then $\mu _ v$ is a smooth positive probability measure, and $v$ solves the normalized equation for $\mu _ v$ with scalar $M_ v$. Uniqueness of the scalar and theorem 12.2.3 give $\mathcal V_{\mu _ v}(\omega )=M_ v$. Hence, if the volume does not depend on the measure, neither does the mass. title: 12.15.3 Upper and lower masses
text: As the probability measure varies, the smooth equation realizes the mass of every smooth strictly positive potential, by the proof of proposition 12.15.2 . The extrema of the volume over all measures are therefore the extrema of these masses, and regularization of bounded potentials identifies them with the lower and upper masses $v_-(\omega )$ and $v_+(\omega )$ of definition 13.14.14 . The infimum simplifies further: at each Gauduchon metric an explicit measure maximizes the denominator, and this removes the density from the formula entirely. Throughout this subsection $\omega $ is a Hermitian form on $X$, and $\mathscr M$ denotes the set of smooth strictly positive probability measures on $X$. Theorem 12.15.4 . B6CA5669E402 One has \[  \inf _{\mu \in \mathscr M}\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )=v_-(\omega ), \qquad \sup _{\mu \in \mathscr M}\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )=v_+(\omega ),  \] where the supremum may be infinite. Moreover, AE720210AADD 12.15.5 \begin{equation}  v_-(\omega )^{1/n} =\inf _{\gamma \text{ Gauduchon}} \frac{\displaystyle \int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{\displaystyle \left(\int _ X\gamma ^ n\right)^{(n-1)/n}}. \end{equation} Proof. For each $\mu \in \mathscr M$, the smooth normalized equation realizes $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )$ as the mass $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ of a smooth potential $v$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$. Conversely, every such potential realizes its mass as $\mathcal V_{\mu _ v}(\omega )$ for the measure $\mu _ v$ in the proof of proposition 12.15.2 . Thus the set of volumes $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )$, $\mu \in \mathscr M$, coincides with the set of these smooth masses. It remains to show that the smooth masses have the same extrema as the masses of bounded potentials, which define $v_\pm (\omega )$. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty $, theorem 5.32.1 gives uniformly bounded smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $u_ j$ decreasing to $u$. Their Monge–Ampère measures converge by the monotone continuity of bounded products, and so do their total masses, since $X$ is compact. Every bounded mass is therefore a limit of smooth strictly positive masses. Conversely, smooth potentials are bounded. This proves the first two identities; no uniform bound on the masses is needed. For the last formula, take $n$th roots and interchange the infima over $\mu $ and over $\gamma $ in theorem 12.2.3 . For a fixed Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, Hölder's inequality and $\int _ X\mu =1$ give \[  D_\mu (\gamma ) \leq \left(\int _ X\gamma ^ n\right)^{(n-1)/n},  \] with equality for the smooth probability measure $\mu =\gamma ^ n/\int _ X\gamma ^ n$. The numerator is positive and does not depend on $\mu $, so the infimum of the quotient over $\mu $ is obtained by maximizing the denominator. This gives ( 12.15.5 ). For $n=1$ both denominators equal one, and the same argument applies. $\square$ Thus $v_-(\omega )>0$ if and only if $\int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}$ has a positive lower bound over all Gauduchon metrics $\gamma $ with $\int _ X\gamma ^ n=1$. This lower bound fails on the threefold constructed in theorem 12.19.1 . By corollary 15.27.5 , positivity of $v_-(\omega )$ is also equivalent to solvability, in the background $\omega $, of the normalized equation for every nonzero finite non-pluripolar measure. In the same way, each individual volume $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )$ is finite, while their supremum $v_+(\omega )$ can be infinite. Proposition 12.15.6 . 87CB9377C0BB The infimum in ( 12.15.5 ) is attained if and only if the infimum of the masses $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ over smooth functions $v$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$ is attained. For every such minimizing potential $v$, the metric $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is Gauduchon. Proof. Suppose that a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ attains the infimum in ( 12.15.5 ), and put $m=v_-(\omega )^{1/n}$. The numerator of its quotient is strictly positive, so $m>0$. For the measure $\mu _\gamma =\gamma ^ n/\int _ X\gamma ^ n$, equality holds in the Hölder inequality above, so the test $\gamma $ gives $\lambda _{\mu _\gamma }(\omega )\leq m$. Theorem 12.15.4 gives the opposite inequality. Hence the solution of the smooth equation for $\mu _\gamma $ has mass $m^ n=v_-(\omega )$, which gives a minimizing smooth potential. For $n\geq 2$, $\gamma $ also minimizes the quotient for $\mu _\gamma $, so by theorem 12.2.3 the solution form is conformal to $\gamma $. Since both have volume forms proportional to $\mu _\gamma $, the conformal factor is constant, and the solution metric is Gauduchon. Conversely, let $v$ be a smooth potential minimizing the mass. For every smooth real $f$, the potentials $v\pm tf$ are admissible for sufficiently small $t>0$. The vanishing of the first variation of the mass therefore gives \[  \int _ X f\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl ((\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-1}\bigr )=0 \quad \hbox{for every smooth real }f.  \] Thus $\Omega =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is Gauduchon. Taking $\gamma =\Omega $ in the quotient and using Stokes' theorem for the Gauduchon metric $\Omega $ gives \[  \frac{\int _ X\omega \wedge \Omega ^{n-1}}{(\int _ X\Omega ^ n)^{(n-1)/n}} =(\int _ X\Omega ^ n)^{1/n}=v_-(\omega )^{1/n},  \] so the infimum in ( 12.15.5 ) is attained. In dimension one all metrics are Gauduchon and all masses equal $\int _ X\omega $. $\square$ The infimum over densities also makes sense beyond the positive cone. For a pseudoeffective smooth real $(1,1)$-form $\theta $ on $X$, put \[  \lambda _*(\theta )= \inf _{\gamma \text{ Gauduchon}} \frac{\int _ X\theta \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{(\int _ X\gamma ^ n)^{(n-1)/n}}.  \] The Hölder argument above proves \[  \lambda _*(\theta )=\inf _{\mu \in \mathscr M}\lambda _\mu (\theta ).  \] Like each $\lambda _\mu $, the function $\lambda _*$ is finite, nonnegative, concave, positively homogeneous, and invariant under smooth $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ changes of $\theta $. Suppose $\theta $ is nef, fix a Hermitian form $h$, and for real $\epsilon >0$ choose a Hermitian representative $\omega _\epsilon $ of $\theta +\epsilon h$. Interchanging the infima over the test metric and over $\epsilon >0$, as in theorem 12.11.1 , gives \[  \lambda _*(\theta ) =\lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0}\lambda _*(\theta +\epsilon h) =\lim _{\epsilon \downarrow 0}v_-(\omega _\epsilon )^{1/n}.  \] By gauge invariance, the last expression does not depend on the choice of representatives. This extends the lower-mass formula to the nef boundary. We do not compare $\lambda _*$ with other notions of lower volume for singular classes.

title: Theorem 12.15.4
text: Theorem 12.15.4 . B6CA5669E402 One has \[  \inf _{\mu \in \mathscr M}\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )=v_-(\omega ), \qquad \sup _{\mu \in \mathscr M}\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )=v_+(\omega ),  \] where the supremum may be infinite. Moreover, AE720210AADD 12.15.5 \begin{equation}  v_-(\omega )^{1/n} =\inf _{\gamma \text{ Gauduchon}} \frac{\displaystyle \int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{\displaystyle \left(\int _ X\gamma ^ n\right)^{(n-1)/n}}. \end{equation} Proof. For each $\mu \in \mathscr M$, the smooth normalized equation realizes $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )$ as the mass $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ of a smooth potential $v$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$. Conversely, every such potential realizes its mass as $\mathcal V_{\mu _ v}(\omega )$ for the measure $\mu _ v$ in the proof of proposition 12.15.2 . Thus the set of volumes $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )$, $\mu \in \mathscr M$, coincides with the set of these smooth masses. It remains to show that the smooth masses have the same extrema as the masses of bounded potentials, which define $v_\pm (\omega )$. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,\omega )\cap L^\infty $, theorem 5.32.1 gives uniformly bounded smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic functions $u_ j$ decreasing to $u$. Their Monge–Ampère measures converge by the monotone continuity of bounded products, and so do their total masses, since $X$ is compact. Every bounded mass is therefore a limit of smooth strictly positive masses. Conversely, smooth potentials are bounded. This proves the first two identities; no uniform bound on the masses is needed. For the last formula, take $n$th roots and interchange the infima over $\mu $ and over $\gamma $ in theorem 12.2.3 . For a fixed Gauduchon metric $\gamma $, Hölder's inequality and $\int _ X\mu =1$ give \[  D_\mu (\gamma ) \leq \left(\int _ X\gamma ^ n\right)^{(n-1)/n},  \] with equality for the smooth probability measure $\mu =\gamma ^ n/\int _ X\gamma ^ n$. The numerator is positive and does not depend on $\mu $, so the infimum of the quotient over $\mu $ is obtained by maximizing the denominator. This gives ( 12.15.5 ). For $n=1$ both denominators equal one, and the same argument applies. $\square$

title: Equation 12.15.5
text: AE720210AADD 12.15.5 \begin{equation}  v_-(\omega )^{1/n} =\inf _{\gamma \text{ Gauduchon}} \frac{\displaystyle \int _ X\omega \wedge \gamma ^{n-1}}{\displaystyle \left(\int _ X\gamma ^ n\right)^{(n-1)/n}}. \end{equation}

title: Proposition 12.15.6
text: Proposition 12.15.6 . 87CB9377C0BB The infimum in ( 12.15.5 ) is attained if and only if the infimum of the masses $\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ over smooth functions $v$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v>0$ is attained. For every such minimizing potential $v$, the metric $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is Gauduchon. Proof. Suppose that a Gauduchon metric $\gamma $ attains the infimum in ( 12.15.5 ), and put $m=v_-(\omega )^{1/n}$. The numerator of its quotient is strictly positive, so $m>0$. For the measure $\mu _\gamma =\gamma ^ n/\int _ X\gamma ^ n$, equality holds in the Hölder inequality above, so the test $\gamma $ gives $\lambda _{\mu _\gamma }(\omega )\leq m$. Theorem 12.15.4 gives the opposite inequality. Hence the solution of the smooth equation for $\mu _\gamma $ has mass $m^ n=v_-(\omega )$, which gives a minimizing smooth potential. For $n\geq 2$, $\gamma $ also minimizes the quotient for $\mu _\gamma $, so by theorem 12.2.3 the solution form is conformal to $\gamma $. Since both have volume forms proportional to $\mu _\gamma $, the conformal factor is constant, and the solution metric is Gauduchon. Conversely, let $v$ be a smooth potential minimizing the mass. For every smooth real $f$, the potentials $v\pm tf$ are admissible for sufficiently small $t>0$. The vanishing of the first variation of the mass therefore gives \[  \int _ X f\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl ((\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-1}\bigr )=0 \quad \hbox{for every smooth real }f.  \] Thus $\Omega =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is Gauduchon. Taking $\gamma =\Omega $ in the quotient and using Stokes' theorem for the Gauduchon metric $\Omega $ gives \[  \frac{\int _ X\omega \wedge \Omega ^{n-1}}{(\int _ X\Omega ^ n)^{(n-1)/n}} =(\int _ X\Omega ^ n)^{1/n}=v_-(\omega )^{1/n},  \] so the infimum in ( 12.15.5 ) is attained. In dimension one all metrics are Gauduchon and all masses equal $\int _ X\omega $. $\square$

title: 12.16 Curvature conditions for mass extrema
text: We now ask when the lower and upper masses are attained by smooth potentials. At a smooth local extremum of the mass, the first variation forces the metric $\Omega =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ to be Gauduchon, and the second variation gives a sign for $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-2})$. On a threefold these necessary conditions are also sufficient, because the mass is then a polynomial of degree two in the variation. Fix a Hermitian form $\omega $, and recall from section 11.1 the set $\mathcal H_\omega $ of smooth real functions $u$ with $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u>0$ and the mass functional $\mathrm M_\omega (u)=\int _ X(\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$. For $n\geq 2$, theorem 11.1.7 , proposition 12.15.2 give the differential conditions under which $\mathcal V_\mu (\omega )$ is independent of the smooth positive probability measure $\mu $. By proposition 11.38.3 , the same conditions characterize when the difference $H_0-\operatorname {Ent}_{\mathrm{d}V}$ considered there is constant on probability measures of finite entropy, for a fixed smooth positive probability volume $\mathrm{d}V$; it suffices to test smooth positive probability measures. In dimension one the mass is always $\int _ X\omega $, so both conclusions hold automatically. Recall that a smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $T$ is nonnegative, written $T\geq 0$, if $\mathrm i\alpha \wedge \bar\alpha \wedge T\geq 0$ for every $(1,0)$-covector $\alpha $; in this bidegree this is the usual notion of positivity. The second variation of the mass produces integrals of the form $\int _ X\mathrm df\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge T$, and the following elementary lemma shows that their signs detect the sign of $T$. Lemma 12.16.1 . 744D35F9BE16 Suppose a smooth real $(n-1,n-1)$-form $T$ satisfies \[  \int _ X \mathrm{d}f\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge T\geq 0 \quad \hbox{for every smooth real }f.  \] Then $T\geq 0$. Proof. Suppose instead that $\mathrm i\alpha \wedge \bar\alpha \wedge T<0$ at a point $x_0$ for some $(1,0)$-covector $\alpha $. Every $(1,0)$-covector is the $(1,0)$-part of a real covector, so we can choose a real linear function $\ell $ in local real coordinates around $x_0$ whose differential has $(1,0)$-part $\alpha $ at $x_0$. Then $\mathrm{d}\ell \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\ell $ is a positive multiple of $\mathrm i\alpha \wedge \bar\alpha $ at $x_0$, and after shrinking the coordinate ball, $\mathrm{d}\ell \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\ell \wedge T$ is strictly negative on it. Choose a nonzero smooth cutoff function $\chi $ supported in this ball and, for positive integers $k$, set \[  f_ k=k^{-1}\chi \sin (k\ell ),  \] extended by zero to $X$. Since $\mathrm{d}\ell $ is a constant nonzero covector in these coordinates, \[  \mathrm{d}f_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f_ k =\chi ^2\cos ^2(k\ell )\, \mathrm{d}\ell \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\ell +O(k^{-1}),  \] where $k$ times the remainder has uniformly bounded coefficients. In $\cos ^2(k\ell )=(1+\cos (2k\ell ))/2$, the oscillatory part contributes integrals tending to zero, as one sees by integrating by parts in a coordinate direction in which $\ell $ has nonzero derivative. Hence \[  \lim _{k\to \infty }\int _ X\mathrm{d}f_ k\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f_ k\wedge T =\frac12\int _ X\chi ^2\mathrm{d}\ell \wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\ell \wedge T<0,  \] which contradicts the hypothesis. $\square$ Proposition 12.16.2 . CE7BE3992C5F Let $n\geq 3$, and let $v\in \mathcal H_\omega $ be a local minimum of $\mathrm M_\omega $ for the $C^2$ topology. Then $\Omega =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ satisfies \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-1})=0, \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-2})\leq 0.  \] At a local maximum the first condition still holds and the second inequality is reversed. Proof. For every smooth real $f$, the potentials $v+tf$ lie in $\mathcal H_\omega $ for all sufficiently small $|t|$. The vanishing of the first variation therefore gives the Gauduchon condition. The second variation is \[  \begin{aligned}  \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}t^2}\right|_{t=0}\mathrm M_\omega (v+tf) & =n(n-1)\int _ X(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^2\wedge \Omega ^{n-2}\\ & =-n(n-1)\int _ X\mathrm{d}f\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-2}), \end{aligned}  \] where the last equality follows by integrating by parts twice, using that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-2})$ is both $\mathrm{d}$-closed and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$-closed. At a local minimum this second variation is nonnegative for every $f$, and lemma 12.16.1 , applied to $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-2})$, gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\Omega ^{n-2})\leq 0$. The case of a maximum is identical, with the opposite sign. $\square$ In dimension three these necessary conditions are also sufficient, and every local extremum is global. Theorem 12.16.3 . 26629526444F Assume $n=3$ and $v\in \mathcal H_\omega $. The following are equivalent: $v$ is a local minimum of $\mathrm M_\omega $; $v$ is a global minimum of $\mathrm M_\omega $ on $\mathcal H_\omega $; $\Omega =\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ is Gauduchon and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \leq 0$. In this case $v_-(\omega )=\int _ X\Omega ^3$, and the infimum in ( 12.15.5 ) is attained. The corresponding statements for maxima hold with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \geq 0$, and then $v_+(\omega )=\int _ X\Omega ^3<+\infty $. Proof. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Omega =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $, the preceding proposition shows that the first condition implies the third. Conversely, if $\Omega $ is Gauduchon, expanding the cube and integrating by parts gives, for every smooth real $f$, D5CA82478984 12.16.4 \begin{equation}  \int _ X(\Omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f)^3-\int _ X\Omega ^3 =-3\int _ X\mathrm{d}f\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega . \end{equation} The form $\mathrm{d}f\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f$ is nonnegative, so the right side is nonnegative if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega \leq 0$; then $v$ is a global minimum, and in particular a local one. By theorem 12.15.4 , regularization identifies the infimum of the masses of smooth strictly $\omega $-plurisubharmonic potentials with $v_-(\omega )$, and proposition 12.15.6 proves attainment in ( 12.15.5 ). Reversing the sign in the same identity proves the statements for maxima, including the equality of $\int _ X\Omega ^3$ with the supremum over bounded potentials. $\square$ These conditions characterize smooth minimizers when they exist; neither argument produces a Gauduchon metric of the form $\omega +\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$ in an arbitrary background. For the Hopf metric $\omega $ and the pulled-back Fubini–Study form $\alpha $ of section 23.1 , one has $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega =-\alpha ^2\leq 0$, and $\omega $ is Gauduchon. Thus the minimum of the mass is attained by the constant potential and equals $6$, while the upper mass is infinite. On a surface, by contrast, the mass $\int _ X\omega ^2+2\int _ Xv\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\omega $ is affine in the potential, so a local extremum exists precisely when $\omega $ is Gauduchon, and then all masses are equal. In dimension $n\geq 4$ the sign condition of proposition 12.16.2 does not control the terms of order three and higher in the mass polynomial, and the argument above does not show that the conditions are sufficient.

title: 12.17 Curvature pairs and positive lower mass
search_title: Curvature pairs and positive lower mass
section: 12.17 Curvature pairs and positive lower mass
text: On a threefold, the lower mass can be bounded below by a curvature condition. Consider a principal elliptic bundle over a Kähler surface, with a connection form $\eta $ whose curvature has real and imaginary parts $\alpha $ and $\beta $. If $\alpha ^2+\beta ^2$ is semipositive, the split metric $g$ built from the base metric and $\eta $ satisfies $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=0$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\leq 0$. A cubic energy identity for bounded potentials then shows that no bounded potential has mass below $\int _ Xg^3$, and the determinant estimate of theorem 12.9.2 transfers this lower bound to every Hermitian form on the manifold. The same curvature sign excludes pluriclosed metrics on these manifolds. In this section $X$ is a connected compact complex threefold and $\mathrm dV$ is a smooth positive probability volume form. Products of bounded potentials are those of proposition 5.28.2 . For a Hermitian form $h$, $\mathscr G_ h$ denotes the compact convex set of normalized Gauduchon currents of section 11.7 , and $k_ T$ is the determinant density of $T\in \mathscr G_ h$ relative to $\mathrm dV$, as in theorem 12.9.1 .

title: 12.17.1 The bounded cubic identity
section: 12.17 Curvature pairs and positive lower mass
text: When the square of a Hermitian metric $g$ is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$-closed, the mass of a bounded $g$-plurisubharmonic function differs from $\int _ Xg^3$ by a term that is linear in $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$. Its coefficient is a positive current playing the role of $\mathrm du\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u$. Lemma 12.17.2 . 3BBBC535BFA2 Let $g$ be a Hermitian form with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=0$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,g)$ be bounded. The current \[  E_ u=\tfrac 12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u^2)-u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u  \] is positive, and 649C88380858 12.17.3 \begin{equation}  \int _ X(g+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =\int _ Xg^3-3\int _ XE_ u\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g. \end{equation} If $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\geq 0$, then $v_-(g)=\int _ Xg^3$. Proof. Locally write $u=p-a$, with $p$ bounded plurisubharmonic and $a$ smooth. Expanding in $p$ and $a$ and using multilinearity, we obtain closed currents $C_ r=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ r$, not necessarily positive, with $C_0=1$. The recursive definition of bounded products, expanded in the same way, gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uC_ r)=C_{r+1},\qquad r=0,1,2.  \] By lemma 5.27.2 and invariance under smooth corrections, the weighted product $u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ does not depend on the local decomposition. On a smaller ball choose smooth bounded plurisubharmonic $p_ j$ decreasing to $p$, and put $u_ j=p_ j-a$. The same lemma gives $u_ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\to u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, while boundedness gives $u_ j^2\to u^2$ in $L^1$. Hence \[  \mathrm du_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u_ j =\tfrac 12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ j^2)-u_ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\longrightarrow E_ u.  \] The smooth currents on the left are positive, so their weak limit $E_ u$ is positive and has order zero. Now expand the cube. Repeated use of distributional Stokes gives \[  \int _ XC_3=0,\qquad \int _ Xg^2\wedge C_1=\int _ Xu\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=0, \qquad \int _ Xg\wedge C_2=\int _ XuC_1\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g.  \] Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ is closed, $\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u^2)\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=0$, so the last integral equals $-\int _ XE_ u\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$. This proves ( 12.17.3 ). If $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\geq 0$, the correction term is nonnegative, and $u=0$ attains the lower bound $\int _ Xg^3$. $\square$ Lemma 12.17.4 . 73E13B1F9B7A Let $g,h$ be Hermitian forms with $v_-(g)=V>0$ and $h\geq c g$ for some $c>0$. Then 6344C84663CF 12.17.5 \begin{equation}  \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_ h}\| k_ T\| _{L^{3/2}(\mathrm dV)} \leq c^{-1}V^{-1/3},\qquad v_-(h)\geq c^3V. \end{equation} Proof. We first check that the determinant measure in ( 12.7.1 ) does not depend on the Hermitian form used to express it. Let $T$ be a positive $(2,2)$-current, and let $\sigma _ h=h\wedge T$ and $P=P_ h$ be its trace measure and coefficient matrix relative to $h$, as in section 12.7 . In an $h$-unitary frame let $G$ be the matrix of $g$, and set \[  a=\tfrac 13\operatorname {tr}(GP),\qquad \sigma _ g=a\sigma _ h,\qquad P_ g=a^{-1}G^{1/2}PG^{1/2}.  \] Comparing the defining trace pairings shows that $\sigma _ g=g\wedge T$ and $P_ g$ are the trace measure and coefficient matrix of $T$ relative to $g$, with $\operatorname {tr}P_ g=3$. Since $G>0$ and $\operatorname {tr}P=3$, one has $a>0$ even where $P$ is singular. Moreover $\det P_ g=a^{-3}\det G\det P$ and $g^3=\det G\, h^3$, so the factors $a$ and $\det G$ cancel in $\Gamma _0(T)$. The calculation applies to the matrix density on the whole trace measure, including its singular part. For $T\in \mathscr G_ h$ put $m=\int _ Xg\wedge T$. Then $0<m\leq c^{-1}$ and $U=T/m\in \mathscr G_ g$. By homogeneity, $k_ T=m k_ U$. Applying theorem 12.9.2 to $g$ gives the norm bound, and applying it again to $h$ gives the lower-mass bound. The supremum here is taken over all of $\mathscr G_ h$, including singular and degenerate currents. $\square$

title: Lemma 12.17.2
section: 12.17 Curvature pairs and positive lower mass
text: Lemma 12.17.2 . 3BBBC535BFA2 Let $g$ be a Hermitian form with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=0$, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,g)$ be bounded. The current \[  E_ u=\tfrac 12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u^2)-u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u  \] is positive, and 649C88380858 12.17.3 \begin{equation}  \int _ X(g+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =\int _ Xg^3-3\int _ XE_ u\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g. \end{equation} If $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\geq 0$, then $v_-(g)=\int _ Xg^3$. Proof. Locally write $u=p-a$, with $p$ bounded plurisubharmonic and $a$ smooth. Expanding in $p$ and $a$ and using multilinearity, we obtain closed currents $C_ r=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ r$, not necessarily positive, with $C_0=1$. The recursive definition of bounded products, expanded in the same way, gives \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uC_ r)=C_{r+1},\qquad r=0,1,2.  \] By lemma 5.27.2 and invariance under smooth corrections, the weighted product $u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ does not depend on the local decomposition. On a smaller ball choose smooth bounded plurisubharmonic $p_ j$ decreasing to $p$, and put $u_ j=p_ j-a$. The same lemma gives $u_ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\to u\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, while boundedness gives $u_ j^2\to u^2$ in $L^1$. Hence \[  \mathrm du_ j\wedge \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}u_ j =\tfrac 12\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ j^2)-u_ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\longrightarrow E_ u.  \] The smooth currents on the left are positive, so their weak limit $E_ u$ is positive and has order zero. Now expand the cube. Repeated use of distributional Stokes gives \[  \int _ XC_3=0,\qquad \int _ Xg^2\wedge C_1=\int _ Xu\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=0, \qquad \int _ Xg\wedge C_2=\int _ XuC_1\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g.  \] Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ is closed, $\int _ X\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u^2)\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=0$, so the last integral equals $-\int _ XE_ u\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$. This proves ( 12.17.3 ). If $-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\geq 0$, the correction term is nonnegative, and $u=0$ attains the lower bound $\int _ Xg^3$. $\square$

title: Lemma 12.17.4
section: 12.17 Curvature pairs and positive lower mass
text: Lemma 12.17.4 . 73E13B1F9B7A Let $g,h$ be Hermitian forms with $v_-(g)=V>0$ and $h\geq c g$ for some $c>0$. Then 6344C84663CF 12.17.5 \begin{equation}  \sup _{T\in \mathscr G_ h}\| k_ T\| _{L^{3/2}(\mathrm dV)} \leq c^{-1}V^{-1/3},\qquad v_-(h)\geq c^3V. \end{equation} Proof. We first check that the determinant measure in ( 12.7.1 ) does not depend on the Hermitian form used to express it. Let $T$ be a positive $(2,2)$-current, and let $\sigma _ h=h\wedge T$ and $P=P_ h$ be its trace measure and coefficient matrix relative to $h$, as in section 12.7 . In an $h$-unitary frame let $G$ be the matrix of $g$, and set \[  a=\tfrac 13\operatorname {tr}(GP),\qquad \sigma _ g=a\sigma _ h,\qquad P_ g=a^{-1}G^{1/2}PG^{1/2}.  \] Comparing the defining trace pairings shows that $\sigma _ g=g\wedge T$ and $P_ g$ are the trace measure and coefficient matrix of $T$ relative to $g$, with $\operatorname {tr}P_ g=3$. Since $G>0$ and $\operatorname {tr}P=3$, one has $a>0$ even where $P$ is singular. Moreover $\det P_ g=a^{-3}\det G\det P$ and $g^3=\det G\, h^3$, so the factors $a$ and $\det G$ cancel in $\Gamma _0(T)$. The calculation applies to the matrix density on the whole trace measure, including its singular part. For $T\in \mathscr G_ h$ put $m=\int _ Xg\wedge T$. Then $0<m\leq c^{-1}$ and $U=T/m\in \mathscr G_ g$. By homogeneity, $k_ T=m k_ U$. Applying theorem 12.9.2 to $g$ gives the norm bound, and applying it again to $h$ gives the lower-mass bound. The supremum here is taken over all of $\mathscr G_ h$, including singular and degenerate currents. $\square$

title: 12.17.6 The curvature criterion
section: 12.17 Curvature pairs and positive lower mass
text: We now describe threefolds on which the hypotheses of lemma 12.17.2 hold. Let $\pi :X\to B$ be a holomorphic principal elliptic bundle over a compact connected Kähler surface $(B,\omega )$, with fiber the elliptic curve $E=\mathbb C/\Lambda $ and fiber coordinate $z$. Assume that there is a smooth $(1,0)$-form $\eta $ on $X$, invariant under the action of $E$ and restricting to $\mathrm dz$ on every fiber, such that \[  \mathrm d\eta =\pi ^*F,\qquad F=\alpha +\mathrm i\beta ,  \] where $\alpha ,\beta $ are smooth closed real $(1,1)$-forms on $B$. Put \[  Q=\alpha ^2+\beta ^2,\qquad e=\mathrm i\eta \wedge \bar\eta , \qquad g=\pi ^*\omega +s e,\quad s>0, \qquad A_ E=\int _ E\mathrm i\, \mathrm dz\wedge \mathrm d\bar z.  \] We call $g$ the split metric. Theorem 12.17.7 . 7EC7E0C62DF9 Suppose $Q\geq 0$ and $Q\not\equiv 0$. The split form $g$ is Hermitian, and its lower mass is D97FFD43BE5D 12.17.8 \begin{equation}  v_-(g)=V=3sA_ E\int _ B\omega ^2. \end{equation} Every bounded $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X,g)$ satisfies \[  \int _ X(g+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^3 =V+\frac{3s}{2\pi }\int _ XE_ u\wedge \pi ^*Q\geq V.  \] Every Hermitian form $h\geq c g$, with $c>0$, satisfies ( 12.17.5 ). Thus the endpoint estimate of theorem 12.9.2 holds for every Hermitian form on $X$, with a constant depending on the form. The manifold $X$ admits no pluriclosed Hermitian metric. Proof. We suppress pullbacks in the curvature calculation. Comparing types in $\mathrm d\eta =F$ gives $\partial \eta =0$, $\bar\partial \eta =F$, $\partial \bar\eta =\bar F$ and $\bar\partial \bar\eta =0$. Hence \[  \partial e=-\mathrm i\eta \wedge \bar F,\qquad \bar\partial e=\mathrm iF\wedge \bar\eta , \qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}e=-\frac1{2\pi }F\wedge \bar F=-\frac1{2\pi }Q.  \] Since $e^2=0$ and the base has dimension two, \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=-\frac{s}{2\pi }\pi ^*Q,\qquad \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(g^2)=-\frac{s}{\pi }\pi ^*(\omega \wedge Q)=0, \qquad g^3=3s\pi ^*(\omega ^2)\wedge e.  \] The form $g$ is positive, because $\pi ^*\omega $ is positive on directions transverse to the fibers and $e$ is positive on the vertical line. Fiber integration of $g^3$ gives $V$, and lemma 12.17.2 , lemma 12.17.4 give the mass identity and the endpoint bound. By compactness, every Hermitian form $h$ satisfies $h\geq cg$ for some $c>0$. Finally, $S=-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g$ is smooth, semipositive and not identically zero. If a Hermitian form $b$ were pluriclosed, Stokes' theorem would give \[  0=\int _ Xg\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b =\int _ Xb\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g=-\int _ Xb\wedge S<0,  \] where the last inequality holds because $b$ is strictly positive and $S$ is semipositive and nonzero on an open set. $\square$ Proposition 12.17.9 . A60EEF389BCA The split metric $g$ is balanced if and only if $\omega \wedge \alpha =\omega \wedge \beta =0$. For such a primitive pair one has $Q\leq 0$, with strict inequality wherever the pair is nonzero. In particular, a balanced split metric never satisfies the hypothesis $Q\geq 0$, $Q\not\equiv 0$ of theorem 12.17.7 . Proof. One has $\mathrm d(g^2)=2s\pi ^*\omega \wedge \mathrm de$, and $\mathrm de$ has one component containing $\eta $ and one containing $\bar\eta $. These two vertical types are independent, so $\mathrm d(g^2)=0$ if and only if $\omega \wedge F=0$, which is equivalent to the two stated real identities. A primitive real $(1,1)$-form on a surface has eigenvalues $\lambda ,-\lambda $ in an $\omega $-unitary frame, so its square is $-\lambda ^2\omega ^2$. Applying this to $\alpha $ and to $\beta $ gives the sign of $Q$. In this case $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}g\geq 0$, so ( 12.17.3 ) bounds the masses of bounded potentials from above rather than from below, and gives no information on the lower mass. $\square$
